10474.q: How can you recognise the robust, so-called tufted capuchins especially easily?
a: By tufts or a crest of hair on the head
10474.e: Robust capuchins have tufts of hair or a crest on the head, hence the name “tufted”. Slender capuchins usually have a smooth cap.
10474.m: Tufted capuchins have a crest of hair on their head.

10475.q: Around 2012, which method did researchers use to show that robust and slender capuchins belong in separate genera?
10475.e: Comparisons of genetic material showed how long the two lines have been separate. After that, the robust forms were put in their own genus, Sapajus.
10475.m: DNA comparisons split the capuchin monkeys into two genera.

10476.q: According to genetic estimates, how long ago did the lines of robust and slender capuchins split?
10476.e: Studies estimate the split at about 6.2 million years. That is roughly as long ago as the split between the lines of humans and chimpanzees.
10476.m: Robust and slender capuchins have gone separate ways for about six million years.

10477.q: Which forest, home to several threatened capuchin monkeys, survives today at only about an eighth of its size?
a: The rainforest of the Congo Basin
10477.e: Only about an eighth of the Atlantic Forest (Mata Atlântica) on Brazil’s coast is left. The Congo and Borneo lie outside the capuchins’ range, and most of the Amazon rainforest still survives.
10477.m: Most of Brazil’s Atlantic Forest has been destroyed.

10478.q: Where does the capuchin monkey get its name from?
a: From the habits of the Capuchin friars
From a hood-shaped fold of skin
10478.e: The colouring, with a dark head and pale face or shoulders, reminded people of the brown hooded habits of the Capuchin order. So European sailors gave the friars’ name to the monkeys.
10478.m: Capuchin monkeys are named after the habits of the Capuchin friars.

10479.q: Which well-known drink is named, like the capuchin monkey, after the habit of the Capuchin friars?
10479.e: The brown colour of cappuccino reminded people of the habits of the Capuchin friars. The capuchin monkeys also owe their name to this habit.
10479.m: Cappuccino and the capuchin monkey are both named after the Capuchin friars.

10480.q: Roughly how many species of capuchin monkey are recognised today?
10480.e: Depending on the classification, just over 20 species are recognised, about 15 in the genus Cebus and 7 in the genus Sapajus. The exact number of species is disputed among experts.
10480.m: About 20 species of capuchin monkey are recognised today.

10481.q: How heavy do adult capuchin monkeys usually get?
10481.e: Capuchin monkeys usually weigh between about 1.5 and 4.5 kg. The males are usually much heavier than the females.
10481.m: A capuchin monkey usually weighs only a few kilograms.

10482.q: Roughly how long is a capuchin monkey’s body without its tail?
10482.e: The head and body length is about 30 to 56 cm. The tail is about as long as the body.
10482.m: Without its tail, a capuchin is about as long as an adult’s forearm and hand.

10483.q: What is special about the capuchin monkey’s tail compared with that of spider monkeys?
a: It can grip but has no bare touch pad at the tip
It is completely stiff and used only for balance
It is shorter than ten centimetres
It has a bare touch pad at the tip like a finger
10483.e: Capuchin monkeys can hold on with their tail, for example while eating. Unlike spider monkeys, though, they lack the hairless patch of skin under the tail that makes a fully gripping tail.
10483.m: The capuchin has a tail that can grip but has no bare touch pad.

10484.q: Which feature of their hands makes capuchin monkeys especially skilful?
a: A movable thumb that allows a precision grip
Fused fingers that cannot move separately
Sharp claws instead of flat nails
No thumb, as in spider monkeys
10484.e: The capuchin’s thumb is considered pseudo-opposable, but it is so movable that they can hold small things between thumb and index finger. This lets them grip and work on stones or nuts very precisely.
10484.m: Thanks to their movable thumb, capuchins can grip very precisely.

10485.q: What is the capuchin monkey’s brain known for among experts?
a: It is exceptionally large relative to body size
It is the largest of all primates in absolute terms
It is especially small relative to the body
10485.e: Relative to their body, capuchin monkeys have one of the largest brains among non-human primates. They are considered the most intelligent New World monkeys.
10485.m: For its body size, the capuchin has a remarkably large brain.

10486.q: How do most capuchin monkeys see colours?
a: All males see two colour channels, some females three
All animals see three colour channels like humans
All animals see only shades of grey
All males see three colour channels, all females two
10486.e: In capuchin monkeys, a gene for colour vision pigments sits on the X chromosome. Males, with only one X chromosome, therefore have two-colour vision, while females with two different versions can have three-colour vision.
10486.m: In capuchins, only some females can tell red from green.

10487.q: Which features do robust capuchins of the genus Sapajus have as an adaptation to hard food?
a: Strong jaws and, in males, a skull crest
Long, thin canines and a narrow jaw
Cheek pouches and a ruminant stomach
A horny beak instead of incisors
10487.e: Sapajus species have stronger lower jaws and shorter, sturdier canines, and the males have a crest on the skull for large chewing muscles. This lets them crack hard nuts and palm fruits.
10487.m: Robust capuchins have strong jaws for hard nuts.

10488.q: How far does the range of capuchin monkeys reach overall?
a: From Mexico to Tierra del Fuego
10488.e: Capuchin monkeys live from Central America, from about Honduras, through the Amazon Basin to south-eastern Brazil and northern Argentina. Brazil has the most capuchins.
10488.m: Capuchin monkeys live from Honduras to northern Argentina.

10489.q: Which capuchin monkey has the northernmost range of its group?
10489.e: White-faced capuchins live in the far north-west of South America and in Central America as far as Honduras. The Central American animals are now often split off as a separate species, the Panamanian white-faced capuchin (Cebus imitator); no other capuchin lives so far north.
10489.m: The white-faced capuchin lives furthest north of all capuchins.

10490.q: In which countries can you see white-faced capuchins in the wild?
10490.e: White-faced capuchins live in Central America, for example in Costa Rica and Panama, and in north-western South America. They are often seen in Costa Rica’s national parks.
10490.m: White-faced capuchins live mainly in Central America.

10491.q: How does the tufted capuchin differ in build from the slender white-faced capuchin?
a: It is sturdier and has stronger jaws
It is bigger than a chimpanzee
It has no tail at all
It has gliding membranes between its legs
10491.e: The tufted capuchin is one of the robust capuchins. With its strong jaws it can crack hard nuts and palm fruits.
10491.m: The tufted capuchin is a robust capuchin with strong jaws.

10492.q: In which habitats are capuchin monkeys found?
a: In rainforests, dry forests and even mangroves
Only in mountain forests above 3,000 metres
Only in open grassy steppes with no trees
10492.e: Capuchin monkeys are very adaptable and live in rainforests, dry deciduous forests, mangroves and mountain forests. This flexibility is one reason why many species are less threatened than other New World monkeys.
10492.m: Capuchin monkeys live in many different types of forest.

10493.q: What is a capuchin monkey’s daily routine typically like?
a: They are active by day and sleep high in trees at night
They are active at night and sleep in burrows by day
They are active at dusk and sleep in rock crevices
They hibernate for several months in winter
10493.e: Capuchin monkeys are day-active tree dwellers. They spend the night in tall trees and often change their sleeping places.
10493.m: Capuchin monkeys are active by day and sleep in the treetops at night.

10494.q: How is the capuchin monkey’s diet best described?
10494.e: Capuchin monkeys mainly eat fruit, plus seeds, flowers, insects, spiders, eggs and small vertebrates. In the dry season, seeds and hard nuts become more important.
10494.m: Capuchin monkeys are omnivores that especially like fruit.

10495.q: How do wild capuchin monkeys crack hard palm nuts?
a: With a hammer stone on a surface used as an anvil
By letting birds open the nuts
By stamping on the nuts with their back legs
By soaking the nuts in water for weeks
10495.e: Capuchin monkeys put the nut on a flat stone or tree trunk and hit it with a heavy stone. They are thought to be the only New World monkeys that regularly use such tools in the wild.
10495.m: Capuchin monkeys crack nuts with a stone hammer and anvil.

10496.q: What do capuchin monkeys choose their hammer stones by?
10496.e: Experiments showed that capuchin monkeys choose stones by weight and size and prefer heavier stones for hard nuts. Some animals carry suitable stones over long distances.
10496.m: Capuchin monkeys check a stone’s weight before using it as a hammer.

10497.q: According to archaeological digs in Brazil (2019), how old at least is the stone-tool tradition of wild capuchin monkeys?
10497.e: In Serra da Capivara National Park, researchers found capuchins’ hammer stones that are about 3,000 years old. The size of the stones changed over time, which points to changing food.
10497.m: Capuchin monkeys have used stone tools for at least 3,000 years.

10498.q: What did researchers discover in 2016 in capuchin monkeys of the species Sapajus libidinosus that bashed stones together?
a: They accidentally made sharp stone flakes like early human tools
They deliberately sharpened knives for cutting meat
They lit small fires with the sparks
They built small walls out of the stones
10498.e: The monkeys struck quartzite stones against rocks and then licked them. This produced sharp-edged flakes that look like early human tools, but the monkeys never used them for cutting.
10498.m: Capuchin monkeys make sharp stone flakes without using them as knives.

10499.q: What do capuchin monkeys on islands off the coast of Panama crack with stones?
a: Sea urchins they collect by diving
Sea turtle eggs in the sand
Shellfish from coral reefs at great depth
10499.e: In Coiba National Park, white-faced capuchins use stones as hammers for crabs, snails and hard fruit. They do not dive for them.
10499.m: Capuchin monkeys in Panama crack crabs and snails with stones.

10500.q: Why do wedge-capped capuchins in Venezuela rub crushed millipedes into their fur?
a: To protect themselves from mosquitoes and other insects
To attract females with the scent
10500.e: The millipedes give off defensive chemicals that keep insects such as mosquitoes away. Capuchins do this rubbing mainly in the rainy season, when there are many mosquitoes about.
10500.m: Capuchin monkeys use millipedes as a natural mosquito repellent.

10501.q: How large are groups of capuchin monkeys usually?
10501.e: Capuchin monkeys usually live in groups of about 10 to 35 animals with several adult males and females. Depending on the species, the average group has about 15 to 20 animals.
10501.m: Capuchin monkeys live in groups of usually 10 to 35 animals.

10502.q: In capuchin monkeys, which sex normally leaves the birth group?
10502.e: In capuchin monkeys the females stay in their birth group, while the males move away around sexual maturity. So the groups are built around related females.
10502.m: In capuchins the females stay and the males move away.

10503.q: How is the ranking in a group of white-faced capuchins usually organised?
a: An alpha male leads, the females have their own ranking
All animals are completely equal in rank
The youngest animal always leads the group
The ranking changes randomly every day
10503.e: In the group there is a top-ranking male, who often keeps his position for many years. Alongside this, the females form their own clear ranking.
10503.m: In white-faced capuchins, an alpha male leads the group.

10504.q: What do capuchin monkeys mark the core area of their territory with?
a: Piles of droppings on the ground
10504.e: Capuchin monkeys mark the core of their home range with urine and defend it against other groups. In the outer zones, the areas of neighbouring groups often overlap.
10504.m: Capuchin monkeys mark their territory with urine.

10505.q: Roughly how long is a capuchin monkey’s pregnancy?
10505.e: Pregnancy lasts about 150 to 180 days, so a good five to six months. Usually a single baby is born.
10505.m: A female capuchin is pregnant for about half a year.

10506.q: How often does a female capuchin monkey usually have a baby?
10506.e: Females usually have a single baby about every two years. The long care of the young explains these long gaps.
10506.m: A female capuchin has a baby about every two years.

10507.q: In capuchin monkeys, which sex becomes sexually mature later?
a: Both at the same time, at one year
Both at the same time, at ten years
10507.e: Females become sexually mature at about four years, males often much later, at up to about eight years. Males also first have to establish themselves in a new group.
10507.m: Male capuchin monkeys grow up later than females.

10508.q: How old can capuchin monkeys live to be in captivity?
10508.e: In zoos and research facilities, some capuchin monkeys have reached an age of over 50 years. In the wild they usually live much shorter lives.
10508.m: In captivity, capuchin monkeys can live over 50 years.

10509.q: Which bird of prey is considered the main enemy of the tufted capuchin?
10509.e: The harpy eagle is a mighty bird of prey of the South American rainforests and specifically hunts monkeys in the treetops. Big cats and snakes also catch capuchin monkeys.
10509.m: The harpy eagle is the tufted capuchin’s most dangerous enemy.

10510.q: What did the famous experiment by Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal (2003) with capuchin monkeys show?
a: They refused cucumber when a partner got grapes for the same task
They did not recognise themselves in a mirror
They learnt sign language in a few days
10510.e: The monkeys swapped tokens for food. If the partner got a much-wanted grape for the same task, many animals refused their slice of cucumber, which is interpreted as a sense of unfair treatment.
10510.m: Capuchin monkeys react angrily to unequal rewards.

10511.q: Which ability did capuchin monkeys show in experiments at Yale University around 2005?
a: They learnt to swap tokens for food like money
They learnt to forge metal tools
They learnt to say simple words
10511.e: After a few months of training, the capuchins used coins deliberately to trade and even reacted to price changes. This suggests a simple understanding of money.
10511.m: Capuchin monkeys can learn to use coins like money.

10512.q: What did the organisation Helping Hands in the USA train capuchin monkeys for from 1979?
a: As helpers for people with paralysis
As search animals for earthquake victims
10512.e: Helping Hands in Boston trained capuchin monkeys to help people with paralysis in everyday life, for example by fetching things. In 2021 the organisation stopped placing monkeys for good and has used technical aids since then.
10512.m: Capuchin monkeys used to be trained as helpers for paralysed people.

10513.q: According to the IUCN, what is the status of the tufted capuchin (Sapajus apella) as a species?
10513.e: The tufted capuchin has a huge range and is very adaptable. So the IUCN classes the species as a whole as not threatened, even though some subspecies are at risk.
10513.m: The tufted capuchin as a whole is not considered threatened.

10514.q: Why are capuchin monkeys on small islands especially at risk of dying out?
a: Small populations cannot move away and quickly lose genetic diversity
On islands it is always too cold for monkeys
They drink sea water and get ill from it
10514.e: Only a few animals live on an island, and they cannot move away if the forest is lost. Small populations also lose genetic diversity and become more prone to disease.
10514.m: Small island populations die out more easily.

10515.q: How do zoos help highly threatened capuchin monkeys such as the yellow-breasted capuchin?
a: By crossing them with other monkey species
10515.e: Zoos breed threatened species such as the yellow-breasted capuchin in joint programmes, so that a healthy reserve population survives. They also support conservation projects in Brazil.
10515.m: Conservation breeding in zoos helps threatened capuchin monkeys.

10516.q: The blond capuchin was “rediscovered” in Brazil in 2006. What does that mean?
a: For a long time it was known only from old descriptions and was found again in the wild
It was bred anew from fossils
It had died out in all zoos
It was genetically modified for the first time
10516.e: The blond capuchin had been described since the 18th century but was considered lost. In 2006 it was found again in remnants of forest in north-eastern Brazil.
10516.m: A rediscovered species is found again in the wild after a long time.

10517.q: What does the IUCN status “Critically Endangered”, which some capuchin monkeys have, mean?
a: The species has an extremely high risk of soon dying out in the wild
The species now lives only in zoos
The species is common but protected
10517.e: “Critically Endangered” is the highest threat level before “Extinct in the Wild”. Species such as the Ka’apor capuchin urgently need protection.
10517.m: Critically Endangered is the highest threat level on the Red List.

10518.q: Which threats endanger many capuchin species the most?
a: Logging, hunting and the illegal pet trade
10518.e: Many species are losing their forest to farming and logging. Capuchin monkeys are also hunted for bushmeat and are among the wild animals most often traded illegally in Brazil.
10518.m: Forest loss, hunting and the pet trade threaten capuchin monkeys.

10519.q: Which famous TV character was played by a white-faced capuchin?
a: The monkey Marcel in the series “Friends”
The monkey King Louie in “The Jungle Book”
The monkey Rafiki in “The Lion King”
10519.e: Marcel, Ross’s pet in the series “Friends”, was played by a white-faced capuchin. Abu, King Louie and Rafiki, on the other hand, are drawn cartoon characters.
10519.m: Marcel from “Friends” was a capuchin monkey.

10520.q: Which family do squirrel monkeys (genus Saimiri) belong to?
10520.e: Squirrel monkeys are placed with the capuchin monkeys in the family Cebidae. Depending on the classification, the marmosets and tamarins are also counted in this family.
10520.m: Squirrel monkeys are close relatives of capuchin monkeys.

10521.q: How do squirrel monkeys mainly differ from the closely related capuchin monkeys?
a: They are much smaller and lighter
They live on a different continent
10521.e: Squirrel monkeys usually weigh under 1.1 kg, capuchins often two to four times as much. Both are day-active group animals in Central and South America. The squirrel monkeys form their own subfamily.
10521.m: Squirrel monkeys are the small relatives of capuchin monkeys.

10522.q: Squirrel monkeys are New World monkeys. Which feature of their nose is typical of this group?
a: The nose is stretched out like a trunk
10522.e: New World monkeys are also called platyrrhines, “flat-nosed”, because their nostrils are separated by a wide septum and point sideways outwards. Squirrel monkeys also have a hairless muzzle.
10522.m: New World monkeys like the squirrel monkey have wide noses with nostrils facing sideways.

10523.q: Where does the squirrel monkey get its German name “Totenkopfaffe” (death’s-head monkey) from?
a: From the black muzzle in its pale, mask-like face
From its night-time call in graveyards
From the dark rings around the eyes of old animals
10523.e: The black muzzle in the white-rimmed face looks like a skull. The animal has a similar name in other Germanic languages too.
10523.m: The squirrel monkey’s face looks like a little skull.

10524.q: Why is the squirrel monkey called a squirrel monkey?
a: Because of its nimble, squirrel-like movements
Because of its liking for nuts and acorns
Because of its bushy red tail
Because of its life in burrows
10524.e: Squirrel monkeys move quickly and nimbly on all fours through the branches. This is reminiscent of squirrels.
10524.m: The squirrel monkey darts through the trees as nimbly as a squirrel.

10525.q: Roughly what does the genus name Saimiri of the squirrel monkeys mean?
10525.e: The name comes from South America (from Tupi or the Portuguese spoken there) and was a term for small monkeys.
10525.m: Saimiri is a South American word for a small monkey.

10526.q: Roughly how many species of squirrel monkey are distinguished today?
10526.e: Until 1984 all South American squirrel monkeys were regarded as one species. Today, depending on the classification, about five to seven species are distinguished.
10526.m: Today several species of squirrel monkey are distinguished.

10527.q: How can the two groups of squirrel monkeys be told apart, among other things?
a: By the shape of the white patch above the eyes
By the length of the ears
By the colour of the tongue
10527.e: In the boliviensis group the white patch above the eyes forms a round arch, in the sciureus group a pointed arch.
10527.m: The shape of the eye patch shows which group a squirrel monkey belongs to.

10528.q: At the site of La Venta in Colombia fossils of close relatives of the squirrel monkeys were found. What do these finds show?
a: This line of monkeys has lived in South America for millions of years
Squirrel monkeys originally come from Europe
Squirrel monkeys used to be as big as gorillas
Squirrel monkeys have existed only since the last Ice Age
10528.e: The fossils from La Venta date from the middle Miocene and are about 12 to 13 million years old. Some experts even place them directly in the genus Saimiri.
10528.m: Over ten million years ago relatives of the squirrel monkeys already lived in Colombia.

10529.q: About how long is the body (head and trunk, without the tail) of a squirrel monkey?
10529.e: The head and body length is about 26 to 36 cm. Squirrel monkeys are thus among the smaller New World monkeys.
10529.m: Without its tail a squirrel monkey is about as long as a school ruler.

10530.q: How does the length of the squirrel monkey’s tail compare with its body length?
a: The tail is longer than head and trunk
The tail is only half as long
The tail is a short stub
The tail is exactly the same length
10530.e: The tail measures about 35 to 43 cm and is thus longer than the head and trunk at about 26 to 36 cm.
10530.m: The squirrel monkey’s tail is longer than its whole body.

10531.q: What do adult squirrel monkeys mainly use their tail for?
a: As a balancing aid when climbing and jumping
As a prehensile tail for holding on to branches
As a fly swatter against insects
As a support when walking upright
10531.e: Only young animals can still use the tail a little for gripping. Adults use it as a balancing pole.
10531.m: In the adult squirrel monkey the tail is a balancing pole and not a gripping tool.

10532.q: About how heavy do male squirrel monkeys grow at most?
10532.e: Males weigh about 750 to 1100 g, females at about 500 to 750 g clearly less.
10532.m: A fully grown squirrel monkey weighs hardly more than a litre of milk.

10533.q: Which statement about the squirrel monkey’s thumb is correct?
a: It is especially long and opposable
It carries a large grooming claw
10533.e: Squirrel monkeys have short fingers, and the thumb cannot be placed opposite the other fingers. They therefore grip less precisely than Old World monkeys.
10533.m: The squirrel monkey cannot oppose its thumb to its fingers as we can.

10534.q: How are the squirrel monkey’s eyes positioned, and what does that help it with?
a: Facing forwards, for good depth vision
At the sides of the head, for all-round vision
On top of the head, for looking into the canopy
Wide apart, for seeing in the dark
10534.e: Like all monkeys, the squirrel monkey has forward-facing eyes. The fields of vision overlap, so it can judge distances well when jumping. The eye sockets are even so close together that an opening in the bone remains between them.
10534.m: Forward-facing eyes let the squirrel monkey judge distances well.

10535.q: What ratio of brain mass to body mass is often given for squirrel monkeys?
10535.e: With a ratio of about 1 to 17, squirrel monkeys have one of the largest brains relative to body size among the primates.
10535.m: Relative to its body the squirrel monkey has a very large brain.

10536.q: Where do squirrel monkeys have sweat glands that help with sweating?
a: Only on the palms and soles of the feet
All over the body like humans
10536.e: Squirrel monkeys sweat only on the palms and soles of the feet. They therefore have to cool down mainly through their behaviour.
10536.m: A squirrel monkey sweats only on its hands and feet.

10537.q: What is so-called “urine washing” in squirrel monkeys?
a: They rub urine from their hands onto their feet
They bathe in puddles full of urine
They spray enemies with urine on purpose
10537.e: Squirrel monkeys urinate onto their hands and rub it onto their feet. The evaporation cools them, and the behaviour increases in heat. It also serves as scent marking.
10537.m: With urine washing the squirrel monkey cools itself and leaves scent trails.

10538.q: How do male squirrel monkeys see colours?
a: All males see only shades of grey
10538.e: The gene for one of the visual pigments in the cones lies on the X chromosome. Males have only one and therefore always see in two colours, like red-green colour-blind people.
10538.m: Male squirrel monkeys are naturally red-green colour-blind.

10539.q: What share of female squirrel monkeys see in three colours (trichromatic)?
10539.e: About two thirds of the females are trichromatic, about a third see only in two colours like the males. This depends on the two X chromosomes.
10539.m: Only some female squirrel monkeys see colours as we do.

10540.q: What was the result of a gene therapy in adult male squirrel monkeys?
a: Afterwards they could tell colours apart like three-colour seers
Afterwards they could see in the dark
10540.e: Researchers introduced the human gene for a red visual pigment into the retina of adult males. Afterwards these showed colour vision like trichromats, which is important for research into colour blindness.
10540.m: Squirrel monkeys showed that gene therapy can cure colour blindness.

10541.q: Where do most species of squirrel monkey live?
a: In the Atlantic rainforest of Argentina
10541.e: Most species live in the Amazon basin, roughly from southern Colombia and French Guiana to Bolivia and central Brazil.
10541.m: The home of most squirrel monkeys is the Amazon basin.

10542.q: Where does the isolated population of the Central American squirrel monkey live?
a: On the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and Panama
On the Caribbean coast of Mexico
10542.e: Saimiri oerstedii occurs only on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and in the adjoining west of Panama, far separated from its South American relatives.
10542.m: The Central American squirrel monkey lives only on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and Panama.

10543.q: In which national parks in Costa Rica does the Central American squirrel monkey mainly live?
10543.e: The most important populations live in the Manuel Antonio and Corcovado national parks on the central and southern Pacific coast.
10543.m: Central American squirrel monkeys can be watched in Manuel Antonio and Corcovado.

10544.q: By how much is the population of the Central American squirrel monkey estimated to have shrunk since the 1970s?
a: From about 2 million to 1 million animals
10544.e: According to estimates about 200,000 animals lived there in the 1970s, today there are fewer than 5000. The reasons are deforestation, hunting and capture for the pet trade.
10544.m: Only a small fraction of the Central American squirrel monkey is left.

10545.q: What status does the Central American squirrel monkey (Saimiri oerstedii) have on the IUCN Red List?
10545.e: The IUCN lists Saimiri oerstedii as endangered. The main reason is loss of habitat through deforestation.
10545.m: The Central American squirrel monkey is endangered.

10546.q: Why is the black squirrel monkey (Saimiri vanzolinii) especially vulnerable?
a: It lives only in a very small area in Brazil
It eats only a single species of plant
It has a young only every ten years
10546.e: The species lives only at the mouth of the Rio Japurá into the Solimões in the Mamirauá Reserve. Its range is among the smallest of all primates.
10546.m: The black squirrel monkey lives in only a single reserve in Brazil.

10547.q: Which type of forest is the habitat of the black squirrel monkey (Saimiri vanzolinii)?
10547.e: The species lives in the várzea, a forest that is flooded every year by the high water of the rivers. Unusually long floods can therefore threaten it.
10547.m: The black squirrel monkey lives in the flooded forest on the Amazon.

10548.q: In which forests are squirrel monkeys generally found especially often?
a: In flooded river forests and secondary forests
In coniferous forests of the mountains
10548.e: Squirrel monkeys inhabit various types of forest but are often found in seasonally flooded forests by rivers and in regrown secondary forests.
10548.m: Squirrel monkeys like forests by rivers and regrown forests.

10549.q: In which layer of the forest and at what time of day are squirrel monkeys mostly active?
a: By day in the middle and lower layers of the trees
At night in the highest treetops
By day mainly on the ground
10549.e: Squirrel monkeys are diurnal tree dwellers and mostly stay in the middle and lower layers of the forest, rarely on the ground.
10549.m: Squirrel monkeys are out and about by day in the middle and lower layers of the trees.

10550.q: How big can groups of squirrel monkeys get at the most?
10550.e: Groups usually include a few dozen animals but can exceed 100 and, according to some reports, reach up to 500. Large groups often split into smaller troops.
10550.m: Squirrel monkeys live in very large groups.

10551.q: How is a group of squirrel monkeys made up?
a: Several males, several females and young
Only females, while the males live alone
10551.e: Squirrel monkeys live in mixed groups of several males, several females and their offspring.
10551.m: In a squirrel monkey group many males and many females live together.

10552.q: How is the group life of many squirrel monkeys organised?
a: Around the females, with the males staying more at the edge
Around a single leading male in the middle
Without any rank order among the animals
10552.e: The groups are centred on the females, who form a stable rank order. The males often stay at the edge of the group.
10552.m: In squirrel monkeys the females are at the centre of the group.

10553.q: What does the diet of squirrel monkeys mainly consist of?
10553.e: Squirrel monkeys eat mainly insects and fruit, with the shares varying by season. Added to that are nectar, flowers, buds, eggs and small vertebrates.
10553.m: The squirrel monkey likes insects and fruit best.

10554.q: How much of their day can squirrel monkeys spend hunting insects?
a: Up to half of the day
Almost the whole day without a break
No time at all, they eat only fruit
10554.e: The search for insects can take up to 50 per cent of the day, while eating fruit makes up only about 10 per cent.
10554.m: Squirrel monkeys spend a lot of time hunting insects.

10555.q: Which tooth shape shows that squirrel monkeys also eat insects?
10555.e: The molars of squirrel monkeys have pointed cusps. With them they can crush the hard shells of insects well.
10555.m: Pointed molars help the squirrel monkey to crack insects.

10556.q: From which enemies do squirrel monkeys warn each other with special calls?
a: From birds of prey such as hawks
10556.e: Squirrel monkeys give alarm calls when birds of prey such as hawks appear. Other enemies are snakes and cats.
10556.m: Birds of prey are among the most dangerous enemies of squirrel monkeys.

10557.q: Besides birds of prey, which bird is among the enemies of young Central American squirrel monkeys?
10557.e: Besides birds of prey, young animals are also taken by toucans, tayras, opossums, coatis, snakes and even spider monkeys.
10557.m: Even toucans can be dangerous to young squirrel monkeys.

10558.q: How do male squirrel monkeys change before the mating season?
a: They put on up to about 20 per cent in weight
10558.e: Before the short mating season the males become clearly heavier and more aggressive. The trigger is a seasonal rise in male hormones such as testosterone.
10558.m: Before the mating season male squirrel monkeys put on a lot of weight.

10559.q: Which male squirrel monkeys in a group usually father the most young?
a: Those that put on the most weight before the mating season
Those that have lived in the group longest
10559.e: A few males usually father most of the offspring. They are usually those that gained the most weight before the mating season.
10559.m: In squirrel monkeys the fattest males have the greatest breeding success.

10560.q: About how long does gestation last in the squirrel monkey?
10560.e: Gestation lasts about 150 to 170 days, that is about five to five and a half months. The births fall in the rainy season.
10560.m: A female squirrel monkey is pregnant for about five months.

10561.q: What is typical of births within a group of squirrel monkeys?
a: They often take place within a few days
They are spread evenly over the whole year
Only one female a year has young
They always take place at full moon
10561.e: Because the mating season is short, the young of a group are often born almost at the same time, within a few days.
10561.m: In a squirrel monkey group the young are born almost at the same time.

10562.q: About how much does a newborn squirrel monkey weigh?
10562.e: Newborns weigh about 100 g. That is quite heavy relative to the mother, who weighs only about 500 to 750 g.
10562.m: A newborn squirrel monkey weighs about as much as a bar of chocolate.

10563.q: Who looks after the young in squirrel monkeys?
a: The mother, partly helped by other females
All the males of the group in turn
Nobody, the young are independent at once
10563.e: The mother takes over the rearing, and sometimes other females help. The fathers hardly take part, unlike in many marmosets, for example.
10563.m: In squirrel monkeys the females bring up the young.

10564.q: For about how long are young squirrel monkeys suckled?
a: Several months to over a year
Not at all, they eat insects at once
10564.e: Young Central American squirrel monkeys are weaned after about 4 months, Bolivian squirrel monkeys only after about 18 months.
10564.m: Young squirrel monkeys drink their mother’s milk for months.

10565.q: Which sex becomes sexually mature later in the squirrel monkey?
a: Both at the same time at one year
10565.e: Females become sexually mature at about 2 to 3 years, males only at about 3.5 to 5 years.
10565.m: Male squirrel monkeys take longer to reach sexual maturity than females.

10566.q: About how old do squirrel monkeys get in the wild?
10566.e: In the wild squirrel monkeys live about 15 years. In human care they can live over 20, sometimes even over 30 years.
10566.m: A wild squirrel monkey lives about fifteen years.

10567.q: Which animal did the squirrel monkey “Miss Baker” fly into space with aboard a Jupiter rocket in 1959?
10567.e: Miss Baker and the female rhesus monkey Able survived a flight on a Jupiter rocket on 28 May 1959. They were among the first monkeys to survive a spaceflight alive.
10567.m: Miss Baker was a squirrel monkey that survived a rocket flight.

10568.q: How old did the space-flight squirrel monkey “Miss Baker”, who died in 1984, become?
10568.e: Miss Baker was born in Peru around 1957 and died in 1984 at the age of 27. She is buried at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center in Huntsville, Alabama.
10568.m: The space monkey Miss Baker lived to a great age for a squirrel monkey.

10569.q: Which well-known film role was played by a squirrel monkey?
a: King Kong from the film of the same name
10569.e: In the film versions of Astrid Lindgren’s Pippi Longstocking books, Mr Nilsson was played by a squirrel monkey.
10569.m: Mr Nilsson from Pippi Longstocking was played by a squirrel monkey.

10570.q: Which bird family do the Andean condor and the California condor belong to?
10570.e: Both species of condor belong to the New World vultures, the family Cathartidae. They are only distantly related to the vultures of Africa and Eurasia.
10570.m: Condors are New World vultures of the family Cathartidae.

10571.q: Which of the two condors is larger and heavier?
a: Both are exactly the same size
10571.e: With a wingspan of over 3 m and up to about 15 kg, the Andean condor is the larger of the two. It is one of the heaviest flying birds.
10571.m: The Andean condor is the larger of the two condors.

10572.q: Where do California condors fly in the wild again today?
a: In California, Arizona, Utah and Baja California
In the Andes of South America
10572.e: After being saved through breeding, California condors were released in California, Arizona, Utah and Baja California (Mexico).
10572.m: California condors are flying again in the south-west of North America.

10573.q: The genus name Gymnogyps ends with the Greek word for vulture. Which feature does the first part “Gymno” refer to?
10573.e: “Gymnos” means naked in Greek, as in the word gymnastics, which used to be done naked. Gymnogyps therefore means naked vulture, because of the featherless head.

10574.q: From which language does the word “condor” come?
10574.e: The word condor goes back to the Quechua word “kuntur”. Quechua is still spoken in the Andes today.
10574.m: The word condor comes from the Quechua word kuntur.

10575.q: What does the Andean condor need its strong, hooked beak for?
a: To tear open the tough skin of carcasses
To spear live fish out of the water
10575.e: As a scavenger the condor has to open the thick hides of large animals. Its strong hooked beak is ideal for that.
10575.m: With its hooked beak the condor tears carcasses open.

10576.q: Which famous naturalist described the Andean condor scientifically in 1758?
10576.e: Carl Linnaeus described the Andean condor in 1758 in the 10th edition of his work “Systema Naturae”. This work is regarded as the starting point of zoological naming.
10576.m: Linnaeus gave the Andean condor its scientific name in 1758.

10577.q: How big can the wingspan of an Andean condor be at most?
10577.e: Large male Andean condors reach a wingspan of a good 3 m, with maximum values around 3.3 m. On average it is about 2.8 m.
10577.m: The Andean condor reaches a wingspan of over three metres.

10578.q: About how heavy can a male Andean condor grow at most?
10578.e: Male Andean condors usually weigh 11 to 15 kg. That makes the Andean condor one of the heaviest flying birds.
10578.m: A male Andean condor weighs up to about 15 kilos.

10579.q: Which bird has an even greater wingspan than the Andean condor?
10579.e: The wandering albatross reaches a wingspan of up to about 3.5 m and so surpasses the Andean condor. Among land birds, however, the Andean condor is one of the leaders.
10579.m: The wandering albatross surpasses the Andean condor in wingspan.

10580.q: What is unusual about the difference in size between the sexes in the Andean condor, for a bird of prey or vulture?
a: The male is larger than the female
The female is twice as large
Both are exactly the same weight
The young birds are larger than the parents
10580.e: In most birds of prey the females are larger. In the Andean condor it is the other way round: the males are clearly larger and heavier.
10580.m: In the Andean condor the male is the larger partner.

10581.q: How can you recognise an adult male Andean condor at a glance?
a: By the fleshy comb on its head
10581.e: Male Andean condors have a fleshy comb on the forehead and beak as well as a wattle. Females lack this comb.
10581.m: Only the male Andean condor has a comb on its head.

10582.q: What colour are the eyes of female Andean condors?
10582.e: Female Andean condors have deep red eyes, the males brown ones. So the sexes can also be told apart by the eye.
10582.m: Female Andean condors can be recognised by their red eyes.

10583.q: What colour is the fluffy neck ruff of an adult Andean condor?
10583.e: Adult Andean condors have a white ruff of feathers at the base of the neck. In young birds it is still brownish and only turns white over the years.
10583.m: The adult Andean condor has a white neck ruff.

10584.q: Where are the large white wing patches in the Andean condor compared with the California condor?
a: In the Andean condor on the upper side of the wing, in the California condor on the underside
In both on the underside of the wing
In the Andean condor on the underside, in the California condor on the upper side
10584.e: The Andean condor shows white patches on the upper side of the wings. In the California condor a white triangle can be seen on the underside of the wing.
10584.m: The Andean condor has white on top, the California condor white underneath.

10585.q: What colour is the bare head skin of an adult California condor?
10585.e: Adult California condors have yellowish to orange-red head skin, which glows more strongly during courtship. Young birds have a grey head.
10585.m: The adult California condor has an orange head.

10586.q: Why is the head of condors featherless?
a: It stays cleaner more easily when feeding in carrion
It serves as camouflage in snow
10586.e: Condors stick their heads deep into carcasses. A bare head gets less dirty and dries quickly, and the sun helps to kill germs. It also plays a part in regulating heat.
10586.m: The bare head keeps the condor clean when feeding.

10587.q: How do the feet of condors differ from those of an eagle?
a: They are rather flat and hardly suited to gripping
They have especially long, sharp claws for killing
10587.e: Condors have comparatively weak feet with blunt claws. They do not kill prey with their feet but walk and stand on them at carcasses.
10587.m: Condors cannot grip with their feet as eagles do.

10588.q: What can condors not do for lack of a syrinx, the voice organ of birds?
a: Sing or call properly; they only hiss and grunt
10588.e: New World vultures such as condors lack a developed syrinx. They can therefore only hiss, snarl and grunt.
10588.m: Condors hiss and grunt because they lack the voice organ.

10589.q: How do condors cool down in the heat, as storks do?
a: They excrete onto their legs so that evaporation cools them
They dip their heads in water
10589.e: This behaviour is called urohidrosis. The liquid waste evaporates on the legs and draws heat from the body, which is why the legs often look streaked with white.
10589.m: Condors cool their legs with their own droppings.

10590.q: What do condors mainly feed on?
10590.e: Condors are scavengers and prefer the carcasses of large animals such as cattle, guanacos or deer. They rarely kill prey themselves.
10590.m: Condors live on the carrion of large animals.

10591.q: What do Andean condors like to eat on the coast of Chile and Peru?
a: Stranded marine mammals such as whales and seals
10591.e: On the Pacific coast Andean condors search the beaches for washed-up whales, seals and sea lions. Eggs of seabirds are also on the menu.
10591.m: On the coast the Andean condor eats dead whales and seals.

10592.q: How do condors mainly find their food?
a: By sight, often by following other vultures
10592.e: Condors have a weak sense of smell and search with their sharp eyes. They often follow turkey vultures, which can smell carrion, and then displace them.
10592.m: Condors see their food instead of smelling it.

10593.q: How many kilometres can an Andean condor cover in a day when looking for food?
10593.e: Andean condors can soar more than 200 km a day in search of carrion. They use updrafts and use hardly any energy.
10593.m: An Andean condor often flies hundreds of kilometres a day.

10594.q: According to a 2020 study, how much of their flight time do Andean condors actively flap their wings?
10594.e: Researchers fitted Andean condors in Patagonia with measuring devices. The birds flapped their wings for only about 1 per cent of flight time, mostly at take-off.
10594.m: The Andean condor almost always soars and hardly flaps its wings.

10595.q: What distance did an Andean condor cover in the 2020 study without a single wingbeat?
10595.e: One bird soared for about five hours over some 172 km without flapping its wings even once. It used thermals and slope updrafts to do so.
10595.m: An Andean condor once soared 170 kilometres without a wingbeat.

10596.q: Over which mountain range does the range of the Andean condor extend?
a: The Andes from Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego
10596.e: The Andean condor lives along the Andes from Venezuela and Colombia to Tierra del Fuego. In the south it also occurs in the lowlands of Patagonia and on the coast.
10596.m: The Andean condor lives along the whole Andes chain.

10597.q: Up to what height does the Andean condor breed in the Andes?
a: Up to about 5000 m above sea level
Only up to about 500 m above sea level
Up to about 9000 m above sea level
10597.e: Andean condors often nest and roost between 3000 and 5000 m above sea level. Rock faces offer protection and good take-off conditions there.
10597.m: The Andean condor breeds at heights up to 5000 metres.

10598.q: Where does the Andean condor mostly lay its egg?
a: On a rock ledge or in a rock niche
In a hole in the ground in the forest
In a tree hollow in the rainforest
10598.e: Andean condors hardly build a nest. They lay their egg on bare rock ledges or in niches in steep rock faces.
10598.m: The Andean condor breeds on rock ledges.

10599.q: How many eggs does a female condor normally lay per brood?
10599.e: Condors normally lay only a single egg. If it is lost early on, a replacement egg can sometimes be laid.
10599.m: A female condor lays only one egg per brood.

10600.q: How often does a pair of condors normally breed?
10600.e: Because rearing a young bird takes a very long time, condors usually breed only every second year. This makes their reproduction very slow.
10600.m: Condors usually raise a young bird only every two years.

10601.q: About how long does incubation last in the Andean condor?
10601.e: Both parents take turns incubating the egg for about 54 to 58 days. For birds that is a long incubation period.
10601.m: A condor egg is incubated for almost two months.

10602.q: At what age can a young Andean condor fly for the first time?
10602.e: Young Andean condors fledge after about six months. After that they often stay with their parents for a long time.
10602.m: A young condor flies after about half a year.

10603.q: At what age do condors become sexually mature?
10603.e: Andean condors and California condors only become able to breed at about 5 to 8 years. This late age makes it harder for populations to recover.
10603.m: Condors only become adult after several years.

10604.q: How old did the Andean condor “Thaao”, one of the oldest known birds, become in a US zoo?
10604.e: Thaao died in 2010 at the Beardsley Zoo in Connecticut at the age of about 79. He is regarded as one of the longest-lived birds of all.
10604.m: An Andean condor in human care lived to almost 80 years.

10605.q: What status does the Andean condor have on the IUCN Red List?
10605.e: The IUCN has classed the Andean condor as vulnerable since 2020. Before that it was regarded as near threatened.
10605.m: The Andean condor has been regarded as vulnerable since 2020.

10606.q: What status does the California condor have on the IUCN Red List?
10606.e: The California condor is regarded as critically endangered. Despite an increase, the free-living population still depends heavily on human help.
10606.m: The California condor is critically endangered.

10607.q: How many California condors were left in the world in 1987?
10607.e: In 1987 only 27 California condors were left. All were taken to breeding centres to save the species.
10607.m: In 1987 there were only 27 California condors left.

10608.q: What happened in 1987 to the last free-living California condor, called AC-9?
a: It was captured for breeding in human care
It was stuffed and put on display
It was taken to South America
It was fitted with a transmitter and stayed free
10608.e: AC-9 was captured on Easter Sunday 1987. After that there was no California condor left in the wild until the releases began.
10608.m: With AC-9 the last wild California condor was captured in 1987.

10609.q: In which zoos did the breeding of the last California condors begin from 1987?
a: The San Diego Zoo Wild Animal Park and the Los Angeles Zoo
The Bronx Zoo and Berlin Zoo
The zoos of Toronto and Mexico City
10609.e: The last condors went to the San Diego Wild Animal Park and the Los Angeles Zoo. Later other institutions took part, such as the World Center for Birds of Prey in Idaho.
10609.m: San Diego and Los Angeles saved the California condor.

10610.q: From which year were California condors released into the wild in California again?
10610.e: In the early 1990s, from 1992, the first condors bred in human care were released in California. Arizona, Utah and Mexico followed later.
10610.m: Since 1992 bred condors have been flying in California again.

10611.q: What is the most common known cause of death in free-living California condors?
a: Lead poisoning from ammunition fragments in carrion
10611.e: Condors eat carcasses and the gut piles of shot animals and swallow lead fragments as they do so. In adult condors, according to a 2012 study, about two thirds of known deaths are due to lead poisoning.
10611.m: Lead ammunition is the greatest danger to the California condor.

10612.q: Roughly how many California condors are there in total today (in the mid-2020s)?
10612.e: Thanks to breeding and releases the population rose to about 600 animals, almost two thirds of them in the wild. At the end of 2025 there were 607 condors, 392 of them free-living.
10612.m: Today there are again about 600 California condors.

10613.q: In which Mexican area were California condors reintroduced?
a: In the Sierra de San Pedro Mártir in Baja California
10613.e: In the Sierra de San Pedro Mártir National Park in Baja California, California condors are flying again. The species used to live there naturally.
10613.m: California condors are flying again in Baja California too.

10614.q: Which disease killed about 21 California condors in Arizona and Utah in 2023?
10614.e: In 2023, 21 condors died of the highly contagious bird flu H5N1. After that, condors were vaccinated against bird flu for the first time.
10614.m: Bird flu killed many California condors in 2023.

10615.q: What surprising discovery did researchers make in 2021 with California condors at the San Diego Zoo?
a: Two chicks had hatched from unfertilised eggs (parthenogenesis)
10615.e: Genetic analyses showed that two chicks had come about without a father, although their mothers had breeding-capable males. It was the first evidence of this virgin birth in condors.

10616.q: Why do keepers use hand puppets that look like adult condors when rearing condors?
a: So that the chicks do not get used to humans
So that the chicks grow faster
10616.e: Chicks that see humans as parents later behave wrongly in the wild. The condor puppet makes sure they imprint on their own kind.
10616.m: Puppets stop condor chicks from taking humans for parents.

10617.q: In which countries is the Andean condor shown on the national coat of arms?
a: Cuba, Panama, Costa Rica and Honduras
10617.e: The Andean condor adorns the coats of arms of Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador and Colombia. In many Andean countries it is a national symbol.
10617.m: Four Andean states carry the condor on their coat of arms.

10618.q: What is the famous Peruvian piece of music named after the condor called?
10618.e: “El Cóndor Pasa” comes from the Peruvian composer Daniel Alomía Robles and dates from 1913. It became world famous through the version by Simon and Garfunkel.
10618.m: The condor gave the song “El Cóndor Pasa” its name.

10619.q: Where was the California condor found during the last Ice Age?
a: Across large parts of North America, as far as Florida
Only on an island off California
10619.e: In the Pleistocene, condors of the genus Gymnogyps were spread over large parts of North America. As large Ice Age animals died out, their range shrank sharply.
10619.m: The California condor used to live across the whole of North America.

10620.q: Which wind belt of the Southern Hemisphere do albatrosses use for their long flights around Antarctica?
a: The westerly zone of the “Roaring Forties”
The trade winds at the equator
The monsoon in the Indian Ocean
10620.e: Between about 40 and 60 degrees south, strong westerly winds blow almost constantly. Albatrosses let them carry them right around the globe.
10620.m: Albatrosses sail with the strong westerly winds of the Southern Ocean.

10621.q: Which bird order do albatrosses belong to?
10621.e: Like petrels and storm petrels, albatrosses are tubenoses. The order is named after the tube-shaped nostrils on the beak.

10622.q: Which seabirds are closely related to albatrosses and also have tube-shaped nostrils on the beak?
10622.e: Albatrosses, petrels and storm petrels together form the order of tubenoses. Gulls, pelicans and cormorants belong to other groups of birds.

10623.q: With what simple measure can longline fishing greatly reduce the bycatch of albatrosses?
a: With fluttering bird-scaring lines above the bait
10623.e: Coloured streamers on a line over the stern keep the birds away from the bait. Together with weighted lines and setting the lines at night, far fewer albatrosses die.
10623.m: Bird-scaring lines protect albatrosses from the hooks.

10624.q: What do young albatrosses do after they have left the nest?
a: They stay at sea for several years without setting foot on land
They stay with their parents until death
They breed as early as the next year
They move into forests on the coast
10624.e: Young albatrosses spend their first years almost uninterruptedly over the open sea. Only after years do they return to the colony.
10624.m: Young albatrosses live only on the sea for years.

10625.q: What do large albatrosses need in order to take off from the ground?
a: A tall tree as a launch place
10625.e: With their long wings and high weight, large albatrosses cannot take off from standing. They run into the wind until they have enough lift.
10625.m: Albatrosses take off with a run-up into the wind.

10626.q: Why do albatrosses mostly avoid the sea areas around the equator?
a: There is often too little wind there for their soaring flight
The water there is too salty
It is too bright for them there
10626.e: In the doldrums at the equator it is often windless. Without wind, albatrosses would have to flap their wings, which takes a lot of strength.
10626.m: Without wind albatrosses hardly get anywhere.

10627.q: After which figure from Greek legend did Linnaeus name the albatross genus Diomedea?
10627.e: According to legend, the companions of the hero Diomedes were turned into birds. Linnaeus took over this name for the genus of the great albatrosses.
10627.m: The genus Diomedea recalls the Greek hero Diomedes.

10628.q: What word does the name “albatross” probably go back to?
a: The English “all across” for a world voyage
10628.e: The Spanish-Portuguese “alcatraz”, which goes back to an Arabic word, referred to large seabirds such as pelicans and frigatebirds. The word reached English through the language of seafarers, probably influenced by Latin “albus” for white.
10628.m: The name albatross comes from the Iberian word “alcatraz”.

10629.q: Which albatross species has the greatest wingspan of all birds alive today?
10629.e: With wingspans of over 3 metres the wandering albatross holds the record among all living birds. The North Pacific species reach only about 2 metres.
10629.m: The wandering albatross has the greatest wingspan of all birds.

10630.q: How big can the wingspan of a wandering albatross get?
10630.e: On average the wingspan of a wandering albatross is about 3.1 m. Individual animals reach a good 3.5 m.
10630.m: A wandering albatross can reach a wingspan of about three and a half metres.

10631.q: What danger does plastic waste in the sea mean for albatross chicks?
a: The parents feed them plastic pieces that fill the stomach
Plastic attracts predators to the islands
Plastic makes the sea water too warm
10631.e: Albatrosses collect food at the sea surface and mistake plastic for food. The chicks are fed it and can starve even though their stomach is full.
10631.m: Plastic waste can make albatross chicks starve despite a full stomach.

10632.q: Who described the wandering albatross scientifically in 1758?
10632.e: Carl Linnaeus listed the wandering albatross in 1758 in his work “Systema Naturae”. That year is regarded as the starting point of zoological naming.
10632.m: Linnaeus described the wandering albatross in 1758.

10633.q: How heavy can a fully grown wandering albatross get?
10633.e: Adult wandering albatrosses weigh about 6 to 12 kg. Albatrosses are thus among the heaviest flying birds.
10633.m: A wandering albatross can weigh about twelve kilograms.

10634.q: Which anatomical feature allows albatrosses to hold their wings outstretched almost without muscle power?
a: A tendon sheet that locks the shoulder joint
Hollow wing feathers filled with air
An additional breast muscle made of fat
An ossified elbow joint with no movement
10634.e: A tendon sheet in the shoulder locks into place when the wing is fully extended. In this way the albatross saves a lot of energy when soaring for hours.
10634.m: A tendon lock in the shoulder keeps the albatross’s wings outstretched.

10635.q: What is the flying technique called with which albatrosses gain energy from different wind speeds over the sea?
10635.e: In dynamic soaring the albatross climbs into the wind and glides back down with the wind. It makes use of the fact that the wind blows more weakly near the water than higher up.

10636.q: According to studies, what distance can individual wandering albatrosses cover within a year?
10636.e: Some wandering albatrosses circle the Southern Ocean three times in a year. In doing so they cover more than 120,000 km.
10636.m: A wandering albatross can fly three times round Antarctica in a year.

10637.q: How does an albatross get rid of the excess salt it takes in with sea water and food?
a: Through a salt gland whose solution drips from the nasal tubes
Through sweat glands on the feet
Through tears running from the eyes
10637.e: Above the eyes there is an enlarged nasal gland that filters salt from the blood. The concentrated salt solution comes out through the nasal tubes on the beak.
10637.m: Albatrosses excrete salt through a gland and the nasal tubes.

10638.q: Which sense especially helps albatrosses to find food on the wide ocean?
10638.e: Unlike most birds, tubenoses such as albatrosses have a well-developed sense of smell. With it they can scent food over great distances.
10638.m: Albatrosses also find their food with their noses.

10639.q: What is the stomach oil that albatrosses produce?
a: An energy-rich oil made from digested prey
A secretion for oiling the feathers
A poison for fending off predators
A lure for finding a mate
10639.e: The stomach oil is made from digested prey and contains a lot of energy for little weight. Albatrosses feed their chicks with it on long supply flights.
10639.m: With stomach oil albatrosses carry a lot of energy for little weight.

10640.q: Which prey animals make up the largest part of the diet of many albatross species?
10640.e: Albatrosses eat mainly squid, as well as fish, krill and other crustaceans. Some species also take carrion and fishing waste.
10640.m: Squid are the main food of many albatrosses.

10641.q: Where do most albatrosses catch their food?
a: At or just below the surface of the water
In the deep sea at over 500 m
On land in the breeding colonies
In flight, from swarms of insects
10641.e: Albatrosses land on the water and snatch squid and fish at the surface. Only a few species dive a few metres deep.
10641.m: Albatrosses hunt mainly at the sea surface.

10642.q: How many eggs does a female albatross lay per brood?
10642.e: Albatrosses lay only a single, large egg per brood. If it is lost, usually no new one is laid in the same season.
10642.m: An albatross lays only one egg per brood.

10643.q: About how long does incubation last in the wandering albatross?
10643.e: The wandering albatross’s egg is incubated for about 78 days. Both parents take turns.
10643.m: The wandering albatross incubates its egg for about eleven weeks.

10644.q: About how long does a young wandering albatross stay in the colony after hatching until it fledges?
10644.e: In the great albatrosses it takes up to about 280 days for the chick to fledge. It spends the whole southern winter at the nest and is fed by its parents at long intervals.
10644.m: A young wandering albatross stays at the nest for about nine months.

10645.q: Why do large albatross species such as the wandering albatross usually breed only every two years?
a: Because breeding and rearing take about a year
Because the females form eggs only every two years
Because the colonies are flooded every second year
Because the partners have to find each other again every year
10645.e: From building the nest to the independence of the young takes about a full year. After that the parents need a break to recover at sea.
10645.m: Large albatrosses breed only every second year because of the long rearing.

10646.q: At what age do large albatross species usually breed for the first time?
10646.e: Wandering albatrosses usually breed for the first time only at 11 to 15 years. Before that, young birds return to the colony for years to look for a partner.
10646.m: Large albatrosses begin breeding only at about ten years.

10647.q: What is the pair bond like in albatrosses, typically?
a: It lasts only a single breeding season
A male always has several females
10647.e: Albatross pairs usually stay together until one partner dies. A separation is rare and usually follows several unsuccessful broods.
10647.m: Albatrosses usually stay faithful to their partner for life.

10648.q: What is part of the courtship ritual of many albatross species?
a: A dance with bill clapping and calls
Handing over stones as a gift
A joint dive into the sea
10648.e: Albatrosses perform ritualised dances with bowing, pointing, calling and bill clapping. Young birds practise these dances for years before they choose a partner.
10648.m: Albatrosses court with a dance of bill clapping and calls.

10649.q: How does the plumage of the wandering albatross change with increasing age?
a: It stays the same brown for life
10649.e: Young wandering albatrosses are mainly brown and become increasingly white over the years. They reach full colouring only after many years.
10649.m: Wandering albatrosses become whiter with age.

10650.q: Which species is the famous albatross “Wisdom”, regarded as the oldest known wild bird?
10650.e: Wisdom is a female Laysan albatross that breeds on Midway Atoll in the Pacific. She is regarded as the oldest known bird in the wild.
10650.m: The oldest known wild bird is the Laysan albatross Wisdom.

10651.q: How old was the Laysan albatross “Wisdom” estimated to be when she laid an egg again on Midway at the end of 2024?
10651.e: Wisdom was ringed in 1956 as an already adult bird. When she laid her probably 60th egg in late autumn 2024, she was estimated to be about 74 years old.
10651.m: At about 74 years Wisdom was still a mother.

10652.q: Where does the greatest part of all Laysan albatrosses breed?
10652.e: About 99 per cent of Laysan albatrosses breed on the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Midway Atoll alone is home to about 70 per cent of the world population.
10652.m: Laysan albatrosses breed almost only on the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.

10653.q: What did researchers observe in a Laysan albatross colony on the Hawaiian island of Oahu?
a: About a third of the pairs consisted of two females
The males raised the chicks alone
The birds bred in tree hollows
The pairs laid two eggs every year
10653.e: In this colony there were more females than males, and about 31 per cent of the pairs consisted of two females. Such pairs raise chicks together.
10653.m: On Oahu many Laysan albatross pairs consist of two females.

10654.q: In which sea area are albatrosses now completely missing as breeding birds?
10654.e: Albatrosses today live mainly in the Southern Hemisphere and the North Pacific. In the North Atlantic only stray individuals turn up now and then.
10654.m: No albatrosses breed in the North Atlantic today.

10655.q: Which wing shape is typical of albatrosses?
a: Long, narrow wings like a glider’s
Short, round wings like a hen’s
Broad wings with spread flight feathers like an eagle’s
Small, stiff flipper-wings like a penguin’s
10655.e: Long, narrow wings produce a lot of lift with little air resistance. In this way albatrosses can glide long distances without flapping their wings.
10655.m: Albatrosses have long, narrow soaring wings.

10656.q: Why was the short-tailed albatross declared extinct in 1949?
a: Because feather hunters had almost wiped it out
Because an oil spill destroyed its colony
Because introduced rats ate all the eggs
Because a typhoon killed all the adult birds
10656.e: From the late 19th century, feather hunters killed millions of these birds. Some young birds, however, survived at sea and founded the population anew.
10656.m: The short-tailed albatross only just survived the feather hunt.

10657.q: Why did researchers move chicks of the short-tailed albatross from its most important breeding island to another island?
a: Because a volcanic eruption could wipe out the main colony
Because the island had become too cold
Because tourists disturbed the nests there
Because the chicks could find no water there
10657.e: Most short-tailed albatrosses breed on an active volcanic island near Japan. With a second colony, a single eruption should not endanger the whole species.
10657.m: A second colony protects the short-tailed albatross from a volcanic eruption.

10658.q: What is special about the habitat of the waved albatross?
a: It is the only albatross species that lives entirely in the tropics
It is the only species that lives in fresh water
It is the only species that breeds in Antarctica
It is the only species that lives in the North Atlantic
10658.e: The Galápagos Islands lie on the equator. The cool Humboldt Current provides food-rich water there, which allows the waved albatross to live in the tropics.
10658.m: The waved albatross is the only tropical albatross.

10659.q: What conservation status does the waved albatross have on the IUCN Red List?
10659.e: The waved albatross has been regarded as critically endangered since 2007. Because it breeds almost only on one island, a single disaster could make the population collapse.
10659.m: The waved albatross is critically endangered.

10660.q: What is different about the breeding of the waved albatross compared with most albatross species?
a: It builds no nest and lays the egg on the ground
It breeds in burrows in the ground
It lays its eggs in rock crevices on cliffs
10660.e: The waved albatross lays its egg without a nest in a hollow on the bare ground and sometimes even moves it around within its territory. Most other albatrosses build nests of earth, peat or plants.
10660.m: The waved albatross breeds entirely without a nest.

10661.q: What behaviour does the waved albatross show regularly as the only tubenose?
a: It robs boobies of their prey
It eats the eggs of other albatrosses
It catches fish in fresh water
10661.e: Waved albatrosses regularly harass boobies until they drop their prey. This stealing of food is called kleptoparasitism.
10661.m: The waved albatross steals food from boobies.

10662.q: Which introduced animals eat the chicks of the Tristan albatross on Gough Island?
10662.e: On Gough Island house mice attack the large albatross chicks and eat them alive. The Tristan albatross is therefore regarded as critically endangered.
10662.m: House mice threaten the chicks of the Tristan albatross.

10663.q: Why do albatross populations recover only very slowly after heavy losses?
a: They start breeding late and raise few young
Their eggs need ten years to hatch
They breed only at full moon
Their chicks can never learn to fly
10663.e: Large albatrosses start breeding only at about ten years, lay only one egg and sometimes breed only every two years. Every adult bird killed is therefore missed for a long time.
10663.m: Few young make albatrosses very vulnerable.

10664.q: Why was the Amsterdam albatross recognised as a species of its own only late?
a: It looks very like the wandering albatross and was regarded as a form of it
It lives only in the deep sea
It is active only at night
It was only recently bred from an egg in a zoo
10664.e: The Amsterdam albatross breeds only on Amsterdam Island in the southern Indian Ocean. For a long time it was regarded as a form of the wandering albatross; only in 1983 was it described as a species of its own.
10664.m: The Amsterdam albatross was long confused with the wandering albatross.

10665.q: What is special about the albatross colony at Taiaroa Head near Dunedin in New Zealand?
a: It is on the mainland, whereas most albatrosses breed on remote islands
Albatrosses spend the winter in snow there
Albatrosses breed there together with penguins in caves
10665.e: At Taiaroa Head northern royal albatrosses breed on the mainland. That is very rare, because albatrosses otherwise prefer islands without predators.
10665.m: Taiaroa Head is a rare albatross colony on the mainland.

10666.q: Which fishing method is regarded as the greatest threat to albatrosses?
10666.e: Albatrosses snap at the bait on the hooks, are pulled under water and drown. According to estimates, about 100,000 albatrosses die this way every year.
10666.m: Longlines with bait kill very many albatrosses every year.

10667.q: Which international agreement, which came into force in 2004, protects albatrosses?
a: The Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP)
The Montreal Protocol on the ozone layer
The Bern Convention on European wildlife
10667.e: ACAP was agreed in 2001 and came into force in 2004. The signatory states undertake, among other things, to reduce the bycatch of seabirds.
10667.m: The ACAP agreement protects albatrosses and petrels.

10668.q: What conservation status does the wandering albatross have on the IUCN Red List?
10668.e: The wandering albatross is regarded as vulnerable. Its numbers have fallen above all through bycatch in longline fishing.
10668.m: The wandering albatross is regarded as vulnerable.

10669.q: Which poem of 1798 made the albatross famous in literature?
a: “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner” by Coleridge
“The Erlking” by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
10669.e: In Coleridge’s poem a sailor kills an albatross and so brings misfortune on his ship. This is the origin of the English expression “an albatross around one’s neck”, an image for a heavy burden.
10669.m: Coleridge’s poem of the sailor made the albatross famous.

10670.q: How many species alive today does the pelican family (Pelecanidae) include?
10670.e: The family Pelecanidae consists of the single genus Pelecanus with eight living species. These include, for example, the great white pelican, the Dalmatian pelican and the brown pelican.
10670.m: There are eight species of pelican worldwide.

10671.q: Which birds belong, like the pelican, to the order Pelecaniformes today?
10671.e: Besides the pelicans, the order Pelecaniformes today includes herons, ibises, the shoebill and the hamerkop. Cormorants and boobies used to be counted in it.
10671.m: Herons and ibises are relatives of the pelican.

10672.q: Which birds are, according to molecular studies, the closest relatives of the pelicans?
10672.e: Genetic analyses show that the shoebill and hamerkop are most closely related to the pelicans. Cormorants, boobies and frigatebirds used to be counted with them but now belong in another order.
10672.m: The strange shoebill is a close relative of the pelican.

10673.q: From which ancient Greek word does the name “pelican” derive?
10673.e: “Pelican” comes from Greek pelekan, which goes back to pelekys for “axe”. In antiquity the word was used both for the pelican and for the woodpecker.
10673.m: The name of the pelican contains the Greek word for axe.

10674.q: Which naturalist described the pelican genus Pelecanus in 1758?
10674.e: Carl Linnaeus established the genus Pelecanus in 1758 in the tenth edition of his work “Systema Naturae”. That year is regarded as the starting point of zoological naming.
10674.m: Linnaeus gave the pelicans their scientific genus name in 1758.

10675.q: Which pelican species is regarded as the heaviest and is among the heaviest flying birds in the world?
10675.e: The Dalmatian pelican weighs about 9.5 kg on average, large animals up to about 15 kg. It is thus among the heaviest birds that can still fly.
10675.m: The Dalmatian pelican is the heavyweight among pelicans.

10676.q: Which is the smallest of the eight pelican species?
10676.e: The brown pelican usually weighs only 2 to 5 kg. Small animals have a wingspan of just under 2 m.
10676.m: The brown pelican is the smallest pelican.

10677.q: Which pelican species has the longest bill of all birds, at up to about 50 cm?
10677.e: In the Australian pelican the bill of large males reaches about 50 cm. No other bird has a longer bill.
10677.m: The longest bird bill in the world belongs to the Australian pelican.

10678.q: About how much water can the stretchy throat pouch of a large pelican hold?
10678.e: Depending on species and source, the pouch holds about 11 to 13 litres of water along with fish. Before the pelican swallows, it lets the water drain out at the sides.
10678.m: The pelican’s throat pouch is a catching net and not a storage bag.

10679.q: What job do the many air sacs have that reach under the skin and into the bones of the pelican?
a: They give buoyancy in the water
They serve as a food store
10679.e: A network of air sacs under the skin of the chest, throat and wings makes pelicans very light and able to float. It probably also cushions the impact when plunge-diving.
10679.m: Thanks to its air sacs the pelican floats like a cork.

10680.q: What is special about the feet of pelicans?
a: All four toes are joined by webbing
The toes have lobes instead of webs
The hind toe is missing completely
10680.e: Pelicans have totipalmate feet, in which all four toes are joined by webbing. This gives large paddles for powerful swimming.
10680.m: In the pelican even all four toes are joined by webbing.

10681.q: How does a pelican cool down in great heat?
a: It flutters the skin of the throat and throat pouch
It bathes its feet in mud
It spreads the feathers on its back
It pants with its tongue stuck out
10681.e: With its beak open, the pelican makes the thin skin of the throat and throat pouch vibrate quickly. Water evaporates in the process and the body cools down.
10681.m: The pelican fans itself cool with its throat pouch.

10682.q: Up to what height can pelicans climb with the help of thermals?
10682.e: Pelicans circle in rising warm air, saving energy, up to 3000 m and higher. From there they glide on almost without flapping.
10682.m: Pelicans use thermals like a lift into the sky.

10683.q: How far do pelicans fly to their feeding grounds, often in V formation?
10683.e: Pelicans commute up to about 150 km between colony and feeding area. They often fly in V formation, which saves energy.
10683.m: For a good catch pelicans fly up to 150 km.

10684.q: About how long does the incubation of pelican eggs last?
10684.e: Depending on the species, the chicks hatch after about 30 to 36 days. Both parents take turns incubating.
10684.m: Pelican eggs are incubated for about a month.

10685.q: How many eggs does a female pelican usually lay?
10685.e: A pelican clutch usually comprises one to three eggs, rarely up to six. Often, though, only one chick survives.
10685.m: A pelican nest usually holds only a few eggs.

10686.q: What do pelicans use to warm their eggs when incubating?
a: Their feet, on or under which the eggs lie
A bare brood patch on the belly
10686.e: Pelicans lay the eggs on or under their well-supplied webbed feet. In this way they pass the warmth directly to the eggs.
10686.m: Pelicans incubate their eggs with their feet.

10687.q: How old do pelicans typically get in the wild?
10687.e: In the wild pelicans usually reach an age of 15 to 25 years. The main dangers are lack of food, disturbance and accidents.
10687.m: A wild pelican can live to a quarter of a century.

10688.q: How old can pelicans get in human care?
10688.e: A pelican in a zoo has been proven to reach 54 years. That is more than twice as old as most wild pelicans.
10688.m: In a zoo a pelican lived to over fifty years.

10689.q: About how much fish does a great white pelican need per day?
10689.e: A great white pelican eats about 0.9 to 1.4 kg of fish a day. It eats mainly fish but also takes other prey if it is easy to get.
10689.m: A great white pelican gets through a good kilo of fish every day.

10690.q: How do great white pelicans often hunt together?
a: They drive fish together in a horseshoe shape
They dive down singly from a great height
They lie in wait motionless on the shore like herons
They dive deep to the bottom of the water
10690.e: Groups of about six to eight great white pelicans form a horseshoe and drive fish into shallow water. Then they all dip their bills in at the same time.
10690.m: Great white pelicans fish as a team, as if with a net.

10691.q: Which pelican species is famous for catching fish by plunging from the air?
10691.e: The brown pelican plunges headfirst into the sea, sometimes going completely under. Most other species fish swimming at the surface.
10691.m: The brown pelican is the plunge-diver among pelicans.

10692.q: From what height does a brown pelican usually plunge into the water?
10692.e: Brown pelicans scan for fish from about 10 to 20 m up and then plunge into the water bill first. The air sacs cushion the impact.
10692.m: The brown pelican jumps, so to speak, from the ten-metre board.

10693.q: How does the American white pelican catch its prey, unlike the brown pelican?
a: By plunging from a great height
By poking about in the shore grass
10693.e: The American white pelican does not dive from the air. It fishes swimming and often herds the fish together with others of its kind.
10693.m: The American white pelican fishes from the water.

10694.q: Which pelican species grows a horn-like plate on its upper bill during the breeding season?
10694.e: Both sexes of the American white pelican carry a flat horny growth on the bill in the breeding season. It is not known in any other pelican species.
10694.m: Only the American white pelican has a bill horn in the breeding season.

10695.q: What happens to the bill horn of the American white pelican after mating and egg laying?
