11181.e: Males have much larger spurs than females. They use them to scratch and stimulate the female and to bring her into the right position when mating.
11181.m: Male pythons use their spurs when mating.

11182.q: What are the many backward-curved teeth of the python used for?
11182.e: The python is non-venomous and does not chew. Its backward-curved teeth hold the prey fast while it coils round it and swallows it.
11182.m: The python's teeth hold the prey fast.

11183.q: What is special about the python's lung compared with many more advanced snakes such as colubrids?
a: Besides the right lung, a left lung is also present
The python breathes mainly through its skin
The python has three lungs of equal size
The python has no lung, it uses gills
11183.e: In most more advanced snakes, the left lung has almost completely disappeared. As more primitive snakes, pythons still have a smaller left lung.

11184.q: Roughly how often does a large python eat in the wild?
a: Only every few weeks to months
11184.e: After a large meal, a python digests for a long time and needs little energy. Large animals therefore go without food for weeks or even months.
11184.m: A large python can go a long time without food.

11185.q: How does a python kill its prey?
a: It coils round it and tightens the coils more and more
It paralyses it with a nerve poison
It always drowns it under water
It wounds it with fangs and waits
11185.e: Pythons are non-venomous constrictors. They seize the prey with their teeth, coil round it and tighten the coils each time the prey breathes out.
11185.m: The python is a non-venomous constrictor.

11186.q: Which feature of the lower jaw allows the python to swallow very large prey?
a: The two halves of the lower jaw are joined at the front only by a stretchy ligament
The lower jaw is made of a single rigid bone
The lower jaw can detach completely from the skull and grow back
The lower jaw is joined at the front by a firm ball-and-socket joint
11186.e: The halves of the lower jaw are not fused at the front but joined elastically. Together with movable skull bones, this lets the python open its mouth enormously wide.
11186.m: The halves of the python's lower jaw are only loosely joined at the front.

11187.q: What does the discovery of a python about 47 million years old in the Messel Pit in Germany show?
a: Pythons also used to live in Europe
Pythons used to live only in the sea
11187.e: The fossil find Messelopython freyi was described in 2020. It shows that pythons once also occurred in Europe, when a warm climate prevailed there.
11187.m: The oldest known python comes from the Messel Pit.

11188.q: In which country were vertebrae of the extinct European python (Python europaeus) from the Miocene found?
11188.e: Python europaeus is known from trunk vertebrae from the Miocene, discovered at sites in France.
11188.m: Pythons once lived in France too.

11189.q: Which python species is regarded as the smallest of its family?
11189.e: The Australian pygmy python only grows to about 50 cm long and weighs about 200 g. It is also called the anthill python because it often lives in termite mounds.
11189.m: The smallest python is the pygmy python from Australia.

11190.q: Which python is regarded as the longest snake in the world?
11190.e: The reticulated python of South-East Asia reaches the greatest reliably measured lengths of any snake. The green anaconda is heavier, but not longer.
11190.m: The reticulated python is the longest snake in the world.

11191.q: Roughly how long was the longest reliably measured wild reticulated python?
11191.e: A reticulated python from East Kalimantan measured 6.95 m under anaesthetic. Older claims of 10 m and more are regarded as exaggerated.
11191.m: The longest measured reticulated python was almost 7 m long.

11192.q: Where does the reticulated python get its name?
a: From the net-like pattern on its skin
Because it steals fish from fishing nets
Because it often gets caught in nets
Because it builds nets out of slime
11192.e: The reticulated python has a fine, net-like pattern of light and dark patches. Its species name reticulatus also means “net-like”.
11192.m: The reticulated python is named after its skin pattern.

11193.q: Roughly how many eggs does a female reticulated python lay?
11193.e: Depending on size, female reticulated pythons lay about 15 to 80 eggs. At 31 to 32 °C, the young hatch after around 88 days.
11193.m: A reticulated python lays up to about 80 eggs.

11194.q: How does the IUCN classify the reticulated python?
11194.e: Because of its large range, the reticulated python is regarded as Least Concern, even though it is heavily hunted for its skin.
11194.m: The reticulated python is regarded as Least Concern despite hunting.

11195.q: When and where was it first fully documented that a reticulated python had swallowed an adult human?
11195.e: In March 2017, a farmer in West Sulawesi was found in the stomach of a reticulated python. It was the first fully confirmed case of its kind.
11195.m: In 2017 on Sulawesi it was first reliably documented that a reticulated python ate a human.

11196.q: On which Caribbean island has the reticulated python become established as an introduced species?
11196.e: Besides the Burmese python in Florida, there is an introduced population of reticulated pythons on Puerto Rico.
11196.m: Reticulated pythons also live on Puerto Rico as an introduced species.

11197.q: Which ability has helped the reticulated python colonise many small islands in South-East Asia?
a: As an egg, it survives months of drying out in salt water
11197.e: Reticulated pythons swim very well and have been seen far out at sea. This is how they reached numerous islands.
11197.m: The reticulated python is an outstanding swimmer.

11198.q: Which python species, named after its native country Burma (Myanmar), became a pest in Florida?
11198.e: The Burmese python is named after its homeland Burma (Myanmar). The ball python and the reticulated python are different species.
11198.m: The Burmese python is named after Burma (Myanmar).

11199.q: Which part of the world does the Burmese python, which now lives in Florida, originally come from?
11199.e: The Burmese python is native to South-East Asia, for example Myanmar and Thailand. It came to Florida through the pet trade.
11199.m: The Burmese python comes from South-East Asia.

11200.q: How does the IUCN classify the Burmese python in its Asian homeland?
11200.e: Since 2012, the Burmese python has been regarded as vulnerable. Wild populations in Asia have fallen sharply through hunting and loss of habitat.
11200.m: In Asia the Burmese python is vulnerable, in Florida it is a pest.

11201.q: Which event contributed to the spread of the Burmese python in Florida in 1992?
a: Hurricane Andrew destroyed a breeding facility
A cargo ship carrying snakes sank off Miami
A zoo released pythons to control rats
A forest fire drove pythons out of a laboratory
11201.e: Hurricane Andrew destroyed a breeding facility and a zoo in 1992. Escaped animals, together with released pets, strengthened the population in the Everglades.
11201.m: Hurricane Andrew helped the pythons in Florida in 1992.

11202.q: According to a 2012 study, by how much did the raccoon population in parts of the Everglades fall since the spread of the Burmese python?
11202.e: The study found declines of over 99 per cent in raccoons and almost 99 per cent in opossums. The pythons are regarded as the main cause.
11202.m: In the Everglades, the raccoons almost completely disappeared.

11203.q: According to estimates, how many Burmese pythons live in Florida?
11203.e: Because the snakes are very well camouflaged, their number is hard to determine. Estimates range from about 30,000 to 300,000 animals.
11203.m: Tens of thousands of Burmese pythons probably live in Florida.

a: An annual competition in which participants catch pythons
A breeding programme to save the Burmese python
A swimming competition with tame pythons
A research prize for snake genetics
11204.e: In this competition in Florida, participants search for introduced pythons for about ten days. There are prizes for the most and the longest animals.
11204.m: In the Florida Python Challenge, introduced pythons are hunted.

11205.q: How do researchers in Florida use so-called “scout pythons”?
a: Males fitted with transmitters lead them to females ready to mate
Tame pythons are used as bait for alligators
Young pythons show where water is polluted
11205.e: Males with radio transmitters seek out females in the mating season. This is how researchers find large females able to breed and remove them.
11205.m: Python males fitted with transmitters reveal where the females are.

11206.q: What did the USA decide in 2012 against the Burmese python and other giant snakes?
a: A ban on import and transport between states
A bounty for every snake in the pet trade
A requirement to vaccinate all pythons
11206.e: In 2012, the Department of the Interior classed four giant snakes as injurious, including the Burmese python and rock pythons. This bans their import and transport between states.
11206.m: Since 2012, Burmese pythons may no longer be imported into the USA.

11207.q: How heavy was the heaviest female Burmese python caught in Florida, which was carrying 122 eggs?
11207.e: The female was about 5.5 m long and weighed around 98 kg. With 122 developing eggs, she also set a record.
11207.m: The heaviest python in Florida weighed around 98 kg.

11208.q: How long was the longest Burmese python caught in Florida (caught in 2023)?
11208.e: In July 2023, a Burmese python 5.79 m long was caught in Big Cypress National Preserve.
11208.m: The longest python in Florida measured almost 5.8 m.

11209.q: What happens to the gut and heart of the Burmese python after a large meal?
a: They stop working altogether for days
11209.e: After eating, the metabolism rises sharply. The gut and heart grow within days, the ventricle by about 40 per cent, and later shrink back again.
11209.m: After a meal, the python's heart grows noticeably.

11210.q: Why is the royal python also called the “ball python”?
a: It rolls itself into a ball when in danger
It lays perfectly round, hard eggs
It prefers to hunt round animals such as hedgehogs
11210.e: When stressed, the royal python coils up tightly and hides its head in the middle. This makes a ball.
11210.m: The royal python rolls into a ball when in danger.

11211.q: What is the maximum length of the royal python, the smallest African python?
11211.e: The royal python reaches at most about 182 cm. Most animals stay considerably smaller.
11211.m: The royal python is the smallest python in Africa.

11212.q: How does the IUCN classify the royal python, and what is the main threat?
a: Near Threatened, mainly through the pet trade
Least Concern, as it is not caught
Extinct in the Wild, because of diseases
11212.e: The royal python is classed as Near Threatened. Mass collecting for the international pet trade puts pressure on populations in West Africa.
11212.m: The pet trade threatens the royal python.

11213.q: How old was the oldest known royal python in captivity?
11213.e: One royal python reached 62 years, 59 of them at the Saint Louis Zoo in the USA. Well-cared-for animals usually live 15 to 30 years.
11213.m: A royal python can live to over 60.

11214.q: Roughly how long does it take for the eggs of a royal python to hatch?
11214.e: The female lays about 3 to 11 eggs and guards them. After around 55 to 60 days, the young hatch.
11214.m: Royal python eggs take just under two months to hatch.

11215.q: Which python is the largest snake in Africa?
a: The Southern African rock python (Python natalensis)
11215.e: The African rock python usually grows to 3 to 3.5 m, with individual animals over 6 m. This makes it Africa's largest snake.
11215.m: The African rock python is the largest snake in Africa.

11216.q: What behaviour, unusual for snakes, does the female African rock python show after hatching?
a: She guards the young for up to about two weeks
She feeds the young with regurgitated prey
She carries the young in her mouth to the water
She immediately eats some of the young
11216.e: The female first guards the clutch for about 90 days and then the young for up to about two weeks. Such care is rare in snakes.
11216.m: Rock python mothers guard their newly hatched young.

11217.q: Who is the species name sebae of the African rock python named after?
a: The Dutch natural history collector Albertus Seba
11217.e: The species name honours Albertus Seba, an apothecary and collector from 18th-century Amsterdam, who depicted animals in a famous illustrated work.
11217.m: The rock python carries the name of Albertus Seba.

11218.q: What colour change does the green tree python (Morelia viridis) go through in the course of its life?
a: The yellow or red young later turn green
The green young turn black with age
It switches daily between green and brown
It turns white first at every shed
11218.e: Young green tree pythons are bright yellow or red. They usually turn green in their first year. The species resembles the South American emerald tree boa, an example of convergent evolution.
11218.m: Green tree pythons are yellow or red when young.

11219.q: What do the Australian pythons of the genus Aspidites, which includes the woma and the black-headed python, lack?
a: The heat-sensing pits on the lips
The teeth in the upper jaw
The anal spurs in the males
11219.e: The genus Aspidites is also called the “pitless pythons”. Unlike most other pythons, they have no labial pits.
11219.m: The woma and the black-headed python have no heat pits.

11220.q: How do boas such as the boa constrictor differ in reproduction from the similar-looking pythons?
a: Boas give birth to live young, pythons lay eggs
Boas lay eggs, pythons give birth to live young
11220.e: Boas and pythons are both constrictors but form separate families. One clear difference: boas bear live young, pythons lay eggs.
11220.m: Boas give birth to live young, pythons lay eggs.

11221.q: Who scientifically described the boa constrictor as Boa constrictor in 1758?
11221.e: Carl Linnaeus described the species in 1758 in the 10th edition of his work “Systema Naturae”. That year is regarded as the starting point of zoological naming.
11221.m: Linnaeus gave the boa constrictor its scientific name in 1758.

11222.q: What does the species name “constrictor” mean in the boa constrictor?
11222.e: “Constrictor” comes from the Latin word for squeezing together. The name describes its way of hunting, in which the boa clasps its prey in coils of its body.
11222.m: The name “constrictor” means strangler, because the boa coils round its prey.

11223.q: Where does the German name “Abgottschlange” (literally “idol snake”) for the boa constrictor come from?
a: From its role in religious cults
11223.e: The snake played a role in the cults of indigenous peoples and of Africans brought to South America by force. An “Abgott” is a worshipped idol.
11223.m: The German name means “idol snake” because it was worshipped in cults.

11224.q: Which language does the word “boa”, found in the name boa constrictor, come from?
11224.e: “Boa” is a Latin word for a large snake, already used by Pliny the Elder. Its actual origin is unknown.

11225.q: What is meant by a folk etymology, as occurs with the word “boa”?
a: A false but plausible explanation of a word's origin
The scientifically proven origin of a word
A word from a Native American language
A word that occurs only in dialect
11225.e: In the Middle Ages, “boa” was linked to the Greek “bous” for ox. Such plausible but false derivations are called folk etymology.
11225.m: A folk etymology is a plausible but false derivation of a word.

11226.q: According to a 2015 study, what does the prey of a boa constrictor mainly die of?
11226.e: Researchers showed that the pressure of the coils stops the blood flow to the heart and brain. The prey dies much faster this way than from simple suffocation.
11226.m: The boa kills its prey by cutting off its blood circulation.

11227.q: How does a constricting boa constrictor know it can release its prey?
a: It feels that the heart is no longer beating
It hears the prey fall silent
11227.e: The boa feels the prey's heartbeat through its body. Only when the heart stops does it loosen its grip.
11227.m: The boa constricts until it feels no more heartbeat.

a: Yes, it has fangs at the front of the jaw
Yes, it has fangs at the back of the jaw
11228.e: The boa constrictor has no venom glands and no fangs. It kills its prey solely by coiling round it.
11228.m: The boa constrictor is non-venomous and kills by constriction.

11229.q: What are the backward-curved teeth of the boa constrictor used for?
a: Holding the prey and pushing it down
11229.e: The many sharp teeth point backwards and stop the prey escaping. When swallowing, they help pull the animal into the throat bit by bit.
11229.m: The boa's teeth hold the prey fast but do not chew.

11230.q: How does the boa constrictor bring its young into the world?
a: It gives birth to live young
It lays eggs in an earth nest
It lays eggs and incubates them
It lays eggs in the water
11230.e: The eggs develop inside the mother's body, and the young are born alive. At birth they are enclosed only in a thin egg membrane.
11230.m: The boa constrictor bears live young.

11231.q: Roughly how many young does a female boa constrictor give birth to per litter?
11231.e: A litter contains about 10 to 65 young, on average around 25. Some of them may be stillborn or unfertilised.
11231.m: A boa gives birth to about 25 young on average.

11232.q: Roughly how long is a newborn boa constrictor?
11232.e: Young boas measure about 38 to 51 cm at birth. They are independent at once and hunt alone.
11232.m: Newborn boas are already around half a metre long.

11233.q: Roughly how long does gestation last in the boa constrictor?
11233.e: Depending on the source and how it is counted, gestation lasts around 100 to 150 days. That is about three to five months.
11233.m: A boa carries its young for around three to five months.

11234.q: At what age does a boa constrictor become sexually mature?
11234.e: Boas become sexually mature at about three to four years. By then they have grown considerably.
11234.m: Boa constrictors reach maturity at three to four years.

11235.q: What was observed in the genetic material of young boa constrictors when a female had offspring without a male?
a: The young had genetic material only from the mother
The young had genetic material from two fathers
The young had no genetic material at all
11235.e: In parthenogenesis, young develop without fertilisation. They therefore carry genetic material only from the mother.
11235.m: In parthenogenesis, the genetic material comes only from the mother.

11236.q: Which special form of reproduction was described in a boa constrictor in 2010?
11236.e: In 2010, researchers reported a female that had young without fertilisation. This is called parthenogenesis.
11236.m: A boa can, exceptionally, reproduce by parthenogenesis.

11237.q: What are the small spurs beside the cloaca of the boa constrictor?
11237.e: The anal spurs are leftovers of a pelvis and hind legs. They show that snakes descend from ancestors with legs.
11237.m: The boa's spurs are remains of its former hind legs.

11238.q: What do male boa constrictors use their anal spurs for?
a: Scratching and holding the female when mating
11238.e: Males have longer spurs than females. During courtship they scratch the female's flanks with them until she lifts her tail.
11238.m: Male boas use their spurs when mating.

11239.q: How does the boa constrictor sense the heat radiation of prey?
a: Through sensory cells in the lips, without pit organs
Through deep pit organs between eye and nostril
Through heat sensors in the tip of the tongue
Through special cells in the eyes
11239.e: Unlike many other boas, Boa constrictor has no lip pits. Heat-sensitive cells in the lips, however, do a similar job.
11239.m: The boa constrictor senses heat with its lips but has no pits.

11240.q: How are the lungs of the boa constrictor formed?
a: The right one is large, the left one much reduced
It has only a single central lung
The left is large, the right is missing
11240.e: The boa constrictor has two lungs. The right one is enlarged and does the work, the left is small and hardly functional.
11240.m: In the boa, the right lung does the main work.

11241.q: How long do fully grown female boa constrictors usually get?
11241.e: Adult females usually measure 2.1 to 3 metres. Lengths over 4 metres are very rare.
11241.m: Female boas usually grow two to three metres long.

11242.q: Which sex is usually larger in the boa constrictor?
a: Both are always the same size
11242.e: In the boa constrictor, females are usually considerably longer and heavier than males. Males are on average around 30 to 40 cm shorter.
11242.m: In the boa, females are larger than males.

11243.q: How heavy are adult female boa constrictors usually?
11243.e: Females usually weigh 10 to 15 kg, large animals up to around 27 kg. Weights over 45 kg are very unusual.
11243.m: An adult female boa usually weighs 10 to 15 kg.

11244.q: Why are length figures for dried snake skins often too large?
a: Skins stretch when they are removed and dried
Head and tail are always measured twice
Skins absorb water and swell as they dry
11244.e: When a snakeskin is removed and dried, it can stretch considerably. The living animal was therefore usually shorter than the skin.
11244.m: Dried snakeskins are longer than the living animal.

11245.q: What later turned out about a supposedly 5.6-metre-long boa constrictor?
a: It was a wrongly identified green anaconda
It was a reticulated python from Asia
It was a forgery made from two skins
It was a boa from Mexico
11245.e: The reported record animal was in fact a green anaconda. True boa constrictors do not reach such lengths.
11245.m: The supposed 5.6-metre record boa was an anaconda.

11246.q: How old do boa constrictors usually get in captivity?
11246.e: In zoos and terrariums, boas usually live 20 to 30 years. Some animals have reached over 40 years.
11246.m: A boa can live 20 to 30 years in captivity.

11247.q: What is the maximum age a boa constrictor can reach in captivity?
11247.e: Boas in zoos and terrariums usually live 20 to 30 years. A boa at Philadelphia Zoo reached over 40 years.
11247.m: A boa can live to over 40.

11248.q: Where is the natural range of Boa constrictor in the narrow sense?
a: In South America, from Colombia to Argentina
In the south of the USA
11248.e: Boa constrictor lives in large parts of South America, from Colombia to Argentina. The boas of Central America and Mexico are now regarded as a separate species.
11248.m: The boa constrictor is at home in South America.

11249.q: Roughly up to what altitude does the boa constrictor occur?
a: Up to about 1000 m above sea level
Only up to about 50 m above sea level
Up to about 3500 m above sea level
Up to about 5000 m above sea level
11249.e: The boa constrictor lives from sea level up to around 1000 m. Above that, it becomes too cool for this heat-loving snake.
11249.m: The boa lives from the lowlands up to about 1000 m.

11250.q: At what time of day is the boa constrictor mainly active?
11250.e: By day, the boa hides in burrows, hollow trees or other shelters. It comes out mainly to bask in the sun and hunts at dusk and at night.
11250.m: The boa constrictor is active at dusk and at night.

11251.q: How does the boa constrictor's way of life change from young animal to adult?
a: Young ones live more in trees, adults more on the ground
Young ones live in water, adults in trees
Young ones live underground, adults in water
Young ones live on the ground, adults only in trees
11251.e: Young boas climb a lot and live mostly in trees. As they grow larger and heavier, they increasingly become ground dwellers.
11251.m: Young boas climb, old boas prefer to stay on the ground.

11252.q: What trick do young boa constrictors use to lure lizards?
a: They move the tip of the tail like a worm
They give off a sweet scent
11252.e: Young boas wiggle the end of their tail, which then looks like a worm. Curious lizards come closer and are seized.
11252.m: Young boas lure lizards with a worm-like tail.

11253.q: Which prey animals does the boa constrictor eat most often?
11253.e: Rodents make up the main part of its diet. Besides these, it eats birds, lizards, frogs and mammals up to the size of small monkeys.
11253.m: The boa constrictor eats mainly rodents.

11254.q: Which well-armed reptile can a boa constrictor, according to observations, even catch?
11254.e: The boa eats almost anything it can overpower, apart from insects and spiders. This even includes small caimans.
11254.m: A boa can even catch small caimans.

11255.q: Roughly how long does it take the boa constrictor to digest a meal?
11255.e: A meal is digested after around 4 to 6 days. After that, the snake can go a long time without food.
11255.m: A boa digests its meal in about four to six days.

11256.q: How long can a boa constrictor go without food after a large meal?
11256.e: As a cold-blooded animal, the boa uses little energy. After a large meal, it often eats nothing for a week to several months.
11256.m: A well-fed boa can fast for months.

11257.q: Which hunting strategies does the boa constrictor use?
a: Lying in ambush and following scent trails
Fishing by diving in the sea
11257.e: The boa either waits hidden for prey to pass by or follows its scent trail. It picks up smells with its tongue.
11257.m: The boa hunts from ambush or follows scent trails.

11258.q: Where does the name “red-tailed boa” for some boa constrictors come from?
a: The saddle patches on the tail are reddish
The tail turns red when in danger
The tip of the tail is bright red and venomous
Only the females have a red tail
11258.e: The dark saddle patches become clearer towards the tail and are often reddish brown. That is why these boas are also called red-tailed boas in the trade.
11258.m: Red-tailed boas have reddish patches on the tail.

11259.q: How can the boa constrictor change its colouring in the short term?
a: It becomes lighter or darker depending on temperature
It changes colour like a chameleon
It takes on a new colour at every shed
It cannot change its colour at all
11259.e: Depending on temperature, the boa can lighten or darken its colouring somewhat. This affects how much heat it absorbs.
11259.m: The boa becomes lighter or darker depending on temperature.

11260.q: How does the IUCN classify the boa constrictor in the Red List?
11260.e: The IUCN lists Boa constrictor as Least Concern. The species is widespread and adaptable.
11260.m: According to the IUCN, the boa constrictor is not threatened.

11261.q: What does the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES), which also covers boas, regulate?
a: International trade in endangered animals and plants
11261.e: CITES regulates which animals and plants may be traded internationally. Most boas are in Appendix II: trade only with a permit.
11261.m: CITES regulates worldwide trade in endangered species.

11262.q: Where does the Argentine boa (Boa constrictor occidentalis) live?
a: In the Amazon basin of Brazil
11262.e: The Argentine boa lives in the south of the range, mainly in the north and centre of Argentina and in the Paraguayan Chaco. Since 2024 it has in part been treated as a species of its own.
11262.m: The Argentine boa lives in the south of South America.

11263.q: What is the boa of Central America called, which is now treated as a separate species from Boa constrictor?
11263.e: The boas of Central America are now classed as Boa imperator. Genetic data show clear differences from the South American animals.
11263.m: The boa of Central America is Boa imperator.

11264.q: Which event separated the ancestors of the boa constrictor and the Central American boa millions of years ago?
a: The uplift of the northern Andes
The formation of the Amazon delta
11264.e: About 3.5 million years ago, the northern Andes were folded upwards. The mountains separated the populations, which developed into separate species.
11264.m: Mountains such as the Andes can separate animal species from one another.

11265.q: Why do separate boa species often develop on remote islands such as Dominica or St Lucia?
a: The animals are isolated and develop separately
There is more oxygen on islands
11265.e: When populations are separated from one another for a long time, they develop differently. This is how separate boa species arose on several Caribbean islands.
11265.m: Isolation on islands promotes the formation of new species.

11266.q: What does it mean when a boa species on St Lucia is “endemic”?
11266.e: Endemic means that a species occurs only in a particular area. Boa orophias lives exclusively on St Lucia.
11266.m: Endemic species occur only in one particular area.

11267.q: Which method is mainly used today to split boas into new species?
a: By the weight of the animals
11267.e: Genetic studies show how closely related populations are. In 2024, for example, the boa of the Atlantic rainforest was described as a species of its own.
11267.m: Genetic comparisons are reorganising the relationships of the boas.

11268.q: Which advanced civilisation of South America revered large snakes such as boas and anacondas in its myths?
11268.e: The Incas linked boas and anacondas with the mythical serpent Amaru. Rulers are said even to have received boas as tribute.
11268.m: Among the Incas, large snakes had a mythical meaning.

11269.q: On which island has the boa constrictor become established as an invasive species through human action?
11269.e: On Aruba, boas were introduced by people and form a stable population there. The species did not originally occur there.
11269.m: On Aruba, the boa is an introduced species.

11270.q: Which snake is regarded as the heaviest in the world?
11270.e: The green anaconda has a very bulky build. The reticulated python can grow longer, but is much slimmer and lighter.
11270.m: The green anaconda is the heaviest snake in the world.

11271.q: Which snake family does the anaconda belong to?
11271.e: The anaconda is a boa and so belongs to the family Boidae. Pythons are similar, but form a family of their own and live in the Old World.
11271.m: The anaconda is a boa and not a python.

11272.q: Which snake can grow longer than the anaconda but has a slimmer build?
11272.e: The reticulated python of South-East Asia is regarded as the longest snake in the world and can grow over 6 m long. The anaconda, however, is much heavier.
11272.m: The reticulated python is the longest snake, the anaconda the heaviest.

11273.q: Who first scientifically described the green anaconda in 1758?
11273.e: Carl Linnaeus described the species in 1758 in the 10th edition of his work “Systema Naturae”. This makes it one of the oldest scientifically named snakes.
11273.m: Linnaeus described the green anaconda as early as 1758.

11274.q: How do female and male green anacondas differ?
a: The females are much larger and heavier
The males are much larger and heavier
Both are exactly the same size
11274.e: Female anacondas can weigh several times as much as males. Large females give birth to more and larger young.
11274.m: In the anaconda, the females are the giants.

11275.q: Which smaller anaconda species lives further south, for example in the Pantanal and in Paraguay?
11275.e: The yellow anaconda is yellowish with black spots and stays much smaller than the green anaconda. It lives in wetlands in the south of South America.
11275.m: The smaller yellow anaconda lives in the south of South America.

11276.q: Which region did the word “anaconda” originally refer to, before it passed to South American snakes?
11276.e: The word appears in 1693 in John Ray for a giant snake from Ceylon, today's Sri Lanka. Only later was it transferred to the South American giant snakes.
11276.m: The name anaconda originally comes from Sri Lanka.

11277.q: What does the Tamil expression, from which “anaconda” is said to derive according to one theory, mean?
11277.e: According to one theory, the word comes from the Tamil “anai-kondra”, which means “elephant killer”. Another theory traces it back to a Sinhalese word.
11277.m: One theory interprets anaconda as “elephant killer”.

11278.q: How long do fully grown female green anacondas usually get?
11278.e: Large females usually reach 4 to 5 m, and only a few grow longer than 6 m. Reports of anacondas 10 m long have never been confirmed.
11278.m: A large anaconda usually measures four to five metres.

11279.q: How heavy can very large female green anacondas get?
11279.e: The heaviest reliably weighed female tipped the scales at almost 100 kg. This makes the anaconda heavier than any other snake.
11279.m: A large anaconda can be as heavy as a grown man.

11280.q: How does the green anaconda move on land compared with in water?
a: On land rather clumsily, in water fast and agile
On land very fast, in water hardly at all
Equally fast on land and in water
It can never leave the water
11280.e: The water supports the anaconda's heavy body. On land, it has to move its whole weight itself and is therefore slower.
11280.m: In water, the heavy anaconda is in its element.

11281.q: What colouring does the green anaconda have?
a: Olive green with dark, round patches
11281.e: The olive-green skin with dark patches camouflages the anaconda in murky water and among plants. This makes it easy for prey to overlook.
11281.m: Its olive-green, spotted skin camouflages the anaconda in water.

11282.q: What can the anaconda do with its nostrils when diving?
a: Close them so no water gets in
Use them to suck in prey
Draw them into the skin to save heat
11282.e: The anaconda can close its nostrils when it dives. This lets it stay under water for a long time without getting water into its airways.
11282.m: The anaconda closes its nostrils when diving.

11283.q: What have researchers occasionally observed in female anacondas after mating?
a: They build a nest of branches
They guard the males for months
11283.e: As the females are much larger, they can overpower a male. The prey provides energy for the long pregnancy, during which they hardly eat.

11284.q: How does an anaconda survive the dry season when its water dries up?
a: It buries itself in the mud and rests
It travels as far as the sea
It lies in the blazing sun
It climbs trees and eats fruit
11284.e: In the Llanos, many waters dry up. Some anacondas then bury themselves in damp mud and stay there until the next rainy season.
11284.m: In the dry season, the anaconda rests in the mud.

11285.q: How dangerous is the green anaconda to humans?
a: Attacks on humans are very rare
It kills thousands of people every year
11285.e: The anaconda is non-venomous and mostly avoids people. Well-documented attacks are extremely rare, despite the many horror stories and films.
11285.m: The anaconda is far less dangerous than its reputation.

11286.q: In which part of South America does the green anaconda live?
11286.e: The green anaconda occurs in the lowlands east of the Andes. It is absent west of the Andes and in the cool south of the continent.
11286.m: The green anaconda lives east of the Andes.

11287.q: In which two large river systems is the green anaconda especially widespread?
a: The Rio Grande and the Colorado
11287.e: The main areas of occurrence are the basins of the Amazon and the Orinoco. There it finds plenty of calm water and prey.
11287.m: The Amazon and the Orinoco are the home of the green anaconda.

11288.q: On which Caribbean island does the green anaconda occur naturally?
11288.e: Trinidad lies just off the coast of Venezuela and is part of the range. The anaconda is absent from the other large Antillean islands.
11288.m: The green anaconda also lives on Trinidad.

11289.q: Which habitat is typical of the green anaconda?
11289.e: The anaconda prefers calm, warm waters such as swamps, oxbow lakes and flooded grasslands. There it can lie in wait and let itself drift.
11289.m: The anaconda loves calm, warm water.

11290.q: Which adaptation allows the anaconda to breathe and watch while almost completely submerged?
a: Its eyes and nostrils sit on top of the head
It has gills behind the head
It breathes through the skin of the tail
Its lung stores air for a day
11290.e: Because the eyes and nostrils sit on top of the head, only a small part sticks out of the water. This keeps the anaconda well camouflaged and still able to breathe.
11290.m: On the anaconda, only the eyes and nose stick out of the water.

11291.q: Which hunting strategy does the green anaconda use?
a: It chases prey over long distances
It filters food out of the water
11291.e: The anaconda waits well hidden in the water until an animal comes close enough. Then it lunges, seizes the prey and coils round it.
11291.m: The anaconda is a patient ambush hunter.

11292.q: How does the anaconda kill larger prey?
a: By a bite to the spinal cord
11292.e: The anaconda is a non-venomous constrictor. It coils round its victim with several loops and squeezes until it dies.
11292.m: The anaconda kills without venom by coiling round its prey.

11293.q: What allows the anaconda to swallow prey that is wider than its own head?
a: Stretchy ligaments between the jaw bones
Teeth that chop up the prey
A second stomach in the neck
11293.e: The jaw bones of the anaconda are joined by elastic ligaments. This lets it open its mouth very wide and swallow large animals whole.
11293.m: Thanks to elastic jaw ligaments, the anaconda swallows huge mouthfuls.

11294.q: Which large prey animals can a fully grown green anaconda overpower?
11294.e: Large anacondas catch capybaras, caimans, deer and even tapirs, among others. All these animals live in South America, like the anaconda.
11294.m: Even caimans and capybaras are on the anaconda's menu.

11295.q: Why does an anaconda shed its skin again and again?
a: Because its outer layer of skin does not grow with it
Because this is how it changes its colour
Because it grows fur in winter
Because this is how it gets rid of venom
11295.e: The outermost horny layer of snake skin does not grow along with the animal. That is why the anaconda sheds it regularly, usually in one piece.
11295.m: Snakes shed because their horny skin does not grow with them.

11296.q: How heavy is the prey of the green anaconda typically in relation to its own body weight?
11296.e: Typical prey animals weigh roughly one seventh to half of the snake. Such large meals are only possible thanks to its stretchy body.
11296.m: The anaconda often eats prey up to half its own weight.

11297.q: How long can a green anaconda go without food after a large meal?
11297.e: As a cold-blooded animal, the anaconda uses little energy. After a large prey, it can therefore fast for weeks to months.
11297.m: After a big catch, the anaconda can fast for a long time.

a: It gives birth to live young
It lays eggs in an earth nest
It lays spawn in the water
It incubates eggs like a python
11298.e: Anacondas are ovoviviparous: the eggs develop inside the mother's body, and the young are born alive. Pythons, on the other hand, lay eggs.
11298.m: The anaconda gives birth to live young.

11299.q: How many young does a female green anaconda usually give birth to?
11299.e: A litter usually contains 20 to 40 young. In exceptional cases, there can be almost 100.
11299.m: An anaconda usually has twenty to forty young at once.

11300.q: Roughly how long does pregnancy last in the green anaconda?
11300.e: The young develop for about half a year inside the mother's body. After the birth, the female has often lost up to half her weight.
11300.m: An anaconda carries its young for about half a year.

11301.q: Roughly how long are newborn green anacondas?
11301.e: Young anacondas are born around 70 to 80 cm long. They are independent at once and hunt small animals.
11301.m: Even at birth, an anaconda is almost a metre long.

11302.q: How much parental care do young anacondas receive after birth?
a: The father guards them for a year
11302.e: Young anacondas are on their own from birth. Many are eaten by predators during this time.
11302.m: Young anacondas have to survive without help from their parents.

11303.q: What is meant by a “breeding ball” in the green anaconda?
a: Several males coil around a female
Two females fight over a territory
A male wraps itself around its clutch
11303.e: In the mating season, up to about a dozen males gather around a single female. The ball can last for two to four weeks.
11303.m: In a breeding ball, many males struggle for one female.

11304.q: What unusual behaviour has been documented in the green anaconda after or during mating?
a: Males carry the young in their mouths
Females lay eggs in other snakes' nests
11304.e: Cannibalism has been observed in the green anaconda; usually a large female eats a smaller male. This gives her energy for the long pregnancy.
11304.m: In anacondas, the male can become the female's meal.

11305.q: Which form of reproduction was demonstrated in 2014 in a green anaconda in an English safari park?
a: Egg laying instead of live birth
11305.e: A female at West Midland Safari Park had young without having had contact with a male. Such parthenogenesis is possible in the species but rare.
11305.m: An anaconda can, in rare cases, have young without a male.

11306.q: Which sex is larger in the green anaconda?
a: The females, and by a clear margin
The males, and by a clear margin
Both are exactly the same size
11306.e: Adult females reach on average about 4.6 m, males only around 3 m. Females are also many times heavier.
11306.m: In the anaconda, the females are the giants.

11307.q: Which record does the green anaconda hold among snakes?
a: It is regarded as the heaviest snake
It is regarded as the fastest snake
It is regarded as the most venomous snake
It is regarded as the smallest snake
11307.e: The green anaconda has a very bulky build and is therefore regarded as the heaviest snake in the world. In length, however, it is surpassed.
11307.m: No snake is as heavy as the green anaconda.

11308.q: Which snake grows longer than the green anaconda but is much slimmer?
11308.e: The South-East Asian reticulated python is regarded as the longest snake in the world. The anaconda is shorter but much heavier.
11308.m: The reticulated python is longer, the anaconda heavier.

11309.q: Roughly how long are the largest reliably measured wild female anacondas?
11309.e: Researchers in Venezuela measured hundreds of wild anacondas. The largest female was about 5.2 m long and weighed around 97 kg; much larger figures are mostly not documented.
11309.m: Documented giant anacondas are a good five metres long.

11310.q: Why are many reports of huge anaconda skins regarded as exaggerated?
a: Skins stretch a lot during tanning
Skins were sewn together from pythons
Skins were only estimated, never seen
11310.e: During tanning, a snakeskin can stretch by more than 50 %. Length figures based on skins are therefore unreliable, and claims over 6 m are hardly documented.
11310.m: A tanned skin makes any anaconda bigger than it was.

11311.q: Which animals are among the natural enemies of adult green anacondas?
11311.e: Adult anacondas are occasionally preyed on by jaguars, black caimans and Orinoco crocodiles. Young animals have many more enemies.
11311.m: Even the anaconda has to beware of the jaguar.

11312.q: How does the IUCN classify the green anaconda?
11312.e: The green anaconda is widespread and, according to the IUCN, is Least Concern. Locally, however, it suffers from habitat loss and persecution.
11312.m: The green anaconda is regarded as not threatened worldwide.

11313.q: The green anaconda is listed in Appendix II of the CITES species protection agreement. What does this mean for international trade?
a: It is allowed but needs a permit
It is free with no controls at all
It is only allowed between zoos
11313.e: Species in Appendix II are not directly threatened with extinction, but their trade is monitored. Anyone wanting to take anacondas across borders needs a CITES permit.
11313.m: Trade in anacondas is only allowed with a CITES permit.

11314.q: What is the situation of the green anaconda in the US state of Florida?
a: Individual animals have been seen, but no established population
It has always been native there
It has completely taken over the Everglades
11314.e: In Florida, individual released or escaped animals have been found, but an established population has not been documented. Since 2021, the species has been listed there as a prohibited species.
11314.m: In Florida, the green anaconda is an unwelcome guest.

11315.q: In which large wetland of South America does the yellow anaconda, the smaller relative of the green anaconda, live?
11315.e: The yellow anaconda lives mainly in the catchment area of the Río Paraguay with the Pantanal. It occurs in Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, Argentina and the north of Uruguay.
11315.m: The yellow anaconda is at home in the Pantanal.

11316.q: How long does an adult yellow anaconda grow on average?
11316.e: As an adult, the yellow anaconda measures around 3.7 m on average. This makes it much smaller and lighter than the green anaconda.
11316.m: The yellow anaconda stays smaller than its green relative.

11317.q: In which landscape of Venezuela did Jesús Rivas study wild green anacondas for years?
11317.e: A large part of what we know about wild anacondas comes from the Llanos, the seasonally flooded grasslands of Venezuela. There Rivas and his team caught and measured hundreds of animals.
11317.m: The Llanos of Venezuela are an open-air laboratory for anaconda research.

11318.q: How old can green anacondas get in captivity?
11318.e: In the wild, anacondas often reach only about 10 years. In zoos, however, they can live over 30 years.
11318.m: In a zoo, an anaconda lives much longer than in the wild.

11319.q: Which extinct giant snake from Colombia, about 13 m long and so far larger, is often compared with the anaconda?
11319.e: Titanoboa lived about 60 million years ago in what is now Colombia and was related to the boas. It was more than twice as long as today's anacondas.
11319.m: The prehistoric snake Titanoboa put every anaconda in the shade.

11320.q: Which snake family does the rattlesnake belong to?
11320.e: Rattlesnakes belong to the viper family. Within this family, they are counted among the pit vipers.

11321.q: Which subfamily of the vipers does the rattlesnake belong to?
11321.e: Rattlesnakes are pit vipers, named after the heat-sensitive pits on the head. This subfamily also includes lancehead vipers and cottonmouths.
11321.m: Rattlesnakes are counted among the pit vipers.

11322.q: Which feature do only rattlesnakes have, and no other snakes?
a: A rattle of horny rings at the end of the tail
11322.e: All pit vipers have pit organs, many snakes have fangs and all snakes have a forked tongue. The tail rattle exists only in rattlesnakes.
11322.m: The rattle is the identifying mark of rattlesnakes.

11323.q: What does the Greek word “krotalon”, from which the rattlesnake's genus name Crotalus comes, mean?
11323.e: In ancient Greek, krotalon was a kind of castanet or clapper. The name alludes to the tail rattle of the rattlesnake.
11323.m: Crotalus is named after a Greek clapper.

11324.q: What does the genus name Sistrurus mean among the rattlesnakes?
11324.e: Sistrurus is the Latinised form of the Greek “seistrouros”, that is “tail-rattler”. The word is related to the sistrum, an ancient Egyptian rattle.

11325.q: Who described the rattlesnake genus Crotalus in 1758?
11325.e: Carl Linnaeus set up the genus Crotalus in 1758 in the 10th edition of his work “Systema Naturae”. This work is regarded as the starting point of zoological naming.
11325.m: Linnaeus named the genus Crotalus in 1758.

11326.q: What important role do rattlesnakes play in their ecosystem?
a: They spread seeds over long distances
11326.e: Rattlesnakes eat many mice, rats and ground squirrels. This limits rodent plagues and also the diseases that rodents transmit.

11327.q: How does a rattlesnake usually react when a person approaches?
a: It rattles as a warning and tries to withdraw
It attacks at once without warning
It chases the person over long distances
11327.e: Rattlesnakes are not aggressors. They warn with the rattle and usually bite only when cornered or trodden on.
11327.m: A rattlesnake would rather warn than bite.

11328.q: What material is the rattle of the rattlesnake made of?
11328.e: The rattle consists of hollow, interlocking segments of keratin. The same material also forms our fingernails and hair.
11328.m: The rattlesnake's rattle is made of keratin.

11329.q: When does the rattlesnake form a new rattle segment?
11329.e: At every shed, a piece of the old skin of the tail tip stays on as a new segment of the rattle. Depending on food and growth, rattlesnakes shed several times a year.
11329.m: Every shed gives the rattlesnake a new rattle segment.

11330.q: Why can't you tell a rattlesnake's age from the number of its rattle segments?
a: It sheds several times a year and segments break off
The rattle only grows in males
The segments are completely renewed every year
The number of segments is innate and fixed
11330.e: Several segments can be added per year, and in the end segments keep breaking off. The number of segments therefore says little about age.
11330.m: Rattle segments are not a reliable measure of age.

11331.q: What does a newborn rattlesnake have at the tip of its tail?
a: A fully working rattle with five segments
Nothing, the rattle only grows after a year
A spine that falls off later
11331.e: Young animals are born with a single button, the “prebutton”. Only when another segment is added through shedding can the rattle make a sound.
11331.m: Young rattlesnakes cannot rattle at first.

11332.q: Roughly how many times per second do the shaker muscles at the tail of the rattlesnake contract when rattling?
11332.e: The specialised shaker muscles contract on average around 50 times per second, and for up to three hours. They are among the fastest known muscles in vertebrates.
11332.m: The rattlesnake's tail muscles shake around 50 times per second.

11333.q: According to a 2021 study, what does a rattlesnake do with its rattling when a person approaches quickly?
a: It suddenly jumps to a much higher frequency
It rattles only in long pauses
It rattles more and more quietly
11333.e: Researchers around Boris Chagnaud (University of Graz) showed that the frequency first rises and then jumps to about 60 to 100 hertz. People therefore judge the snake to be closer than it really is.
11333.m: With a jump in frequency, the rattlesnake fakes closeness.

11334.q: Where are the pit organs of the rattlesnake?
a: On the tip of the tongue
At the end of the tail
11334.e: On each side of the head, there is a pit between eye and nostril. These organs gave the pit vipers their name.
11334.m: The pit organs sit between eye and nostril.

11335.q: What does the rattlesnake sense with its pit organs?
11335.e: A thin membrane in the pit reacts to heat radiation. This lets the snake locate warm-blooded prey even in complete darkness.
11335.m: The rattlesnake sees heat with its pit organs.

11336.q: How sensitive are the pit organs of the rattlesnake?
a: They detect temperature differences of fractions of a degree
They sense only differences of about 10 degrees
They react only to open fire
11336.e: The pit organs detect even tiny differences in heat radiation. This lets the snake spot a mouse even in complete darkness.
11336.m: Rattlesnakes sense the smallest differences in heat.

11337.q: How are the fangs of the rattlesnake built?
a: Short, fixed and at the front of the jaw
Grooved and at the back of the upper jaw
Not present at all, the venom drips from the lip
11337.e: Rattlesnakes have tube-shaped fangs that lie folded against the roof of the mouth at rest. When biting, they swing forward and inject the venom deep into the tissue.
11337.m: The rattlesnake's fangs swing forward when it bites.

11338.q: Which effect is in the foreground in the venom of most North American rattlesnakes?
a: Tissue destruction and disturbed blood clotting
11338.e: The venom of most species acts mainly as a haemotoxin. It destroys tissue, can cause necrosis and disturbs blood clotting.
11338.m: Rattlesnake venom attacks mainly tissue and blood.

11339.q: Why is the Mojave rattlesnake regarded as especially dangerous?
a: Its venom often contains a strong nerve poison
It is the largest of all rattlesnakes
It can spit its venom for metres
11339.e: Many Mojave rattlesnakes have Mojave toxin, a strong nerve poison. Unlike the venom of most other rattlesnakes, it can cause paralysis and breathing problems.
11339.m: The Mojave rattlesnake often has a strong nerve poison.

11340.q: In which habitats does the South American rattlesnake mainly live?
a: In mangroves right by the sea
11340.e: The South American rattlesnake prefers open, dry landscapes such as savannas and scrubland. It largely avoids the damp, dense rainforest.
11340.m: The South American rattlesnake likes it open and dry.

11341.q: What should you do after a rattlesnake bite?
a: Stay calm and get medical help at once
Suck the venom out of the wound
Tie the arm or leg tightly
11341.e: Sucking, tying off and cutting do more harm than good. What matters is to stay calm and get quickly to a hospital, where antivenom is available.
11341.m: After a snakebite: stay calm and go to hospital.

11342.q: How does the rattlesnake bring its young into the world?
a: It gives birth to live young
It lays eggs in the sand
It lays eggs and incubates them
It lays eggs in other snakes' nests
11342.e: Rattlesnakes are ovoviviparous: the eggs develop inside the mother's body. The young hatch there and are born alive.

11343.q: How long can a female rattlesnake store sperm?
a: For months, until fertilisation the next spring
Not at all, fertilisation happens at once
11343.e: Females often mate in late summer or autumn and store the sperm over winter. The egg cells are only fertilised the following spring.
11343.m: Female rattlesnakes keep sperm over the winter.

11344.q: How often do female rattlesnakes in cool areas typically reproduce?
a: Often only every three to four years
Every year in spring and autumn
11344.e: A female needs a long time to build up enough fat reserves for a litter. In timber rattlesnakes in the Adirondacks (New York), there was on average a good four years between two litters.

11345.q: How do females of the Arizona black rattlesnake (Crotalus cerberus) behave after giving birth?
a: They often stay with their young for several weeks
They eat their young at once
They leave the young before the birth
They carry the young around in their mouths
11345.e: In this species, mothers often stay in the hideout with their offspring for weeks. Such brood care was long thought unlikely in snakes.
11345.m: Some rattlesnake mothers stay with their young for weeks.

11346.q: Where do many rattlesnakes in the north of their range spend the winter?
a: In shared winter dens, sometimes with over 1000 animals
11346.e: In rock crevices and earth burrows, called hibernacula, sometimes over 1000 snakes hibernate together. Many return to the same den every year.
11346.m: Rattlesnakes often hibernate in large groups.

11347.q: How does a rattlesnake typically hunt larger prey such as mice?
a: It bites, lets go and then follows the scent trail
It strangles the prey like a boa
It chases the prey over long distances
It lures the prey with the rattle
11347.e: Rattlesnakes lie in wait, bite in a flash and let the prey go straight away. The poisoned animal runs a short way, and the snake follows its trail with its tongue.
11347.m: The rattlesnake bites, lets go and then seeks the prey with its tongue.

11348.q: According to research, how does the rattlesnake find its bitten prey among many scent trails?
a: Substances in its venom change the prey's smell
It marks the prey with droppings
The prey glows in the dark
11348.e: A 2013 study showed that disintegrins in the venom change the smell of the bitten animal. This lets the snake follow exactly this trail.
11348.m: The rattlesnake's venom also marks the prey.

11349.q: Which is the largest rattlesnake species?
11349.e: The eastern diamondback rattlesnake is the largest and heaviest rattlesnake. Lengths of up to about 2.4 metres have been reported.
11349.m: The eastern diamondback is the largest rattlesnake.

11350.q: In whose burrows does the eastern diamondback rattlesnake in Florida often seek shelter?
11350.e: The gopher tortoise digs deep earth tunnels that serve many animals as shelter. The eastern diamondback uses them as a hideout and winter quarters.
11350.m: The diamondback likes to be a lodger of the gopher tortoise.

11351.q: Where does the western diamondback rattlesnake get the nickname “coontail”?
a: From the black and white rings on the tail
11351.e: Just before the rattle, the species usually has four to six black bands with pale gaps. This is reminiscent of the ringed tail of a raccoon (“coon” for short).
11351.m: The western diamondback has a raccoon tail.

11352.q: Which rattlesnake species causes the most snakebites in the USA?
11352.e: The western diamondback is common, large and often lives close to people. Its large venom glands deliver a lot of venom in a bite.
11352.m: Most rattlesnake bites in the USA are due to the western diamondback.

11353.q: Which rattlesnake is among the smallest rattlesnake species?
11353.e: Adult pygmy rattlesnakes usually measure only 40 to 60 centimetres, with a record length of just under 80 centimetres. Their rattle is correspondingly tiny and hardly audible.
11353.m: The pygmy rattlesnake is the smallest rattlesnake.

11354.q: How does the rattlesnake species sidewinder (Crotalus cerastes) move on loose sand?
a: Sideways in loops, leaving J-shaped tracks
Hopping on the tip of its tail
Only straight forward like a caterpillar
11354.e: In sidewinding, only a few parts of the body touch the hot, loose sand. This leaves typical, parallel J-shaped tracks.
11354.m: The sidewinder crawls sideways across the sand.

11355.q: What are the “horns” above the eyes of the sidewinder rattlesnake?
11355.e: The horns are enlarged scales above the eyes. They probably protect the eyes from sand and fold down under pressure.

11356.q: What is unusual about the sidewinder compared with most rattlesnakes of the USA?
a: The females are larger than the males
11356.e: In most US rattlesnakes, the males are larger. In the sidewinder, it is the other way round: the females reach the greater length.
11356.m: In the sidewinder, the females are the larger ones.

11357.q: What special feature does the Santa Catalina rattlesnake from the Gulf of California have?
11357.e: In this island species, the end segment falls off at every shed instead of building up a rattle. On its island without large enemies or hoofed animals, it probably does not need a warning rattle.
11357.m: The Santa Catalina rattlesnake is a rattlesnake without a rattle.

11358.q: What IUCN status does the Santa Catalina rattlesnake have?
11358.e: The species lives only on an island of about 43 square kilometres. Because of this tiny range, the IUCN classes it as Critically Endangered.
11358.m: The Santa Catalina rattlesnake is critically endangered.

11359.q: Roughly how many adult Aruba rattlesnakes are estimated to still live in the wild?
11359.e: The Aruba rattlesnake occurs only on the Caribbean island of Aruba. With fewer than 250 adult animals, it is among the rarest rattlesnakes in the world.
11359.m: The Aruba rattlesnake is one of the rarest rattlesnakes.

11360.q: In which habitat does the massasauga rattlesnake typically live?
a: In high mountains above the tree line
In the sea at coral reefs
11360.e: The massasauga lives in damp meadows, swamps and bogs. Its name from the Ojibwe language alludes to a river mouth.
11360.m: The massasauga is a rattlesnake of the wetlands.

11361.q: What threatens the eastern massasauga rattlesnake most in the USA and Canada?
a: The destruction of wetlands and prairies
11361.e: Many wetlands have been drained and turned into farmland or housing. That is why the eastern massasauga is regarded as threatened in the USA.
11361.m: The loss of wetlands threatens the massasauga.

11362.q: Which rattlesnake is shown on the famous Gadsden flag of 1775?
11362.e: The yellow flag shows a coiled timber rattlesnake with the motto “Don't Tread on Me”. Its thirteen rattle segments stand for the thirteen colonies.
11362.m: On the Gadsden flag, a timber rattlesnake threatens.

11363.q: What did Benjamin Franklin propose in a satirical newspaper item about rattlesnakes in 1751?
a: Sending rattlesnakes to Great Britain in thanks for convicts
Introducing rattlesnakes as a national dish
11363.e: At the time, Great Britain was sending convicts to the colonies. Franklin mockingly proposed sending rattlesnakes to England in return.
11363.m: Franklin wanted to send rattlesnakes to England as a mocking gift.

11364.q: How do California ground squirrels warn a rattlesnake, which can see heat?
a: They heat up their tail and wave it
They sing high notes in ultrasound
11364.e: A 2007 study showed that ground squirrels pump more blood into the tail when waving it. The heat signal works only on rattlesnakes with their pit organs.
11364.m: Ground squirrels warn rattlesnakes with a hot tail.

11365.q: Which snakes eat rattlesnakes and are largely unaffected by their venom?
11365.e: Kingsnakes coil round rattlesnakes and crush them. They are largely resistant to the venom of pit vipers.
11365.m: The kingsnake is a natural enemy of the rattlesnake.

11366.q: Roughly how many people are bitten by venomous snakes each year in the USA, with rattlesnakes the main culprits?
11366.e: In the USA, there are an estimated 7,000 to 8,000 venomous snakebites per year. Thanks to good treatment, only about five people a year die of them.
11366.m: Rattlesnake bites are common in the USA but rarely fatal.

11367.q: Roughly what share of rattlesnake bites involve no venom being delivered?
11367.e: In about a fifth of bites, the snake injects no venom; these are called “dry bites”. Even so, every bite must be checked by a doctor.
11367.m: Not every rattlesnake bite is venomous.

11368.q: On which continents do rattlesnakes occur naturally?
a: Only in North, Central and South America
11368.e: Rattlesnakes live only in the Americas. Their range stretches from the south of Canada to central Argentina.
11368.m: Rattlesnakes exist only in the Americas.

11369.q: In which country is the timber rattlesnake regarded as extinct, although it used to occur there?
11369.e: The timber rattlesnake used to live in the south of Ontario and Québec as well. Today it is regarded as extirpated in Canada.
11369.m: In Canada, the timber rattlesnake has disappeared.

11370.q: Which group of animals do chameleons belong to?
11370.e: Chameleons are lizards and belong to the squamates. They form their own family, Chamaeleonidae.

11371.q: Which family of lizards is regarded as the closest relative of the chameleons?
11371.e: Chameleons and agamas are grouped together as Acrodonta. Among other things, they share the special attachment of the teeth to the jaw bone.
11371.m: The closest relatives of the chameleons are the agamas.

11372.q: How are the teeth attached in the chameleon's jaw?
a: They sit on top of the jaw bone (acrodont)
They are fused to the inner side of the jaw
They are anchored only in the gum
11372.e: Chameleons have acrodont teeth, which have grown directly onto the edge of the jaw. These teeth are hardly ever replaced, as in the agamas.
11372.m: Chameleon teeth sit directly on the jaw bone.

11373.q: What does the Greek origin of the word “chameleon” mean literally?
11373.e: The word comes from the Greek “chamai” meaning “on the ground” and “leon” meaning “lion”. So it means a “lion on the ground”.
11373.m: The name chameleon originally means earth lion.

11374.q: Roughly how many chameleon species have been described today?
11374.e: The family now contains over 200 described species, and new ones keep being added. Many of them were only discovered in recent decades.
11374.m: There are now over 200 chameleon species.

11375.q: What share of all chameleon species lives exclusively on Madagascar?
11375.e: Madagascar is the centre of chameleon diversity: around half of all species occur only there. Most of the other species live on the African mainland.
11375.m: Around half of all chameleon species are endemic to Madagascar.

11376.q: Which chameleon species is native to southern Europe, for example southern Spain and southern Portugal?
11376.e: The common or European chameleon lives around the Mediterranean, in Europe for example in southern Spain, southern Portugal, on Crete and Cyprus. The other species come from Madagascar, Arabia and East Africa.
11376.m: The common chameleon is the chameleon of Europe.

11377.q: On which Mediterranean island was the common chameleon probably introduced by humans in the 19th century?
11377.e: The common chameleon was introduced to Malta around 1880 and then spread across the main island. Jesuit priests are regarded as responsible.
11377.m: Malta owes its chameleons to humans.

11378.q: Roughly how long does it take for the eggs of the common chameleon to hatch?
11378.e: The females bury the eggs in the ground, where they take around 10 to 12 months to hatch. This is a very long development time for lizards.
11378.m: The eggs of the common chameleon take almost a year to hatch.

11379.q: On which island do both the largest and the smallest chameleons in the world live?
11379.e: Oustalet's chameleon grows up to about 68 cm long, Brookesia nana only about 2 cm. Both live on Madagascar.
11379.m: Madagascar is the home of the largest and smallest chameleons.

11380.q: Which chameleon was described in 2021 as one of the smallest reptiles in the world?
11380.e: The male of Brookesia nana from Madagascar measures only about 22 mm in total length. It was described in 2021 by a German-Malagasy research team.
11380.m: Brookesia nana is so small that it fits on a fingertip.

11381.q: What are the horns, which grow on the head of some male chameleons such as Jackson's chameleon, used for?
11381.e: Males use their horns in fights with rivals, for example to push the opponent off the branch. They are also used to impress.
11381.m: Chameleon horns are weapons in rival fights.

11382.q: According to current knowledge, what is the main function of the chameleon's rapid colour change?
a: Communication with others of its kind and temperature regulation
Mainly perfect adaptation to any background
11382.e: Chameleons use colours to show mood, rank and readiness to mate, and to regulate their body heat. The idea that they match any background is a myth.
11382.m: Chameleons change colour mainly to communicate and to control heat.

11383.q: Why does a chameleon often turn darker on a cool morning?
a: Dark skin absorbs more heat from the sun
Dark skin protects against drying out
Dark skin makes it invisible to birds
11383.e: As a cold-blooded animal, the chameleon depends on external warmth. A darker colouring absorbs more solar radiation and heats the body faster.
11383.m: A dark chameleon soaks up the sun's heat faster.

11384.q: According to research, which structures in the skin are crucial for the brilliant colour changes of the panther chameleon?
a: Blood vessels that widen and narrow
11384.e: In special cells, the iridophores, nanocrystals of guanine lie in a lattice. If the animal changes their spacing, light of a different wavelength is reflected.
11384.m: Chameleons change colour with shiftable nanocrystals.

11385.q: At which Swiss university was the crystal mechanism of the chameleon's colour change decoded in 2015?
11385.e: A team around Michel Milinkovitch at the University of Geneva showed in the panther chameleon that photonic crystals enable the colour change. The study appeared in 2015 in “Nature Communications”.
11385.m: Researchers in Geneva revealed the chameleons' colour secret.

11386.q: Which colour do the crystals in the relaxed panther chameleon reflect at first, before yellow pigments turn it green?
11386.e: At rest, the guanine crystals lie close together and reflect blue light. Together with yellow pigment cells above them, the skin looks green.
11386.m: The chameleon's green comes from blue and yellow.

11387.q: What does a male chameleon usually show when it suddenly turns dark and dull in a dispute with a rival?
11387.e: Victorious males glow in strong colours, defeated ones turn dark and pale. This allows fights to end without injuries.
11387.m: A dark, dull male chameleon gives up.

11388.q: What does a pregnant female chameleon of many species signal to males with a striking, dark colouring?
a: That she is no longer ready to mate
That she is looking for a territory
That she wants to share food
11388.e: Many females switch to a high-contrast colouring after fertilisation. Males recognise from this that mating is being refused.
11388.m: Pregnant female chameleons say a clear no with colour.

11389.q: How long can a chameleon's tongue typically shoot out in relation to its body length without the tail?
11389.e: In most species, the tongue reaches 1.5 to 2 times the head-and-body length. Small species even manage more than double.
11389.m: The chameleon's tongue is longer than its whole body without the tail.

11390.q: Which chameleons shoot out their tongue most powerfully in relation to body size?
a: Only the young of large species
11390.e: A 2016 study showed that small chameleons reach the highest accelerations, a tiny species over 260 times the acceleration of gravity.
11390.m: The smaller the chameleon, the more explosive the tongue.

11391.q: How does the chameleon manage its extremely fast tongue shot?
a: With tension stored in elastic collagen sheaths
With air pressure from the lung
With blood pressure that inflates the tongue
With an explosion of saliva gas
11391.e: The accelerator muscle pre-tensions elastic layers of collagen around a process of the hyoid bone. On release, the energy is freed in a flash, as with a catapult.
11391.m: The chameleon's tongue works like a tensioned catapult.

11392.q: On which bony part does the chameleon's tongue slide forward when fired?
a: On a process of the hyoid bone
11392.e: The so-called entoglossal process is part of the hyoid bone and serves as a launch ramp. The tongue muscles slide forward along it.
11392.m: The hyoid bone is the launch ramp of the chameleon's tongue.

11393.q: Why does the chameleon's tongue shot still work well at cool temperatures?
a: Because it relies on elastic energy instead of direct muscle power
Because the tongue has its own heating
Because chameleons live only in the tropics
Because the tongue is insulated with fat
11393.e: Muscles become slow in the cold, elastic tissue hardly at all. Shooting out therefore stays fast, while pulling the tongue back in becomes much slower in the cold.
11393.m: Thanks to elastic energy, the chameleon's tongue shoots out fast even in the cold.

11394.q: What makes the saliva at the tip of the chameleon's tongue so special?
a: It is around 400 times more viscous than human saliva
It is acidic and digests the prey at once
11394.e: In 2016, researchers found that the tongue mucus is extremely sticky. Together with the suction-cup-like tongue tip, even heavy prey can be held fast.
11394.m: The sticky saliva makes the chameleon's tongue a flypaper.

11395.q: What do most chameleons mainly feed on?
11395.e: Chameleons are mainly ambush hunters of insects such as grasshoppers, flies and beetles. Large species occasionally also eat small vertebrates or fruit.
11395.m: Chameleons are first and foremost insect hunters.

11396.q: How do chameleons mostly drink in the wild?
a: They drink from puddles on the ground
They absorb water through the skin of the belly
11396.e: Chameleons often do not recognise standing water as a source of drink. They lick dew and rain drops from leaves, which is why keepers spray plants.
11396.m: Chameleons like drinking drops from leaves best.

11397.q: Which ability of the chameleon's eyes is especially striking among lizards?
a: They move independently of each other
11397.e: Each eye can look in a different direction. This lets the chameleon watch almost its whole surroundings without moving its head.
11397.m: A chameleon can look elsewhere with each eye.

11398.q: Roughly how large is a chameleon's field of view thanks to its rotating eyes?
11398.e: The cone-shaped eyes can be turned far. Together they cover almost a full circle.
11398.m: A chameleon sees almost all the way round.

11399.q: How are the chameleon's eyelids built?
a: They are fused and leave only a small hole for the pupil
They are transparent as in snakes
They open sideways as in birds
11399.e: The lids form a scaly cone around the eye. Only a small opening is left for the pupil, which protects the eye well.
11399.m: The chameleon's eye looks out through a small peephole.

11400.q: How does a chameleon mainly judge the distance to its prey?
a: By how a single eye focuses
By heat sensors on the head
11400.e: Studies showed that chameleons can judge distances precisely even with only one eye. They use how much the eye has to focus.
11400.m: A chameleon measures distances by the focusing of its eye.

11401.q: Which light can chameleons additionally perceive, unlike humans?
11401.e: Besides visible light, chameleons also see UV light. In them, UV light promotes activity, social behaviour and reproduction.

11402.q: What did researchers discover in 2018 in many chameleons under UV light?
a: Bony bumps on the head glow blue
11402.e: In many species, especially of the genus Calumma, bony bumps fluoresce blue through the thin skin. This could serve to recognise others of the same species.
11402.m: Under UV light, the head bones of many chameleons glow blue.

11403.q: How are the five toes on a chameleon's front feet arranged?
a: In two bundles: three on the inside and two on the outside
All five spread side by side
In two bundles: four on the inside and one on the outside
In three bundles of two toes each
11403.e: The toes are fused into two opposing groups and grip like pincers. On the hind feet, the arrangement is reversed: two on the inside, three on the outside.
11403.m: Chameleon feet grip branches like pincers.

11404.q: Why is the tail of many tree-dwelling chameleons called a “fifth leg”?
a: Because it can wrap round branches as a prehensile tail
Because it is used for swimming
Because it stores fat for the winter
11404.e: The prehensile tail serves as an extra hold when climbing. Unlike many lizards, chameleons cannot shed their tail.
11404.m: The prehensile tail gives the chameleon an extra hold.

11405.q: How does a chameleon often move forward along a branch?
11405.e: Many chameleons rock back and forth as they walk. They probably imitate a leaf in the wind this way and attract less attention from enemies.
11405.m: A chameleon sways as it walks like a leaf in the wind.

11406.q: What is the hearing of chameleons like?
a: They have no eardrum but perceive low sounds
They have large outer ear flaps
11406.e: Chameleons lack an external ear opening with an eardrum. Even so, they perceive low frequencies of about 200 to 600 hertz.
11406.m: Chameleons are not deaf, but hear only low sounds.

11407.q: How do most chameleon species reproduce?
a: They lay eggs, which they bury in the ground
They all give birth to live young
They lay eggs in tree hollows and incubate them
11407.e: Most chameleons are egg-laying. The female digs a hole, often 10 to 30 cm deep, and leaves the clutch afterwards.
11407.m: Most chameleons bury their eggs in the ground.

11408.q: Which chameleon, whose male has three horns, gives birth to live young?
11408.e: The East African Jackson's chameleon bears live young and has up to about 30 young. The males have three striking horns on the head.
11408.m: Jackson's chameleon has three horns and gives birth to live young.

11409.q: Why do some chameleons in cool areas give birth to live young instead of laying eggs?
a: Eggs would develop poorly in the cool ground
Because there is no soil there
Because birds would otherwise eat the young
Because the females are larger there
11409.e: In cold ground, eggs develop slowly or not at all. Inside the mother's body, the young are warmer, as in the dwarf chameleons of South Africa.
11409.m: In cool areas, live birth is an advantage for chameleons.

11410.q: What is special about the life cycle of Labord's chameleon (Furcifer labordi) from Madagascar?
a: After hatching it lives only about 4 to 5 months
It lays eggs only every ten years
11410.e: Labord's chameleon has one of the shortest lives of any land vertebrate. It spends the larger part of its life, around 8 to 9 months, in the egg.
11410.m: Labord's chameleon spends more of its life in the egg than outside.

11411.q: How long can the eggs of Parson's chameleon take to hatch?
11411.e: In the large Malagasy Parson's chameleon, development in the egg usually lasts around 400 to 660 days. This is among the longest development times in the egg of any reptile.
11411.m: Parson's chameleons need over a year to develop in the egg.

11412.q: Which region does the veiled chameleon (Chamaeleo calyptratus) originally come from?
11412.e: The veiled chameleon lives in the wild in Yemen and the south-west of Saudi Arabia. A typical feature is the tall casque on the head.
11412.m: The veiled chameleon comes from the Arabian Peninsula.

11413.q: What is the panther chameleon from Madagascar especially known for?
a: Males differ greatly in colour depending on where they come from
It lives in groups of over a hundred animals
It can fly like a flying dragon
It is the only venomous chameleon
11413.e: Male panther chameleons show quite different basic colours depending on the region, such as red, blue or green. These colour varieties are named after the places where they are found.
11413.m: In the panther chameleon, the colour often reveals the origin.

11414.q: Where does the genus Brookesia, the stump-tailed chameleons, mainly live?
a: On the ground in the leaf litter of Madagascar's forests
In the treetops of West Africa
11414.e: The small, mostly brown Brookesia species in Madagascar live mainly on the forest floor and on low plants. Their short tail is hardly suited to gripping.
11414.m: Stump-tailed chameleons live in the leaf litter on the forest floor.

11415.q: How do many stump-tailed chameleons (Brookesia) behave when in danger?
a: They squirt blood from their eyes
They puff up into a ball and roll away
They attack with a loud hiss
11415.e: When threatened, Brookesia often drop to the ground and lie rigid. In the brown leaf litter, they then look like a dry leaf.
11415.m: Stump-tailed chameleons play dead leaf when in danger.

11416.q: According to a 2014 IUCN assessment, what share of chameleon species was regarded as threatened?
11416.e: Of the assessed species with sufficient data, about 36 per cent were threatened. Including Near Threatened species, over half were affected.
11416.m: About one in three chameleons is threatened with extinction.

11417.q: What is the greatest threat to many chameleon species?
11417.e: Many species have very small ranges, especially on Madagascar. If their forest is cleared, a whole species can disappear.
