11417.m: Chameleons lose their home mainly through deforestation.

11418.q: What does it mean for a chameleon species to be in Appendix I of CITES?
a: It may only be shown in zoos
11418.e: Appendix I covers the most threatened species. Commercial international trade in them is practically banned, for example for the stump-tailed chameleon Brookesia perarmata.
11418.m: CITES Appendix I bans trade in highly threatened species.

11419.q: Where does the East African Jackson's chameleon now also live as an introduced species?
11419.e: Jackson's chameleons were brought to Hawaii through the animal trade in the 1970s and released there. Today they live wild on several islands and also eat native insects.
11419.m: In Hawaii, Jackson's chameleons live as an introduced species.

11420.q: Which family does the green iguana (Iguana iguana) belong to?
11420.e: The green iguana is the namesake member of the family Iguanidae. It also includes marine iguanas, spiny-tailed iguanas and desert iguanas.
11420.m: The green iguana belongs to the iguana family.

11421.q: Who scientifically described the green iguana in 1758?
11421.e: Carl Linnaeus described the species in 1758 in the 10th edition of his work “Systema Naturae”. This edition is regarded as the starting point of zoological naming.
11421.m: Linnaeus described the green iguana as early as 1758.

11422.q: Which language does the word “iguana”, the genus name of the green iguana, come from?
a: Taíno, a language of the Caribbean
11422.e: The word goes back to “iwana”, the Taíno name for this animal. The Spaniards took it over and made “iguana” of it.
11422.m: The name iguana comes from the Taíno word “iwana”.

11423.q: What does an adult green iguana mainly feed on?
11423.e: Adult green iguanas are almost pure plant eaters. Bacteria in their gut help to digest the tough leaves.
11423.m: The green iguana is a plant eater.

11424.q: How long does a fully grown green iguana typically get from snout to tail tip?
11424.e: Most adult animals measure 1.2 to 1.7 m in total. Some large males reach about 2 m.
11424.m: An adult green iguana is usually well over a metre long.

11425.q: What share of the total length does the tail make up in the male green iguana?
11425.e: The tail of the green iguana is very long and makes up about two thirds of the total length in males. The body itself usually measures only 30 to 45 cm.
11425.m: Most of a green iguana is its tail.

11426.q: How heavy do very large male green iguanas get?
11426.e: Typical males weigh about 4 kg, females considerably less. Some very large males reach 8 to 10 kg.
11426.m: Large male green iguanas can weigh over 8 kilograms.

11427.q: Which feature do many green iguanas from Central America have on the snout?
a: Small horn-like scales between eyes and nostrils
Long, soft whiskers like a cat
A bright blue shield above the nostrils
11427.e: Many green iguanas from Central America have small horn-like scales between the eyes and nostrils. These animals were formerly classed as a separate subspecies, Iguana iguana rhinolopha.
11427.m: Many Central American green iguanas have little horns on the snout.

11428.q: Which two features most easily tell the green iguana from the Lesser Antillean iguana (Iguana delicatissima)?
a: A round shield under the ear and a ringed tail
A blue tongue and a forked tail tip
No dorsal crest and red eyes
A short tail and a dewlap without spines
11428.e: The green iguana has a large round scale under the ear, the subtympanic shield, and a dark-banded tail. The Lesser Antillean iguana has neither.
11428.m: The ear shield and tail rings give away the green iguana.

11429.q: What can the parietal eye (“third eye”) on the head of the green iguana do?
a: Sense light and dark and movements from above
Produce sharp colour images of the surroundings
Locate the heat radiation of prey
11429.e: The parietal eye has only a simple retina and lens and produces no images. It does, however, register changes of light and shadows, for example from birds of prey.
11429.m: The green iguana's third eye warns of shadows from above.

11430.q: What functions does the dewlap of the green iguana have?
a: Signals in courtship and territory defence, and heat regulation
Storing water for the dry season
Producing loud calls as a resonating sac
11430.e: The dewlap is raised in threat displays and in courtship. It also helps to take in or give off heat.
11430.m: With its dewlap, the green iguana threatens, courts and regulates heat.

11431.q: What does a green iguana raise its large dewlap for?
a: As a signal when threatening, showing off and courting
To store water in it for dry seasons
To glide like a parachute when jumping
To catch insects as with a net
11431.e: The dewlap is stretched by a process of the hyoid bone. The iguana shows it to rivals, enemies and females, and can also take in or give off heat with it.
11431.m: With the dewlap, the green iguana sends signals.

11432.q: What are the femoral pores on the underside of the green iguana's thighs used for?
a: Taking up water from damp ground
11432.e: The femoral pores secrete a waxy substance with scent compounds. With it, the iguana marks its territory and gives chemical signals to others of its kind.
11432.m: The green iguana leaves scent marks through its thigh pores.

11433.q: How can you recognise an adult male green iguana compared with the female?
a: A taller dorsal crest, a larger dewlap and larger femoral pores
A shorter tail and no dorsal crest
A light blue tongue and spines on the belly
A smaller head and no dewlap
11433.e: Males have longer dorsal spines, a larger dewlap, stronger cheeks and better-developed femoral pores. Females are also usually lighter.
11433.m: Male green iguanas have the larger crest.

11434.q: How are the teeth of the green iguana shaped?
a: Leaf-shaped, flat and finely serrated at the edge
Broad, flat grinding plates without edges
11434.e: The teeth are leaf-shaped, broad and serrated and suited to cutting off parts of plants. There is hardly any real chewing; the pieces are usually swallowed whole.
11434.m: With serrated leaf-shaped teeth, the green iguana cuts off plants.

11435.q: What happens to lost teeth in the green iguana?
a: They are replaced continually throughout life
They are replaced only once in life as in humans
They are replaced by horny plates
11435.e: In the green iguana, the teeth sit on the inside of the jaw bone. Teeth that fall out or wear down are replaced again and again throughout life.
11435.m: The green iguana keeps getting new teeth.

11436.q: What does an adult green iguana mainly feed on?
11436.e: The green iguana is largely a plant eater and uses over 100 plant species. It takes animal food at most occasionally.
11436.m: The green iguana is a plant eater.

11437.q: How does the green iguana digest the hard-to-digest plant fibre?
a: By fermentation with microbes in the hindgut
By chewing the cud in a forestomach
By swallowed stones in a muscular stomach
By venom glands that dissolve fibres
11437.e: In the enlarged large intestine, micro-organisms break down cellulose by fermentation. This is called hindgut fermentation, as in the horse.
11437.m: In the green iguana's hindgut, microbes ferment the plant fibres.

11438.q: Why do young green iguanas eat the droppings of adult animals?
a: To take in gut microbes for digesting plants
To meet their need for water
To take on the smell of the group
To scare off enemies with the smell
11438.e: Newly hatched iguanas do not yet have the necessary gut bacteria. They take in these microbes through the droppings of the adults.
11438.m: Young green iguanas get their gut flora from the droppings of adults.

11439.q: What calcium-to-phosphorus ratio does a green iguana need in its food?
11439.e: For healthy bones, the green iguana needs about twice as much calcium as phosphorus. A wrong ratio often leads to bone disease in captivity.
11439.m: A green iguana needs twice as much calcium as phosphorus.

11440.q: How does the green iguana excrete excess salts that it takes in with its plant food?
a: Through a salt gland in the nose, often by “sneezing”
Through sweat glands in the skin
Through the dewlap as a salt crust
Through the femoral pores on the legs
11440.e: Plant food contains a lot of potassium. A gland at the side of the nose gives off excess potassium and sodium salt, which the iguana sneezes out.
11440.m: The green iguana simply sneezes out excess salt.

11441.q: Why do green iguanas in terrariums need a UVB lamp?
a: So that they can make vitamin D3 for their calcium balance
So that their eggs hatch faster
So that the parietal eye does not go blind
So that they see better at night
11441.e: Under UVB light, the skin makes vitamin D3, which is needed to absorb calcium. If it is missing, serious bone disease threatens.
11441.m: Without UVB light, a green iguana gets too little vitamin D.

11442.q: In which temperature range does the green iguana, as a cold-blooded animal, feel most comfortable?
11442.e: As a tropical, cold-blooded reptile, the green iguana needs high ambient temperatures. It basks to raise its body temperature.
11442.m: The green iguana loves tropical warmth.

11443.q: What happens to green iguanas in Florida on especially cold nights with only a few degrees above zero?
a: They become rigid and can fall from the trees
11443.e: Below about 10 °C, green iguanas become sluggish, and at even lower temperatures unable to move. On cold nights they then fall from trees, but often recover as they warm up.
11443.m: In the cold, green iguanas go stiff and fall from trees.

11444.q: Where is the natural range of the green iguana?
a: From southern Mexico to Paraguay and central Brazil, and parts of the Caribbean
In southern Africa and on Madagascar
In South-East Asia and northern Australia
11444.e: The green iguana originally lives in Central and South America and on several Caribbean islands. In the south, its range reaches Paraguay and Bolivia.
11444.m: The green iguana comes from Central and South America.

11445.q: Up to what altitude does the green iguana typically occur in its range?
a: Up to about 1000 metres above sea level
Up to about 100 metres above sea level
Up to about 3500 metres above sea level
Up to about 5000 metres above sea level
11445.e: The green iguana is an animal of the warm lowlands. Altitudes above around 1000 m are usually too cool for it.
11445.m: The green iguana mostly stays below 1000 metres in altitude.

11446.q: Which habitat does the green iguana prefer?
a: Trees in tropical forests, often near water
Rocky high mountains above the tree line
11446.e: The green iguana is active by day in treetops and likes to stay by rivers and lakes. When in danger, it jumps from branches into the water.
11446.m: The green iguana is a tree dweller near water.

11447.q: From what height can a green iguana, according to observations, fall without injury?
11447.e: Green iguanas survive falls from up to about 15 m unharmed. They try to grab branches with the claws of their hind legs.
11447.m: A green iguana survives falls from around 15 metres.

11448.q: How does the green iguana swim?
a: With its legs held back and sideways beats of the tail
With strong paddling strokes of all four legs
Only at the surface, by drifting
11448.e: When swimming, the iguana holds its legs against its body. The powerful tail snakes from side to side and drives it forward.
11448.m: The green iguana swims with its tail.

11449.q: Roughly how long can a green iguana hold its breath?
11449.e: Green iguanas can stay under water for about half an hour. This is how they escape enemies after jumping into the water.
11449.m: A green iguana can dive for around half an hour.

11450.q: What happens when an enemy seizes a green iguana by the tail?
a: The tail can break off and partly grows back
The iguana squirts blood from its eyes
The iguana puffs up into a ball
The tail gives off a paralysing venom
11450.e: Like many lizards, the green iguana can shed part of its tail (autotomy). The regrown tail, however, never quite reaches the original shape.
11450.m: If need be, the green iguana sacrifices a piece of its tail.

11451.q: Besides bites and claws, which weapon does a threatened green iguana use?
a: A venomous spine on the dorsal crest
A foul-smelling secretion from the mouth
Loud roars to scare off enemies
11451.e: The long, powerful tail can be used like a whip. Such blows are painful for attackers.
11451.m: The green iguana strikes with its tail like a whip.

11452.q: What do green iguanas use the typical head-bobbing for?
a: Communication in greeting, courtship and territorial behaviour
Chopping up food in the mouth
11452.e: Head-bobbing in different rhythms is a signal among others of the species. It occurs in greeting, courtship and threat behaviour.
11452.m: Green iguanas talk to each other by bobbing their heads.

11453.q: How does the colouring of male green iguanas often change in the mating season?
a: They turn orange to reddish in places
11453.e: In the mating season, many males turn orange on the head, legs or back. The colour serves as a signal to females and rivals.
11453.m: In the mating season, many male iguanas wear orange.

11454.q: In which season does the green iguana mate in large parts of its range?
a: All year round with no fixed time
11454.e: Mating mostly falls in the dry season. This means the young hatch later, at the start of the rainy season, when a lot of fresh greenery grows.
11454.m: Green iguanas mate in the dry season.

11455.q: Roughly how many eggs does a female green iguana lay per clutch?
11455.e: A clutch usually contains between about 20 and 70 eggs. Large females lay more eggs than small ones.
11455.m: A green iguana lays dozens of eggs at once.

11456.q: Where does a female green iguana lay her eggs?
a: In burrows she digs herself, partly at shared nesting sites
In tree hollows high above the ground
11456.e: The females dig tunnels in sandy or loose soil and lay the eggs there. Often several females use the same nesting site.
11456.m: Green iguanas bury their eggs in the ground.

11457.q: Roughly how long does it take for the eggs of the green iguana to hatch?
11457.e: Depending on temperature, the young hatch after about 8 to 15 weeks. The warmth of the ground incubates the eggs.
11457.m: Iguana eggs take around two to three months to hatch.

11458.q: What brood care does the female green iguana provide after laying her eggs?
a: She guards the nest until hatching
She carries the young on her back
She feeds the young with plant mash
11458.e: After burying the eggs, the female takes no further care of the clutch. The young are independent when they hatch.
11458.m: Young green iguanas have to cope alone from the start.

11459.q: How is sex determined in the green iguana?
a: Genetically, by X and Y chromosomes
By the size of the egg
By a change of sex in old age
11459.e: Unlike in many turtles and crocodilians, sex does not depend on temperature. Green iguanas have an XY system, in which the males carry two different sex chromosomes.
11459.m: In the green iguana, the chromosomes determine sex.

11460.q: How do young green iguanas live in their first year?
a: Often in small groups with siblings
Always completely alone from the first day
In the mother's burrow under her protection
11460.e: In their first year, young animals often stay in groups. This can give them protection from enemies.
11460.m: Young green iguanas like to live in company.

11461.q: How many vertebrate species have been recorded as predators of the green iguana?
11461.e: Studies list at least 108 vertebrate species that eat green iguanas, including birds of prey, snakes and caimans. Eggs and young animals are especially at risk.
11461.m: Over a hundred animal species hunt the green iguana.

11462.q: How old can green iguanas get in human care?
a: Around 10 to 20 years, some even older
11462.e: In captivity, green iguanas usually live 10 to 20 years, some over 20 years. Many pets, however, die much earlier because of wrong care.
11462.m: A well-kept green iguana can live well over ten years.

11463.q: What status does the green iguana have on the IUCN Red List?
11463.e: Because of its huge range, the green iguana is regarded as Least Concern. Locally, however, it has become rare through hunting.
11463.m: The green iguana is regarded as not threatened worldwide.

11464.q: What does the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) regulate for the green iguana?
a: International trade in it needs a permit
Keeping it as a pet is banned worldwide
It may only be shown in zoos
It may no longer be eaten in its homeland
11464.e: The green iguana is in Appendix II of CITES. Trade across borders is allowed, but only with a permit and proof, so that wild populations are not overused.
11464.m: Trade in green iguanas needs a CITES permit.

11465.q: What nickname is the green iguana given in Central and South America because of its meat?
11465.e: The meat and eggs of the green iguana are eaten in many places. Because the meat is reminiscent of chicken, it is called “chicken of the trees”.
11465.m: In Latin America, the green iguana is also called tree chicken.

11466.q: Why is the green iguana regarded as a danger to the Lesser Antillean iguana (Iguana delicatissima)?
a: It interbreeds with it and displaces it through hybridisation
It passes on a venom through its bite
It destroys its nests by digging in the water
11466.e: Introduced green iguanas cross with the critically endangered Lesser Antillean iguana. On some islands, such as Les Saintes, the pure species has disappeared as a result.
11466.m: Crossing with the green iguana threatens the Lesser Antillean iguana.

11467.q: How did green iguanas reach the Caribbean island of Anguilla in 1995, where they had not been before?
a: Through a deliberate release for hunting
Swimming over a land bridge at low tide
11467.e: After Hurricanes Luis and Marilyn, at least 15 iguanas drifted on uprooted trees about 300 km from Guadeloupe to Anguilla. This observed case supports the idea that animals can colonise islands this way.
11467.m: Green iguanas reached Anguilla as castaways on driftwood.

11468.q: In which US state is the green iguana especially widespread and controlled as an introduced species?
11468.e: In the south of Florida, large populations have formed from escaped and released pets. There they damage gardens, banks and infrastructure.
11468.m: In the south of Florida, the green iguana is an introduced pest.

11469.q: What does the name “melanoderma” mean, for the strikingly dark iguanas of the Caribbean islands of Saba and Montserrat?
11469.e: The name is formed from Greek: “melas” means black (as in melanin), “derma” means skin. Whether these island iguanas are a species of their own is disputed.

11470.q: Which reptile family does the Komodo dragon belong to?
11470.e: The Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis) belongs to the monitor family within the squamates. All monitors are grouped in the genus Varanus.
11470.m: The Komodo dragon is a monitor of the genus Varanus.

11471.q: In which country does the Komodo dragon live exclusively in the wild?
11471.e: The Komodo dragon is endemic to Indonesia. In the wild, it occurs only on a few islands in the province of East Nusa Tenggara.
11471.m: Wild Komodo dragons exist only in Indonesia.

11472.q: Which island group do the home islands of the Komodo dragon belong to?
11472.e: Komodo, Rinca and Flores belong to the Lesser Sunda Islands east of Bali. There the climate is dry and savanna-like.
11472.m: The Komodo dragon lives on the Lesser Sunda Islands.

11473.q: On which of these islands does the Komodo dragon occur naturally?
11473.e: Besides Komodo, Komodo dragons live on Rinca, Flores, Gili Motang and Gili Dasami. There are no wild Komodo dragons on Bali, Sumatra or Borneo.
11473.m: Besides Komodo, Rinca is an important home island of the Komodo dragon.

11474.q: What total length do the largest Komodo dragons reach?
11474.e: Large males grow up to about 3 metres long. The largest measured wild animal was 3.04 metres long.
11474.m: A large Komodo dragon is about 3 metres long.

11475.q: Roughly how heavy do large wild male Komodo dragons get, without stomach contents?
11475.e: The heaviest wild animal weighed was around 87 kg. Average adult males weigh about 79 to 91 kg.
11475.m: A large male Komodo dragon weighs about as much as a grown man.

11476.q: Which record does the Komodo dragon hold among living lizards?
a: It is the largest species of lizard
It is the fastest species of lizard
It is the longest-lived species of lizard
It is the most venomous species of lizard
11476.e: The Komodo dragon is the largest and heaviest living lizard in the world. The Papua monitor can grow similarly long, but is much slimmer and lighter.
11476.m: The Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard in the world.

11477.q: What conservation status does the Komodo dragon have on the IUCN Red List?
11477.e: The IUCN classes the Komodo dragon as “Endangered”. Its populations are small, fragmented and limited to a few islands.
11477.m: The Komodo dragon is regarded as endangered.

11478.q: How may tourists watch Komodo dragons in Komodo National Park?
a: Only at night with a torch
11478.e: Komodo dragons can be dangerous to people. Walks in the park are therefore allowed only with trained rangers, who carry long forked sticks for defence.
11478.m: Komodo dragons are watched only with rangers.

11479.q: Which consequence of climate change especially threatens the habitat of the Komodo dragon?
11479.e: Many habitats of the Komodo dragon lie low on the coast. A rising sea level could flood a large part of them in the coming decades.
11479.m: Rising sea levels threaten the coastal habitats of the Komodo dragon.

11480.q: According to the IUCN assessment of 2021, how many adult Komodo dragons still live in the wild?
11480.e: In the 2021 reassessment, fewer than 1400 adult animals were estimated. Together with young animals, there are a few thousand Komodo dragons.
11480.m: There are only fewer than 1400 adult Komodo dragons left in the wild.

11481.q: What else does Komodo National Park protect besides the Komodo dragons?
11481.e: The national park also includes large marine areas with very species-rich coral reefs, manta rays and dolphins. Orangutans live on Borneo and Sumatra, not in the park.
11481.m: Komodo National Park also protects coral reefs.

11482.q: What does it mean that Komodo National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
a: It is regarded as nature of outstanding value to all humanity
It now belongs to UNESCO and no longer to Indonesia
Nobody may enter it any more
It is an official leisure park
11482.e: World Heritage Sites are places that are to be preserved for all humanity. The country remains the owner and commits to protecting them.
11482.m: World Heritage means: valuable for all humanity.

11483.q: When was the Komodo dragon first documented by Western scientists?
11483.e: A Dutch colonial officer heard in 1910 of a “land crocodile” on Komodo and obtained evidence. Only then did the species become known to science.
11483.m: The West only learned of the Komodo dragon in 1910.

11484.q: Why did the giant lizard, the Komodo dragon, remain unknown to Western science until the 20th century?
a: It lives only on a few remote islands
It only came into existence around 1900
It lives almost entirely under water
It digs itself deep underground most of the time
11484.e: Komodo dragons live only on a few small, remote islands of Indonesia. Only in 1910 did reports of them reach European researchers, and the species was described in 1912.
11484.m: The Komodo dragon stayed unknown for a long time because of its remote home.

11485.q: Where were fossils found which suggest that the Komodo dragon probably originally comes from there?
11485.e: In Queensland, fossils of the Komodo dragon about 4 million years old were found. Researchers suspect that the species arose in Australia and later reached the Indonesian islands.
11485.m: The ancestors of the Komodo dragon lived in Australia.

11486.q: Which language does the genus name Varanus of the Komodo dragon come from?
11486.e: Varanus goes back to the Arabic word “waral” for monitor lizard. The species name komodoensis refers to the island of Komodo.
11486.m: The name Varanus has Arabic roots.

11487.q: Which is the largest island on which wild Komodo dragons live?
11487.e: Komodo dragons live on Komodo, Rinca, Gili Motang, Gili Dasami and in the west and north of Flores. Flores is the largest of these islands. There are no wild Komodo dragons on Java, Bali or Sumatra.
11487.m: Flores is the largest home island of the Komodo dragon.

11488.q: Where are the venom glands in the Komodo dragon?
a: In the upper jaw behind the eyes
At the base of the tail
In the skin of the neck
11488.e: Studies showed two venom glands in the lower jaw. Their secretion reaches the bite wound through ducts between the teeth.
11488.m: The Komodo dragon has its venom glands in the lower jaw.

11489.q: What is the main effect of Komodo dragon venom?
a: It inhibits blood clotting and lowers blood pressure
It immediately paralyses the breathing muscles
It dissolves the bones within minutes
11489.e: The venom proteins prevent clotting and make blood pressure fall. The prey thus loses more blood and goes into a state of shock.
11489.m: Komodo dragon venom inhibits blood clotting.

11490.q: How did researchers show in 2009 that the Komodo dragon is venomous?
a: They found venom glands in the jaw and studied their secretion
They found venom in its droppings
They discovered venom spines on its tail
They saw that bitten animals dropped dead at once
11490.e: Using medical images of the head, researchers found venom glands in the lower jaw and analysed their secretion. Bitten animals do not die at once, however, but are weakened by blood loss.
11490.m: Venom glands in the jaw prove that the Komodo dragon is venomous.

11491.q: Which earlier explanation for the deadly effect of a Komodo dragon bite is regarded as outdated today?
a: Dangerous bacteria in the saliva kill the prey
Deep cuts lead to blood loss
A venom affects the prey's blood
The prey exhausts itself after the bite
11491.e: For a long time it was believed that especially dangerous bacteria in the mouth poisoned the prey. Today it is known that the mouth flora is ordinary and that venom and wounds are decisive.
11491.m: Not bacteria, but venom and wounds make the Komodo dragon's bite dangerous.

11492.q: Roughly how many teeth does a Komodo dragon have?
11492.e: A Komodo dragon has about 60 serrated teeth up to 2.5 cm long. They are curved backwards and suited to slashing.
11492.m: The Komodo dragon has about 60 serrated teeth.

11493.q: Roughly how often is a single tooth of the Komodo dragon replaced?
11493.e: The Komodo dragon's teeth are renewed continually, roughly every 40 days. Behind each tooth, several replacement teeth are already ready.
11493.m: The Komodo dragon gets new teeth about every 40 days.

11494.q: What did researchers discover in 2024 on the tooth tips of the Komodo dragon?
a: Tiny venom cannulas made of lime
11494.e: A 2024 study showed that the tips and serrated edges of the teeth are enriched with iron. This orange layer keeps the cutting edges sharp.
11494.m: The tooth tips of the Komodo dragon are reinforced with iron.

11495.q: What are the osteoderms in the skin of an adult Komodo dragon?
a: Small bony plates that protect like chain mail
Glands that give off a scent substance
11495.e: Osteoderms are ossified plates in the scales. They form a kind of chain mail and only develop with increasing age.
11495.m: Osteoderms armour the Komodo dragon's skin like chain mail.

11496.q: What is the forked tongue of the Komodo dragon mainly used for?
a: It brings scent particles to the Jacobson's organ
It helps in chewing the prey
It cools the body as in a dog
It is used for drinking like a straw
11496.e: The Komodo dragon picks up scent particles from the air with its tongue. The Jacobson's organ in the roof of the mouth analyses them, and the forked shape helps to tell the direction.
11496.m: The Komodo dragon smells with its forked tongue.

11497.q: From what distance can a Komodo dragon, depending on the wind, detect carrion?
11497.e: With its tongue and Jacobson's organ, the Komodo dragon perceives the smell of carrion over several kilometres. The exact distance depends strongly on the wind.
11497.m: A Komodo dragon smells carrion over several kilometres.

11498.q: Up to what distance can a Komodo dragon recognise objects by day?
11498.e: The Komodo dragon sees quite well by day and can tell colours apart. At night, however, its eyesight is poor.
11498.m: The Komodo dragon sees up to about 300 m by day.

11499.q: How well does the Komodo dragon hear compared with humans?
a: Worse, it hears only a narrow range of sounds
Much better, it even hears ultrasound
Not at all, it is completely deaf
11499.e: Like other reptiles, the Komodo dragon has only one ear bone. It therefore hears only a narrow range of sounds and relies more on smell and eyes.
11499.m: The Komodo dragon hears worse than humans.

11500.q: How fast can a Komodo dragon sprint over short distances?
11500.e: Over short distances, the Komodo dragon reaches up to about 20 km/h. It avoids longer chases and prefers to hunt from ambush.
11500.m: The Komodo dragon sprints briefly up to about 20 km/h.

11501.q: How does the Komodo dragon behave in water?
a: It swims well and dives to about 4.5 m deep
It avoids water and cannot swim
It lives mostly in the sea like a marine iguana
It can only survive in fresh water
11501.e: Komodo dragons are good swimmers and can even swim between islands. They dive to about 4.5 m deep.
11501.m: The Komodo dragon is a good swimmer.

11502.q: How much of its body weight can a Komodo dragon eat in a single meal?
11502.e: Thanks to a stretchy stomach and movable jaw joints, the Komodo dragon bolts down huge chunks. A meal can make up to about 80 per cent of its body weight.
11502.m: A Komodo dragon can eat up to 80 per cent of its weight at once.

11503.q: How few meals per year can a large Komodo dragon get by on?
11503.e: As a cold-blooded animal, the Komodo dragon has a low energy consumption. Large animals survive on only about 12 large meals a year.
11503.m: A large Komodo dragon needs only about twelve meals a year.

11504.q: What does the Komodo dragon bring back up after digesting a large meal?
a: A pellet of hair, horns and teeth
A layer of its stomach wall
11504.e: Indigestible remains such as hair, horns and teeth stay behind in the stomach. The Komodo dragon retches them up as a slimy pellet.
11504.m: The Komodo dragon retches up the indigestible as a pellet.

11505.q: Which animals are among the most important prey of adult Komodo dragons?
11505.e: Adult Komodo dragons hunt mainly rusa deer (Rusa timorensis) and wild boar. They also eat water buffalo and carrion.
11505.m: Rusa deer and wild boar are the Komodo dragon's main prey.

11506.q: Roughly what share of the diet of adult Komodo dragons is made up of young of their own species?
11506.e: Komodo dragons are cannibals. Young of their own species make up about 10 per cent of the diet of adult animals.
11506.m: Adult Komodo dragons also eat young of their own species.

11507.q: Where do young Komodo dragons mostly spend their first years?
11507.e: Young animals climb trees and are safe there from adults of their own species. Adults are too heavy to climb.
11507.m: Young Komodo dragons live safely in trees.

11508.q: Which behaviour additionally protects young Komodo dragons from cannibalistic adults?
a: They play dead and stink of carrion
11508.e: Young Komodo dragons roll in dung and gut contents. This smell is thought to stop adult animals from eating them.
11508.m: Young Komodo dragons disguise themselves with the smell of dung.

11509.q: Which sex determination system does the Komodo dragon have?
a: ZW system (females are ZW, males ZZ)
11509.e: In the Komodo dragon, females carry two different sex chromosomes (ZW). Males have two identical ones (ZZ), the reverse of mammals.
11509.m: In the Komodo dragon, females are ZW and males ZZ.

11510.q: What sex are Komodo dragons that arise by parthenogenesis?
11510.e: In parthenogenesis, the egg receives doubled chromosomes from the mother, that is ZZ or WW. WW eggs do not develop, ZZ gives males.
11510.m: Komodo dragons from parthenogenesis are always male.

11511.q: In which zoo did parthenogenesis in the Komodo dragon female Flora become known in 2006?
11511.e: The female Flora at Chester Zoo laid eggs although she had never had contact with a male. Genetic tests proved that the young arose without a father.
11511.m: In 2006, Chester Zoo demonstrated parthenogenesis in the Komodo dragon.

11512.q: How many eggs does a female Komodo dragon lay per clutch on average?
11512.e: A clutch contains about 20 eggs on average. Mating takes place between May and August, and the eggs are usually laid in September.
11512.m: A Komodo dragon clutch has about 20 eggs.

11513.q: Roughly how long does it take for Komodo dragon eggs to hatch?
11513.e: The eggs are laid around September and take about 7 to 8 months. The young usually hatch around April.
11513.m: Komodo dragon eggs take about seven to eight months to hatch.

11514.q: Which nests do female Komodo dragons use especially often for laying eggs?
11514.e: In one study, about 60 per cent of the nests were in incubation mounds of the orange-footed scrubfowl. These mounds of soil and leaves keep the eggs warm.
11514.m: Komodo dragons like to lay their eggs in the mounds of megapodes.

11515.q: Roughly how long are newly hatched Komodo dragons?
11515.e: In one study, newly hatched young were on average about 46 cm long and weighed around 100 g. It takes them many years to grow to the size of their parents.
11515.m: A newly hatched Komodo dragon is about 45 cm long.

11516.q: Roughly how old can a Komodo dragon get in the wild?
11516.e: Wild Komodo dragons live about 30 years, though some estimates are higher. They only become sexually mature at around 8 to 11 years.
11516.m: A Komodo dragon can live to about 30.

11517.q: Which animals are the closest living relatives of the Komodo dragon?
11517.e: Genetic studies show that Australian monitors such as the lace monitor are the closest relatives of the Komodo dragon. Both lines have a common ancestor in Australia.
11517.m: The Komodo dragon is closely related to Australian monitors.

11518.q: Where were the oldest fossils of the Komodo dragon found?
11518.e: Fossils from Queensland are about 3.8 million years old. The species probably arose in Australia and later spread to Indonesia.
11518.m: The Komodo dragon originally comes from Australia.

11519.q: How can female Komodo dragons in zoos have offspring without a male?
a: Not at all, it is impossible
11519.e: In zoos, female Komodo dragons without contact with males laid eggs from which young hatched. This parthenogenesis probably helps the species to colonise new islands.
11519.m: Komodo dragons can reproduce by parthenogenesis.

11520.q: Which family does the Nile crocodile belong to?
11520.e: The Nile crocodile belongs to the genus Crocodylus within the family of true crocodiles. Alligators, caimans and gharials form separate families of the order Crocodilia.
11520.m: The Nile crocodile is a true crocodile of the family Crocodylidae.

11521.q: What does the addition “Laurenti, 1768” after the scientific name Crocodylus niloticus indicate?
a: Who described the species and in which year
Where the first animal was found
Since when the species has been protected
How old the oldest known animal became
11521.e: After the species name come the name of the person who scientifically described the species and the year. The Austrian naturalist Laurenti named the Nile crocodile in 1768.
11521.m: After a species name often come the first describer and the year.

11522.q: Roughly what does the Greek word from which the name “crocodile” comes mean?
11522.e: “Crocodile” goes back to the Greek “kroke” (pebble) and “drilos” (worm). The name probably alludes to the rough, bumpy skin.
11522.m: The word crocodile originally means pebble worm.

11523.q: What does the species name “niloticus” mean in the Nile crocodile?
11523.e: “Niloticus” is Latin and means “belonging to the Nile”. The River Nile was the best-known site of the species for Europeans.
11523.m: The name niloticus points to the Nile.

11524.q: Which crocodile species was formerly counted as the Nile crocodile but is now regarded as a species of its own?
11524.e: Genetic studies showed that the West and Central African populations form a species of their own. It is now listed as the West African crocodile (Crocodylus suchus).
11524.m: The West African crocodile is a species of its own and not a Nile crocodile.

11525.q: Which special source did researchers use in 2011 to show that two species were hidden in the “Nile crocodile”?
a: DNA from ancient Egyptian crocodile mummies
X-ray images of living zoo animals
11525.e: A study around Evon Hekkala in 2011 examined, among other things, DNA from crocodile mummies in museums. In this way, the West African crocodile was rediscovered as a species of its own.
11525.m: Mummy DNA helped to discover a hidden crocodile species.

11526.q: Which crocodiles is the Nile crocodile, according to genetic studies, more closely related to than to the West African crocodile?
a: American Crocodylus species such as the American crocodile
11526.e: Family trees based on DNA data place the Nile crocodile beside the American crocodile, the Cuban crocodile and the Orinoco crocodile. It is assumed that the ancestors of these American species came from Africa across the Atlantic.
11526.m: The closest relatives of the Nile crocodile live in the Americas.

11527.q: Which living reptile grows larger than the Nile crocodile?
11527.e: The Nile crocodile is the largest crocodile in Africa and the second-largest living reptile. Only the saltwater crocodile of South Asia and Australia grows larger.
11527.m: Only the saltwater crocodile surpasses the Nile crocodile in size.

11528.q: How long do adult male Nile crocodiles typically get?
11528.e: Adult males usually measure around 3.3 to 5 metres. Exceptional animals can grow over 6 metres long.
11528.m: A fully grown male Nile crocodile is usually longer than a car.

11529.q: How heavy can large male Nile crocodiles get?
11529.e: Large males often weigh several hundred kilograms. Very large, old males can reach around 1000 kg.
11529.m: A large Nile crocodile weighs as much as a small car.

11530.q: How do females and males differ in size in the Nile crocodile?
a: Females are about 30 per cent smaller
Females are about 30 per cent larger
Both sexes are the same size
Females are only half as long
11530.e: The Nile crocodile shows clear sexual dimorphism. Females stay about 30 per cent smaller than males and usually measure 2.2 to 3.8 metres.
11530.m: In the Nile crocodile, males are clearly larger than females.

11531.q: Roughly how many teeth does a Nile crocodile have?
11531.e: The Nile crocodile has 64 to 68 cone-shaped teeth. Worn or lost teeth are replaced throughout life.
11531.m: The Nile crocodile has around 66 teeth, which keep growing back.

11532.q: How old can Nile crocodiles probably get in the wild?
11532.e: A possible lifespan of 70 to 100 years is assumed for Nile crocodiles. They grow slowly and stay able to breed for a long time.
11532.m: A Nile crocodile can live as long as a human.

11533.q: At what age do Nile crocodiles become sexually mature?
11533.e: Nile crocodiles reach sexual maturity at around 12 to 16 years. What matters most is body size, about 3.3 metres in males.
11533.m: Nile crocodiles only become sexually mature as teenagers.

11534.q: How many eggs does a female Nile crocodile typically lay in a clutch?
11534.e: A clutch usually contains around 25 to 80 eggs. Larger females lay more eggs than smaller ones, very large ones even over 90.
11534.m: The larger the female Nile crocodile, the more eggs she lays.

11535.q: Where does a female Nile crocodile lay her eggs?
a: In a pit she digs herself in the sand on the bank
In a floating nest of plants
In a tree hollow above the water
Freely into the water among water plants
11535.e: The female digs a hole in sandy ground a few metres from the water and covers the eggs again. Some crocodile species, on the other hand, build mound nests of plants.
11535.m: The Nile crocodile buries its eggs in the sand of the bank.

11536.q: Roughly how long does the incubation period of the eggs last in the Nile crocodile?
11536.e: The eggs develop for about three months in the warm ground. The duration depends on the temperature in the nest.
11536.m: Nile crocodile eggs take about three months to hatch.

11537.q: What determines in the Nile crocodile whether a male or a female hatches from an egg?
a: The temperature in the nest during development
The sex chromosomes of the mother
The length of the days during incubation
11537.e: The Nile crocodile has temperature-dependent sex determination. The incubation temperature during a certain phase decides the sex of the embryo.
11537.m: In the Nile crocodile, the nest temperature makes the sex.

11538.q: At which incubation temperatures do male young hatch in the Nile crocodile?
a: Only in a narrow middle range
11538.e: Males arise only in a narrow range of about 31.7 to 34.5 °C. If it is cooler or warmer, females hatch.
11538.m: Only a narrow temperature window gives males in the Nile crocodile.

11539.q: How does a Nile crocodile mother notice that her young want to hatch?
a: The young call from inside the egg
11539.e: Shortly before hatching, the young in the egg make croaking sounds. The mother then digs open the nest and helps to free them.
11539.m: Young Nile crocodiles call their mother from inside the egg.

11540.q: How does a female Nile crocodile bring the newly hatched young to the water?
a: She carries them carefully in her mouth
She lets them ride on her tail
She pushes them with her front legs
She leaves the young to themselves
11540.e: The mother gently takes the hatchlings in her mouth and carries them to the water. Despite her powerful jaws, she does not hurt the young.
11540.m: The Nile crocodile mother carries her babies in her mouth.

11541.q: Roughly how long is a newly hatched Nile crocodile?
11541.e: Hatchlings measure about 28 to 30 cm and weigh around 70 grams. They can later grow into animals of over 4 metres.
11541.m: A baby Nile crocodile is about as long as a ruler.

11542.q: What share of hatched Nile crocodiles is estimated to reach adulthood?
11542.e: Eggs and young are eaten by many predators. It is estimated that only about one per cent of hatchlings become adults.
11542.m: Of a hundred baby Nile crocodiles, only about one becomes an adult.

11543.q: Which reptile especially often plunders the nests of the Nile crocodile?
11543.e: Nile monitors deliberately dig up crocodile nests and eat the eggs. That is why the female guards the nest during the incubation period.
11543.m: The Nile monitor is a feared egg thief for the Nile crocodile.

11544.q: How long can a Nile crocodile hold its breath when completely at rest?
11544.e: Normally, a Nile crocodile dives for only a few minutes. If it does not move at all, the oxygen lasts up to around two hours thanks to its slow metabolism.
11544.m: A resting Nile crocodile can stay under water for a very long time.

11545.q: How fast can a Nile crocodile swim at most?
11545.e: With powerful strokes of its sideways-flattened tail, the Nile crocodile briefly reaches 30 to 35 km/h. When swimming fast, the legs lie against the body.
11545.m: The tail makes the Nile crocodile a fast swimmer.

11546.q: What job do the stones found in the stomach of Nile crocodiles probably have?
a: They serve as ballast when diving and help with grinding
They are digested as a source of lime for the eggs
They are rubbish swallowed by accident, of no use
They serve as heat stores at night
11546.e: Nile crocodiles swallow stones, so-called gastroliths. It is suspected that as ballast they stabilise the position in the water and help to grind up food.
11546.m: Nile crocodiles swallow stones as ballast.

11547.q: Which body structure allows the Nile crocodile to live in brackish water too?
a: A layer of fat under the skin
An extra bladder on the gut
11547.e: True crocodiles have salt glands on the tongue, through which they excrete excess salt. Nile crocodiles have therefore also been seen in mangroves and even in the sea off the coast.
11547.m: Salt glands on the tongue help the Nile crocodile in salt water.

11548.q: What is the nictitating membrane of the Nile crocodile used for?
a: It protects the eye under water like swimming goggles
It closes the ears when diving
It cools the brain in the sun
11548.e: The nictitating membrane is a transparent third eyelid. It slides over the eye when diving and protects it without taking away the view completely.
11548.m: The nictitating membrane is the Nile crocodile's built-in swimming goggles.

11549.q: Why can a Nile crocodile hold prey with its mouth open under water without getting water into its airways?
a: A palatal valve closes the throat
It then breathes through its skin
Its lung fills with air reserves from the tail
11549.e: A fold of skin at the base of the tongue and a palatal valve seal the throat. This stops water getting into the windpipe and stomach, while the nostrils stay above water.
11549.m: In the Nile crocodile, a palatal valve keeps water out of the throat.

11550.q: What can the small dark dots on the jaw scales of the Nile crocodile perceive?
a: The finest pressure waves and movements in the water
11550.e: These skin sense organs are extremely sensitive pressure receptors. With them, the Nile crocodile feels even the smallest ripples, for example from an animal drinking.
11550.m: The Nile crocodile senses prey with sensory dots on its skin.

11551.q: How many heart chambers does the Nile crocodile have?
11551.e: Crocodiles are the only living reptiles with a completely four-chambered heart, like birds and mammals. A special connection allows them to partly bypass the lung when diving.
11551.m: Like us, the Nile crocodile has a heart with four chambers.

11552.q: What are the osteoderms in the skin of the Nile crocodile?
a: Bony plates that act like armour
Colour cells that change the camouflage
11552.e: Osteoderms are bony plates in the dermis, especially on the back. They protect the animal and help it to take in heat from the sun.
11552.m: Bony plates in the skin armour the back of the Nile crocodile.

11553.q: Why do Nile crocodiles often lie on the bank with their mouths wide open?
11553.e: Nile crocodiles are cold-blooded and regulate their temperature through behaviour. With the mouth open, moisture evaporates from the lining of the mouth and cools the body.
11553.m: The open mouth is the Nile crocodile's air conditioning.

11554.q: What does a young Nile crocodile mainly eat in its first months?
11554.e: Young animals are still too small for large prey and hunt mainly insects, crustaceans and small frogs. As they grow, fish and later larger vertebrates are added.
11554.m: Small Nile crocodiles eat insects first.

11555.q: Which form of cooperation has been observed in Nile crocodiles?
a: They form a semicircle in the river to herd fish together
They feed other young with regurgitated food
They take turns incubating the eggs
11555.e: Several Nile crocodiles can line up across the river and block migrating fish. Each animal then catches the fish that come near it.
11555.m: Nile crocodiles sometimes hunt as a team.

11556.q: How does a Nile crocodile tear up large prey even though it cannot chew?
a: It spins around its own axis with the prey in its jaws
It cuts it up with its claws
It dissolves it beforehand with stomach acid
It lets it rot for weeks
11556.e: In the so-called death roll, the crocodile bites hard and rolls around its long axis. This tears out pieces, which it swallows whole.
11556.m: With the death roll, the Nile crocodile tears pieces out of its prey.

11557.q: During which natural event in East Africa do Nile crocodiles lie in wait for especially well-known prey animals?
a: At the wildebeest river crossing at the Mara River
At the migratory bird stopover at Lake Victoria
At the salmon spawning run in the Nile
At the elephant migration in the Congo Basin
11557.e: During the great migration, wildebeest and zebras cross the Mara River in Kenya and Tanzania. There, Nile crocodiles wait for weakened or careless animals.
11557.m: At the Mara River, Nile crocodiles wait for the wildebeest.

11558.q: How do adult male Nile crocodiles behave towards others of their kind?
a: They defend stretches of bank as territory
They live in fixed pairs for life
They wander alone with no fixed area
They live only in all-male groups
11558.e: Males claim stretches of bank, patrol their boundaries and drive off intruders. Females, on the other hand, are not territorial.
11558.m: Male Nile crocodiles defend their stretch of bank.

11559.q: How do Nile crocodiles survive a dry season when their water dries up?
a: They retreat into burrows in the ground
Almost all die and are replaced by young in the rainy season
They always migrate to the sea
They fall into hibernation in trees
11559.e: In drying waters, Nile crocodiles dig burrows in the river bank. In them, sometimes several together, they can sit out the hot dry season.
11559.m: In the dry season, the Nile crocodile hides in a burrow.

11560.q: On which large island does a population of the Nile crocodile of its own live?
11560.e: Nile crocodiles also occur in the west and south of Madagascar. They probably colonised the island from Africa across the sea.
11560.m: Nile crocodiles also live on Madagascar.

11561.q: Where does the Nile crocodile in the Nile now occur only?
a: In the south of Egypt from about Aswan and further upriver
Only in the Nile delta on the Mediterranean
Only in Cairo in the zoo
Everywhere in the Nile as far as the Mediterranean
11561.e: In the past, Nile crocodiles lived throughout the Nile as far as the delta. Today the species is extinct in the Egyptian lower course and occurs only south of Aswan.
11561.m: There are no Nile crocodiles left in the lower Nile today.

11562.q: Which ancient Egyptian god was shown with a crocodile head?
11562.e: Sobek was a god of water and fertility and was shown with a crocodile head. Anubis had a jackal head, Horus a falcon head and Thoth an ibis head.
11562.m: Sobek is the crocodile god of the ancient Egyptians.

11563.q: At which Egyptian temple site were mummified Nile crocodiles found and displayed in a museum of their own?
11563.e: The temple of Kom Ombo was dedicated, among others, to the crocodile god Sobek. Since 2012, a crocodile museum there has displayed well-preserved crocodile mummies.
11563.m: In Kom Ombo you can see mummified Nile crocodiles.

11564.q: Which claim about Nile crocodiles comes from the ancient historian Herodotus?
a: A small bird cleans the crocodile's teeth
Crocodiles shed real tears while eating
11564.e: Herodotus reported that a bird picked food remains out of the open crocodile mouth. For regular behaviour of this kind, however, there is hardly any scientific evidence.
11564.m: The story of the tooth-cleaning bird of the Nile crocodile is hardly documented.

11565.q: How does the IUCN classify the Nile crocodile in the Red List?
11565.e: The IUCN lists the Nile crocodile as Least Concern. Until the 1990s it was still regarded as threatened, because it had been heavily hunted.
11565.m: The Nile crocodile is now regarded as not threatened.

11566.q: How is the Nile crocodile classed in the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES)?
a: In Appendix I or Appendix II, depending on the country
In no appendix, trade is free everywhere
Uniformly only in Appendix III everywhere
Only as a pet, not listed as a wild animal
11566.e: In a large part of the range, the strict protection of Appendix I applies. Countries with well-controlled populations, such as South Africa or Zambia, list it in Appendix II, which allows regulated trade in skins.
11566.m: For the Nile crocodile, trade protection depends on the country.

11567.q: Roughly how many Nile crocodiles are estimated to live in the wild?
11567.e: Estimates put wild Nile crocodiles at 250,000 to 500,000. The species is found in around two dozen African countries.
11567.m: There are still hundreds of thousands of wild Nile crocodiles.

11568.q: Roughly how many Nile crocodiles are estimated to have been killed for leather between the 1950s and the 1980s?
11568.e: The leather industry caused a sharp fall in numbers. Today, a large part of the demand is met by crocodile farms.
11568.m: The hunt for crocodile leather cost millions of Nile crocodiles their lives.

11569.q: What is suspected as the cause of the mass die-off of Nile crocodiles from 2008 in the Olifants River in South Africa?
a: Pollution of the river and spoiled fish
A rabies epidemic among the animals
11569.e: In Kruger National Park, many Nile crocodiles died of an inflammation of the fatty tissue. The exact cause is not clear; spoiled fish and heavy pollution of the river are suspected.
11569.m: Polluted rivers can make even Nile crocodiles ill.

11570.q: Which family does the American alligator belong to?
11570.e: The American alligator belongs to the family Alligatoridae within the order Crocodilia. This family also includes the caimans.
11570.m: The American alligator belongs to the family Alligatoridae.

11571.q: How many living species does the genus Alligator, to which the American alligator belongs, contain?
11571.e: The genus Alligator has only two living species: the American alligator and the Chinese alligator. All other alligatorids are caimans.
11571.m: There are only two living species of alligator.

11572.q: Which US state roughly forms the northern limit of the natural range of the American alligator on the Atlantic coast?
11572.e: The range stretches in the east from North Carolina through Florida to Texas in the west. Further north, the winters are too cold for the alligator.
11572.m: In the north, the alligator's range reaches as far as North Carolina.

11573.q: What is the only other living species of alligator besides the American alligator called?
11573.e: The genus Alligator has only two living species: the American alligator and the rare Chinese alligator on the Yangtze. Gharials, saltwater crocodiles and caimans do not belong to the genus Alligator.
11573.m: The Chinese alligator is the only relative of the American alligator in its genus.

11574.q: Where does the word “alligator” in the name of the American alligator come from?
a: From the Spanish “el lagarto”, the lizard
From the Latin “alligare”, to bind fast
From a Seminole word for river
From the English “all gator”, the eater
11574.e: Spanish sailors called the large lizards “el lagarto”, which means “the lizard”. This became “alligator” in English.
11574.m: Alligator comes from the Spanish expression for the lizard.

11575.q: What IUCN status does the American alligator have today?
11575.e: Thanks to strict protection and controlled use, the population has recovered strongly. The IUCN now classes the species as Least Concern.
11575.m: The American alligator is now regarded as not threatened.

11576.q: Why was the American alligator placed under protection as an endangered species in the USA in 1967?
a: Hunting and loss of habitat had greatly reduced its numbers
A disease had killed almost all the animals
It had already died out in Florida
It was declared the national animal of the USA
11576.e: Decades of hunting, mainly for leather, and the destruction of swamps had made the populations shrink sharply. In 1967, the species was therefore listed as endangered.
11576.m: From 1967, the American alligator was protected as an endangered species.

11577.q: What did the US authorities declare about the American alligator in 1987?
a: Its population is regarded as recovered
It is extinct in the wild
It is placed under protection for the first time
11577.e: In 1987, the population was regarded as recovered, and the species was no longer listed as endangered. It is regarded as a success story of species conservation.
11577.m: Since 1987, the American alligator has been regarded as recovered in the USA.

11578.q: Why is the American alligator still formally listed in the USA despite its recovery?
a: Because of its similarity to endangered crocodile species
Because it is declining sharply again
Because it is extinct outside the USA
Because it is regarded as a pest
11578.e: It is listed as “threatened due to similarity of appearance”. This is meant to prevent skins of endangered, similar-looking crocodile species being traded as alligator leather.
11578.m: The similarity to endangered crocodiles keeps the alligator legally protected.

11579.q: What applies under the CITES species protection agreement to international trade in American alligator skins?
a: It is allowed but needs permits
It is free with no control at all
It is only allowed within the USA
11579.e: The American alligator is in CITES Appendix II. International trade in skins is therefore allowed, but subject to permits and controlled.
11579.m: Trade in alligator skins is allowed, but controlled.

11580.q: What led to the sharp decline of the American alligator in the 19th and early 20th century?
11580.e: From the American Civil War on, the alligator was hunted commercially, mainly for its skin. By around 1900, many populations had collapsed.
11580.m: The hunt for leather almost wiped out the American alligator.

11581.q: How is the American alligator mainly used economically in Louisiana today?
a: Eggs are collected and raised on farms
Only the fat is made into lamp oil
11581.e: In Louisiana, hundreds of thousands of eggs are collected from the wild every year and hatched on farms (ranching). Some of the young are later released again.
11581.m: In Louisiana, many farmed alligators come from collected wild eggs.

11582.q: How large do adult male American alligators typically grow at most?
11582.e: Males rarely reach more than about 4.5 metres in length. Females stay considerably smaller, at around 3 metres at most.
11582.m: Large male alligators grow about 4.5 metres long.

11583.q: How long do female American alligators grow at most?
11583.e: Females rarely exceed about 3 metres in length. Sexual dimorphism is clearly marked in this species.
11583.m: At around 3 metres, female alligators stay smaller than the males.

11584.q: What weight can very large male American alligators reach?
11584.e: Very large males can weigh about 450 kilograms. Females are much lighter and often weigh under 100 kilograms.
11584.m: A large male alligator can weigh almost half a tonne.

11585.q: How long was the largest American alligator from Louisiana ever reported but not documented, in 1890?
11585.e: For a male shot in Louisiana in 1890, about 5.84 metres was claimed. As no evidence has survived, this record is regarded as unconfirmed.
11585.m: The 5.8-metre record alligator of 1890 is not documented.

11586.q: Roughly how many teeth does an American alligator have?
11586.e: An American alligator has 74 to 80 teeth. Worn or lost teeth are replaced again and again throughout life.
11586.m: An alligator has around 80 teeth, which keep growing back.

11587.q: How can you most easily recognise an American alligator with its mouth closed, compared with a true crocodile?
a: The lower jaw teeth are largely hidden
It shows a large fourth lower tooth
It has a pointed, V-shaped jaw
11587.e: In the alligator, the upper jaw is wider, so the lower teeth largely disappear when the mouth closes. In true crocodiles, the fourth lower tooth stays visible.
11587.m: In the alligator, the lower teeth disappear when the mouth is closed.

11588.q: What shape is the snout of the American alligator?
11588.e: The snout of the American alligator is broad, flat and rounded at the front, that is U-shaped. This distinguishes it from the more pointed head of many crocodiles.
11588.m: The American alligator has a broad, U-shaped snout.

11589.q: What are the bony plates in the back skin of the American alligator called?
11589.e: In the skin of the back lie bony plates, the osteoderms. They protect the body and help it take in heat when basking.
11589.m: Osteoderms are the bony plates in the alligator's back.

11590.q: Which sense organs on the jaw help the American alligator perceive the smallest water movements?
a: Small pressure receptors in the skin (ISOs)
Lateral line organs as in fish
11590.e: On the jaw sit numerous small skin sense organs (integumentary sense organs). They react very sensitively to pressure and waves in the water.
11590.m: Skin sense organs on the jaw feel the finest ripples in the water.

11591.q: What is the nictitating membrane of the American alligator used for?
a: It protects the eye under water
11591.e: The nictitating membrane is a transparent third eyelid. It protects the eye when diving without taking away the view completely.
11591.m: The transparent nictitating membrane protects the alligator's eye when diving.

11592.q: What allows the American alligator to open its mouth under water without getting water into its airways?
a: A palatal valve in the throat
An air sac in the tail
11592.e: A valve in the back of the palate closes the throat off from the mouth. This lets the alligator bite under water without drowning.
11592.m: Thanks to the palatal valve, the alligator can open its mouth under water.

11593.q: What is special about the airflow in the lung of the American alligator?
a: The air flows through the lung in one direction
It breathes only through the skin
It breathes only every few days
11593.e: Researchers found that the air in the alligator lung flows largely in one direction. This principle was previously known mainly from birds.
11593.m: In the alligator lung, as in birds, the air flows in one direction.

11594.q: How many chambers does the heart of the American alligator have?
11594.e: Like all crocodiles, the alligator has a heart with four chambers, like birds and mammals. A special connection (the foramen of Panizza) allows blood to be diverted when diving.
11594.m: The alligator's heart has four chambers.

11595.q: Which living group of animals is most closely related to the American alligator, if the crocodiles are left out?
11595.e: Crocodiles and birds together form the archosaurs, which also included the dinosaurs. Lizards and snakes are much more distantly related.
11595.m: Birds are the closest living relatives of the crocodiles.

11596.q: How many toes do the hind feet of the American alligator have?
11596.e: The hind feet have four toes with webbing, the front feet five toes. When swimming, though, it is mainly the powerful tail that drives it.
11596.m: The alligator has four webbed toes at the back.

11597.q: Roughly how long can an American alligator stay under water in the cold?
11597.e: In warm weather, an alligator usually dives for 15 to 20 minutes. In the cold, the metabolism falls so far that it can manage several hours without air.
11597.m: In the cold, the alligator can dive for hours.

11598.q: How does the American alligator survive when the water surface freezes over?
a: It sticks its snout through the ice and breathes
It buries itself in leaves in the forest
It migrates to the sea at once
11598.e: In frost, it stays in shallow water and keeps its nostrils above the surface. If the water freezes over, the snout sticks out through the ice so it can keep breathing.
11598.m: In frost, the alligator breathes through a hole in the ice.

11599.q: Why does the American alligator mostly stay in fresh water?
a: The salt glands in its tongue do not work
It cannot dive in salt water
Its skin dissolves in salt water
It finds no sun in the sea
11599.e: True crocodiles excrete excess salt through glands in the tongue. In the alligator, these glands do not work, so it avoids salt water and goes at most into brackish water.
11599.m: Without working salt glands, the alligator stays in fresh water.

11600.q: Where do the American alligator and the American crocodile occur together naturally?
a: In the Mississippi delta of Louisiana
11600.e: South Florida is the only area where alligators and crocodiles live side by side naturally. The American crocodile is more sensitive to cold and lives there mainly on salty coasts.
11600.m: Only in south Florida do alligators and crocodiles live together.

11601.q: In which US state does the largest population of the American alligator live?
11601.e: With its extensive swamps and marshes, Louisiana has the largest alligator population in the USA. Florida also has a great many animals.
11601.m: Louisiana is the state with the most alligators.

11602.q: Which three US states have declared the American alligator their official state reptile?
11602.e: Florida, Louisiana and Mississippi list the alligator as their official state reptile. It is a symbol of the wetlands in the south of the USA.
11602.m: Florida, Louisiana and Mississippi honour the alligator as a state reptile.

11603.q: What are the so-called “gator holes” of the American alligator?
a: Dug-out water holes that hold water in the dry season
Burrows in the forest for laying eggs
Traps that hunters dig for alligators
11603.e: Alligators dig and keep clear water holes that hold water even in dry spells. Fish, birds and other animals find refuge there.
11603.m: In the gator holes, many animals survive the dry season.

11604.q: How does a male American alligator make the water on its back dance during courtship?
a: By squeezing air out of its skin
11604.e: The male bellows with infrasound, which makes the body vibrate. Droplets of water splash up on the back, which is called the “water dance”.
11604.m: In the water dance, infrasound makes the water on the back splash.

11605.q: How does the female American alligator build her nest?
a: As a mound of plants, twigs and mud
As a pit in dry sand on the beach
As a floating raft of feathers
In a tree hollow above the water
11605.e: The female piles plant material, twigs and mud into a mound. As the plants rot, heat is produced which incubates the eggs.
11605.m: The alligator incubates its eggs in a rotting mound of plants.

11606.q: Roughly how many eggs does a female American alligator lay per clutch?
11606.e: A clutch usually contains 20 to 50 hard, white eggs. They are about as large as goose eggs.
11606.m: An alligator clutch usually contains 20 to 50 eggs.

11607.q: Roughly how long does the incubation period last in the American alligator?
11607.e: Depending on temperature, the eggs take about 60 to 80 days, usually around 65 days. The young hatch in late summer.
11607.m: Alligator eggs take a good two months to hatch.

11608.q: What determines in the American alligator whether a male or a female hatches from an egg?
11608.e: Sex is determined by the incubation temperature. At about 33 °C mainly males arise, at cooler temperatures mainly females.
11608.m: In the alligator, the nest temperature decides the sex.

11609.q: How does a female American alligator notice that it is time to open the nest?
a: The young call from inside the egg
11609.e: Shortly before hatching, the young make sounds from inside the egg. The mother then digs open the nest and helps them to hatch.
11609.m: The calls from the egg summon the alligator mother to the nest.

11610.q: How does a female American alligator transport her newly hatched young to the water?
a: In a fold of skin on her belly
Not at all, they walk alone
11610.e: The mother gently takes the young in her mouth and carries them into the water. Despite her enormous bite force, she does not hurt the little ones.
11610.m: The alligator mother carries her young into the water in her mouth.

11611.q: Roughly how long are newly hatched American alligators?
11611.e: Hatchlings measure about 15 to 20 centimetres. They have striking yellow and black banding for camouflage.
11611.m: Young alligators are only about a hand long when they hatch.

11612.q: Roughly how many of 100 hatched American alligators reach adulthood?
11612.e: The young are eaten by fish, herons, raccoons, otters and even larger alligators. In a study in Florida, only about 8 per cent were still alive after two years, and even fewer make it to adulthood.
11612.m: Only a few young alligators become adults.

11613.q: What do young American alligators mainly eat?
a: Insects, snails and other small animals
11613.e: Young alligators hunt insects, spiders, snails, worms and small fish. Only as they grow larger does the prey become bigger.
11613.m: Young alligators eat mainly small invertebrates.

11614.q: What does an American alligator swallow stones for?
a: To grind up food in the stomach
To obtain lime for the eggshells
11614.e: Swallowed stones, so-called gastroliths, lie in the muscular stomach. There they probably help to grind up hard food such as shells and bones.
11614.m: Stomach stones help the alligator to grind up its food.

11615.q: What unusual hunting behaviour has been observed in the American alligator in Louisiana and Florida?
a: It balances twigs on its snout to lure birds looking for nesting material
It herds fish together with air bubbles
It hunts in packs with otters
11615.e: Researchers around Vladimir Dinets reported in 2013 that alligators balance twigs on their snouts during the heron nesting season. Birds looking for nesting material thus come within reach. A later study with alligators in captivity, however, found no convincing evidence for this.
11615.m: With twigs on their snouts, alligators possibly lure birds.

11616.q: What is especially striking about the jaw of the American alligator?
a: The closing muscles are enormously strong, the opening muscles weak
It can dislocate its jaw sideways
The lower jaw is movable as in snakes
It has only muscles for opening
11616.e: The alligator has one of the strongest bite forces measured in any animal. The muscles for opening the mouth, however, are weak, which is why a closed mouth can be held shut with tape.
11616.m: The alligator bites with enormous force but opens its mouth with little strength.

11617.q: What special feature do the rare leucistic American alligators show?
11617.e: Leucistic alligators have white skin but, unlike albinos, usually blue eyes. They are extremely rare in the wild, because they stand out and get sunburn.
11617.m: Leucistic alligators are white and have blue eyes.

11618.q: Which American alligator survived the bombing of Berlin Zoo in the Second World War and died in 2020 at a great age?
11618.e: Saturn came to Berlin in the 1930s, survived the destruction of the zoo and lived in Moscow Zoo from 1946. He died there in 2020 at over 80 years old.
11618.m: Saturn survived the war in Berlin and died in Moscow in 2020.

11619.q: Which zoo did the American alligator Muja, who became known as one of the oldest alligators in captivity, come to in the 1930s?
a: The Bronx Zoo in New York
11619.e: Muja came to Belgrade Zoo in Serbia around 1937 and survived several bombings there. In 2020, the zoo celebrated his 83rd year there; after the death of Saturn, he was regarded as the oldest known alligator in captivity.
11619.m: Muja from Belgrade is among the oldest known alligators in zoos.

11620.q: Which order of amphibians does the axolotl belong to?
11620.e: The axolotl is a salamander and so belongs to the Caudata. Frogs and toads and caecilians are the other two orders of amphibians.
11620.m: The axolotl is a caudate like all salamanders and newts.

11621.q: How does the axolotl mostly get about?
a: It walks along the bottom or swims with its tail
It glides over the water surface
It burrows through the mud like an earthworm
11621.e: The axolotl walks slowly along the bottom of the water on its four short legs. For fast movements, it undulates with its powerful paddle tail.
11621.m: The axolotl walks along the bottom and swims with its tail.

11622.q: What does the scientific species name “mexicanum” of the axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) reveal?
11622.e: The species name mexicanum points to Mexico. In the wild, the axolotl lives only in the lakes near Mexico City.
11622.m: The species name mexicanum reveals the axolotl's home.

11623.q: Which well-known North American group of salamanders is the axolotl closely related to?
11623.e: The axolotl belongs to the genus Ambystoma and is closely related to the tiger salamander. The two have even been crossed experimentally.
11623.m: The axolotl is a close relative of the tiger salamander.

11624.q: What is the phenomenon called in which the axolotl becomes sexually mature as a larva?
11624.e: In neoteny, an animal keeps larval features and still becomes sexually mature. The axolotl normally does not undergo metamorphosis into a land animal.
11624.m: Thanks to neoteny, the axolotl stays a sexually mature larva all its life.

11625.q: Which hormone can artificially trigger metamorphosis into a land salamander in the axolotl?
11625.e: If the thyroid hormone thyroxine is given to the axolotl, it can change into a land-living salamander form. Normally, the necessary hormone release is missing.
11625.m: Thyroxine from the thyroid can make the axolotl transform.

11626.q: Which organs serve the axolotl as its most striking breathing organs?
a: Three pairs of external gill branches
One pair of internal gill arches
Two pairs of skin flaps on the back
11626.e: On each side of the head, the axolotl has three feathery external gill branches. They are its best-known feature.
11626.m: The axolotl has three pairs of feathery gills on its head.

11627.q: Which breathing routes does the axolotl use in addition to the external gills?
11627.e: Besides the gills, the axolotl has simple lungs and can gulp air at the surface. It also takes in oxygen through the skin.
11627.m: The axolotl breathes through gills, skin and simple lungs.

11628.q: What is striking about the eyes of an adult axolotl?
a: They sit together on top of the head
11628.e: The small eyes of the axolotl have no eyelids. Eyelids develop only in animals that undergo metamorphosis.
11628.m: The axolotl cannot blink because it has no eyelids.

11629.q: How long does a fully grown axolotl usually get?
11629.e: Adult axolotls usually measure around 20 to 30 cm, most often about 23 cm. Animals over 30 cm are rare.
11629.m: A fully grown axolotl is about as long as a ruler.

11630.q: In which two lakes near Mexico City does the axolotl occur naturally?
11630.e: The axolotl is endemic to Lake Xochimilco and Lake Chalco in the Valley of Mexico. Lake Chalco has now largely disappeared.
11630.m: The axolotl lives only in the remains of Lakes Xochimilco and Chalco.

11631.q: What does it mean that the axolotl is “endemic” to Mexico?
a: It occurs naturally only there in the world
11631.e: Endemic means that a species occurs naturally only in a narrowly limited area. In the wild, the axolotl lives only in the Valley of Mexico.
11631.m: The axolotl is endemic and lives wild only near Mexico City.

11632.q: What conservation status does the axolotl have on the IUCN Red List?
11632.e: The IUCN classes the axolotl as “Critically Endangered”. This is the highest level before “Extinct in the Wild”.
11632.m: The wild axolotl is regarded as critically endangered by the IUCN.

11633.q: Why is the axolotl common in aquariums worldwide although it has almost disappeared in the wild?
a: It is caught in huge numbers in Mexico every year
It occurs wild in many countries
11633.e: Axolotls breed without trouble in aquariums and laboratories. Almost all animals in the trade come from captive breeding, and trade is also controlled under the CITES agreement.
11633.m: Almost all axolotls in aquariums come from captive breeding.

11634.q: By how much did the number of wild axolotls in Lake Xochimilco fall between 1998 and 2008?
a: Not at all, it stayed the same
11634.e: Surveys found about 6000 animals per square kilometre in 1998 and only about 100 in 2008. That is a collapse of around 98 per cent within ten years.
11634.m: Within ten years, most axolotls disappeared from Lake Xochimilco.

11635.q: Which introduced fish especially harm the wild axolotl?
11635.e: Released tilapia and carp eat axolotl eggs and young and compete for food. They are regarded as one of the main causes of the decline.
11635.m: Introduced tilapia and carp are a serious threat to the axolotl.

11636.q: Which threat to the axolotl's habitat comes directly from the city of millions, Mexico City?
a: Frequent volcanic eruptions in the lake area
Strong tides from the nearby ocean
11636.e: The growth of Mexico City led to lakes being drained, water being extracted and sewage pollution. As a result, the axolotl's habitat shrank massively.
11636.m: The growing city robs the axolotl of water and habitat.

11637.q: What are the “chinampas”, which are important for protecting the axolotl in Xochimilco?
a: Artificial farming islands made of mud and plants
Concrete tanks of a breeding station
11637.e: Chinampas are traditional, seemingly floating farming islands made of mud and plants in the canals. Protected zones for the axolotl are being set up in their canals.
11637.m: The old farming islands of the chinampas offer the axolotl refuge.

11638.q: Which special ability makes the axolotl so interesting for medical research?
a: It can regrow limbs and parts of organs
It can spray venom from its skin
It can regulate its body temperature itself
11638.e: The axolotl regenerates whole legs, the tail, and parts of the spinal cord, heart and even brain. Researchers hope to gain insights for medicine from this.
11638.m: The axolotl can completely regrow lost body parts.

11639.q: How large is the axolotl's genome compared with that of humans?
a: About a thousand times as large
11639.e: The axolotl genome has about 32 billion base pairs, the human one around 3 billion. It is one of the largest animal genomes decoded so far.
11639.m: The axolotl genome is about ten times as large as the human one.

11640.q: What is the axolotl called in Spanish in Mexico?
11640.e: In Mexican Spanish, the axolotl is called “ajolote”. The word is derived from the Nahuatl name āxōlōtl.
11640.m: In Mexico, the axolotl is called ajolote in Spanish.

11641.q: Why was decoding the axolotl genome so difficult for so long?
a: It is huge and contains many repeating sections
Axolotl cells could not be obtained
The genetic material occurs only in the gills
It consists of RNA instead of DNA
11641.e: The axolotl genome is about ten times as large as the human one and full of repeats. Only in 2018 did an international team succeed in decoding it completely.
11641.m: The huge axolotl genome was only decoded in 2018.

11642.q: Which language does the name “axolotl” come from?
11642.e: The name comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. It is often translated as “water monster” or “water dog”.
11642.m: The name axolotl comes from the Aztec language Nahuatl.

11643.q: Which Aztec god is contained in the name of the axolotl?
11643.e: The name combines “atl” (water) with Xolotl, the Aztec god of fire and lightning. According to legend, Xolotl turned himself into an axolotl while fleeing.
11643.m: The Aztec god Xolotl is in the name axolotl.

11644.q: What does the part of the name “atl” in the word axolotl mean?
11644.e: In Nahuatl, “atl” means water. So the axolotl is, in a way, the “Xolotl of the water”.
11644.m: The word atl in the axolotl's name stands for water.
