11645.q: Which famous naturalist sent the first preserved axolotls to Europe at the start of the 19th century?
11645.e: Alexander von Humboldt sent preserved axolotls at the start of the 19th century to the zoologist Georges Cuvier in Paris. Living animals only came to Europe decades later.
11645.m: Alexander von Humboldt brought the first axolotls to Europe.

11646.q: Where were about 34 living axolotls from Mexico shipped to in the 1860s?
a: To the Jardin des Plantes in Paris
11646.e: A group of about 34 animals reached the Jardin des Plantes in Paris. Many of the axolotls later kept in laboratories all over Europe descend from them.
11646.m: Many laboratory axolotls descend from a small group in Paris.

11647.q: What astonishing thing was observed in some axolotls in the Jardin des Plantes in Paris from 1865?
a: They grew over a metre long
They gave birth to live young
11647.e: The zoologist Auguste Duméril noticed animals with reduced gills that went onto land. This showed that the axolotl is really a sexually mature larval form.
11647.m: In Paris it emerged that axolotls can transform.

11648.q: Besides hormone doses, what can trigger transformation into a land salamander in axolotls?
a: Changed environmental conditions such as falling water levels
11648.e: From 1874, the zoologist Marie von Chauvin brought axolotls to transform through changed keeping, such as less water. She is regarded as a pioneer of amphibian research.
11648.m: The environment too can make an axolotl transform.

11649.q: Roughly how many eggs does a female axolotl lay per clutch?
11649.e: Depending on size and condition, a female lays several hundred eggs, sometimes over a thousand, and attaches them singly to water plants. Many are eaten by others of their kind or by fish.
11649.m: A female axolotl lays hundreds of eggs on water plants.

11650.q: How does fertilisation take place in the axolotl?
a: The female picks up the male's sperm packet with her cloaca
The male fertilises the eggs freely in the water
The female gives birth to live young
The eggs develop without any fertilisation
11650.e: The male deposits sperm packets (spermatophores) on the bottom. The female picks them up with her cloaca, so fertilisation takes place inside the body.
11650.m: In the axolotl, fertilisation takes place inside the female's body via a sperm packet.

11651.q: After roughly how long do axolotl larvae hatch from the egg?
11651.e: Depending on the water temperature, the larvae hatch after about two to three weeks, later in cool water. After that, they live briefly on the yolk supply.
11651.m: Axolotl larvae hatch after about two to three weeks.

11652.q: Which misleading English nickname is the axolotl also known by?
11652.e: In English, the axolotl is also called the “Mexican walking fish”. The name is misleading, because the axolotl is not a fish but an amphibian with legs.
11652.m: The axolotl is also called the Mexican walking fish in English, but it is not a fish.

11653.q: At what age do axolotls usually become sexually mature?
a: In their first or second year
11653.e: In captivity, axolotls often become sexually mature before their first birthday. Wild animals need about a year and a half.
11653.m: Axolotls become sexually mature in their first or second year.

a: Usually 10 to 15 years, sometimes up to nearly 20
11654.e: Wild axolotls are estimated to live 10 to 15 years. Well-cared-for animals in captivity can also reach nearly 20 years.
11654.m: With good care, an axolotl can live well over ten years.

11655.q: How does the axolotl eat its prey?
a: It sucks it in by opening its mouth quickly
It chews it with strong molars
It shoots out a sticky tongue
It paralyses it with a venomous bite
11655.e: The axolotl opens its mouth in a flash, creating suction that pulls the prey in. Its small teeth serve only for holding, not for chewing.
11655.m: The axolotl sucks its prey into its mouth in a flash.

11656.q: What does the wild axolotl mainly feed on?
a: Invertebrates, small fish and amphibian larvae
Plankton that it filters from the water
11656.e: The axolotl is a carnivore and eats crustaceans, insect larvae, worms, snails, small fish and larvae of other amphibians. It does not even spurn others of its own kind.
11656.m: The axolotl is a predator that eats almost anything that fits in its mouth.

11657.q: Which sensory system helps the axolotl to perceive water movements made by prey?
11657.e: Like fish and many water-living amphibian larvae, the axolotl has a lateral line system. With it, it senses the finest currents and movements in the water.
11657.m: With the lateral line, the axolotl senses movements in the water.

11658.q: What water temperature does Lake Xochimilco, the home of the axolotl, rarely exceed?
11658.e: The water in the highland Lake Xochimilco rarely gets warmer than about 20 °C. In winter it can cool to 6 to 7 °C.
11658.m: The axolotl comes from cool highland water.

11659.q: What water temperature is considered ideal for keeping axolotls?
11659.e: Axolotls feel comfortable at a cool 16 to 18 °C. Temperatures above about 24 °C cause stress and can be fatal.
11659.m: An axolotl needs cool water and cannot tolerate warmth.

11660.q: At roughly what altitude does the Valley of Mexico, the home of the axolotl, lie?
11660.e: The Valley of Mexico, with Mexico City and Xochimilco, lies at around 2,200 to 2,300 m above sea level. That explains the cool water in the axolotl's habitat.
11660.m: The axolotl lives in a high valley at over 2,000 metres.

11661.q: What is the pink captive-bred form of the axolotl with dark eyes called?
11661.e: Leucistic axolotls are pale pink to white but have dark eyes. Albinos, by contrast, have light, reddish eyes.
11661.m: A pink axolotl with dark eyes is leucistic.

11662.q: What colouring do wild axolotls normally have?
a: Dark greyish brown to olive green, mottled
11662.e: Wild animals are marbled dark greyish brown to olive and lighter on the belly. The pink animals in aquariums are captive-bred forms.
11662.m: Wild axolotls are inconspicuously dark, not pink.

11663.q: How did the albino gene find its way into axolotl breeding?
a: Through crossing with an albino tiger salamander
Through wild catches from a cave
11663.e: In the 1960s, the geneticist Rufus R. Humphrey crossed an albino female tiger salamander with axolotls. That is how the albino gene entered axolotl breeding.
11663.m: The albino gene came to the axolotl through a cross with the tiger salamander.

11664.q: On which Mexican banknote has an axolotl been shown since 2021?
11664.e: In 2021, the Banco de México issued a new 50 peso note with an axolotl. It became very popular in Mexico.
11664.m: In Mexico, the 50 peso note shows an axolotl.

11665.q: Which Pokémon, regarded as inspired by the axolotl, first appeared in 1999 in Pokémon Gold and Silver?
11665.e: Wooper appeared in 1999 in Pokémon Gold and Silver and is modelled on an axolotl. Mudkip is also associated with the axolotl.
11665.m: The Pokémon Wooper is modelled on an axolotl.

11666.q: What do researchers especially hope to gain from studying the axolotl genome?
a: To understand which genes control the regrowth of body parts
To breed axolotls as livestock for meat
To find a remedy for short-sightedness
To make axolotls insensitive to warmth
11666.e: The axolotl can regrow legs and parts of the heart and brain. Researchers look in the genome for the genes that control this and hope for insights for medicine.
11666.m: The axolotl genome is meant to reveal the secret of regeneration.

11667.q: Which Latin American writer wrote the famous short story “Axolotl”?
11667.e: The Argentinian Julio Cortázar published the story “Axolotl” in 1956 in the volume “Final del juego”. In it, a man who watches axolotls in the Jardin des Plantes in Paris turns into an axolotl himself.
11667.m: Julio Cortázar made the axolotl the hero of a famous story.

11668.q: What did a four-month search for wild axolotls in Lake Xochimilco, whose result became known in early 2014, find?
a: At first not a single animal was found
Over a million animals were counted
A new axolotl species was discovered
11668.e: In a search lasting four months, researchers at first found no free-living axolotls. Shortly afterwards, a few individual animals were spotted in canals again.
11668.m: Wild axolotls are so rare that researchers can hardly find them any more.

11669.q: In which year was it announced that the axolotl would come to the video game Minecraft?
11669.e: Axolotls were announced in 2020 and came into the game in 2021 with an update. That made the animal even better known among young people worldwide.
11669.m: Since an update, axolotls also swim through the world of Minecraft.

11670.q: By what second name are poison dart frogs also known?
11670.e: Poison dart frogs are also called poison frogs and form the family Dendrobatidae. Glass frogs, clawed frogs and paddle frogs are other groups of frogs.
11670.m: Poison dart frogs are also called poison frogs.

11671.q: In which region of the world do poison dart frogs live naturally?
11671.e: Poison dart frogs live in the rainforests from Nicaragua to Bolivia and Brazil. The similarly colourful mantellas of Madagascar are not closely related to them.
11671.m: Poison dart frogs are at home in the rainforests of Central and South America.

11672.q: Roughly how many species does the family of poison dart frogs (Dendrobatidae) include today?
11672.e: The family now includes around 200 species in 16 genera. AmphibiaWeb currently lists a little over 210 species, as new ones keep being described.
11672.m: The family of poison dart frogs has around 200 species.

11673.q: What does the genus name Dendrobates, after which the poison dart frogs are named, mean?
11673.e: The name comes from Greek: “dendron” means tree and “bates” walker or climber. That is also why they are called tree climbers in some languages.

11674.q: What does the species name “terribilis” in the golden poison frog mean?
a: It refers to the deadly skin poison
It refers to the loud call
It refers to the large eyes
It refers to the fast tongue
11674.e: “Terribilis” is Latin for terrible and refers to the extremely strong toxicity of the skin secretions.
11674.m: The golden poison frog gets its name from its deadly poison.

11675.q: Where does the name “poison dart frog” come from?
a: Indigenous hunters smeared blowgun darts with the skin poison
The frogs shoot poison like darts
The poison acts as fast as an arrow
11675.e: Indigenous peoples in Colombia used the skin secretion of some Phyllobates species to poison the tips of blowgun darts for hunting.
11675.m: The name poison dart frog comes from poisoned blowgun darts.

11676.q: Were all species of poison dart frogs used for poisoned blowgun darts?
a: No, only a few especially poisonous species
Yes, all species of the family
No, only their spawn was used
11676.e: Only three species of the genus Phyllobates are documented as dart poison, such as the golden poison frog. The name poison dart frog is therefore actually misleading for the whole family.
11676.m: Only a few poison dart frog species supplied real dart poison.

11677.q: In which country does the golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) live exclusively?
11677.e: The species is endemic to the Pacific coast of Colombia, in the Chocó rainforest of the departments of Cauca and Valle del Cauca.
11677.m: The golden poison frog lives only in Colombia.

11678.q: Roughly how large is the range of the golden poison frog?
11678.e: The species occurs only in a small area of less than 5,000 square kilometres in the Chocó. The small range is a main reason for its endangered status.
11678.m: The golden poison frog has a tiny range.

11679.q: At what altitude does the golden poison frog live?
a: From sea level to about 200 m
11679.e: Phyllobates terribilis inhabits humid lowland rainforests on the Pacific coast from sea level to around 200 m altitude.
11679.m: The golden poison frog is a lowland dweller.

11680.q: About how large does an adult golden poison frog grow?
11680.e: Adult animals mostly reach about 4.5 to 5.5 cm, large females up to around 6 cm. Females are usually somewhat larger than males.
11680.m: The golden poison frog is only about five centimetres long.

11681.q: Which poison makes the golden poison frog so dangerous?
11681.e: The skin of Phyllobates contains batrachotoxin, one of the strongest known nerve poisons. Tetrodotoxin is known from the pufferfish, bufotoxin from toads.
11681.m: Phyllobates frogs carry batrachotoxin in their skin.

11682.q: What does the word part “batracho” in the poison name batrachotoxin mean?
11682.e: Greek “batrachos” means frog. So batrachotoxin literally means frog poison.

11683.q: How does batrachotoxin, the poison of the golden poison frog, act in nerve cells?
a: It keeps sodium channels permanently open
11683.e: Batrachotoxin opens sodium channels in nerve and muscle cells practically irreversibly. Muscles stay cramped, and paralysis, heart fibrillation and heart failure threaten.
11683.m: Batrachotoxin keeps sodium channels open and thus disables nerves and muscles.

11684.q: How much poison does a wild golden poison frog carry on average?
11684.e: A wild Phyllobates terribilis contains on average around one milligram of poison. Even this tiny amount is extremely dangerous.
11684.m: A golden poison frog carries around one milligram of poison.

11685.q: How many people could the poison of a single golden poison frog kill, according to estimates?
11685.e: The roughly one milligram of batrachotoxin in a wild animal is estimated to be enough to kill 10 to 20 people.
11685.m: A single golden poison frog could kill over ten people.

11686.q: How long do darts stay poisonous when they have been smeared with the secretion of the golden poison frog?
11686.e: According to reports, the poisoned dart tips stay deadly for two years or even longer.
11686.m: Darts smeared with frog poison stay effective for years.

11687.q: Which Indigenous people in Colombia are known for preparing blowgun darts with the poison of the golden poison frog?
11687.e: The Emberá (formerly often called Chocó Indians) live in the Chocó region on the Pacific coast of Colombia and used the frog poison for blowgun hunting.
11687.m: The Emberá poisoned their darts with frog poison.

11688.q: How does a poison dart frog get its poison?
a: It takes up alkaloids through poisonous prey
It makes the poison itself from plant sap
It inherits the finished poison from its parents
It absorbs the poison from the water
11688.e: Poison dart frogs do not make their alkaloids themselves but take them in with prey such as ants, mites and beetles and store them in skin glands (sequestration).
11688.m: Poison dart frogs eat their way to their poison.

11689.q: What happens to a golden poison frog that grows up in captivity on ordinary feeder insects?
a: It becomes even more poisonous than wild animals
It dies from the missing poison
11689.e: Without the poisonous prey from the rainforest, the raw materials for the poison are missing. Captive-bred animals are therefore regarded as non-poisonous.
11689.m: A poison dart frog from a terrarium is not poisonous.

11690.q: Which group of insects makes up the main part of the golden poison frog's diet?
11690.e: Phyllobates terribilis eats mainly small ants, for example of the genera Brachymyrmex and Paratrechina, as well as other small invertebrates.
11690.m: The golden poison frog eats mainly ants.

11691.q: Which animals from New Guinea also contain batrachotoxin and are seen as a clue to the poison source of poison dart frogs?
11691.e: Batrachotoxin was found in beetles of the genus Choresine from New Guinea. It is suspected that related beetles in Colombia are the frogs' poison source.
11691.m: Beetles carry the same poison as the most dangerous poison dart frogs.

11692.q: Which animal can eat young golden poison frogs without coming to harm?
11692.e: The snake Erythrolamprus epinephelus (formerly Leimadophis epinephelus) is resistant to several frog poisons and has been observed eating young frogs.
11692.m: A resistant snake can eat poison dart frogs.

11693.q: What conservation status does the golden poison frog have on the IUCN Red List?
11693.e: The IUCN classes Phyllobates terribilis as endangered, mainly because of habitat destruction in its tiny range.
11693.m: The golden poison frog is endangered.

11694.q: According to the IUCN, what is the main threat to the golden poison frog?
11694.e: Logging and other habitat destruction in the small range are the greatest danger. The IUCN considers the animal trade less important, as mostly captive-bred animals are traded.
11694.m: Habitat loss threatens the golden poison frog most.

11695.q: When was the golden poison frog scientifically described?
11695.e: Charles W. Myers, John W. Daly and Borys Malkin described Phyllobates terribilis only in 1978, although the Emberá had long known the frog.
11695.m: The golden poison frog was described only in 1978.

11696.q: Which researcher studied the skin poisons of poison dart frogs for decades and was one of those who described Phyllobates terribilis?
11696.e: The biochemist John W. Daly identified numerous frog alkaloids, including epibatidine, and took part in 1978 in the description of the golden poison frog.
11696.m: John Daly was the great researcher of frog poisons.

11697.q: Which colours occur in the golden poison frog?
11697.e: Phyllobates terribilis occurs in yellow, mint green and orange colour forms. Red with blue legs is known from the strawberry poison frog, blue from the dyeing poison frog.
11697.m: The golden poison frog is yellow, mint green or orange.

11698.q: What do young golden poison frogs look like?
a: Black with two light stripes on the back
11698.e: Young animals are black with two stripes along the sides of the back. The bright colouring of adults develops only later.
11698.m: Young golden poison frogs are black and striped.

11699.q: What is the striking warning colouration of poison dart frogs called in biology?
11699.e: Aposematism means that garish colours warn predators of toxicity. Many predators avoid the frogs after a single bad experience.
11699.m: Garish colours warn enemies of the poison of poison dart frogs.

11700.q: How did warning colouration arise within the family of poison dart frogs?
a: Several times independently of one another
Only once, in the common ancestor
11700.e: Toxicity and warning colours arose several times independently in the family, probably at least four times. This is an example of convergent evolution.
11700.m: The warning colours of poison dart frogs arose several times independently.

11701.q: The poison dart frog Ranitomeya imitator is itself poisonous and imitates other poisonous species. What is this form of imitation called?
11701.e: When several poisonous species come to resemble one another in colouring, this is called Müllerian mimicry. In Batesian mimicry, a harmless species imitates a poisonous one.
11701.m: Poisonous species that resemble one another show Müllerian mimicry.

11702.q: At what time of day are poison dart frogs typically active?
11702.e: Unlike many frogs, poison dart frogs are active by day. Thanks to their poison and warning colours, they do not need to hide in the daytime.
11702.m: Poison dart frogs are active by day.

11703.q: How are the eggs of most poison dart frogs fertilised?
a: Externally, after the eggs are laid
Not at all, they develop without fertilisation
Through the water of a stream
11703.e: In poison dart frogs, fertilisation takes place externally, usually right after the eggs are laid on land.
11703.m: Poison dart frogs fertilise their eggs outside the body.

11704.q: How do the tadpoles of many poison dart frogs get into the water?
a: A parent carries them on its back
They are washed away by the rain
They hop to the stream by themselves
The parents carry them in their mouths
11704.e: After hatching, the tadpoles climb onto the back of a parent, which carries them to a body of water. In many species, the male takes on this task.
11704.m: Poison dart frogs carry their tadpoles piggyback.

11705.q: Where do many poison dart frogs raise their tadpoles?
a: In small pools of water in plants such as bromeliads
In large rivers rich in fish
In salty sea water on the coast
11705.e: Tiny bodies of water in plants, for example in the leaf axils of bromeliads, are called phytotelmata. There the tadpoles are protected from fish and other predators.
11705.m: Many poison dart frogs raise their tadpoles in bromeliads.

11706.q: About how long does the development of a poison dart frog tadpole into a young frog take?
11706.e: After roughly 10 to 16 days the larvae hatch, and the metamorphosis into a young frog then takes about 6 to 14 weeks.
11706.m: Poison dart frog tadpoles need a few weeks to become frogs.

11707.q: Which parent of the strawberry poison frog, a poison dart frog, carries the tadpoles to the bromeliads?
11707.e: In the strawberry poison frog, the female carries each tadpole singly to its own bromeliad pool and then feeds it with nutritive eggs. Beforehand, the male guards the clutch and keeps it moist.
11707.m: In the strawberry poison frog, the mother mainly looks after the tadpoles.

11708.q: What does the genus name Oophaga of the strawberry poison frog, a poison dart frog, mean?
11708.e: In Greek, “oon” means egg and “phagein” means to eat. The name describes the tadpoles, which feed on eggs.

11709.q: What do female strawberry poison frogs, a type of poison dart frog, feed their tadpoles?
11709.e: The female regularly lays unfertilised nutritive eggs in the bromeliad pool. The tadpoles depend on this food and even receive poison from their mother this way.
11709.m: Strawberry poison frog mothers feed their tadpoles with eggs.

11710.q: In which region does the strawberry poison frog, a poison dart frog, live?
11710.e: Oophaga pumilio lives in Central America, from eastern Nicaragua through Costa Rica to north-western Panama.
11710.m: The strawberry poison frog lives in Central America.

11711.q: About how big does the strawberry poison frog, a poison dart frog, grow?
11711.e: Oophaga pumilio reaches a body length of only about 17 to 22 mm, which makes it much smaller than the golden poison frog.
11711.m: The strawberry poison frog is only about two centimetres long.

11712.q: What is the strawberry poison frog, a poison dart frog, famous for in the Bocas del Toro archipelago in Panama?
a: Its very many different colour forms
Having the strongest poison of all frogs
11712.e: In total, about 15 to 30 colour forms are known, many of them on individual islands of Bocas del Toro. The red form with blue legs is called “Blue Jeans”.
11712.m: The strawberry poison frog comes in many colours.

11713.q: Which prey animals provide a large part of the pumiliotoxins of the strawberry poison frog, a poison dart frog?
11713.e: Oribatid mites (Oribatida) are an important source of pumiliotoxins. The frogs take in the alkaloids along with these tiny mites.
11713.m: The strawberry poison frog gets its poison from mites.

11714.q: Which poison dart frog is known in German as the “Färberfrosch” (dyeing frog)?
11714.e: Dendrobates tinctorius is the dyeing poison frog; the Latin “tinctorius” means dyeing. It was described in 1797 by Georges Cuvier.
11714.m: The dyeing poison frog is called Dendrobates tinctorius.

11715.q: How did the dyeing poison frog, a poison dart frog, get its name?
a: According to reports, its secretion was used to change the colour of parrot feathers
It turns the water in its bromeliad blue
It was bred for dyeing fabrics
It changes its colour every day
11715.e: Indigenous peoples are said to have plucked feathers from parrots and rubbed the skin with the frog's secretion, after which yellow or red feathers grew back. This method is called tapirage.
11715.m: The dyeing poison frog is said to have been used to change the colour of parrot feathers.

11716.q: In which region of South America does the dyeing poison frog, a poison dart frog, live?
a: In the high Andes of Bolivia
11716.e: Dendrobates tinctorius lives in French Guiana, Suriname, Guyana and neighbouring parts of Brazil, up to a height of about 600 m.
11716.m: The dyeing poison frog lives in the Guiana region.

11717.q: Which blue colour form from the south of Suriname is now usually counted as a dyeing poison frog?
11717.e: The blue poison frog, formerly listed as a separate species, Dendrobates azureus, is now usually regarded as a colour form of the dyeing poison frog.
11717.m: The blue Azureus is a form of the dyeing poison frog.

11718.q: Which alkaloid was first isolated in 1974 from the skin of the Ecuadorian poison dart frog Epipedobates anthonyi and acts as an extremely powerful painkiller?
11718.e: John Daly isolated epibatidine in 1974, but its chemical structure was only worked out in 1992. It relieves pain at least 200 times more strongly than morphine, but is far too toxic to be used as a medicine.
11718.m: Epibatidine from a poison dart frog is an extremely powerful painkiller.

11719.q: What protection do poison dart frogs such as Phyllobates and Dendrobates have in international trade?
a: They are listed in Appendix II of CITES
They are not covered by any agreement
Trade in them is completely free
They are regarded as invasive pests
11719.e: Genera such as Dendrobates and Phyllobates are listed in CITES Appendix II. International trade is allowed, but strictly regulated.
11719.m: Poison dart frogs are protected by CITES.

11720.q: Which family does the olm (Proteus anguinus) belong to?
11720.e: The olm belongs to the family Proteidae. Today it includes only two genera.
11720.m: The olm is a member of the family Proteidae.

11721.q: Where do the mudpuppies, the only living close relatives of the olm, live?
11721.e: Today the family Proteidae includes only the olm in Europe and the mudpuppies (Necturus) in North America.
11721.m: The olm's closest living relatives, the mudpuppies, live in North America.

11722.q: Which order of amphibians does the olm belong to?
11722.e: The olm is a caudate (Caudata), like newts and salamanders. It keeps its tail all its life.
11722.m: Like newts and salamanders, the olm belongs to the caudates.

11723.q: Which of today's countries did the animals come from on which the olm was first scientifically described in 1768?
11723.e: The animals used for the first description came from the area around Stična in present-day Slovenia. Slovenia is still regarded as the olm's homeland today.
11723.m: The olm was described from animals found in what is now Slovenia.

11724.q: What did people take the olm to be when Valvasor reported on it in 1689?
11724.e: In 1689, Johann Weikhard von Valvasor mentioned that locals found olms after floods and took them for baby dragons. People believed that dragons lived in the caves.
11724.m: In the past, the olm was taken for a baby dragon from the depths.

11725.q: Where does the genus name “Proteus” of the olm come from?
a: From a Greek sea god who could change his shape
From a Roman emperor who explored caves
11725.e: In Greek mythology, Proteus is a sea god who could change his shape. The name suits the animal's mysterious, larva-like appearance.
11725.m: The olm bears the name of a shape-shifting Greek sea god.

11726.q: What does the species name “anguinus” in the scientific name of the olm mean?
11726.e: “Anguinus” comes from the Latin “anguis”, meaning snake. It describes the olm's long, slender body.
11726.m: The olm's species name refers to its snake-like body.

11727.q: What is the olm called in Slovenian because of its pale, skin-coloured appearance?
11727.e: In Slovenian it is called “človeška ribica”, which means little human fish. Its pale pink skin is reminiscent of human skin.
11727.m: Because of its skin colour, the olm is called the human fish in Slovenia.

11728.q: How long does a fully grown olm usually grow?
11728.e: Olms usually grow to about 20 to 30 cm in length. Some animals reach up to 40 cm.
11728.m: A grown-up olm is about as long as a ruler.

11729.q: How many fingers does the olm have on each front leg?
11729.e: The olm's small front legs have three fingers each. The limbs are greatly reduced.
11729.m: The olm has three fingers on each front leg.

11730.q: How many toes does the olm have on each hind leg?
11730.e: On its hind legs, the olm has only two toes each. This is a clear reduction compared with other salamanders.
11730.m: At the back, the olm stands on only two toes per leg.

11731.q: How many pairs of external gill tufts does the olm have on its head?
11731.e: The olm has three pairs of external gill tufts behind its head. It keeps them all its life.
11731.m: Three pairs of gill tufts decorate the olm's head.

11732.q: Why do the olm's gills glow red?
a: Oxygen-rich blood shows through the unpigmented skin
Red dyes from its food are stored there
The gills are covered with red scales
Luminous bacteria live on the gill tufts
11732.e: The skin of the gills contains no pigments. That is why you can see the oxygen-rich blood in the vessels shining through in red.
11732.m: In the olm, you can see the blood shining red through the gills.

11733.q: Which developmental feature does the olm show because it keeps larval features such as external gills all its life?
11733.e: In neoteny, animals become sexually mature without losing their larval features. In the olm it is obligate, so it never transforms.
11733.m: Thanks to neoteny, the olm stays larva-like all its life.

11734.q: Why does the olm not go through metamorphosis, even though its thyroid gland works normally?
a: Important tissues do not respond to the hormone thyroxine
It has no thyroid gland at all
Its food contains too little iodine
The cold in the caves stops all development
11734.e: The olm's thyroid gland produces thyroxine. But the target tissues do not respond to it, so the transformation does not happen.
11734.m: In the olm, the transformation hormone has no effect.

11735.q: What are the eyes of an adult olm of the pale nominate form like?
a: Reduced and hidden under the skin
Large and light-sensitive like those of owls
Completely missing, including the optic nerve
11735.e: The eyes are greatly reduced and lie under the skin. They can no longer form an image.
11735.m: The olm carries its stunted eyes under its skin.

11736.q: What can the olm use to sense light even though it is blind?
a: A third eye on its tail
11736.e: The olm's skin contains the light-sensitive protein melanopsin. In bright light, it therefore flees to dark hiding places.
11736.m: The olm senses light with its whole skin.

11737.q: Which sense does the olm probably use to find its way in the dark cave waters, according to experiments from 2002?
a: A heat sense like pit vipers
Colour vision in the infrared range
11737.e: Experiments in 2002 showed that olms align themselves with natural and artificial magnetic fields. This probably helps them find their way in the dark.
11737.m: In the dark, the olm probably also orients itself by the magnetic field.

11738.q: What can the ampullary organs in the olm's skin detect?
a: The salt content of the air
11738.e: Ampullary organs are electroreceptors. With them, the olm can detect weak electric fields, for example from prey animals.
11738.m: With its ampullary organs, the olm senses weak electricity.

11739.q: What does the olm mainly eat?
a: Small crustaceans such as freshwater shrimps and water lice
11739.e: Olms mainly eat small crustaceans such as freshwater shrimps, water lice and cave shrimps. Worms and insect larvae are also on the menu.
11739.m: The olm likes to hunt small crustaceans best.

11740.q: According to experiments, how long can an olm survive without food?
11740.e: In controlled experiments, olms survived up to ten years without food. They greatly reduce their activity and metabolism to do so.
11740.m: The olm can go hungry for years.

11741.q: Which breathing organs does the olm have in addition to its external gills?
a: Simple lungs, and it also breathes through its skin
Gill covers like a bony fish
A breathing tube at the end of its tail
11741.e: Besides the gills, the olm has simple, rudimentary lungs and also absorbs oxygen through its skin. The lungs help above all when the water contains little oxygen.
11741.m: Besides gills, the olm also has small lungs.

11742.q: What maximum lifespan did researchers estimate for the olm in 2010?
11742.e: A study from the Moulis cave laboratory in France estimated the maximum lifespan at over 100 years. That is extraordinary for such a small amphibian.
11742.m: An olm can probably live to be over a hundred years old.

11743.q: At about what age do female olms become sexually mature in the wild?
11743.e: Studies at about 10 °C showed sexual maturity after around 14 to 16 years. The cold slows down development greatly.
11743.m: An olm takes about fifteen years to become an adult.

11744.q: On average, how often does a female olm reproduce, according to observations in the Moulis cave laboratory?
11744.e: In the Moulis laboratory, females laid eggs only about every 12.5 years on average. This slow reproduction suits their long lives.
11744.m: A female olm lays eggs only very rarely.

11745.q: What is the maximum number of eggs a female olm lays per clutch?
11745.e: A clutch contains up to about 70 eggs, around 35 on average. The female attaches them under stones.
11745.m: An olm clutch holds at most around seventy eggs.

11746.q: About how long does it take for olm eggs to develop until they hatch?
11746.e: At around 10 °C, embryonic development takes about 140 to 180 days, depending on the source. In warmer water it goes faster.
11746.m: Olm eggs need several months to hatch.

11747.q: What water temperature is typical in the olm's cave waters?
11747.e: The cave waters are cool and even all year round, usually about 8 to 11 °C. Temperatures of around 14 °C are rarely reached.
11747.m: The olm lives in cool water at around ten degrees.

11748.q: Above what water temperature can olm eggs and larvae no longer develop?
11748.e: Above 18 °C, eggs and larvae cannot develop. Warming of the waters is therefore a danger to the species.
11748.m: Water that is too warm prevents the olm from having young.

11749.q: In which mountain region does the olm's natural range lie?
11749.e: The olm naturally lives only in the Dinaric Karst east of the Adriatic. The area stretches from Italy through Slovenia and Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.
11749.m: The olm's home is the Dinaric Karst.

11750.q: In which river catchment area are the olm's north-westernmost natural populations in Italy?
11750.e: The Italian populations lie in the catchment area of the Isonzo, called the Soča in Slovenian, near Trieste. The north-western limit of the range runs there.
11750.m: In Italy, the olm reaches the area of the Isonzo.

11751.q: What special feature does the olm have among the amphibians of Europe?
a: It is the only European amphibian that lives exclusively in caves
It is the only European amphibian that lives in the sea
It is the only poisonous European amphibian
It is the only European amphibian with scales
11751.e: The olm is Europe's only amphibian that spends its whole life in caves. Such animals are called troglobitic.
11751.m: No other European amphibian lives so completely in caves as the olm.

11752.q: What historical rank does the olm hold in cave biology?
a: It was the first scientifically described animal species living only in caves
It was the first animal bred in a cave
It was the first amphibian whose fossil was found
It was the first animal with proven colour vision
11752.e: With its description in 1768, the olm is regarded as the first cave-dwelling animal species in the world to be described. The region around Postojna is therefore regarded as the cradle of biospeleology.
11752.m: The study of cave animals began with the olm.

11753.q: When was the black form of the olm discovered?
11753.e: Members of the Slovenian Karst Research Institute discovered the black olm in 1986 at a karst spring. The find was a scientific sensation.
11753.m: The black olm was only discovered in 1986.

11754.q: What does the black olm, with its functioning eyes, reveal about the pale cave form?
a: Its ancestors could see, and the eyes shrank in the dark
The pale form will grow eyes again over time
Olms only develop eyes when they see light
The two forms are not related at all
11754.e: The black olm is more like the ancestors that lived at the surface. In the pale form, the eyes and skin colour have shrunk away in the eternal darkness of the caves.
11754.m: In the darkness of the caves, the pale olm has lost its eyes and colour.

11755.q: How does the black olm differ from the pale cave olm?
a: It has dark pigmentation and developed eyes
It is twice as long and has six legs
It has no gills and breathes only with lungs
It lives exclusively in the sea
11755.e: The black olm has dark skin and functioning eyes. It also has a shorter head and lives partly in waters close to the surface.
11755.m: The black olm has dark skin and visible eyes.

11756.q: In which country does the tiny range of the black olm lie?
11756.e: The black olm lives only in waters near Črnomelj in the Bela krajina region in south-eastern Slovenia. Its range covers less than 100 km².
11756.m: The black olm lives only in a small area in Slovenia.

11757.q: What conservation status does the olm have on the IUCN Red List?
11757.e: The IUCN classes the olm as vulnerable, including in the latest assessment. Its small range and water pollution threaten it.
11757.m: The IUCN regards the olm as vulnerable.

11758.q: What does it mean that the olm is strictly protected in the EU?
a: It may not be caught and its habitat may not be destroyed
It may only be caught in winter
It may be freely sold as a pet
It may only live in zoos
11758.e: The olm is listed in the EU Habitats Directive and counts as a priority species. Catching it, disturbing it and destroying its habitats are forbidden.
11758.m: The olm is strictly protected in the EU.

11759.q: How long has the olm been legally protected in Slovenia?
11759.e: Slovenia placed the olm under protection as early as 1922. It is therefore one of the early protected animal species in Europe.
11759.m: Slovenia has protected the olm for over a hundred years.

11760.q: What is regarded as the main threat to the olm?
11760.e: Karst waters hardly filter out pollutants, so they quickly reach the habitat. In olms, PCBs and raised arsenic levels, for example, have been found.
11760.m: Clean groundwater is vital for the olm's survival.

11761.q: What role does the olm play in Slovenia?
a: It is a national symbol of the country
It is regarded as a pest in wells
It is eaten as a delicacy
It is regarded as bad luck
11761.e: The olm is a national symbol of Slovenia. For example, it was shown on a Slovenian coin and is a landmark of the Postojna Cave.
11761.m: The olm is a landmark of Slovenia.

11762.q: What happened to olms in the Postojna Cave in Slovenia in 2016?
a: Young hatched from eggs in the show aquarium
The last animals died of a virus
A black olm was found there for the first time
All the animals were moved to Italy
11762.e: A female had laid eggs in the show aquarium, and the first young hatched there in 2016. The media spoke of “baby dragons”.
11762.m: In 2016, young olms hatched in front of an audience in Postojna.

11763.q: How big is the olm's genome compared with the human genome?
11763.e: Decoding it revealed a genome about 15 times longer than that of humans. It is one of the largest genomes sequenced so far.
11763.m: The olm has a huge genome.

11764.q: In which German cave were olms released in 1932, which can still be seen there today?
11764.e: In 1932, olms from Istria were released in the Hermannshöhle near Rübeland. A few animals still live there today in a tank.
11764.m: In the Hermannshöhle, olms live far from their homeland.

11765.q: In which country is the Moulis cave laboratory, where a released population of olms is studied?
11765.e: The laboratory in Moulis lies in the French Pyrenees. Olms were observed and bred there over decades.
11765.m: Much of what we know about the olm comes from a cave laboratory in France.

11766.q: How long can an olm survive in water with no oxygen at all?
11766.e: The olm survives complete lack of oxygen for up to about 12 hours. This is an adaptation to changing conditions in the karst.
11766.m: The olm can do without oxygen for a surprisingly long time.

11767.q: In a study from Herzegovina (2020), how long did an olm stay in the same place without moving any further away?
11767.e: Researchers found an animal in the same place over 2500 days, so about seven years. Olms move very little and so save energy.
11767.m: The olm is an extreme stay-at-home.

11768.q: What behaviour do male olms show towards others of their kind?
a: They migrate to the sea every year
They build nests out of mud
11768.e: Sexually active males defend small territories against rivals, about 80 cm across in an aquarium. Courtship also takes place in these territories.
11768.m: Male olms defend their small territory.

11769.q: From which geological period does the fossil Mioproteus, a relative of the olm from the Caucasus, come?
11769.e: Mioproteus caucasicus was found in Miocene layers in the Caucasus. This shows that olms used to be more widespread.
11769.m: Fossil relatives of the olm lived as early as the Miocene.

11770.q: How does the whale shark breathe?
a: With gills, and it does not have to surface to breathe
With lungs, and it has to surface regularly
11770.e: As a cartilaginous fish, the whale shark breathes with gills. It belongs to the order of carpet sharks, which also includes wobbegongs.
11770.m: As a fish, the whale shark breathes with gills.

11771.q: The whale shark is the only living species of its family. What does that mean?
a: It has no close living relatives
It is the only species of shark
There is only a single whale shark left
It lives in only a single sea
11771.e: Rhincodon is the only genus of the family Rhincodontidae, and the whale shark is its only living species. This is called a monotypic family.
11771.m: The whale shark stands completely alone in its family.

11772.q: What record does the whale shark hold among today's living fish?
11772.e: The whale shark is the largest living shark and also the largest living fish of all. Today only some whales are bigger, but they are mammals.
11772.m: No fish alive today is as big as the whale shark.

11773.q: Despite its name, which class of vertebrates does the whale shark belong to?
11773.e: The whale shark is a shark and therefore a cartilaginous fish that breathes with gills. It is not closely related to whales, which are mammals.
11773.m: The whale shark is a fish, not a whale.

11774.q: Where does the name “whale shark” come from?
a: From its size and filter feeding, as in baleen whales
From its ability to breathe air
From its song, as in humpback whales
From its close relationship with whales
11774.e: The name refers to its enormous size and its way of feeding by filtering, which is reminiscent of baleen whales. It is not related to whales.
11774.m: The whale shark has “whale” in its name only because of its size and way of feeding.

11775.q: Why is the whale shark regarded as a “gentle giant” despite its size?
a: It eats only plankton and small animals and is harmless to humans
It swims only at night and avoids light
It has no teeth at all
It lives only in freshwater lakes
11775.e: The whale shark filters plankton, krill and small fish out of the water. Divers can swim with it without being in danger.
11775.m: The whale shark is harmless to humans.

11776.q: How should snorkellers behave when they meet whale sharks?
a: Keep their distance and not touch the animals
Feed the animals so that they stay
Take photos with a flash close to the eye
Hold on to the dorsal fin
11776.e: Touching can damage the sensitive mucus layer of the skin and disturb the animals. Many countries therefore require a minimum distance.
11776.m: Whale sharks are watched from a distance and without touching.

11777.q: What does the Greek word part “odon” in the genus name Rhincodon of the whale shark mean?
11777.e: “Odous” means tooth in Greek, as in mastodon. Rhincodon probably means rasp tooth, after the tiny teeth arranged like a rasp.
11777.m: The whale shark is called Rhincodon because of its rasp-like little teeth.

11778.q: Which length counts as the greatest reliably documented body length of a whale shark?
11778.e: An animal about 18.8 m long is regarded as the largest reliably documented specimen. Most whale sharks seen in gatherings are much smaller, often around 6 to 8 m.
11778.m: A whale shark can grow almost 19 metres long.

11779.q: How heavy can big whale sharks get?
11779.e: Big whale sharks weigh more than 10 tonnes, and about 15 tonnes was given for an animal around 12 m long. But they come nowhere near the 150 tonnes of a blue whale.
11779.m: A big whale shark weighs as much as several elephants.

11780.q: How thick can a whale shark's skin get?
11780.e: A whale shark's skin can be up to about 15 cm thick. It is regarded as the thickest skin in the animal kingdom and protects the body.
11780.m: The whale shark has the thickest skin of all animals.

11781.q: In how many rows are the tiny teeth in a whale shark's mouth arranged?
11781.e: The whale shark has around 3600 very small teeth, arranged in over 300 rows. They are only a few millimetres in size.
11781.m: The whale shark has thousands of tiny teeth in hundreds of rows.

11782.q: What role do the whale shark's teeth play when it feeds?
a: They hold on to wriggling seals
11782.e: The whale shark filters its food out of the water and swallows it whole. Its tiny teeth are not needed for this.
11782.m: The whale shark feeds without using its teeth.

11783.q: With which structures does the whale shark sieve food out of the water?
a: With about 20 filter pads on its gills
With horny baleen plates in its upper jaw
11783.e: The whale shark has about 20 sponge-like filter pads attached to its gill arches. They hold back plankton and small animals while the water flows out through the gills.
11783.m: The whale shark filters its food with pads on its gills.

11784.q: Which feature runs along the length of each side of the whale shark's body?
11784.e: The whale shark has three conspicuous long ridges on each side. They are a typical identifying feature of the species.
11784.m: Three ridges on each side give away the whale shark.

11785.q: How is the whale shark's tail fin built?
a: The upper lobe is bigger than the lower one
Both lobes are exactly the same size
The lower lobe is much bigger
It consists of only one lobe
11785.e: The tail fin is heterocercal, which means that the upper lobe is bigger. This build is typical of many sharks.
11785.m: In the whale shark, the upper part of the tail fin is the bigger one.

11786.q: Where is the whale shark's mouth, unlike in most other sharks?
a: Right at the front of the head
At the side behind the eyes
11786.e: In most sharks, the mouth is on the underside of the head. In the whale shark, the broad mouth is at the very front, which makes filtering while swimming easier.
11786.m: The whale shark has its broad mouth right at the front of its head.

11787.q: What did researchers discover on the whale shark's eyeballs in 2020?
11787.e: The whale shark's eyeballs are covered with small skin teeth (denticles). They differ in structure from those on the body and protect the eye from injury.
11787.m: Even the whale shark's eyes carry little teeth.

11788.q: Why is the whale shark's pattern of spots useful for research?
a: It is unique to each animal
11788.e: Every whale shark has its own pattern of pale dots and stripes. Researchers can therefore recognise individual animals in photos.
11788.m: You can recognise every whale shark by its spot pattern, like a fingerprint.

11789.q: Which field does a computer method used to compare photos of whale sharks come from?
11789.e: For comparing the spot patterns, an algorithm was adapted that originally recognises star patterns in images from the Hubble Space Telescope. The dots on the shark are treated like stars.
11789.m: Whale sharks are recognised with software from astronomy.

11790.q: To which light is the whale shark's visual pigment rhodopsin particularly tuned?
11790.e: The whale shark's rhodopsin is particularly sensitive to blue light. This helps it see at very different depths, where mainly blue light arrives.
11790.m: The whale shark sees especially well in the blue light of the deep.

11791.q: Which two other shark species feed by filtering, like the whale shark?
a: Great white shark and tiger shark
11791.e: Only three shark species filter plankton: the whale shark, the basking shark and the megamouth shark. All three are very large.
11791.m: The whale shark shares filter feeding only with the basking shark and the megamouth shark.

11792.q: What can the whale shark do when feeding that the basking shark cannot?
a: Actively suck water into its mouth
Chop up prey with its teeth
Filter plankton out of the water
11792.e: The basking shark filters only passively while swimming forwards. The whale shark can also actively suck in water and so feed while staying in one place.
11792.m: The whale shark can suck in its food instead of only swimming through it.

11793.q: About how much water can a whale shark filter per hour when feeding?
11793.e: Measurements showed filtering rates of around 300 to over 600 cubic metres of water per hour. Only in this way does the animal get enough plankton.
11793.m: Every hour, a whale shark sieves a whole swimming pool of water.

11794.q: What does the whale shark mainly eat?
11794.e: The whale shark eats plankton, krill, fish eggs as well as small fish and squid. It cannot swallow large prey.
11794.m: The biggest fish lives on the smallest sea creatures.

11795.q: How does the whale shark reproduce?
a: It is ovoviviparous and gives birth to live young
It lays egg cases on the seabed
It spawns freely into open water
It incubates eggs in its mouth
11795.e: The eggs develop inside the female's body, where the young also hatch. Fully developed little whale sharks are born.
11795.m: Whale shark young hatch inside the mother and are born alive.

11796.q: Roughly how many embryos did a pregnant female whale shark caught off Taiwan in the 1990s carry?
11796.e: A female about 10.6 m long, caught off Taiwan in the mid-1990s, carried around 300 embryos at different stages of development. This find proved that the whale shark gives birth to live young.
11796.m: A female whale shark can carry hundreds of young at once.

11797.q: About how long is a newborn whale shark?
11797.e: Young whale sharks are about 40 to 60 cm long at birth. They take decades to grow to the size of their parents.
11797.m: A whale shark begins life hardly bigger than a forearm.

11798.q: At about what body length do male whale sharks become sexually mature?
11798.e: According to the data so far, males become sexually mature at a length of about 8 to 9 m. Females mature at a similar or greater length.
11798.m: A male whale shark is only grown up at about eight metres.

11799.q: Which sex grows bigger in the whale shark?
a: Both grow exactly the same size
It depends only on the sea
11799.e: A study at Ningaloo Reef in 2020 showed that females grow bigger than males. The largest animals are therefore usually females.
11799.m: In the whale shark, the females are the giants.

11800.q: How old can a whale shark get, according to current estimates?
11800.e: Life expectancy is estimated at around 80 to 130 years. Whale sharks grow slowly and become sexually mature late.
11800.m: A whale shark can live to be over a hundred years old.

11801.q: What was used in 2020 to confirm that the rings in a whale shark's vertebrae form once a year?
a: Counts of the rows of teeth
11801.e: The atomic bomb tests of the 1950s and 1960s left raised C-14 levels, which were deposited in the vertebrae. This made it possible to show that one ring forms per year.
11801.m: Atomic bomb tests helped to determine the age of whale sharks.

11802.q: According to the age study of 2020, about how old was a female whale shark 10 m long?
11802.e: Analysis of the vertebral rings gave an age of around 50 years for a female 10 m long. A male of almost the same length was about 35 years old.
11802.m: A whale shark ten metres long already has half a century behind it.

11803.q: Why is almost nothing known about the mating of whale sharks?
a: It has hardly ever been observed in the wild
Whale sharks mate only in aquariums
Whale sharks mate only under the ice of the Arctic
11803.e: Whale shark mating has hardly ever been observed. In 2019, a pilot photographed from the air what was probably mating behaviour off Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia.
11803.m: The mating of the whale shark is one of the great mysteries of the sea.

11804.q: Which whale sharks are found seasonally at Darwin Island in the Galápagos archipelago?
11804.e: At Darwin Island, large adult females appear regularly, many of them pregnant. The place is therefore important for research into reproduction.
11804.m: At the Galápagos, mainly pregnant female whale sharks swim.

11805.q: What distance did the female whale shark “Anne” cover on the longest known migration?
11805.e: The female “Anne”, tagged in 2011, swam over 20,000 km in 841 days. It is the longest whale shark migration ever documented.
11805.m: A whale shark can travel half way around the Earth.

11806.q: Which water temperature does the whale shark prefer?
11806.e: Whale sharks live in tropical and subtropical seas and prefer water of around 21 to 25 °C. They avoid cold polar seas.
11806.m: The whale shark feels at home in warm seawater.

11807.q: What diving depth has already been recorded for whale sharks?
11807.e: Although whale sharks often feed near the surface, tags recorded dives to depths of over 1000 m.
11807.m: The whale shark dives deeper than you would expect of a plankton eater.

11808.q: What did measurements of the body temperature of whale sharks off Okinawa show?
a: It stayed above 19 °C although the water was 14 °C
It dropped at once to the water temperature
It rose above 37 °C as in mammals
It varied by more than 20 °C a day
11808.e: Over about twelve hours, the body temperature did not fall below 19 °C despite water at 14 °C. The huge body stores heat and cools down only slowly.
11808.m: Thanks to its size, the whale shark stays warm even in cool water.

11809.q: How fast does a whale shark normally swim?
11809.e: The whale shark is a calm, slow swimmer and usually moves at about 5 km/h. It does not need speed for filter feeding.
11809.m: The whale shark glides through the sea at about walking pace.

11810.q: In which sea region does most of the world's whale shark population live?
11810.e: An estimated 75% of all whale sharks belong to the Indo-Pacific subpopulation. The rest live mainly in the Atlantic.
11810.m: Most whale sharks live in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.

11811.q: Off which peninsula have seasonal gatherings of over 400 whale sharks been observed?
11811.e: Off Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, over 400 whale sharks gather at certain times of year to eat fish spawn. It is one of the largest known gatherings.
11811.m: Off Yucatán, hundreds of whale sharks gather for a feast.

11812.q: How has the IUCN Red List classed the whale shark since 2016?
11812.e: Since 2016, the IUCN has listed the whale shark as “Endangered”. Its numbers are still falling.
11812.m: The whale shark has been regarded as endangered since 2016.

11813.q: By how much has the whale shark population shrunk over about 75 years, according to the IUCN?
11813.e: The IUCN assumes a decline of more than half over about 75 years. The main causes are fishing, bycatch and collisions with ships.
11813.m: In three generations, the whale shark has lost more than half its population.

11814.q: Which danger particularly threatens whale sharks because they often feed near the surface of the water?
11814.e: Because whale sharks often filter just below the surface, they are rammed by ships or injured by propellers. Ship collisions are regarded as an important cause of death.
11814.m: At the surface, ships are a deadly danger for the whale shark.

11815.q: What does it mean that the whale shark has been listed in the species protection agreement CITES since 2003?
a: International trade in it requires permits
Every whale shark gets a tag
Whale sharks may no longer be observed
The whale shark has been regarded as extinct since then
11815.e: Since 2003, the whale shark has been in Appendix II of CITES. International trade in it and its products therefore requires a permit and is monitored.
11815.m: Trade in whale sharks has been monitored internationally since 2003.

11816.q: Which country banned commercial trade in whale sharks as early as 1998?
11816.e: The Philippines banned the trade in 1998, India followed in 2001 and Taiwan in 2007. Today, whale shark watching is an important branch of tourism in the Philippines.
11816.m: The Philippines protected the whale shark as early as 1998.

11817.q: What behaviour of orcas towards whale sharks has been observed?
a: They turn them over and eat their liver
They follow them to share plankton
They use them as shelter from storms
They clean parasites off their skin
11817.e: Orcas have been seen turning whale sharks on their backs and deliberately eating the nutrient-rich liver. Tiger sharks and great white sharks also occasionally prey on weaker whale sharks.
11817.m: Even the huge whale shark has a dangerous enemy in the orca.

11818.q: Which aquarium holds the record for the longest time a whale shark has been kept in human care?
11818.e: In the Okinawa Churaumi Aquarium, a whale shark had lived for over 26 years by 2021. This is the longest known period in captivity.
11818.m: In Okinawa, a whale shark lived in an aquarium for over a quarter of a century.

11819.q: According to the specialist literature, which is the only aquarium outside Asia that has kept whale sharks?
a: Sea Life Konstanz on Lake Constance
11819.e: The Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta is the only facility outside Asia that has looked after whale sharks. The huge animals need enormous tanks.
11819.m: Outside Asia, only the Georgia Aquarium shows whale sharks.

11820.q: The tiger shark's scientific name is Galeocerdo cuvier. What does the second part of this name indicate?
11820.e: In the system of naming introduced by Linnaeus, the genus (Galeocerdo) comes first, then the species name (cuvier). Together they make up the unique name of a species.
11820.m: A scientific species name consists of the genus and the species.

11821.q: What do sharks such as the tiger shark lack, unlike most bony fish?
11821.e: Sharks have no gas-filled swim bladder. Buoyancy comes mainly from their large, oil-rich liver, and they have to keep swimming so as not to sink.
11821.m: Instead of a swim bladder, the tiger shark has an oil-rich liver.

11822.q: How many living species does the genus Galeocerdo, to which the tiger shark belongs, include?
a: Only one, the tiger shark itself
11822.e: The genus Galeocerdo is monotypic today, so the tiger shark is its only living species. Other Galeocerdo species are known only as fossils.
11822.m: The tiger shark is the only living member of its genus.

11823.q: Why do more recent classifications place the tiger shark in a family of its own instead of with the requiem sharks?
a: It differs clearly from them in several features
It is the only shark that lives only in freshwater
It is more closely related to rays
It is really a bony fish
11823.e: The tiger shark, for example, has spiracles and a different way of reproducing from the requiem sharks. More recent classifications therefore give it its own family, Galeocerdonidae.
11823.m: More recent classifications give the tiger shark its own family called Galeocerdonidae.

11824.q: The tiger shark was described in 1822 as Squalus cuvier and later placed in a different genus. Why?
a: Squalus was then a catch-all name for many sharks
At that time it was thought to be a ray
The name had already been given to a whale
11824.e: The naturalists Péron and Lesueur described the species in 1822 as Squalus cuvier, at that time a catch-all name for many sharks. Only later was it placed in its own genus, Galeocerdo.
11824.m: The tiger shark was originally described as Squalus cuvier.

11825.q: Johannes Müller and Jakob Henle set up the tiger shark's genus in 1837. Which group of animals did their great work deal with?
11825.e: Müller and Henle wrote a great work on the classification of cartilaginous fish, that is, sharks and rays. In it, they introduced the genus Galeocerdo in 1837.
11825.m: Müller and Henle gave the tiger shark its genus name in 1837.

11826.q: In honour of which famous naturalist does the tiger shark bear the species name “cuvier”?
11826.e: The species name honours the French naturalist Georges Cuvier, a founder of comparative anatomy and palaeontology. It is unusual that the name appears without the usual genitive ending.
11826.m: The tiger shark's species name recalls the scientist Georges Cuvier.

11827.q: The tiger shark's genus name Galeocerdo roughly means “fox shark”. Which language do its word parts come from?
11827.e: Galeocerdo is a made-up word from the Greek galeos for shark and kerdo for fox. Many scientific names are formed from Greek or Latin words.
11827.m: The genus name Galeocerdo roughly means “fox shark”.

11828.q: Where does the tiger shark get its name from?
a: From the dark vertical stripes, especially in young animals
From its roar when it attacks
11828.e: Young tiger sharks have clear dark stripes and spots that are reminiscent of a tiger's coat. In older animals these stripes fade more and more.
11828.m: The tiger shark is named after the tiger-like stripes of its young.

11829.q: What does the tiger shark's snout look like?
a: Narrow and extended like a trunk
11829.e: The tiger shark has a strikingly short, broad and blunt snout, which gives its head an almost wedge-like shape. Many other requiem sharks have a much more pointed snout.
11829.m: You can recognise the tiger shark by its short, blunt snout.

11830.q: What is the colouring of the tiger shark, with a dark back and pale underside, which camouflages it in the water, called?
11830.e: From above, the dark back blends into the depths, and from below, the pale belly blends into the light of the surface. This countershading is widespread among predators of the sea.
11830.m: Countershading makes the tiger shark hard to see from above and below.

11831.q: How long do fully grown tiger sharks typically grow?
11831.e: Most adult tiger sharks measure around 3.5 to 4.7 metres. Only exceptionally large females grow longer than 5 metres.
11831.m: An adult tiger shark is usually between 3.5 and 4.7 metres long.

11832.q: Which sex grows bigger in the tiger shark?
a: Both grow exactly the same size
It depends only on the water temperature
11832.e: In the tiger shark, the females are the bigger sex. Males rarely reach more than about 4 metres, while females can grow longer than 5 metres.
11832.m: In the tiger shark, females are bigger than males.

11833.q: How heavy do fully grown tiger sharks typically get?
11833.e: Typical adult tiger sharks weigh around 300 to 900 kilograms. Especially large females can even reach over 1300 kilograms.
11833.m: A fully grown tiger shark usually weighs several hundred kilograms.

11834.q: Where does the tiger shark rank in size among predatory sharks?
a: It is the second largest after the great white shark
It is the largest of all sharks
It is smaller than the blacktip reef shark
It is the second largest after the whale shark
11834.e: Among predatory sharks, only the great white shark grows bigger than the tiger shark. The whale shark and basking shark are bigger, but they feed on plankton.
11834.m: Among predatory sharks, only the great white shark is bigger than the tiger shark.

11835.q: How big was the unconfirmed record tiger shark said to have been caught in the South China Sea in 1957?
11835.e: The female is said to have been 7.4 metres long and to have weighed 3110 kilograms. However, these figures are regarded as unconfirmed.
11835.m: The supposed record tiger shark of 1957 is said to have been over 7 metres long.

11836.q: What shape are the tiger shark's teeth?
a: Cockscomb-shaped with a tip curved to the side and a serrated edge
Long, thin and needle-like with no serrated edge
11836.e: The tiger shark's teeth are broad, strongly serrated and have a tip pointing obliquely to the side. This shape resembles a cockscomb.
11836.m: The tiger shark's teeth look like a serrated cockscomb.

11837.q: What are the tiger shark's serrated teeth especially well suited for?
a: Cutting through hard prey such as turtle shells
Filtering plankton out of the water
11837.e: With its serrated, sideways-curved teeth, the tiger shark can cut through even the shells of sea turtles, as with a saw. In doing so, it often shakes its head back and forth.
11837.m: The tiger shark's saw teeth can even crack turtle shells.

11838.q: What is a spiracle, as the tiger shark has behind its eyes?
a: An opening through which breathing water can reach the gills
A nozzle for quick escape jumps
11838.e: Spiracles are small openings behind the eyes, a relic of a gill slit. In rays they are large, in the tiger shark they are small, and the other requiem sharks lack them.
11838.m: The tiger shark has spiracles, which the other requiem sharks lack.

11839.q: What are the sense organs on the tiger shark's head called, with which it detects weak electric fields from prey?
11839.e: The ampullae of Lorenzini are gel-filled pores on the snout that sense electric fields. In this way, the tiger shark can even find prey hidden in the sand.
11839.m: With the ampullae of Lorenzini, the tiger shark detects electric fields.

11840.q: With which sensory system does the tiger shark detect water movements and vibrations?
11840.e: The lateral line organ runs along the body and registers pressure waves in the water. Incidentally, sharks have no swim bladder.
11840.m: The lateral line organ tells the tiger shark of every movement in the water.

11841.q: Which layer in the eye helps the tiger shark see well in little light?
11841.e: The tapetum lucidum is a reflective layer behind the retina that sends incoming light through the sensory cells a second time. This is especially useful for a hunter active at night.
11841.m: Thanks to the tapetum lucidum, the tiger shark also sees well at dusk.

11842.q: What protects the tiger shark's eyes when it attacks wriggling prey?
11842.e: Like other requiem sharks, the tiger shark has a nictitating membrane, a movable third eyelid. It slides protectively over the eye when the shark bites.
11842.m: When the tiger shark bites, the nictitating membrane protects its eye.

11843.q: How does the tiger shark reproduce?
a: Ovoviviparous, the young hatch inside the mother
It lays egg cases on the seabed
The young are nourished through a yolk-sac placenta
It spawns thousands of eggs into open water
11843.e: In the tiger shark, the eggs develop inside the mother, the young hatch there and are born alive. In this it differs from most requiem sharks, which form a yolk-sac placenta.
11843.m: The tiger shark gives birth to live young that hatched inside the mother.

11844.q: How many young can a female tiger shark give birth to in one litter?
11844.e: Tiger sharks are very fertile for sharks: a litter usually contains between about 10 and 80 young. Larger females tend to have more offspring.
11844.m: A female tiger shark can have dozens of young at once.

11845.q: How long is the gestation period in the tiger shark?
11845.e: The tiger shark's gestation period lasts around 13 to 16 months, depending on the source. That is much longer than in most mammals.
11845.m: A female tiger shark is pregnant for more than a year.

11846.q: How big are newborn tiger sharks?
11846.e: Young tiger sharks are born about half a metre to three quarters of a metre long. They are independent at once and receive no parental care.
11846.m: A newborn tiger shark is already over half a metre long.

11847.q: How often does a female tiger shark usually have young?
a: About every two to three years
11847.e: According to common figures, female tiger sharks give birth only about every three years, while more recent observations in the Maldives point to about every two years. This slow reproductive cycle makes the species vulnerable to overfishing.
11847.m: A female tiger shark has offspring only every few years.

11848.q: At roughly what body length do female tiger sharks become sexually mature?
11848.e: Female tiger sharks become sexually mature at around 2.5 to 3.5 metres, males somewhat earlier at around 2.3 to 2.9 metres. Several years pass before then.
11848.m: A female tiger shark has to be several metres long before she can have young.

11849.q: Why is the tiger shark regarded as a shark with one of the widest diets?
a: It eats fish, turtles, seabirds, marine mammals and even carrion
It lives only on plankton and krill
It eats only squid in the deep sea
11849.e: The tiger shark is an extreme generalist feeder. Its menu includes bony fish, other sharks, rays, cephalopods, crabs, sea turtles, seabirds, dolphins, seals and carrion.
11849.m: The tiger shark eats almost everything it meets in the sea.

11850.q: What nickname does the tiger shark have because of the inedible things found in its stomach?
11850.e: In tiger sharks' stomachs, number plates, tyres and baseballs have been found. That is why it is also called the “rubbish bin of the sea”.
11850.m: Because it even swallows rubbish, the tiger shark is called the “rubbish bin of the sea”.

11851.q: Which group of animals does the tiger shark eat more often than any other shark?
a: Marine reptiles such as sea turtles and sea snakes
11851.e: No other shark preys on sea turtles and sea snakes as regularly as the tiger shark. Its strong saw teeth are ideal for this.
11851.m: The tiger shark is the greatest turtle hunter among sharks.

11852.q: Which prey do tiger sharks deliberately lie in wait for every summer in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands?
a: Young albatrosses on their first flying attempts
11852.e: When young Laysan and black-footed albatrosses learn to fly, many land on the water while practising. Tiger sharks then gather off the islands and prey on them.
11852.m: In Hawaii, tiger sharks hunt young albatrosses that have just learned to fly on the water.

11853.q: Which large plant-eating marine mammal is part of the tiger shark's prey in Shark Bay in Western Australia?
11853.e: In Shark Bay, tiger sharks prey on dugongs, among other animals. Researchers found dugong tissue there in the stomachs of several tiger sharks.
11853.m: In Western Australia, dugongs are also on the tiger shark's menu.

11854.q: What ecological effect did research in Shark Bay show: how does the presence of tiger sharks affect dugongs and sea turtles?
a: The animals avoid dangerous seagrass meadows, which spares the seagrass
The animals leave the bay altogether and never return
The animals become bigger and heavier as a result
The animals form feeding partnerships with the tiger sharks
11854.e: For fear of tiger sharks, dugongs and turtles graze risky spots less. In this way, the predator indirectly influences the whole seagrass ecosystem, which is called a “landscape of fear”.
11854.m: The mere presence of the tiger shark indirectly protects the seagrass meadows.

11855.q: At what time of day does the tiger shark mainly hunt?
a: Only in daytime during a full moon
11855.e: The tiger shark is mostly active at night. At night it swims into shallow coastal waters, and by day it often retreats into deeper water.
11855.m: The tiger shark goes hunting mainly at night.

11856.q: How does the tiger shark live socially?
a: In schools of several hundred animals
In pairs that stay together for life
11856.e: Tiger sharks are mostly loners. Only at especially rich feeding places, for example at a whale carcass, do several animals meet.
11856.m: The tiger shark mostly roams the sea alone.

11857.q: How does the tiger shark normally swim, and how does it still surprise its prey?
a: It usually swims slowly but can accelerate in a flash
It swims constantly at top speed
It lies motionless on the bottom and never swims
It only drifts passively with the current
11857.e: Tiger sharks seem sluggish and slow when patrolling. Shortly before they strike, however, they can put on a quick sprint.
11857.m: The slow tiger shark can strike in a flash at the decisive moment.

11858.q: In which sea regions is the tiger shark found?
a: Worldwide in tropical and warm temperate seas
Only in freshwater lakes in Africa
11858.e: The tiger shark occurs around the globe in tropical, subtropical and warm temperate seas. In the Mediterranean, by contrast, it is very rare.
11858.m: The tiger shark lives in warm seas all over the world.

11859.q: Which waters does the tiger shark particularly prefer?
a: Murky coastal waters and river mouths
11859.e: The tiger shark likes to stay in murky coastal waters, lagoons and river mouths. There it finds plenty of prey and can sneak up well.
11859.m: The tiger shark likes murky coastal waters and river mouths.

11860.q: What is the greatest depth at which individual tiger sharks have been recorded?
11860.e: Although tiger sharks often live near the coast, individual animals have been recorded at depths of almost 900 metres. Usually, however, they stay in much shallower water.
11860.m: Tiger sharks can dive down to almost 900 metres.

11861.q: According to a satellite study from 2015, what distance did tagged tiger sharks near Bermuda cover each year?
11861.e: The tiger sharks tagged with transmitters travelled each year between the coral reefs of the Caribbean and the open North Atlantic. In doing so, they covered round trips of over 7500 kilometres.
11861.m: Some tiger sharks travel thousands of kilometres every year, like migratory birds.

11862.q: Off which island does the largest known gathering of tiger sharks in the world live?
11862.e: Off Fuvahmulah in the Maldives, a study identified around 240 different tiger sharks. Well over 80 per cent of them are females, which probably also stay there during pregnancy.
11862.m: Particularly many tiger sharks live off the Maldives island of Fuvahmulah.

11863.q: Which animal is the only known natural enemy of adult tiger sharks?
11863.e: Orcas turn tiger sharks on their backs, which sends them into a rigid state called tonic immobility. They then eat mainly the nutrient-rich liver.
11863.m: Only the orca is a match for the adult tiger shark as an enemy.

11864.q: What status does the tiger shark have on the IUCN Red List (2019 assessment)?
11864.e: Since 2019, the IUCN has classed the tiger shark as near threatened. In some regions, for example the Arabian Sea, numbers have fallen sharply.
11864.m: According to the IUCN, the tiger shark is near threatened.

11865.q: Which parts of the tiger shark are especially sought after in fishing?
11865.e: Tiger sharks are caught for their fins for shark fin soup, their liver rich in vitamin A and their skin for leather. The meat is also used.
11865.m: Fins, liver and skin make the tiger shark a target for fishing.

11866.q: Which shark is responsible for more recorded unprovoked attacks on humans than the tiger shark?
11866.e: In the statistics of unprovoked shark attacks, the tiger shark comes second after the great white shark. Fatal accidents are nevertheless very rare.
11866.m: After the great white shark, the tiger shark is involved in the most recorded attacks.

11867.q: What did the shark control programme in Hawaii, in which over 4000 sharks were killed from 1959 to 1976, show?
a: The number of encounters with tiger sharks did not noticeably fall as a result
Afterwards there were never any more sharks around Hawaii
The tiger sharks became much more aggressive as a result
The tiger sharks were wiped out in Hawaii
11867.e: Despite the killing of 4668 sharks, including many tiger sharks, incidents with humans did not fall measurably. Such control programmes are now regarded as not very effective.
11867.m: Killing tiger sharks in large numbers in Hawaii brought no noticeable safety.

11868.q: How far back does the fossil record of the genus Galeocerdo, to which the tiger shark belongs, go?
a: Back to the Eocene about 50 million years ago
Back to the last ice age 20,000 years ago
Back to the Cambrian 500 million years ago
Only back to the Middle Ages
11868.e: The oldest fossils of the genus Galeocerdo come from the early Eocene, that is, from about 50 million years ago. The present-day species is much younger.
11868.m: The ancestors of the tiger shark were already hunting about 50 million years ago.

11869.q: Which artist exhibited a tiger shark preserved in formaldehyde as a famous work of art in 1991?
11869.e: Damien Hirst's work “The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living” shows a tiger shark in a formaldehyde tank. It is one of the best-known works of contemporary art.
11869.m: Damien Hirst turned a preserved tiger shark into a famous work of art.

11870.q: Which large group of cartilaginous fish do the sawfishes (family Pristidae) belong to in classification?
11870.e: Despite their shark-like body, sawfishes are rays. You can tell this from, among other things, the gill slits on the underside.
11870.m: The sawfish looks like a shark, but it is a ray.

11871.q: Which rays, which also have a shark-like body, are the closest relatives of the sawfishes?
11871.e: Together with the guitarfishes and their relatives, sawfishes form an order of their own. These rays all have an elongated, shark-like body.
11871.m: The closest relatives of the sawfishes are the guitarfishes.

11872.q: How many living species of sawfish are usually distinguished today?
11872.e: Today five species are recognised: four in the genus Pristis and one in the genus Anoxypristis.
11872.m: There are only five species of sawfish.

11873.q: What is the basic difference between sawfishes and sawsharks?
a: Sawfishes are rays, sawsharks are true sharks
Sawfishes are bony fish, sawsharks are cartilaginous fish
Sawfishes live in freshwater, sawsharks only in the deep sea
There is no difference, they are two names for the same animal
11873.e: Sawfishes (genera Pristis and Anoxypristis) are rays, while sawsharks (Pristiophorus and Pliotrema) are true sharks. Both developed a saw independently of each other.
11873.m: A sawfish is a ray, a sawshark is a shark.

11874.q: Where are the gill slits in the sawfish, and where are they in the similar-looking sawshark?
a: In the sawfish underneath, in the sawshark at the sides
In the sawfish at the sides, in the sawshark underneath
In both at the sides of the head
11874.e: Like all rays, the sawfish has its five gill slits on the underside. Sawsharks are true sharks and have them at the sides of the neck.
11874.m: Gills underneath mean sawfish, gills at the sides mean sawshark.

11875.q: Which feature on the saw does the sawshark have but the sawfish lack?
a: A light organ at the tip
A movable flap at the end
11875.e: Sawsharks have two long barbels in the middle of their saw, with which they feel the ground. Sawfishes have no barbels on the saw.
11875.m: Only the sawshark has barbels on its saw.

11876.q: How do the teeth on the sawfish's saw differ from those of a sawshark?
