a: They are about the same size
They alternate between large and small
They are hook-shaped and curved backwards
They sit only at the tip
11876.e: In the sawfish, the teeth at the sides of the saw are about the same size. In the sawshark, large and small teeth alternate.
11876.m: Saw teeth of equal size give away the sawfish.

11877.q: What happens when a sawfish loses a tooth on its saw?
a: A tooth from the mouth moves forward
It is replaced by two smaller ones
11877.e: The teeth of the saw keep growing all through life, but lost teeth are not replaced. In the sawshark, by contrast, lost saw teeth grow back.
11877.m: A lost saw tooth does not come back in the sawfish.

11878.q: What did the teeth at the sides of the sawfish's saw develop from?
a: From hardened scales as in bony fish
11878.e: The saw teeth are greatly enlarged, modified skin teeth (placoid scales). They sit in hollows in the cartilage of the saw.
11878.m: The sawfish's saw teeth are enlarged skin teeth.

11879.q: About what share of the total length does the saw (the rostrum) of a sawfish make up?
a: About a quarter to a third
11879.e: Depending on the species and animal, the rostrum is about a quarter to a third as long as the whole fish. In an animal 6 m long, the saw can therefore measure well over 1.5 m.
11879.m: The saw makes up about a quarter to a third of the sawfish.

11880.q: What is the “saw” of a sawfish?
a: A lengthened, flat snout with teeth
11880.e: The saw is the rostrum, a greatly lengthened, flat snout made of cartilage. At the sides, depending on the species, it has about 14 to 37 teeth per side.
11880.m: The sawfish's saw is a lengthened snout.

11881.q: With which sense organs on the saw does the sawfish detect hidden prey?
11881.e: The saw is covered with thousands of ampullae of Lorenzini. With them, the sawfish detects weak electric fields from prey, even in murky water or in sand.
11881.m: The sawfish's saw is also an electric sense organ.

11882.q: From roughly what distance can a sawfish detect prey with its electric sense?
11882.e: Electroreception works only over a short distance. In the sawfish, according to studies, it reaches about 40 cm.
11882.m: The sawfish's electric sense works only over a short distance.

11883.q: How does a sawfish typically use its saw when hunting schools of fish?
a: It swings it sideways through the school
It impales prey with it like a spear
11883.e: With quick sideways strikes, the sawfish injures or stuns fish in the school. It then picks up the prey, often pressing it to the bottom with the saw.
11883.m: The sawfish swings its saw sideways into schools of fish.

11884.q: How does a sawfish usually eat its prey?
a: It saws it into small pieces
11884.e: Sawfishes usually swallow their prey whole. The size of the mouth therefore limits how large the prey animals they can eat are.
11884.m: The sawfish swallows its prey whole.

11885.q: What is mainly on the sawfish's menu?
11885.e: Sawfishes eat mainly fish, as well as crustaceans and molluscs from the bottom. The saw helps them to find and catch their prey.
11885.m: The sawfish eats mainly fish and bottom-dwelling animals.

11886.q: What length can the largest sawfish species, such as the largetooth sawfish, reach?
11886.e: Several species reach about 7 m, and a few reports go up to 7.6 m. This makes sawfishes some of the largest rays of all.
11886.m: The largest sawfishes grow to about seven metres long.

11887.q: How heavy can very large sawfishes get?
11887.e: Large animals of the largest species weigh about 500 to 600 kg. This makes sawfishes some of the heaviest rays of all.
11887.m: A large sawfish weighs several hundred kilograms.

11888.q: At most, how big do sawsharks get compared with the large sawfishes?
11888.e: Sawsharks usually reach at most about 1.5 m. Large sawfishes, by contrast, can grow about 7 m long.
11888.m: Sawsharks are much smaller than large sawfishes.

a: They are ovoviviparous and give birth to live young
They lay egg cases on the seabed
They nourish the young through a placenta
11889.e: The embryos develop in eggs inside the mother and feed on the yolk. They are then born alive.
11889.m: Sawfishes give birth to live young.

11890.q: How many young can a female sawfish give birth to per litter?
11890.e: Litter size is about 1 to 23 young, depending on the species and female. Births take place every year or every two years.
11890.m: A female sawfish has at most about two dozen young.

11891.q: About how long are young sawfishes at birth?
11891.e: Newborn sawfishes measure about 60 to 90 cm. They are therefore already quite big at birth.
11891.m: Young sawfishes are born almost a metre long.

11892.q: What prevents unborn sawfishes from injuring their mother with their saw?
a: The saw is surrounded by a soft sheath
The saw grows only after birth
The young are born tail first without a saw
The saw teeth lie flat in a groove
11892.e: In unborn sawfishes, the saw is flexible and the teeth are enclosed in a sheath. This comes off shortly after birth.
11892.m: A protective sheath around the saw spares the mother at birth.

11893.q: Which special form of reproduction was proved in 2015 in wild smalltooth sawfishes in Florida?
a: Sex change from male to female
11893.e: Genetic studies showed that about 3 per cent of the young examined had come about by virgin birth (parthenogenesis). It was one of the first proofs of this in free-living vertebrates.
11893.m: Some female sawfishes have young without any males.

11894.q: At about what age do sawfishes of the genus Pristis become sexually mature?
a: Just a few weeks after birth
11894.e: Pristis species become sexually mature only at about 7 to 12 years. This late maturity makes the populations especially vulnerable to overfishing.
11894.m: Sawfishes become sexually mature only late.

11895.q: Why do the populations of the large sawfishes recover only very slowly from overfishing?
a: They become sexually mature late and have few young
They lay eggs only every ten years
Their young survive only in coral reefs
11895.e: Pristis species become sexually mature only at about 7 to 12 years and have only a few young per litter. Losses through fishing can therefore hardly be made up.
11895.m: Late maturity and few young: that is why sawfishes recover so slowly.

11896.q: How old can sawfishes of the genus Pristis get, according to estimates?
11896.e: For Pristis species, a lifespan of about 30 to over 50 years is estimated. A smalltooth sawfish lived for over 42 years in human care.
11896.m: Sawfishes can live to be several decades old.

11897.q: At what water depth do sawfishes mostly stay?
a: Mostly at depths of less than 10 m
Mostly at depths of 200 to 500 m
Mostly in the deep sea below 1000 m
Mostly in the open ocean far from the coast
11897.e: Sawfishes live mainly in shallow coastal waters, river mouths and rivers, mostly at depths of less than 10 m. They are only rarely found deeper than 100 m.
11897.m: Sawfishes are inhabitants of shallow water.

11898.q: Which habitat is particularly often used by young sawfishes as a nursery?
a: Shallow mangrove coasts and river mouths
Coral reefs in the open sea
11898.e: Young sawfishes often grow up in shallow water among mangroves and in river mouths. There they find food and protection from large predators.
11898.m: Mangroves are the nursery of many sawfishes.

11899.q: How far upstream in the Amazon has the largetooth sawfish been recorded?
a: All the way to the source in the Andes
11899.e: The largetooth sawfish tolerates freshwater very well. In the Amazon it has been reported about 1340 km inland.
11899.m: The largetooth sawfish swims far into rivers.

11900.q: In which great lake in Central America did well-known populations of the largetooth sawfish once live?
11900.e: Largetooth sawfishes migrated up the Río San Juan into Lake Nicaragua. Because of intensive fishing, they have almost disappeared there today.
11900.m: Sawfishes once even lived in Lake Nicaragua.

11901.q: How many years do young largetooth sawfishes usually spend in the freshwater of rivers?
11901.e: The young usually grow up in rivers for about 3 to 5 years, sometimes several hundred kilometres inland. Adults then live more along the coast.
11901.m: Young largetooth sawfishes grow up in rivers.

11902.q: How can you tell sawfishes from the similar-looking sawsharks at first glance?
a: Their gill slits are on the underside
Their saw has no teeth at all
They have long barbels on the saw
11902.e: In sawfishes, the gill slits are on the underside of the body. Sawsharks have gill slits at the sides and long barbels on the saw.
11902.m: Sawfishes have their gill slits on the underside.

11903.q: What does the sawfish mainly use its saw for?
a: To locate prey and stun it with sideways strikes
To saw holes in coral reefs
11903.e: The saw has many sense organs that detect weak electric fields from prey. With quick sideways strikes, the sawfish stuns or injures fish in a school.
11903.m: The saw is a locating device and a weapon at the same time.

11904.q: Where in the USA does the smalltooth sawfish now live almost exclusively?
11904.e: In the past, the species occurred from Texas to New York. Today, in the USA, it is essentially restricted to the waters of Florida.
11904.m: In the USA, the smalltooth sawfish has its last refuge in Florida.

11905.q: What has applied in the USA since the smalltooth sawfish was placed under the Endangered Species Act in 2003?
a: Catching, killing and trading it is forbidden
It may only be caught with a rod
It may only be kept in aquariums
It may only be fished in winter
11905.e: As an endangered species, the smalltooth sawfish is under strict protection. Animals caught by accident must be released as unharmed as possible.
11905.m: In the USA, the smalltooth sawfish is strictly protected.

11906.q: Which group of fish do the sawfishes belong to, even though they look like sharks?
11906.e: Sawfishes have a shark-like body but belong to the rays. The swordfish, by contrast, is a bony fish, and its sword carries no teeth.
11906.m: The sawfish is a ray with a saw.

11907.q: What status do all five sawfish species have on the IUCN Red List since the reassessment completed in 2023?
11907.e: After a reassessment completed in December 2023 with the narrow sawfish, all five species are regarded as critically endangered. Previously, two species were still classed as endangered.

11908.q: Which country is regarded today as one of the last strongholds of sawfishes?
11908.e: In northern Australia, comparatively many sawfishes still live, and so do they in Florida. According to a study from 2021, they have already disappeared from 46 countries.
11908.m: Northern Australia is one of the last strongholds of sawfishes.

11909.q: According to the 2021 study, what share of their former worldwide coastal range have sawfishes lost?
11909.e: Sawfishes have disappeared from about half of the coastal waters where they used to live.
11909.m: Sawfishes have lost half of their habitat.

11910.q: Why do sawfishes particularly easily become bycatch in fishing?
a: Their saw easily gets tangled in nets
They follow fishing boats because of the waste
They often jump into the boats
11910.e: The toothed saw quickly gets tangled in gill nets and trawl nets. In addition, sawfishes live in shallow coastal waters, where a lot of fishing takes place.
11910.m: The saw proves fatal to the sawfish in fishing nets.

11911.q: In which appendix of the Washington Convention on species protection, CITES, are all sawfishes listed?
a: In Appendix I with a trade ban
In Appendix II with trade control
In Appendix III at the request of individual countries
11911.e: Sawfishes have been listed in Appendix I since 2007, and the largetooth sawfish fully since 2013. International commercial trade is therefore forbidden.
11911.m: Sawfishes may not be traded internationally.

11912.q: For which product are sawfish fins in demand on the market?
11912.e: Sawfish fins are regarded as especially valuable for shark fin soup. This increases the incentive to keep animals that have been caught.
11912.m: The fins make the sawfish valuable to fishermen.

11913.q: For what, among other things, were individual teeth from sawfish saws sold?
11913.e: The hard saw teeth were traded in Peru and Ecuador as artificial spurs for cockfights, in 2014 sometimes for up to 220 US dollars. Whole saws are sold as souvenirs and trophies.
11913.m: Even individual saw teeth are traded at high prices.

11914.q: What does the Ancient Greek word “prístēs”, from which the sawfish's genus name Pristis comes, mean?
11914.e: “Prístēs” means “saw” or “sawyer”. Like the German name, the scientific name therefore describes the striking saw.

11915.q: Since when have sawfishes existed, according to clear fossil finds?
11915.e: Sawfish genera that can be clearly identified are about 60 million years old. Even older finds from the Cretaceous are disputed in their classification.
11915.m: Sawfishes have existed for about 60 million years.

11916.q: Where did archaeologists find dozens of sawfish saws as offerings of an ancient American civilisation?
a: In the Aztec Templo Mayor in Mexico City
11916.e: In the Aztec Templo Mayor, a total of 77 saws had been found by 2018, among other places in an offering from the time of the ruler Ahuitzotl. For the Aztecs, the sawfish linked earth and sea.
11916.m: The Aztecs sacrificed saws of sawfishes.

11917.q: How often had sawfishes been successfully bred in human care by 2023?
11917.e: Until then, breeding had succeeded only twice: in 2012 in the Bahamas with four young smalltooth sawfishes and in 2023 at SeaWorld Orlando with three young.
11917.m: Sawfishes can hardly be bred in human care.

11918.q: Which animals leave bite marks on about 60 per cent of young sawfishes in Australia's Fitzroy River?
11918.e: Studies in the Fitzroy River showed that about 60 per cent of the young bore bite marks from bull sharks or crocodiles. The saw is also used to defend against such enemies.
11918.m: Young sawfishes are hunted by bull sharks and crocodiles.

11919.q: Why has there been an international Sawfish Day every year since 2017?
a: Because all sawfish species are threatened with extinction
Because the first species was discovered on this day
Because the sawfishes then migrate into the rivers
Because trade was allowed again on this day
11919.e: Sawfish Day is held each year on 17 October. It is meant to draw attention to the severely threatened animals and their protection.
11919.m: Sawfish Day draws attention to the threatened animals.

11920.q: Despite its name, is the electric eel a true eel?
a: No, it belongs to the South American knifefishes
Yes, it is a freshwater relative of the European eel
No, it is a water snake
No, it is an amphibian like the newt
11920.e: The electric eel is a bony fish from the order of New World knifefishes. It is not closely related to true eels such as the European eel; it just looks similar to them.
11920.m: The electric eel is a knifefish and not a true eel.

11921.q: On which continent does the electric eel live in the wild?
11921.e: Electric eels live in freshwater in the north of South America, mainly in the Amazon and Orinoco regions. In Africa, another electric fish lives, the electric catfish.
11921.m: The electric eel is a South American.

11922.q: With which group of fish is the electric eel more closely related than with true eels?
11922.e: Like catfishes and carp-like fishes, the knifefishes belong to the superorder Ostariophysi. The catfishes are regarded as the sister group of the knifefishes.
11922.m: The electric eel is more a relative of the catfishes than of the eels.

11923.q: How many species of electric eel have been distinguished since the revision of 2019?
11923.e: In 2019, a research team led by C. David de Santana split the one species known until then into Electrophorus electricus, E. voltai and E. varii.
11923.m: Since 2019, there have been three species of electric eel.

11924.q: What distinguishes most other New World knifefishes from the electric eel?
a: They produce only weak electric fields
They live exclusively in the sea
11924.e: Almost all New World knifefishes, such as the genus Gymnotus, use only weak discharges for orientation and communication. The electric eel is the only one in this order that gives strong shocks for hunting and defence.
11924.m: Among the knifefishes, only the electric eel is a strong producer of electricity.

11925.q: What peak voltage was measured in Volta's electric eel (Electrophorus voltai)?
11925.e: With about 860 volts, Electrophorus voltai holds the record for the strongest known electric discharge of any animal. The old record was about 650 volts.
11925.m: About 860 volts is the record of Volta's electric eel.

11926.q: Why is a shock from an electric eel dangerous to a human even though it lasts only a very short time?
a: A voltage of several hundred volts can paralyse, and you can drown
The shock burns the skin down to the bones
The electric eel injects poison at the same time
The shock makes you blind for ever
11926.e: Depending on the species, electric eels produce about 480 to 860 volts. A shock can make muscles cramp, so that a person in the water can fall and drown.
11926.m: An electric eel's shock is dangerous mainly in the water.

11927.q: One electric eel species honours the inventor of the first battery. What is it called?
11927.e: The Italian physicist Alessandro Volta built the first battery, the voltaic pile, around 1800. The species Electrophorus voltai, described in 2019, honours him.
11927.m: Volta's electric eel bears the name of the inventor of the battery.

11928.q: What decides to whom a newly discovered animal species such as Electrophorus varii is dedicated?
a: The researchers who describe it choose the name
The country in which it lives decides it
11928.e: Whoever describes a species scientifically may choose the name according to fixed rules. Electrophorus varii honours the fish researcher Richard Vari of the Smithsonian.
11928.m: New species are often named after distinguished researchers.

11929.q: How many electric eel species are distinguished since the 2019 reassessment based on genetics and voltage?
a: Three species in different regions of South America
A single species in all of South America
Two species, one in the sea and one in freshwater
11929.e: In 2019, the electric eel was divided into three species: Electrophorus electricus on the Guiana Shield, E. voltai on the Brazilian Shield and E. varii in the Amazon lowlands.
11929.m: There are three electric eel species in different regions of South America.

11930.q: In which waters does the electric eel live?
a: In freshwater such as rivers and swamps
11930.e: Electric eels inhabit rivers, streams, floodplains and swamps of South America. They do not go into the sea.
11930.m: The electric eel is a freshwater fish.

11931.q: Which waters does the electric eel Electrophorus varii typically inhabit?
a: Cold highland lakes of the Andes
11931.e: Electrophorus varii lives in the Amazon lowlands in slow-flowing, murky water with little oxygen and a muddy or sandy bottom.
11931.m: Electrophorus varii likes murky, low-oxygen lowland water.

11932.q: By which method did researchers recognise in 2019 that there is more than one electric eel species?
a: By genetic analyses and comparisons of body build and voltage
With satellite images of the rivers
11932.e: The team compared DNA, body features and the measured voltage of over 100 animals. This showed that three separate lines exist, which split from each other millions of years ago.

11933.q: Which naturalist introduced the two-part scientific names for animals such as the electric eel?
11933.e: In the 18th century, Carl Linnaeus established binomial nomenclature, made up of a genus name and a species name. He described the electric eel in 1766 as Gymnotus electricus.
11933.m: Linnaeus gave living things double names made up of genus and species.

11934.q: What does a scientific species name such as Electrophorus electricus consist of?
a: A genus name and a species epithet
A family name and a country name
The first name and surname of the discoverer
11934.e: The first part names the genus, the second the species. The genus Electrophorus was created in 1864 specially for the electric eel.
11934.m: A species name consists of a genus and a species epithet.

11935.q: What does the genus name Electrophorus of the electric eel mean?
11935.e: The name comes from Greek: “elektron” and “phoros”, which means “bearing”.

11936.q: What length can a large electric eel reach?
11936.e: Large electric eels grow about 2 metres long, and maximum figures give about 2.5 metres.
11936.m: A large electric eel can be longer than a person is tall.

11937.q: How heavy can a large electric eel get?
11937.e: A maximum weight of about 20 kilograms is given for electric eels.
11937.m: A large electric eel weighs about as much as a school-age child.

11938.q: Which sex grows bigger in the electric eel?
11938.e: Males are clearly bigger than females. They become sexually mature only at about 1.2 metres, females already at about 70 centimetres.
11938.m: In the electric eel, the males are the giants.

11939.q: What share of the body length is taken up by electric organs in the electric eel?
11939.e: The vital organs lie in the short front part of the body. The long tail section consists largely of electric organs.
11939.m: The electric eel is mostly a living power station.

11940.q: How many different electric organs does the electric eel have?
11940.e: The electric eel has three paired electric organs: the large main organ, the Hunter's organ and the Sachs' organ. They produce strong shocks or weak locating pulses.
11940.m: The electric eel has three different electric organs.

11941.q: What is the Sachs' organ of the electric eel mainly used for?
11941.e: The Sachs' organ produces weak discharges of about 10 volts. They probably serve for orientation and communication.
11941.m: With the Sachs' organ, the electric eel scans its surroundings electrically.

11942.q: Why do organs of the electric eel have names such as Hunter's organ or Sachs' organ?
a: They are named after researchers who studied them
They are named after places in South America
They are brand names of batteries
They are named after their shape
11942.e: The Hunter's organ honours the Scottish surgeon John Hunter, who studied the electric eel in 1775. The Sachs' organ is named after the physiologist Carl Sachs.
11942.m: Many body parts are named after their researchers.

11943.q: From which tissue did the electric eel's electrocytes develop?
11943.e: Electrocytes are modified muscle cells that no longer contract but produce voltage.
11943.m: The electric eel's battery cells were originally muscles.

11944.q: A single electrocyte of the electric eel delivers only a little over 0.1 volt. How does it still reach hundreds of volts?
a: Thousands of cells are connected in series
The cells are charged by sunlight
It stores electricity from the water
A single giant cell amplifies the voltage
11944.e: In the main organ, about 6000 electrocytes lie in a row. As with batteries in series, their voltages add up.
11944.m: Cells connected in series add up their voltage.

11945.q: What does the electric eel mainly use its strong electric shocks for?
a: To paralyse prey and for defence
To attract partners over long distances
11945.e: With strong shocks of several hundred volts and about one ampere, the electric eel paralyses fish and fends off enemies. For orientation, it uses weak pulses.
11945.m: Strong shocks serve for hunting and defence.

11946.q: How does an electric eel deliver its electric shocks when attacking?
a: In fast volleys of many short pulses
As a single continuous current lasting minutes
11946.e: When attacking, the main organ fires volleys of up to about 500 pulses per second. Each single pulse lasts only about 2 milliseconds.
11946.m: The electric eel fires its shocks in fast volleys.

11947.q: How does the electric eel get most of its oxygen?
a: It gulps air at the surface
It takes it in through its gills
It stores it in its swim bladder
11947.e: The electric eel is an obligate air breather. It takes in almost 80 per cent of its oxygen through the heavily supplied mucous membrane of its mouth.
11947.m: Without air from the surface, an electric eel would drown.

11948.q: Which fin mainly drives the electric eel when it swims?
11948.e: An anal fin with several hundred rays runs along almost the whole underside. Its wave-like movement lets it swim forwards and backwards.
11948.m: The electric eel swims with an undulating anal fin.

11949.q: Which fins does the electric eel lack?
11949.e: The electric eel has only pectoral fins and the long anal fin. This allows it to keep its body straight when swimming, which is important for electrolocation.
11949.m: An electric eel manages without dorsal and tail fins.

11950.q: What is the electric eel's skin like?
11950.e: The electric eel has no body scales. Only along the lateral line are there small scales.
11950.m: The electric eel has almost no scales.

11951.q: How does the electric eel mainly find its way around with its very small eyes?
11951.e: Its eyes are very small and its eyesight is weak. With weak fields and electroreceptors in its skin, it scans its surroundings.
11951.m: The electric eel sees its world mainly electrically.

11952.q: What do the short double pulses that an electric eel gives off above hidden prey do?
a: The prey twitches and gives itself away
The prey is killed at once
The prey is stunned and cooked
11952.e: Kenneth Catania showed in 2014 that such double pulses trigger involuntary muscle twitches. The movement reveals the hiding place to the electric eel.
11952.m: With double pulses, the electric eel makes hidden prey twitch.

11953.q: How does the electric eel paralyse its prey with high-voltage volleys?
a: It stops its heart with heat
It poisons it through the skin
It destroys its eyes with light
11953.e: The volleys activate the nerves leading to the muscles. As a result, the prey cramps and cannot flee, similar to a stun gun.
11953.m: The electric eel remote-controls the muscles of its prey.

11954.q: Why does an electric eel curl around large prey?
11954.e: By bringing its head and tail close together, the prey lies between the two poles. This concentrates the field and strengthens the effect.
11954.m: Curled up, the electric eel becomes a battery twice as strong.

11955.q: What do electric eels sometimes do when threatened, as Kenneth Catania described in 2016?
a: They leap out of the water at the attacker
They bury themselves in the mud
They release a cloud of ink
11955.e: An electric eel can press itself up the attacker and send the current straight into its body. In this way, the shock works much more strongly than in the water.
11955.m: Threatened electric eels also attack above the water surface.

11956.q: Which researcher described around 1800 in Venezuela how electric eels attacked horses?
11956.e: Humboldt reported how locals drove horses into a pool. The electric eels attacked, and several horses were stunned and drowned.
11956.m: Humboldt witnessed the fight between electric eels and horses.

11957.q: Which physicist studied the electrical properties of an electric eel from Suriname in London in 1839?
11957.e: Michael Faraday experimented at length with an electric eel. He compared one strong shock with the discharge of a battery of 15 Leyden jars.
11957.m: Faraday, too, learned from an electric eel.

11958.q: What did Alessandro Volta call his pile, which was inspired by electric fish such as the electric eel?
11958.e: Volta took his lead from the stacked cells of electric fish and called his invention the “organe électrique artificiel”.
11958.m: The first battery imitated the organs of electric fish.

11959.q: What did researchers observe in Volta's electric eel on the Rio Iriri in Brazil in 2021?
11959.e: Over 100 electric eels herded schools of small tetras together and attacked them jointly with electric shocks. Until then, electric eels were thought to be solitary hunters.
11959.m: Volta's electric eels can hunt in packs.

11960.q: What does the male electric eel build its nest from?
11960.e: In the dry season, the male builds a hidden foam nest from saliva, in which the female lays the eggs.
11960.m: The electric eel builds its nest from saliva.

11961.q: In which season does the electric eel reproduce?
11961.e: Reproduction takes place in the dry season, in parts of the range from about September to December.
11961.m: Electric eels spawn in the dry season.

11962.q: On average, how many young hatch from an electric eel nest?
11962.e: Field observations gave an average of about 1200 hatched young fish per nest. Females can produce up to about 17,000 eggs.
11962.m: An electric eel nest produces over a thousand young.

11963.q: Which parent guards the nest and young in the electric eel?
11963.e: The male energetically defends the nest and young fish, and the parental care can last several months.
11963.m: In the electric eel, the father is the protector.

11964.q: What do newly hatched electric eel larvae feed on first?
a: On eggs laid later in the nest
On algae at the bottom of the water
11964.e: The larvae eat left-over eggs from later clutches in the nest. Only later do they switch to other food.
11964.m: Young electric eels first eat their unhatched siblings.

11965.q: What do adult electric eels mainly feed on?
11965.e: Adult electric eels eat mainly fish, such as armoured catfish and cichlids. Young ones feed mainly on small invertebrates.
11965.m: The adult electric eel is a fish hunter.

11966.q: What status does the electric eel Electrophorus electricus have on the IUCN Red List?
11966.e: The IUCN classes Electrophorus electricus as least concern. The two species described in 2019 have so far been little studied.
11966.m: The electric eel is currently regarded as not threatened.

11967.q: How old can electric eels get in human care?
11967.e: In zoos and aquariums, electric eels have lived for more than 20 years. Their age in the wild is hardly known.
11967.m: In an aquarium, an electric eel can get older than 20.

11968.q: What did the genome analysis of the electric eel show in 2014?
a: Electric organs arose several times independently
Electric eels descend from moray eels
The electric eel has the largest fish genome
11968.e: A team led by Jason Gallant showed that electric organs arose independently in six fish lineages, with similar genetic mechanisms.
11968.m: Evolution invented electric organs several times.

11969.q: For which research were the electric eel's electric organs especially important?
a: Research on ion channels in nerves
11969.e: The electric organs contain very many sodium channels. In 1984, the gene of a voltage-gated sodium channel was decoded from them for the first time.
11969.m: The electric eel helped us understand nerve conduction.

11970.q: Which fish family do the seahorses (genus Hippocampus) belong to?
11970.e: Within the family Syngnathidae, seahorses form the genus Hippocampus. The same family also includes pipefishes and leafy sea dragons.
11970.m: Seahorses are close relatives of the pipefishes.

11971.q: Which order are the seahorses assigned to?
11971.e: The family Syngnathidae with the seahorses belongs to the order Syngnathiformes. It also includes trumpetfishes and cornetfishes.
11971.m: Seahorses belong to the order Syngnathiformes.

11972.q: What does the genus name Hippocampus of the seahorses mean literally?
11972.e: The name comes from Ancient Greek: “hippos” means horse and “kampos” sea monster. In Greek mythology, the hippocampus was a sea creature with the front of a horse.
11972.m: Hippocampus means horse and sea monster when translated.

11973.q: Which region of the human brain was named after the seahorse because of its shape?
11973.e: In the 16th century, the anatomist Giulio Cesare Aranzi compared the curved structure in the temporal lobe with a seahorse. The hippocampus is central to memory and orientation.
11973.m: The hippocampus in the brain bears the name of the seahorse.

11975.q: Where is the male's brood pouch in most seahorses?
a: On the underside at the front part of the tail
On the back behind the head
11975.e: The brood pouch sits on the underside at the transition to the tail. Only in the tiny pygmy seahorses that live on corals is the brood chamber in the trunk.
11975.m: The seahorse's brood pouch is at the front of the tail.

11976.q: Roughly how long does the pregnancy in a male seahorse's brood pouch last, depending on species and temperature?
11976.e: Depending on species and water temperature, development in the brood pouch takes about 9 to 45 days, often about two to four weeks. Warmer water speeds up development.
11976.m: A male seahorse is pregnant for a few weeks.

11977.q: How many young does a male seahorse typically release at one birth?
11977.e: Typically it is about 100 to 1000 young per birth, and in large species considerably more. At birth, the young are tiny, fully developed seahorses.
11977.m: A seahorse father often gives birth to hundreds of young.

11978.q: What share of young seahorses is estimated to reach adulthood?
11978.e: The young are released into open water without further parental care and are often eaten there. Fewer than half a per cent survive to sexual maturity.
11978.m: Very few young seahorses grow up.

11979.q: Which fin do seahorses lack, unlike most fish?
a: The anal fin in all young
11979.e: Seahorses have no tail fin. Instead they have a prehensile tail, with which they hold on to seagrass or corals.
11979.m: Instead of a tail fin, the seahorse has a prehensile tail.

11981.q: What does a seahorse mainly use its pectoral fins for?
11981.e: The pectoral fins sit at the sides of the head and serve mainly for steering and stabilising. Propulsion comes from the rapidly beating dorsal fin.
11981.m: The seahorse steers with its pectoral fins.

11982.q: Which seahorse species is regarded as the slowest fish in the world?
11982.e: The dwarf seahorse from the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean manages only about 1.5 metres per hour. It is therefore regarded as the slowest known fish.
11982.m: The dwarf seahorse is the slowest fish in the world.

11983.q: Roughly how fast does the dwarf seahorse swim?
11983.e: The dwarf seahorse from the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean manages at most about 1.5 metres per hour. It is therefore regarded as the slowest known fish.
11983.m: A dwarf seahorse swims only about a metre and a half per hour.

11984.q: Besides protecting the embryos, what task does the male seahorse's brood pouch take on?
a: It supplies them with oxygen and regulates the salt content
It warms the eggs by muscle shivering
It dyes the young for camouflage
It filters plankton as food for the young
11984.e: The brood pouch supplies the embryos with oxygen, and the salt content of the fluid in it is regulated. The male also gives off nutrients such as fats and calcium.
11984.m: The male's brood pouch supplies the embryos with oxygen.

11985.q: What shape is the cross-section of a seahorse's prehensile tail?
11985.e: The tail is almost square in cross-section. Researchers found that this shape makes it more stable and more resistant to crushing when gripping.
11985.m: The seahorse's tail is angular in cross-section.

11986.q: Which digestive organ does the seahorse lack?
11986.e: Seahorses have no true stomach, and food passes through the intestine very quickly. That is why they have to eat almost constantly.
11986.m: Without a stomach, the seahorse has to eat very often.

11987.q: What are a seahorse's jaws like?
11987.e: Seahorses have toothless jaws at the end of a tube-like snout. They suck in their prey whole.
11987.m: A seahorse eats entirely without teeth.

11988.q: What is the main food of seahorses?
a: Small crustaceans such as copepods and mysid shrimps
11988.e: Seahorses eat mainly tiny crustaceans from the plankton, such as copepods and mysid shrimps. They mostly lie in wait for them motionless.

11989.q: What is the hunting technique called in which a seahorse jerks its head upwards and sucks in prey?
a: Ambush hunting with a poison spine
11989.e: In pivot feeding, the seahorse rotates its head upwards in a flash and creates suction in its tube-like snout. In this way, the prey is sucked in.
11989.m: The seahorse snaps up prey with a lightning-fast tilt of its head.

11990.q: According to a study from 2013, how long does a dwarf seahorse take for one strike at prey?
a: About a thousandth of a second
11990.e: In pivot feeding, the seahorse rotates its head upwards in about a millisecond and sucks in the prey. That is faster than a copepod can flee.
11990.m: A seahorse snaps up prey faster than its prey can react.

11991.q: Why do copepods often fail to notice a seahorse sneaking up on them?
a: The shape of its head creates hardly any water movement in front of the snout
The seahorse paralyses them with poison
The seahorse attracts them with light
The seahorse is transparent like glass
11991.e: The shape of the seahorse's head creates an almost flow-free zone in front of the snout. The little crustaceans therefore feel no pressure wave and do not flee in time.
11991.m: The seahorse's head sneaks up almost without making waves.

11992.q: According to measurements, roughly what is the dwarf seahorse's capture success rate in calm water?
11992.e: In calm water, the dwarf seahorse succeeds in about 90 per cent of its capture attempts. That is one of the highest values measured in fish.
11992.m: The seahorse is an extremely successful hunter.

11993.q: What is special about the seahorse's eyes?
a: They can move independently of each other
They are covered by a bony plate
11993.e: Like a chameleon, the seahorse can move its eyes independently of each other. In this way, it looks for prey and enemies in different directions at the same time.
11993.m: The seahorse looks in a different direction with each eye.

11994.q: What is the crown-like structure on a seahorse's head called?
11994.e: The coronet is a bony outgrowth on the head. Its shape differs from species to species and also between individual animals.
11994.m: Every seahorse wears a coronet on its head.

11995.q: Which seahorse species, at up to about 35 cm long, is among the largest?
11995.e: The big-belly seahorse lives off southern Australia and New Zealand and grows up to about 35 cm long. Its bulging belly is typical.
11995.m: The big-belly seahorse is a giant among seahorses.

11996.q: Which species, at only about 1.5 cm long, is among the smallest seahorses?
11996.e: Denise's pygmy seahorse grows only about 1.3 to 2 cm long. It lives well camouflaged on gorgonians in the western Pacific.
11996.m: Denise's pygmy seahorse is hardly bigger than a fingernail.

11997.q: Which species, at no more than about 1.4 cm long, is regarded as one of the smallest known seahorses?
11997.e: Satomi's pygmy seahorse grows only about 1.4 cm long and is regarded as the smallest known seahorse. It lives in coral reefs of Indonesia and Malaysia.
11997.m: Satomi's pygmy seahorse is hardly bigger than a fingernail.

11998.q: How was Bargibant's pygmy seahorse discovered in 1969?
a: While examining a collected gorgonian in the laboratory
On a deep-sea expedition with a submarine
In the stomach of a caught tuna
At a fish market in Japan
11998.e: Georges Bargibant collected gorgonians in New Caledonia for a museum. Only in the laboratory did people notice the perfectly camouflaged pygmy seahorses on them.
11998.m: Bargibant's pygmy seahorse was so well camouflaged that it was overlooked at first.

11999.q: How many gill openings do pygmy seahorses such as Hippocampus bargibanti have?
a: A single one at the back of the head
Two at the sides of the head
None, they breathe through the skin
11999.e: In pygmy seahorses, the gill openings have fused into a single opening at the back of the head. Larger seahorses have two openings at the sides of the head.
11999.m: Pygmy seahorses breathe through a single gill opening.

12000.q: What do tiny pygmy seahorses such as Hippocampus bargibanti live on?
a: On the backs of sea turtles
12000.e: Pygmy seahorses live on gorgonians and match their colour and little bumps almost perfectly. That is why they were overlooked for a long time.

12001.q: Which two seahorse species occur naturally on European coasts?
a: The short-snouted and the long-snouted seahorse
The big-belly and the dwarf seahorse
The Knysna and the tigertail seahorse
The yellow seahorse and Denise's pygmy seahorse
12001.e: On Europe's coasts live the short-snouted seahorse (Hippocampus hippocampus) and the long-snouted seahorse (Hippocampus guttulatus). Both occur in the Mediterranean and the north-eastern Atlantic.
12001.m: Europe has a short-snouted and a long-snouted seahorse.

12002.q: How did the seahorse Hippocampus fuscus get from the Red Sea into the Mediterranean?
12002.e: Hippocampus fuscus is a so-called Lessepsian migrant. It moved from the Red Sea into the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal.
12002.m: Some seahorses came into the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal.

12003.q: Which habitats do many seahorses prefer?
a: Seagrass meadows, mangroves and coral reefs
Open high seas at great depth
Sandy deserts of the seabed with no growth
12003.e: Seahorses mostly live in shallow, sheltered coastal waters with plant growth. There they find a hold for their prehensile tail and cover from enemies.
12003.m: Seahorses need plants or corals to hold on to.

12004.q: In which region of the world do particularly many seahorse species live in temperate waters?
a: Off southern Australia and New Zealand
12004.e: Many species of the temperate latitudes occur off southern Australia and New Zealand. Overall, seahorses live in tropical and temperate seas worldwide.
12004.m: Australia is a hotspot for seahorses.

12005.q: Which seahorse species lives only in a few estuaries in South Africa and is regarded as severely threatened?
12005.e: The Knysna seahorse occurs only in a few estuaries on the south coast of South Africa. The IUCN classes it as endangered.
12005.m: The Knysna seahorse lives in only a few lagoons in South Africa.

12006.q: Since when has the Washington Convention on species protection, CITES, regulated trade in all seahorses?
a: Since their inclusion in Appendix II in 2002
Since the founding of CITES in 1975
12006.e: In 2002, the whole genus Hippocampus was included in Appendix II of CITES, and the rule came into force in 2004. Since then, international trade has been allowed only with proof of sustainability.
12006.m: Trade in seahorses is controlled by CITES.

12007.q: What is a large part of the traded seahorses used for when dried?
12007.e: Dried seahorses are in demand in traditional Chinese medicine. Millions of animals are caught for this every year.
12007.m: Dried seahorses often end up in traditional medicine.

12008.q: How are most seahorses caught worldwide?
a: As bycatch of bottom trawl fishing
12008.e: A large share of seahorses end up as bycatch in trawl nets, especially in shrimp fishing. The animals are then often sold dried.
12008.m: Trawl nets catch many seahorses on the side.

12009.q: Which organisation researches and protects seahorses worldwide and was co-founded by Amanda Vincent?
12009.e: Project Seahorse was founded in 1996 by Amanda Vincent and Heather Koldewey. The organisation researches seahorses and campaigns for marine conservation.
12009.m: Project Seahorse fights for the protection of seahorses.

12010.q: What special feature did the genome of the tigertail seahorse, decoded in 2016, show?
a: It has changed particularly fast in the course of evolution
It is identical to the genome of pipefishes
It is the largest genome of all animals
It contains genes from land horses
12010.e: The tigertail seahorse's genome was published in “Nature” in 2016. It showed that the seahorse genome has changed particularly fast, which fits their unusual body build.
12010.m: The seahorse genome has changed particularly fast.

12011.q: According to the 2016 genome study, what explains why seahorses have no pelvic fins?
a: They lack a gene that forms the pelvic fins in other fish
They shed their pelvic fins after hatching
The pelvic fins have fused into the brood pouch
They bite each other's pelvic fins off
12011.e: The seahorse lacks the gene tbx4, which is involved in forming the pelvic fins in other fish. In land vertebrates, it controls the development of the hind legs.
12011.m: Without a particular gene, the seahorse has no pelvic fins.

12012.q: Which genes has the seahorse lost, according to genome research, which fits its toothless mouth?
12012.e: The genome study showed that seahorses have lost important genes for tooth enamel proteins. This explains why they do not form teeth.
12012.m: Seahorses have lost the genes for teeth.

12013.q: Roughly how old are the oldest known seahorse fossils from Slovenia?
12013.e: The fossils Hippocampus sarmaticus and Hippocampus slovenicus from the Tunjice Hills in Slovenia date from the middle Miocene. They are about 13 million years old.
12013.m: Seahorses have existed for at least 13 million years.

12014.q: How many eggs can a female seahorse transfer into the male's brood pouch, depending on the species?
12014.e: Depending on the species, the female transfers a few dozen to about 1500 eggs. The eggs are fertilised only in the male's brood pouch.
12014.m: A female seahorse puts many eggs into the male's pouch.

12015.q: How quickly can a male seahorse take on new eggs again after a birth during the breeding season?
a: Often after only hours to a few days
At the earliest after about a year
Not at all, it breeds only once in its life
12015.e: The male usually gives birth at night and can often take over eggs from the female again the next morning during the breeding season. Several broods per season are therefore possible.
12015.m: A seahorse father is often pregnant again soon after giving birth.

12016.q: What do seahorse pairs of some species do every morning during the breeding season?
a: They greet each other with a short dance
They build a nest of seagrass together
12016.e: In some species, the partners greet each other daily with a short dance, in which they brighten their colour and circle each other. This strengthens the pair bond during the breeding season.
12016.m: Many seahorses stay together for a season.

12017.q: How do rival male seahorses fight over a female?
a: They wrestle with their tails and snap with their heads
They ram each other with spines full of poison
They spit jets of water at each other
They do not fight at all, the female chooses only by colour
12017.e: Research by Amanda Vincent showed that males wrestle with their tails and snap at the rival with their snouts. This is how they compete for females.
12017.m: Male seahorses wrestle with their tails.

12018.q: With which adaptation does a seahorse mainly protect itself from predators?
a: Camouflage by changing colour and skin appendages
12018.e: Seahorses can adapt their colour to their surroundings, and some species also have skin filaments. Since they are slow, camouflage is their most important protection.
12018.m: The seahorse hides instead of fleeing.

12019.q: How does a seahorse control its rising and sinking in the water?
a: By changing the volume of gas in its swim bladder
By breathing air in and out at the surface
By taking sand into its intestine
12019.e: The swim bladder works like a buoyancy jacket. By adjusting the amount of gas, the seahorse rises or sinks while staying upright.
12019.m: The seahorse moves up and down with its swim bladder.

12020.q: Which group of bony fish do today's coelacanths of the genus Latimeria belong to?
12020.e: Like the lungfishes, coelacanths belong to the lobe-finned fishes. Their fins sit on fleshy stalks supported by bones.
12020.m: The coelacanth is a lobe-finned fish with stalked fins.

12021.q: How many living species of the coelacanth genus Latimeria are known?
12021.e: There is the Comoran coelacanth (Latimeria chalumnae) and the Indonesian coelacanth (Latimeria menadoensis). All other coelacanths are known only as fossils.
12021.m: Only two species of coelacanth are alive today.

12022.q: Why was the catch of a living coelacanth off South Africa in 1938 a sensation?
a: Coelacanths had been thought extinct for about 66 million years
It was the biggest fish ever caught
It could breathe and walk on land
It was the first fish with bones
12022.e: Coelacanths were known only from fossils, the youngest from the time of the dinosaurs. The catch shortly before Christmas 1938 was regarded as the zoological sensation of the 20th century.
12022.m: Until 1938, the coelacanth was thought to have died out long ago.

12023.q: Which museum curator was the first to recognise in 1938 that the coelacanth that had been caught was something special?
12023.e: Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer was curator at the museum in East London (South Africa). She had the fish secured and informed an expert.
12023.m: Without Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, the coelacanth might have ended up in the rubbish.

12024.q: Why is the coelacanth called a “living fossil”?
a: It closely resembles ancestors that were known only as fossils
It can turn to stone and come back to life
It lives in petrified coral reefs
It lives to be several thousand years old
12024.e: Today's coelacanth looks very similar to its fossil relatives from prehistoric times. That is why it is regarded as a living fossil, even though it has developed further in details.
12024.m: The coelacanth is regarded as a living fossil.

12025.q: Roughly how old are the oldest known fossils of coelacanths?
12025.e: The oldest coelacanths date from the Devonian, the Age of Fishes. They therefore lived long before the dinosaurs.
12025.m: Coelacanths have existed for about 400 million years.

12026.q: Why could the gills and inner skeleton of the first coelacanth of 1938 not be examined?
a: It was stuffed and the innards were thrown away.
It was sold by the fisherman and eaten.
It fell apart completely during transport.
It was immediately petrified in formalin.
12026.e: For lack of refrigeration, the fish was handed to a taxidermist and stuffed. Only a second specimen 14 years later allowed the inner anatomy to be examined.
12026.m: Because the first coelacanth was stuffed, its organs remained a mystery.

12027.q: Where was the second coelacanth found in 1952, which cleared up the origin of the species?
12027.e: A fisherman caught it near the Comoran island of Anjouan. This made it clear that the Comoros are the main range of the species.
12027.m: The second coelacanth led the researchers to the Comoros.

12028.q: What did the South African prime minister make a military aircraft available for in 1952?
a: To fetch the second coelacanth from the Comoros
To search for coelacanths in the sea
To bring fossils to the USA
To arrest fishermen in the Comoros
12028.e: J. L. B. Smith wanted to secure the freshly caught fish as quickly as possible. Prime Minister Malan had him flown to the Comoros in a military aircraft.
12028.m: For the second coelacanth, a military aircraft flew to the Comoros.

12029.q: How did the fishermen in the Comoros see the coelacanth long before science knew it?
a: As a rare, not very tasty bycatch
As a sacred animal that must never be caught
As an expensive delicacy for feasts
12029.e: The fishermen knew the coelacanth under the name “gombessa”. It occasionally ended up on their hooks, but was regarded as a poor food fish.
12029.m: In the Comoros, the coelacanth was long known as the gombessa.

12030.q: What does the local name “raja laut” for the Indonesian coelacanth mean?
12030.e: In North Sulawesi, the fish is called “raja laut”, which translates as “king of the sea”.
12030.m: The Indonesians call the coelacanth the king of the sea.

12031.q: Where did a marine biologist discover the first Indonesian coelacanth in 1997?
a: At a fish market on Sulawesi
On a deep-sea expedition with a robot
12031.e: The marine biologist Mark Erdmann noticed the fish at a market in Manado on his honeymoon. He obtained a second specimen in 1998.
12031.m: The Indonesian coelacanth was discovered at a fish market.

12032.q: What does the species name “menadoensis” of the Indonesian coelacanth refer to?
a: To the city of Manado on Sulawesi
12032.e: The Indonesian coelacanth was described in 1999 as Latimeria menadoensis. The name recalls Manado, where it was discovered at the fish market.
12032.m: The name menadoensis refers to the city of Manado.

12033.q: By what does the Indonesian coelacanth differ most clearly in appearance from the Comoran coelacanth?
a: By its body length, twice as great
12033.e: The Comoran coelacanth is deep blue with pale spots. The Indonesian coelacanth is brownish-grey with golden speckles.
12033.m: The Indonesian coelacanth wears brown instead of blue.

12034.q: According to a genetic study from 2005, about how long have the lines of the Comoran and the Indonesian coelacanth been separated?
12034.e: A study in 2005 compared the genetic material of the two species. From it, researchers estimated a split about 30 to 40 million years ago.
12034.m: The two coelacanth species have gone their separate ways for many millions of years.

12035.q: What maximum body length can a female Comoran coelacanth reach?
12035.e: Females grow up to about 2 metres long, while males stay somewhat smaller at about 1.7 metres.
12035.m: In the coelacanth, the females are the bigger ones.

12036.q: How heavy can very large Comoran coelacanths get?
12036.e: The heaviest documented animal weighed about 95 kilograms. The females are clearly heavier than the males.
12036.m: A large coelacanth weighs as much as a strong person.

12037.q: What does the group name “coelacanth” mean literally from Greek?
12037.e: It is made up of “koilos” (hollow) and “akantha” (spine). It refers to the hollow fin rays, which were already noticed on fossils.
12037.m: Coelacanth means hollow spine when translated.

12038.q: How many fins does a coelacanth have in total?
12038.e: It has two dorsal fins, two pectoral fins, two pelvic fins, one anal fin and one tail fin.
12038.m: With eight fins, the coelacanth is well equipped.

12039.q: What special feature does the coelacanth's tail fin show?
a: It has a small extra middle lobe.
It is strongly asymmetrical as in sharks.
It has been reshaped into a sucker.
12039.e: The tail fin has three parts: a small middle lobe sticks out between the upper and lower lobes. This shape is typical of coelacanths.
12039.m: The coelacanth's tail ends in three lobes.

12040.q: How does the coelacanth move its paired pectoral and pelvic fins when swimming?
a: Diagonally in alternation, like land vertebrates move their legs
All at once like a frog
Not at all, they lie close to the body
Only the pectoral fins beat like wings
12040.e: Researchers observed that the fins move in a diagonal gait, similar to a trotting horse. Even so, the coelacanth does not walk on the seabed.
12040.m: The coelacanth swims in a diagonal gait but never walks.

12041.q: What largely replaces the bony backbone in the coelacanth?
a: A strand of solid bony vertebrae
A row of limy plates in the skin
An air-filled tube in the back
12041.e: Instead of ossified vertebral bodies, it has a thick, hollow notochord filled with fluid that supports the body.
12041.m: Instead of a solid backbone, the coelacanth has an oil-filled notochord.

12042.q: What is the rostral organ in the coelacanth's snout probably for?
a: It produces light to attract prey.
12042.e: The jelly-filled organ probably serves for electroreception. In this way, the fish can locate prey in the dark.
12042.m: With the rostral organ, the coelacanth senses the electricity of its prey.

12043.q: Which unique joint in the skull does the coelacanth have as the only living vertebrate?
a: A joint that divides the skull into a front and a back part
A joint between gills and heart
A ball-and-socket joint between skull and pectoral fin
A joint between the two eye sockets
12043.e: The intracranial joint makes it possible to lift the front part of the skull and open the mouth wide. It probably also increases the suction force when snapping.
12043.m: The coelacanth's skull can bend in the middle.

12044.q: What has become of the lung of its ancestors in today's coelacanth?
a: A small organ filled with fat
12044.e: Fossil coelacanths had a large, calcified lung. In today's Latimeria, it has shrunk and is largely filled with fat.
12044.m: The coelacanth's lung has shrunk to a small bag of fat.

12045.q: How does the coelacanth keep its blood in balance with the salty seawater?
a: It stores a lot of urea in its blood, like sharks.
It constantly drinks freshwater from springs.
It excretes salt through its scales.
It has the same salt concentration as freshwater fish.
12045.e: Like sharks and rays, the coelacanth holds back a lot of urea in its blood. As a result, it loses less water to the salty sea.
12045.m: Urea in the blood protects the coelacanth from drying out in salt water.

12046.q: Which adaptation helps the coelacanth to see in the twilight of the deep sea?
a: A light-reflecting layer behind the retina
A third eye on the top of the head
Tube-shaped eyes as in telescope fish
Its own lamp next to the eye
12046.e: Its large eyes have many rods and a tapetum lucidum. This layer throws the light through the retina a second time, as in cats.
12046.m: Like a cat, the coelacanth uses a reflective tapetum in its eye.

12047.q: How can researchers tell individual Comoran coelacanths apart?
a: By the individual pattern of pale spots
By the number of their fins
By the colour of their eyes
By notches in their tail fin
12047.e: Every Comoran coelacanth has a unique pattern of pale spots that stays the same for life. It works like a fingerprint.
12047.m: The coelacanth's spots are its personal fingerprint.

12048.q: How did the German biologist Hans Fricke study the coelacanths of the Comoros directly in their habitat?
a: By catching them in large trawl nets
With animals in an aquarium on land
12048.e: From the end of the 1980s, Fricke dived down to the coelacanths in the submersible “Jago”. Over 21 years, his team identified about 145 animals.
12048.m: Hans Fricke watched the coelacanths with a submersible.

12049.q: Where do Comoran coelacanths mostly spend their time in the daytime?
a: In caves on steep volcanic slopes
Buried in the sand of the seabed
In open water near the surface
In seagrass meadows in shallow water
12049.e: In the daytime, they rest in lava caves, sometimes more than ten animals together. At night, they leave the caves to look for food.
12049.m: In the daytime, the coelacanth hides in lava caves.

12050.q: How does the coelacanth hunt for prey at night?
a: It drifts slowly with the current and snaps up prey.
It chases prey in a fast sprint.
It digs in the sand for mussels.
It filters plankton out of the water.
12050.e: It is an energy-saving drift hunter that floats just above the bottom and suddenly sucks in prey. In doing so, it can cover several kilometres in one night.
12050.m: The coelacanth hunts at a leisurely pace as a drift hunter.

12051.q: What odd behaviour do coelacanths occasionally show underwater?
a: They stand upside down, vertically, in the water for minutes.
They jump out of the water.
They curl up like a ball.
12051.e: In the so-called headstand, they position themselves vertically with the head down. They probably use the rostral organ in this way to search for prey in crevices.
12051.m: The coelacanth's headstand is probably used for finding prey.

12052.q: What does the coelacanth mainly feed on?
a: On fish and cephalopods such as squid
12052.e: It is a predatory fish. In its stomach, deep-sea fish, eels, small sharks as well as squid and cuttlefish have been found.
12052.m: Fish and squid are on the coelacanth's menu.

12053.q: At what depth range does the Comoran coelacanth occur around the Comoros?
12053.e: Around the Comoros, it lives on steep volcanic slopes at about 150 to 700 metres' depth, mostly around 200 metres. There the water is cool and dim.
12053.m: The coelacanth lives in the twilight zone of the sea.

12054.q: Which water temperature does the coelacanth roughly prefer?
12054.e: It lives in cool water of about 14 to 22 degrees. In warmer water, its blood cannot take up enough oxygen, which is why it avoids the surface.
12054.m: The coelacanth likes it cool, although it lives in the tropics.

12055.q: Where did divers surprisingly discover coelacanths at only about 100 metres' depth in 2000?
a: In Sodwana Bay in South Africa
In the Red Sea off Egypt
12055.e: Technical divers found a group of coelacanths in caves in Sodwana Bay, in what is now the iSimangaliso reserve. It was one of the shallowest sightings ever.
12055.m: In Sodwana Bay, divers met the coelacanth face to face.

a: The eggs develop inside the mother, and the young are born alive.
The female lays spawn on corals.
The male incubates the eggs in his mouth.
The eggs are released freely into the open sea.
12056.e: The coelacanth is ovoviviparous. The embryos grow in the oviduct and hatch there before being born alive.
12056.m: Coelacanths give birth to live young.

12057.q: About how big are the eggs of a female coelacanth?
a: About 9 centimetres across, as big as a grapefruit
About 1 millimetre, as small as a grain of sand
About 5 millimetres, as big as a pea
About 30 centimetres, as big as a football
12057.e: At about 9 centimetres across and over 300 grams, the eggs are among the biggest fish eggs of all. Their yolk feeds the embryo.
12057.m: The coelacanth's egg is as big as a grapefruit.

12058.q: According to a study from 2021, how long does the gestation period last in the coelacanth?
12058.e: French researchers determined the age of embryos from growth rings on the scales. They arrived at about five years, which is among the longest gestation periods in the animal kingdom.
12058.m: A young coelacanth grows for about five years inside its mother.

12059.q: How many young can a female coelacanth carry in one litter?
12059.e: Captured pregnant females carried between 5 and 26 embryos. The newborns are already about 35 centimetres long and independent at once.
12059.m: A coelacanth litter consists of few but large young.

12060.q: What did a paternity test on coelacanth embryos in 2013 show?
a: Each litter came from just one father.
Each embryo had a different father.
The young came about without fertilisation.
12060.e: Researchers examined two litters with 26 and 23 embryos. All the young in a litter came from the same male.
12060.m: A coelacanth litter has only one father.

12061.q: According to the 2021 scale study, at what age does a coelacanth become sexually mature?
12061.e: Analysis of the fine annual rings on the scales showed extremely slow growth. Only at about 55 years can the animals reproduce.
12061.m: The coelacanth becomes an adult only at a grandfather's age.

12062.q: How old can a coelacanth get, according to more recent estimates?
12062.e: The oldest animal examined was 84 years old. In the past, only about 20 years had been assumed, so the lifespan was underestimated about five times over.
12062.m: A coelacanth can live to be a whole century old.

12063.q: What conservation status does the Comoran coelacanth have on the IUCN Red List?
12063.e: The species has a small population and reproduces extremely slowly. The IUCN therefore classes it as critically endangered.
12063.m: The Comoran coelacanth is close to extinction.

12064.q: What IUCN status does the Indonesian coelacanth have?
12064.e: Because of its small range, low numbers and bycatch, it is regarded as vulnerable. It is therefore one level less threatened than its African relative.
12064.m: The Indonesian coelacanth is regarded as vulnerable.

12065.q: How many Comoran coelacanths live off the island of Grande Comore, according to an estimate by the researcher Hans Fricke?
12065.e: After over 20 years of observation with the submersible, Fricke estimated the population at 300 to 400 animals. He regards the population as small but stable.
12065.m: Only a few hundred coelacanths live off Grande Comore.

12066.q: What is the biggest threat to coelacanths today?
12066.e: Coelacanths are hardly eaten, but they end up in deep gill nets and trawl nets as bycatch. With so few animals, every loss is serious.
12066.m: Bycatch is the greatest danger to the coelacanth.

12067.q: What does it mean that the Comoran coelacanth has been in Appendix I of the Washington Convention on species protection (CITES) since 1989?
a: International commercial trade in it is forbidden
It may only be shown in zoos
It may be fished in any quantity
It is officially regarded as extinct
12067.e: Appendix I means a ban on international commercial trade. Even museum specimens may only be sent with a permit.
12067.m: Coelacanths may not be traded internationally.

12068.q: From which geological period do the oldest known coelacanth fossils come?
a: From the Devonian, about 410 million years ago
From the Cretaceous, about 100 million years ago
From the Jurassic, about 170 million years ago
From the Tertiary, about 30 million years ago
12068.e: The earliest coelacanths lived in the early Devonian. The group is therefore older than the dinosaurs.
12068.m: Coelacanths were swimming through the seas even before the dinosaurs.

12069.q: What important insight did the decoding of the coelacanth genome in 2013 provide?
a: Lungfishes are more closely related to land vertebrates than the coelacanth is.
The coelacanth is the direct ancestor of all mammals.
The coelacanth is really a cartilaginous fish.
The coelacanth has not a single gene in common with land animals.
12069.e: The comparison of genetic material showed that lungfishes are the closest living relatives of land vertebrates. In addition, some genes of the coelacanth change strikingly slowly.
12069.m: The lungfish is more closely related to us than the coelacanth is.

12070.q: What is the scientific name of the giant squid?
12070.e: The giant squid's scientific name is Architeuthis dux, and as far as is known today it is the only species of its genus. Dosidicus gigas, by contrast, is the Humboldt squid.
12070.m: The giant squid bears the name Architeuthis dux.

12071.q: What does the species name “dux” in the giant squid's scientific name mean?
12071.e: “Dux” is Latin and means leader or prince. The name stresses the outstanding position of this large cephalopod.

12072.q: Which group of molluscs does the giant squid belong to?
12072.e: Like octopuses and cuttlefish, the giant squid is a cephalopod. In these molluscs, the arms sit directly on the head.
12072.m: The giant squid is a cephalopod.

12073.q: Which phylum of animals does the giant squid belong to?
12073.e: Like all cephalopods, the giant squid is a mollusc. It is therefore more closely related to snails and bivalves than to jellyfish or crustaceans.
12073.m: The giant squid is a mollusc like the snail.

12074.q: How many arms and feeding tentacles does the giant squid have altogether?
a: Eight arms and two long feeding tentacles
Eight arms and no feeding tentacles
Six arms and four feeding tentacles
Ten arms and two feeding tentacles
12074.e: The giant squid belongs to the ten-armed cephalopods (Decabrachia). It has eight shorter arms and two much longer feeding tentacles.
12074.m: The giant squid has eight arms and two feeding tentacles.

12075.q: What served the Danish zoologist Japetus Steenstrup in 1857, among other things, as evidence for the giant squid?
a: The beak of a stranded animal
A photo from the deep sea
A living animal in an aquarium
A film recording by a diver
12075.e: Steenstrup described Architeuthis in 1857 using, among other things, the beak of an animal stranded in Jutland. This turned a sailor's tale into a real animal of science.
12075.m: A beak made the giant squid a case for science in 1857.

12076.q: What is the greatest length of the mantle (the body without head and arms) of a giant squid?
12076.e: In over a hundred animals examined, no mantle was found to be much longer than about 2.25 m. The great total length comes mainly from the long feeding tentacles.
12076.m: The giant squid's mantle measures at most a good two metres.

12077.q: What total length, including feeding tentacles, do the largest female giant squids reach, according to reliable estimates?
12077.e: Reliable estimates assume at most about 12 to 13 m including tentacles for females and about 10 m for males. Figures of 20 m and more are not scientifically supported.
12077.m: A large female giant squid is about 12 m long including tentacles.

12078.q: Why should older length figures of 18 m and more for the giant squid be treated with caution?
a: The tentacles of dead animals can stretch a lot
The animals were always measured in the water then
In the past, males and females were added together
At that time only the track in the sand was measured
12078.e: The muscular feeding tentacles go limp after death and can stretch like rubber bands. Stranded animals therefore often look much longer than they were alive.
12078.m: Dead giant squids look longer than living ones because of stretched tentacles.

12079.q: At most, how heavy does a female giant squid get, according to estimates?
12079.e: About 275 kg is estimated for the largest females and about 150 kg for males. Many animals found weigh much less than 200 kg.
12079.m: A giant squid weighs at most a few hundred kilograms.

12080.q: What diameter can the eyes of the giant squid reach?
12080.e: The giant squid's eyes measure up to about 25 cm, and some sources even give 27 cm. They are therefore among the largest eyes in the whole animal kingdom.
12080.m: A giant squid's eye is about as big as a plate.

12081.q: According to a well-known study from 2012, what does the giant squid probably use its huge eyes for?
a: To spot approaching sperm whales early
To hunt at the surface in daylight
To tell the colours of corals apart
To use the stars for navigation
12081.e: Researchers led by Dan-Eric Nilsson showed that large eyes help above all to see large objects such as sperm whales. When swimming, these set off glowing plankton, which the squid can detect in the depths.
12081.m: The large eyes probably warn the giant squid of sperm whales.

12082.q: What are the giant squid's suckers reinforced with on the inside?
12082.e: Each sucker has a ring of chitin with small teeth. In this way, the giant squid can hold slippery prey such as fish and squid securely.
12082.m: Toothed chitin rings make the giant squid's suckers grippy.

12083.q: What diameter do the largest suckers of the giant squid have?
12083.e: The suckers usually measure 2 to 5 cm. Reports of scars 20 cm across on sperm whales are regarded as unbelievable.
12083.m: The giant squid's largest suckers are about the size of a coin to a golf ball.

12084.q: Why are sucker scars on sperm whales no proof of giant squids 60 m long?
a: The scars grow along with the whale's skin
The scars always come from killer whales
The scars are caused by stones on the seabed
The scars shrink as the whale gets older
12084.e: Scars that a young sperm whale receives get bigger as the whale grows. Large scars on old whales therefore do not necessarily come from huge squids.
12084.m: Sucker scars grow with the sperm whale and exaggerate the squid's size.

12085.q: What does the giant squid's parrot-like beak mainly consist of?
12085.e: The beak consists of hard, chitin-containing material with proteins. It is the only really hard body part of the giant squid.
12085.m: The beak is the hardest part of the giant squid.

12086.q: Why are giant squid beaks so valuable for research?
a: They are preserved undigested in the stomachs of sperm whales
They glow in the dark and are easy to find
They contain the animal's whole brain
They are shed every year and washed ashore
12086.e: Sperm whales digest the soft tissue, but the hard beaks remain in the stomach. From them, the size and number of squids eaten can be estimated.
12086.m: Sperm whale stomachs are an archive full of squid beaks.

12087.q: How does the giant squid keep its buoyancy in the water without using much energy?
a: With an ammonium chloride solution in its tissue that is lighter than seawater
With a gas-filled swim bladder like a fish
With a thick layer of fat under the skin
With an air-filled shell of lime inside the body
12087.e: In the giant squid's muscle tissue, sodium ions are replaced by ammonium ions. The resulting ammonium chloride solution is lighter than seawater and makes it able to float.
12087.m: Ammonium chloride lets the giant squid float in the water.

12088.q: Why is the flesh of the giant squid not suitable as food?
a: It tastes bitter and unpleasant because of the ammonia
It contains a deadly nerve poison
It consists almost only of cartilage
It falls apart into powder when cooked
12088.e: The ammonium-containing tissue smells and tastes strongly of ammonia. The giant squid is therefore regarded as inedible.
12088.m: Ammonia makes the giant squid inedible.

12089.q: At what depths does the giant squid probably live mainly?
12089.e: The giant squid probably inhabits the twilight zone and the upper parts of the lightless deep sea. The observations from Japan lay between about 600 and 900 m.
12089.m: The giant squid usually lives several hundred metres deep.

12090.q: How is the giant squid distributed worldwide?
a: In all the great oceans, often near continental slopes
Only in the Southern Ocean around Antarctica
Only in the river mouths of tropical countries
12090.e: Finds come from all the great oceans, for example off Norway, Newfoundland, Japan, New Zealand and South Africa. Animals are often found on continental slopes and island slopes.
12090.m: The giant squid lives in all the great oceans of the world.

12091.q: Which animal is regarded as the most important natural enemy of adult giant squids?
12091.e: Sperm whales dive deep and deliberately hunt large squid. Giant squid beaks are regularly found in their stomachs.
12091.m: The sperm whale is the giant squid's greatest enemy.

12092.q: According to stomach contents, what does the giant squid mainly feed on?
a: On deep-sea fish and other squid
12092.e: In the stomachs of giant squids, remains of deep-sea fish and squid have been found, in some cases even of their own species. It is therefore a predator.
12092.m: The giant squid hunts fish and other squid.

12093.q: What does the giant squid use its two long feeding tentacles, with the broadened club at the end, for?
a: To seize prey from a distance and pull it towards the arms
To move about on the seabed
To bury eggs in the sand
To pump water into the gills
12093.e: The feeding tentacles have suckers only on the club. With them, the squid snaps up prey and brings it to its eight arms and the beak.
12093.m: The giant squid seizes its prey with its feeding tentacles.

12094.q: How does the giant squid, like other squid, move forward fast?
a: By jet propulsion, by squirting water out of the funnel
By beating its feeding tentacles like fins
By walking on its arms on the seabed
By gas bubbles that it expels
12094.e: Cephalopods suck water into the mantle cavity and expel it forcefully through the funnel. This recoil drives them forward on the jet principle.
12094.m: The giant squid swims by jet propulsion, like a nozzle.

12095.q: How many hearts does the giant squid have, like other cephalopods?
12095.e: Two gill hearts pump the blood through the gills, and one systemic heart supplies the rest of the body. This is typical of cephalopods.
12095.m: The giant squid has three hearts.

12096.q: Why is the giant squid's blood bluish?
a: Because it contains haemocyanin with copper
Because it contains haemoglobin with iron
Because it contains chlorophyll with magnesium
Because it contains melanin from the ink sac
12096.e: As in other cephalopods, copper-containing haemocyanin carries the oxygen. When loaded with oxygen, it colours the blood bluish.
12096.m: Copper in the haemocyanin makes the giant squid's blood blue.

12097.q: What special position does the giant squid's brain have?
a: It surrounds the gullet in a ring
It lies in the tip of the mantle
It is spread over the eight arms with no centre
It sits behind the ink sac
12097.e: In cephalopods, the brain is built in a ring around the gullet. Large bites could therefore injure the brain, which is why prey is broken up with the beak.
12097.m: In the giant squid, the gullet runs right through the brain.

12098.q: By which method do researchers determine the age of a giant squid?
a: By counting growth rings in the statoliths
By counting the suckers on the arms
By measuring the length of the beak alone
By counting the annual rings in the limy cuttlebone
12098.e: Statoliths are small limy bodies in the balance organ. They lay down growth rings, similar to annual rings in trees.
12098.m: Statoliths reveal the age of a giant squid.

12099.q: Roughly how old does a giant squid get, according to current knowledge?
a: Only a few years, about 3 to 5
12099.e: Despite its size, the giant squid grows very fast and lives only a few years. It becomes sexually mature at about three years.
12099.m: The giant squid lives fast and dies young.

12100.q: How do male giant squids transfer their sperm to the female?
a: They inject sperm packets (spermatophores) under the skin of the female's arms
They place the sperm in a nest on the seabed
They release the sperm freely into the water over a clutch
They pass the sperm into the mouth with the beak
12100.e: Male giant squids implant spermatophores into the female's skin. How the eggs are fertilised later has not yet been exactly worked out.
12100.m: Male giant squids implant sperm packets into the skin of females.

12101.q: How big are the individual eggs of the giant squid?
a: About as big as a hen's egg
12101.e: The giant squid's eggs are tiny, but a female can carry over 5 kg of eggs in her ovary. That means an enormous number of offspring.
12101.m: The huge giant squid lays tiny eggs.

12102.q: When were the first photos of a living giant squid taken in its natural habitat?
12102.e: The Japanese researchers Tsunemi Kubodera and Kyoichi Mori photographed an animal at about 900 m depth on 30 September 2004. It was a milestone of deep-sea research.
12102.m: Since 2004, there have been photos of a living giant squid in the depths.

12103.q: Near which island group was a living giant squid first photographed in the depths in 2004?
12103.e: The photos were taken south of Tokyo near the Ogasawara Islands, where sperm whales often hunt. The researchers had lowered their camera into the depths with bait.
12103.m: The Ogasawara Islands are a famous place for giant squid research.

12104.q: In which year was a giant squid first filmed in its natural habitat in the deep sea?
12104.e: In July 2012, a Japanese team filmed a giant squid at about 600 to 900 m depth. The pictures were shown on television worldwide in 2013.
12104.m: In 2012, a giant squid was filmed in the deep sea for the first time.

12105.q: With what trick did the camera “Medusa” attract a giant squid in the Gulf of Mexico in 2019?
a: With a light lure that imitates a jellyfish's alarm glow
With a piece of sperm whale meat as bait
With loud music from an underwater loudspeaker
