12105.e: The team around Edith Widder used red light, which deep-sea animals can hardly see, and a lure that flashes like a glowing jellyfish. In this way, the first footage of a giant squid in US waters was achieved in 2019.
12105.m: An artificial jellyfish glow lured a giant squid in front of the camera in 2019.

12106.q: What did a genetic study from 2013 on giant squids from all over the world show?
a: They probably all belong to a single species
There are at least twenty separate species
They are closely related to octopuses of the genus Octopus
They all descend from a population in the Atlantic that has died out
12106.e: Researchers at the University of Copenhagen compared the genetic material of animals from all over the world and found only very small differences. This points to a single worldwide species, although up to 17 species had been proposed in the past.
12106.m: All giant squids in the world probably belong to one species.

12107.q: How big is the giant squid's genome, decoded in 2020, compared with the human genome?
a: Almost as big as the human one
Only about a hundredth of it
About as small as that of a bacterium
12107.e: The giant squid's genome comprises about 2.7 billion base pairs. The human genome has about 3.1 billion.
12107.m: The giant squid's genome is almost as big as ours.

12108.q: How does the IUCN classify the giant squid on the Red List?
12108.e: The IUCN lists the giant squid as least concern. It is distributed worldwide and is not specifically fished.
12108.m: According to the IUCN, the giant squid is not threatened.

12109.q: Which sea monster from Nordic legends probably goes back to sightings of giant squids?
12109.e: The kraken was a monster in Scandinavian seafarers' stories that attacks ships. Stranded giant squids probably fed these legends.
12109.m: Behind the kraken legend, there is probably the giant squid.

12110.q: In which novel by Jules Verne does the crew fight against a giant squid?
a: “Journey to the Centre of the Earth”
12110.e: In “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea” (1870), the Nautilus is attacked by giant squids. The scene made the giant squid a famous character in fiction.
12110.m: Jules Verne had the Nautilus fight a giant squid.

12111.q: Where is the famous giant squid “Archie”, caught near the Falkland Islands in 2004, on display?
a: In the Natural History Museum in London
In the Natural History Museum of Bern
In the American Museum of Natural History in New York
In the Museum für Naturkunde in Berlin
12111.e: “Archie” is a female about 8.6 m long, preserved in a large tank in the Natural History Museum in London. The name is derived from Architeuthis.
12111.m: The giant squid “Archie” floats preserved in London.

12112.q: Which squid from the Southern Ocean is often compared with the giant squid because it gets even heavier?
12112.e: The colossal squid (Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni) lives in the Southern Ocean. It is shorter than the giant squid, but much bulkier.
12112.m: The colossal squid is the heavy relative of the giant squid.

12113.q: How closely related is the colossal squid to the giant squid?
a: Not particularly closely, it belongs to a different family
It is the male of the giant squid
It is an octopus and not a squid at all
12113.e: The colossal squid belongs to the glass squids, while the giant squid has a family of its own, Architeuthidae. Despite similar size, the two are not particularly closely related.
12113.m: The colossal squid and the giant squid are not close relatives.

12114.q: How heavy was the largest known specimen of the colossal squid, caught in the Ross Sea in 2007?
12114.e: The female caught in 2007 weighed about 495 kg and is the heaviest known invertebrate. It is now on display in the Te Papa museum in New Zealand.
12114.m: The heaviest colossal squid weighed almost half a tonne.

12115.q: How do the giant squid and the colossal squid differ in length and weight?
a: The giant squid is longer, the colossal squid much heavier
The giant squid is longer and also heavier
The colossal squid is longer and also heavier
Both are the same length and the same weight
12115.e: Thanks to its long tentacles, the giant squid reaches the greater total length. But the colossal squid has a bulkier body and gets much heavier.
12115.m: The giant squid is the longest, the colossal squid the heaviest.

12116.q: Which weapon does the colossal squid have on its arms and tentacles that the giant squid lacks?
a: Sharp limy spines on the mantle
12116.e: Besides suckers, the colossal squid also has hooks, some of which can rotate. The giant squid has only suckers with toothed rings.
12116.m: The colossal squid grips with hooks, the giant squid with suckers.

12117.q: Where does the colossal squid live, unlike the worldwide giant squid?
a: In the Southern Ocean around Antarctica
In the Arctic Ocean around Greenland
In the Mediterranean and the Black Sea
12117.e: The colossal squid occurs circumpolar around Antarctica in the Southern Ocean. Giant squids, by contrast, are found in all the great oceans.
12117.m: The colossal squid is an animal of the Southern Ocean.

12118.q: Which animal, a relative of the giant squid, has the largest eyes of all known animals?
12118.e: The colossal squid's eyes are estimated at about 27 to 30 cm and are regarded as the largest known eyes in the animal kingdom. The giant squid's eyes are similarly large.
12118.m: The colossal squid is regarded as the record holder for the largest eyes.

12119.q: When was a living colossal squid, a relative of the giant squid, first reliably filmed in its habitat?
12119.e: In March 2025, a diving robot filmed a young animal about 30 cm long at around 600 m depth near the South Sandwich Islands. Adult animals have never been filmed alive in the depths.
12119.m: Only in 2025 was a living colossal squid filmed.

12120.q: Which class of animals do the nautiluses belong to?
12120.e: Nautiluses are molluscs from the class of cephalopods, which also includes octopuses, squid and cuttlefish. They are the only living cephalopods with an external, chambered shell.
12120.m: The nautilus is a cephalopod with a house.

12121.q: Which extinct group of animals with a chambered shell is related to the nautilus?
12121.e: Like the nautilus, ammonites were cephalopods with a chambered limy shell. They died out at the end of the Cretaceous, but the nautilus survived to the present day.
12121.m: The nautilus is a relative of the extinct ammonites.

12122.q: Which widespread claim about the shape of the nautilus shell turns out to be a myth when measured carefully?
a: That it is a golden spiral
That it is built of chitin
That it never grows any more
That it has only one chamber
12122.e: It is often claimed that the nautilus shell follows the golden ratio. Measurements show, however, that it is a logarithmic spiral, but not a golden one.
12122.m: The nautilus shell is beautiful, but not a golden spiral.

12123.q: Which respiratory pigment carries oxygen in the nautilus's blood and colours it bluish?
12123.e: Like other cephalopods, the nautilus uses copper-containing haemocyanin as its oxygen carrier. When loaded with oxygen, the blood looks bluish.
12123.m: The nautilus has blue blood thanks to haemocyanin.

12124.q: Which type of spiral actually describes the nautilus shell well mathematically?
12124.e: The shell keeps growing in a constant shape, which corresponds to a logarithmic spiral. The distance between the whorls increases steadily.
12124.m: The nautilus grows in a logarithmic spiral.

12125.q: Roughly how many tentacles (cirri) can a nautilus have?
12125.e: Depending on sex and individual, a nautilus has about 50 to over 90 cirri. It therefore has far more tentacles than octopuses with 8 or squid with 10.
12125.m: The nautilus has many more arms than an octopus.

12126.q: What do the nautilus's tentacles lack, unlike the arms of most octopuses?
12126.e: The nautilus's cirri have no suckers. Instead, they stick to prey or the ground with sticky ridges.
12126.m: Nautilus tentacles stick instead of sucking.

12127.q: How are the nautilus's eyes built?
12127.e: The nautilus eye is an open pit with a small opening through which seawater enters. Without a lens, only simple, dim images form.
12127.m: The nautilus sees through a pinhole camera without a lens.

12128.q: Which sense is most important for the nautilus in finding food and finding a mate?
12128.e: Since its pinhole eyes give only rough images, the nautilus relies mainly on its sense of smell. With it, it finds carrion and others of its kind even in the dark.
12128.m: The nautilus finds its food with its nose.

12129.q: Where are the nautilus's small smell organs, with which it detects scent trails in the water?
a: At the tip of the shell
On the gills in the mantle
12129.e: The smell organs, called rhinophores, lie below the nautilus's eyes. With them, it detects scent trails of carrion and others of its kind.
12129.m: The nautilus smells with small organs below its eyes.

12130.q: How many gills does a nautilus have?
12130.e: The nautilus has two pairs of gills, so four gills. That is why it was formerly separated as “Tetrabranchiata” from the other, two-gilled cephalopods.
12130.m: The nautilus breathes with four gills.

12131.q: Which structure closes the shell opening of the nautilus when it withdraws?
a: A horny shield on the foot
12131.e: Two specially shaped tentacles form a tough, leathery hood. When the nautilus withdraws, this hood closes the opening like a door.
12131.m: The hood is the nautilus's front door.

12132.q: What is the strand called that runs through all the shell chambers of the nautilus and regulates buoyancy?
12132.e: The siphuncle is a tube-shaped strand of tissue that runs through every partition. Through it, the nautilus can draw fluid out of the chambers or store it in them.
12132.m: The siphuncle is the swimming regulator in the nautilus shell.

12133.q: By what process does the nautilus remove fluid from the shell chambers?
a: By osmosis with the help of salts
By pumping it out with the heart
By expelling it through the funnel
12133.e: The siphuncle transports salts out of the chamber fluid, so that the water follows by osmosis. Empty chambers fill with gas and increase buoyancy.
12133.m: The nautilus controls its buoyancy with osmosis.

12134.q: In which part of its shell does the nautilus itself live?
a: In the largest, outermost living chamber
In a chamber in the middle of the spiral
12134.e: The body sits in the foremost and largest chamber, the living chamber. The older chambers behind it serve as buoyancy bodies.
12134.m: The nautilus always lives in the front room.

12135.q: Roughly how many chambers does the shell of a fully grown nautilus have?
12135.e: On hatching, a nautilus has only a few chambers, and new ones are added continually as it grows. Adult animals have about 30 or more chambers.
12135.m: An adult nautilus has about 30 chambers.

12136.q: What does the nautilus shell mainly consist of?
12136.e: The shell is built of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate. The inner layer consists of mother-of-pearl, which also consists mainly of aragonite.
12136.m: The nautilus shell is built of lime and mother-of-pearl.

12137.q: Where does the German name “Perlboot” (pearl boat) for the nautilus come from?
a: From the pearly, shimmering inside of the shell
From pearls that it forms in its stomach
From pearl-like eggs at the surface
From pearl divers who discovered it
12137.e: The inside of the nautilus shell is lined with shimmering mother-of-pearl. Together with the boat-like shape, this gave the name “Perlboot”.
12137.m: The Perlboot gets its name from the mother-of-pearl in its shell.

12138.q: What does the Greek word “nautilos”, from which the name nautilus is derived, mean?
12138.e: The Greek “nautílos” means seaman or sailor. The name alludes to the idea that the animal sails across the sea like a ship.

12139.q: How does a nautilus move through the water?
a: By jet propulsion through a funnel
By beating fins on its mantle
By rowing with all its tentacles
12139.e: The nautilus forcefully expels water through its movable funnel. The recoil usually drives it backwards through the water.
12139.m: The nautilus swims by jet propulsion.

12140.q: What does the nautilus lack for defence, unlike octopuses and squid?
12140.e: The nautilus has no ink sac and cannot release a cloud of ink. It protects itself instead with its hard shell and the hood.
12140.m: The nautilus has no ink, but an armoured house.

12141.q: Which ability of many other cephalopods does the nautilus lack?
12141.e: Octopuses and cuttlefish can change colour in a flash thanks to chromatophores. The nautilus lacks these colour cells, and its pattern is fixed on the shell.
12141.m: A nautilus cannot change its colour.

12142.q: What purpose does the colouring of the nautilus shell, with dark stripes on top and a pale underside, serve?
12142.e: From above, the dark upper side blends into the depths, and from below, the pale underside blends into the light. This countershading makes the nautilus harder for enemies to see.
12142.m: The nautilus camouflages itself with a dark back and a pale belly.

12143.q: In which sea region do nautiluses live naturally?
12143.e: Nautiluses occur only in the tropical Indo-Pacific, for example near the Philippines, Indonesia, Australia and New Caledonia. They are absent from the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
12143.m: Nautiluses live only in the tropical Indo-Pacific.

12144.q: In which habitats are nautiluses typically found?
a: On steep slopes of coral reefs
In river mouths with brackish water
In the open ocean above deep-sea trenches
12144.e: Nautiluses live on the deep, steeply sloping outer slopes of coral reefs. There they find the cool depths that they need.
12144.m: Nautiluses live on the steep slopes of the reefs.

12145.q: At what depth do nautiluses mostly stay?
a: Mostly at a few hundred metres' depth
Mostly buried in the sand of the seabed
12145.e: Nautiluses mostly live at depths of a few hundred metres. In some areas, they rarely occur shallower, and the deepest record was about 700 metres.
12145.m: Nautiluses mostly live a few hundred metres deep.

12146.q: From roughly what depth does a nautilus's shell risk breaking under the water pressure?
12146.e: The gas-filled shell can withstand only a limited pressure. From about 800 metres' depth, it implodes, which limits the depth to which a nautilus can dive.
12146.m: Below about 800 metres, the nautilus shell breaks.

12147.q: Which water do nautiluses avoid, which ties them to deeper zones?
12147.e: Nautiluses tolerate warm water badly and mostly avoid temperatures above about 25 °C. That is why in tropical seas they stay in cooler depths.
12147.m: Warm surface water gets too hot for the nautilus.

12148.q: Which daily migration behaviour has been observed in many nautiluses?
a: At night they rise, in the daytime they sink deeper
In the daytime they rise, at night they sink
They migrate thousands of kilometres every year
They stay in one place all their lives
12148.e: Many nautiluses rise to shallower areas at night to look for food. In the daytime, they withdraw to the depths again, although some populations show more complex patterns.
12148.m: The nautilus comes up at night and goes down into the depths by day.

12149.q: What does the nautilus mainly feed on?
a: On carrion, crabs and moulted shells
12149.e: The nautilus is a scavenger and opportunistic hunter. It eats dead animals, hermit crabs and discarded lobster shells.
12149.m: The nautilus is mainly a scavenger.

12150.q: What does the nautilus use to break up its food?
12150.e: Like other cephalopods, the nautilus has a horny, parrot-like beak. Together with the rasping tongue (radula), it breaks up its food with it.
12150.m: The nautilus bites with a beak like a parrot.

12151.q: How do male nautiluses transfer their sperm packets to the female?
a: By releasing them into open water
Through a tube on the shell
Not at all, nautiluses fertilise themselves
12151.e: In male nautiluses, four modified tentacles form an organ, the spadix. With it, they transfer sperm packets to the female.
12151.m: The male nautilus uses modified tentacles for mating.

12152.q: Roughly how long does development in the egg take in the nautilus?
12152.e: At about 21 to 25 °C, nautilus eggs take about 8 to 12 months to hatch. Depending on the temperature, it can also take longer.
12152.m: A nautilus egg takes almost a year to hatch.

12153.q: Roughly how big is a young nautilus on hatching?
12153.e: Young nautiluses hatch with a shell of about 30 millimetres. They already look like little adults and have no larval stage.
12153.m: A newly hatched nautilus is about three centimetres big.

12154.q: How does a female nautilus lay her eggs?
a: Singly, as a few large eggs on the substrate
In large swarms freely into the water
As thousands of eggs in strings of mucus
Not at all, she gives birth to live young
12154.e: Female nautiluses lay only a few large eggs and attach them singly to stones or corals. Development in the egg takes almost a year.
12154.m: The nautilus lays a few large eggs one at a time.

12155.e: Nautiluses can live longer than 20 years. They therefore live much longer than most octopuses and squid, which often live only one to two years.
12155.m: A nautilus lives much longer than most cephalopods without a shell.

12156.q: How big does the shell of a fully grown nautilus usually get?
12156.e: Adult nautiluses usually have a shell about 10 to 25 cm in diameter. The largest species is Nautilus pompilius.
12156.m: A nautilus shell usually fits in two hands.

12157.q: Which nautilus species is the largest and most widespread?
12157.e: Nautilus pompilius, the chambered nautilus, reaches the largest shells and has the largest range. It extends from the Andaman Sea to Fiji.
12157.m: Nautilus pompilius is the largest and commonest nautilus.

12158.q: Who described the chambered nautilus Nautilus pompilius scientifically in 1758?
12158.e: Carl Linnaeus described Nautilus pompilius in 1758 in his work “Systema Naturae”. That year is regarded as the starting point of zoological naming.
12158.m: Linnaeus gave the nautilus its scientific name in 1758.

12159.q: What is the most striking feature of the shell of Allonautilus scrobiculatus?
12159.e: Fresh shells of Allonautilus scrobiculatus have a thick, shaggy layer (periostracum) that is reminiscent of slimy hair. That is why it is also called the “hairy nautilus”.

12160.q: What happened in 2015 to the rare nautilus Allonautilus scrobiculatus?
a: It was sighted again after about three decades
It was bred in a zoo for the first time
It was found in the Atlantic for the first time
12160.e: In 2015, the team led by Peter Ward sighted Allonautilus scrobiculatus off Papua New Guinea. Before that, there had been no confirmed observation for about three decades.
12160.m: The rare Allonautilus turned up again in 2015 after a long time.

12161.q: Why did researchers place the nautilus Allonautilus in a genus of its own beside Nautilus in 1997?
a: Because of differences in shell and body build
Because it is the only one living in the Atlantic
Because its shell has no chambers
12161.e: Peter Ward and W. Bruce Saunders described Allonautilus as a genus of its own in 1997. The reasons were differences in shell, anatomy and reproductive organs.
12161.m: Allonautilus differs clearly in build from Nautilus.

12162.q: In which year did the CITES species protection conference decide to include all nautiluses in Appendix II?
12162.e: At the CITES conference in Johannesburg in 2016, all species of the family Nautilidae were included in Appendix II, in force since the beginning of 2017. Since then, international trade in shells has required permits.
12162.m: Since the CITES decision of 2016, trade in nautiluses has been regulated.

12164.q: What status does the chambered nautilus Nautilus pompilius have on the IUCN Red List?
12164.e: The IUCN classes Nautilus pompilius as vulnerable. The main reason is overfishing for the trade in shells.
12164.m: The chambered nautilus is regarded as vulnerable.

12165.q: What is the greatest threat to wild nautiluses?
a: Catching them for the trade in shells
12165.e: Nautiluses are caught in traps with bait because their shells are in demand as jewellery and decoration. Because of their late maturity and few eggs, populations recover only slowly.
12165.m: The shell trade threatens nautiluses most.

12166.q: What does it mean that the chambered nautilus has been classed as “threatened” in the USA since 2018?
a: It is regarded as threatened, and import and trade are more strictly regulated
It is regarded as extinct and may not be studied
It is regarded as a pest and may be caught
It is regarded as a pet and may be sold freely
12166.e: The US agency NOAA Fisheries classed Nautilus pompilius as “threatened” under the Endangered Species Act in 2018. Stricter rules for import and trade therefore apply in the USA.
12166.m: Since 2018, the nautilus has also been legally protected in the USA.

12167.q: Why are nautiluses often called “living fossils”?
a: Their body plan has hardly changed over a very long time
They can turn to stone and come back to life
They live only in fossil reefs on land
They were bred from fossils only recently
12167.e: Nautiloids arose as early as the Cambrian about 500 million years ago. Today's nautiluses still resemble their fossil relatives closely.
12167.m: The nautilus still looks almost like its ancient ancestors.

12168.q: Which animal, also called the “paper boat” or “paper nautilus”, is in truth not a nautilus?
12168.e: The paper nautilus (Argonauta) is an octopus whose female forms a thin egg case. This case has no chambers and is not related to the nautilus shell.
12168.m: The paper nautilus is an octopus and not a true nautilus.

12169.q: Which famous submarine from a novel by Jules Verne bears the name of the nautilus?
12169.e: In “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea”, Captain Nemo travels in the submarine Nautilus. Later, the world's first nuclear-powered submarine was also given this name.
12169.m: Captain Nemo's submarine is named after the nautilus.

12170.q: Why is the Portuguese man o' war not a true jellyfish?
a: It is a colony of many specialised individual animals
It is a single polyp with no medusa stage
It belongs to the comb jellies, which have no stinging cells
It is a snail with a gas bubble as its shell
12170.e: The Portuguese man o' war is a siphonophore. It consists of many zooids, which together work like a single animal.
12170.m: The Portuguese man o' war is a state made up of many individual animals.

12171.q: Which order does the Portuguese man o' war belong to?
12171.e: The Portuguese man o' war is counted in the order of siphonophores. These form colonial groups of specialised partial animals.
12171.m: The Portuguese man o' war belongs to the siphonophores.

12172.q: How can you tell that the Portuguese man o' war belongs to the cnidarians?
a: It has stinging cells with which it stings
It has a hard limy shell
It breathes with lungs in the air
It has a skeleton of bone
12172.e: All cnidarians, that is jellyfish, corals and sea anemones, have stinging cells. The Portuguese man o' war also catches its prey with them.
12172.m: Stinging cells are the mark of all cnidarians.

12173.q: Which phylum of animals does the Portuguese man o' war belong to?
12173.e: The Portuguese man o' war has stinging cells and therefore belongs to the cnidarians. This phylum also includes corals and jellyfish.
12173.m: The Portuguese man o' war is a cnidarian.

12174.q: When are Portuguese men o' war washed up on beaches particularly often?
a: After strong wind from the sea
12174.e: The Portuguese man o' war has no propulsion of its own and drifts with the wind. If it blows from the sea towards the land for a longer time, many animals often end up on the beach.
12174.m: Wind from the sea drives Portuguese men o' war to the coast.

12175.q: What does the Greek word “physalis”, from which the genus name of the Portuguese man o' war comes, mean?
12175.e: “Physalis” means bladder or little bubble in Greek. The name refers to the striking gas-filled float.
12175.m: Physalia means something like bladder animal.

12176.q: Who first described the Portuguese man o' war scientifically in 1758?
12176.e: Carl Linnaeus described the species in 1758 in the 10th edition of his work “Systema Naturae”. At that time, he still placed it in the genus Holothuria.
12176.m: Linnaeus described the Portuguese man o' war in 1758.

12177.q: What is the system introduced by Linnaeus called, according to which the Portuguese man o' war also has a genus name and a species name?
12177.e: Since Linnaeus, every species has a two-part scientific name made up of genus and species. For the Portuguese man o' war, it is Physalia physalis.
12177.m: Every species has a two-part name made up of genus and species.

12178.q: Which French naturalist, known for an early theory of evolution, gave the Portuguese man o' war its present genus name Physalia in 1801?
12178.e: Lamarck created the genus Physalia in 1801. He is known above all for his idea that living things pass on acquired characteristics.
12178.m: Lamarck gave the Portuguese man o' war its present genus.

12179.q: What does the English name “man o' war” of the Portuguese man o' war recall?
12179.e: The upright gas bubble recalls the sail of an old warship. “Man o' war” was a name for such armed sailing ships.
12179.m: The Portuguese man o' war is named after a sailing ship.

12180.q: Which two tasks does the gas-filled bubble of the Portuguese man o' war fulfil?
a: It keeps the colony afloat and serves as a sail
It digests prey and stores poison
It serves as an eye and as an ear
It attracts prey with light and keeps warm
12180.e: The gas bubble keeps the whole colony at the water surface. At the same time, it catches the wind like a sail.
12180.m: The gas bubble is a float and a sail at the same time.

12181.q: How long is the float of a typical fully grown Portuguese man o' war?
12181.e: The gas bubble of a typical Portuguese man o' war is about 15 to 30 cm long. The tentacles below it, by contrast, are many metres long.
12181.m: The Portuguese man o' war's gas bubble is about 15 to 30 cm long.

12182.q: Where does part of the gas in the Portuguese man o' war's float come from?
a: A gas gland of the colony produces it itself
It gulps air at the surface
Algae in the bubble produce it
12182.e: A gas gland produces, among other things, carbon monoxide and fills the bubble with it. The rest is an air-like gas mixture.
12182.m: The Portuguese man o' war fills its bubble partly with gas that it makes itself.

12183.q: How long are the Portuguese man o' war's tentacles typically?
12183.e: The tentacles usually hang about 10 m deep into the water, and in large colonies even over 30 m. In this way, the colony fishes a large area of water beneath it.
12183.m: The Portuguese man o' war's tentacles are usually about 10 m long.

12184.q: Roughly how many stings by Physalia species such as the Portuguese man o' war are reported per year on the east coast of Australia?
12184.e: On the east coast of Australia, about 10,000 to 30,000 Physalia stings are reported every year. There, it is mainly the related bluebottle that is common.
12184.m: In Australia, there are tens of thousands of Physalia stings every year.

12185.q: How do the many partial animals of a Portuguese man o' war share out the work?
a: There are partial animals for catching prey, digestion and reproduction
All partial animals do all the tasks equally
One partial animal works, all the others rest
The partial animals take turns every day
12185.e: The colony consists of specialised partial animals, the zooids. Catching polyps hunt, feeding polyps digest, and others take care of offspring.
12185.m: In the Portuguese man o' war, every partial animal has its own task.

12186.q: How does the Portuguese man o' war digest its prey?
a: Feeding polyps attach to the prey and break it down with enzymes
It pulls the prey into the gas bubble
Bacteria in the seawater pre-digest it
It only sucks out the prey's blood
12186.e: The feeding polyps each have a mouth. They envelop the paralysed prey and dissolve it with digestive enzymes.
12186.m: Feeding polyps digest the Portuguese man o' war's prey.

12187.q: Why can a single partial animal of the Portuguese man o' war not survive alone?
a: It fulfils only one task and needs the others
It can live only in freshwater
It is too heavy to swim
12187.e: Every partial animal is specialised, for example in catching, digesting or reproducing. Only together do they work like a whole animal.
12187.m: The partial animals of the Portuguese man o' war depend on one another.

12188.q: How does the Portuguese man o' war's prey reach the feeding polyps?
a: The tentacles contract and lift it up
The gas bubble sucks it in through an opening
Waves wash it straight into a stomach
A fish carries it up to the colony
12188.e: After the catch, the tentacles shorten greatly. In this way, the paralysed prey is pulled to the gastrozooids under the bubble.
12188.m: The Portuguese man o' war pulls its prey upwards with its tentacles.

12189.q: What does the Portuguese man o' war mainly feed on?
a: On small fish and fish larvae
12189.e: The Portuguese man o' war is a predator. Besides small fish and fish larvae, it also catches small crustaceans, molluscs and zooplankton.
12189.m: The Portuguese man o' war eats mainly small fish.

12190.q: How does the Portuguese man o' war move?
a: It drifts with wind and current
It swims by jet propulsion like a squid
It glides over the bottom with cilia
12190.e: The Portuguese man o' war has no propulsion of its own. The wind pushes against the bubble as against a sail.
12190.m: The Portuguese man o' war sails only with the wind.

12191.q: At roughly what angle to the wind does the Portuguese man o' war sail?
12191.e: Because of the slanted bubble, the colony drifts about 45 degrees to the side of the wind direction. It therefore does not simply sail with the wind.
12191.m: The Portuguese man o' war sails at an angle to the wind.

12192.q: What does it mean that there are “left-handed” and “right-handed” Portuguese men o' war?
a: Their sail is set as a mirror image to the left or right
They catch prey with only one side of the body
They turn in one direction when swimming
Their gas bubble has an opening on the left or right
12192.e: In the two forms, the sail is laid out as a mirror image. That is why they drift in opposite directions in the same wind.
12192.m: There are Portuguese men o' war with a left sail and with a right sail.

12193.q: What advantage do the two mirror-image forms of the Portuguese man o' war bring?
a: Not the whole population is driven to the same coast
They can swim against the wind
12193.e: Because the two forms drift in different directions in the same wind, the whole population probably never strands in the same place. Researchers regard this as an adaptation that lets part of it survive on the open sea.
12193.m: The two sail forms protect the Portuguese man o' war from stranding.

12194.q: What can the Portuguese man o' war do when it is attacked at the surface?
a: Deflate its gas bubble and dive briefly
Shed its tentacles and fly away
12194.e: The colony can let gas out of the bubble. It then sinks below the surface for a short time.
12194.m: The Portuguese man o' war can dive briefly to escape.

12195.q: How are the sexes distributed in the Portuguese man o' war?
a: Every colony is either male or female
12195.e: The Portuguese man o' war has separate sexes. A colony produces either only eggs or only sperm.
12195.m: A Portuguese man o' war is male or female.

12196.q: How does fertilisation take place in the Portuguese man o' war?
a: Eggs and sperm are released into open water
The colonies mate with their tentacles
The eggs are fertilised in the gas bubble
The sperm are handed over in packets
12196.e: The sex cells are released into the sea, where fertilisation takes place. In the wild, however, this process has never yet been observed directly.
12196.m: The Portuguese man o' war reproduces in open water.

12197.q: What does a whole colony of the Portuguese man o' war develop from?
a: From a single fertilised egg cell
From many larvae that join together
From a polyp on the seabed
12197.e: The whole colony develops from a single embryo. The other zooids arise by budding and are therefore genetically identical.
12197.m: A whole Portuguese man o' war grows from a single egg.

12198.q: How do the many partial animals of a young Portuguese man o' war arise?
a: They bud from the first partial animal
Foreign larvae attach themselves to the colony
Each one hatches from its own egg
They arise from algae in the water
12198.e: From the fertilised egg, an animal with a gas bubble forms first. From it, all the other partial animals bud one after another, which is why they are genetically the same.
12198.m: The partial animals of the Portuguese man o' war arise by budding.

12199.q: What happens when a stinging cell of the Portuguese man o' war is triggered?
a: A tiny tube shoots out and injects poison
It gives off an electric shock
12199.e: The stinging capsule literally explodes on contact. A fine tube pierces the skin and injects poison into it.
12199.m: Stinging cells shoot a poison tube into the skin.

12200.q: Why is a dead Portuguese man o' war lying on the beach still dangerous?
a: Its stinging cells can still fire for hours to days
It gives off poisonous gas as it dries
It comes back to life after stranding
12200.e: The stinging capsules still work for a while even without a living animal. Torn-off tentacles in the water can also still sting.
12200.m: Even a dead Portuguese man o' war can still sting.

12201.q: How long does the pain usually last after a sting from a Portuguese man o' war?
12201.e: The strong pain after a sting from a Portuguese man o' war usually lasts about one to three hours. After that, it gradually fades.
12201.m: A Portuguese man o' war sting usually hurts for a few hours.

12202.q: How dangerous is a Portuguese man o' war sting to healthy adults as a rule?
a: Very painful, but only extremely rarely fatal
12202.e: Stings are very painful, but deaths are extremely rare. Allergies or stings over a large area in small children are more dangerous.
12202.m: The Portuguese man o' war is painful, but rarely fatal.

12203.q: What should you rinse the skin with after a sting from a Portuguese man o' war and carefully removing the tentacle remains?
12203.e: Many first-aid recommendations advise rinsing with seawater and not using freshwater, because freshwater can trigger further stinging capsules. Urine and alcohol are not suitable remedies.
12203.m: After a Portuguese man o' war sting, you rinse with seawater.

12204.q: Which heat treatment is recommended for the pain of a Portuguese man o' war sting?
a: About 20 minutes in water at about 45 °C
12204.e: Hot but not scalding water at about 45 °C for around 20 minutes eases the pain. Studies show that it works better than ice.
12204.m: Warm water at about 45 °C helps against the pain.

12205.q: Which animal has a well-known partnership with the Portuguese man o' war and lives between its tentacles?
12205.e: The man-of-war fish lives between the tentacles and is protected from enemies there. It skilfully dodges the tentacles and tolerates the poison much better than other fish.
12205.m: The man-of-war fish lives between the tentacles of the Portuguese man o' war.

12206.q: Which sea turtle eats the Portuguese man o' war despite its poison?
12206.e: The loggerhead turtle (Caretta caretta) is one of the known predators. Its thick skin protects it from the stinging cells.
12206.m: The loggerhead turtle eats Portuguese men o' war.

12207.q: Which large fish is among the predators of the Portuguese man o' war?
12207.e: The ocean sunfish (Mola mola) likes to eat jelly-like animals. This also includes the Portuguese man o' war.
12207.m: The ocean sunfish eats Portuguese men o' war.

12208.q: Which blue sea slug eats the Portuguese man o' war and stores its stinging cells for its own defence?
12208.e: The blue dragon eats the colony and stores unfired stinging capsules in its body appendages. In this way, it becomes well defended itself.
12208.m: The blue dragon steals the stinging cells of the Portuguese man o' war.

12209.q: Which snail, which floats on a raft of foam that it builds itself, also eats Portuguese men o' war?
12209.e: The violet snail (Janthina) floats at the surface on a raft of mucus bubbles. It feeds on drifting animals such as the Portuguese man o' war.
12209.m: The violet snail hunts the Portuguese man o' war at the surface.

12210.q: What trick do young blanket octopuses use with the Portuguese man o' war?
a: They carry torn-off tentacles as a weapon
They live in its gas bubble
They eat only its gas bubble
They imitate its colour to deceive prey
12210.e: Young blanket octopuses are immune to the poison. They hold on to pieces of the Portuguese man o' war's tentacles and use them to fend off enemies.
12210.m: The blanket octopus arms itself with tentacles of the Portuguese man o' war.

12211.q: Which habitat is typical of the Portuguese man o' war?
a: The surface of the open sea
The bottom of the deep sea
12211.e: The Portuguese man o' war lives in the pleuston, that is, right at the sea surface. Half of it sticks up into the air, half hangs in the water.
12211.m: The Portuguese man o' war lives at the surface of the open sea.

12212.q: In which climate zones is the Portuguese man o' war mainly found?
12212.e: The Portuguese man o' war prefers warm seas. With wind and currents, however, it occasionally reaches European coasts.
12212.m: The Portuguese man o' war loves warm seas.

12213.q: In which ocean is the species Physalia physalis, in the narrower sense, mainly at home?
12213.e: Physalia physalis occurs mainly in the Atlantic, for example off West Africa, the Caribbean and the Azores. In the Indo-Pacific, related Physalia species live.
12213.m: The Portuguese man o' war is found mainly in the Atlantic.

12214.q: What did a worldwide genetic study in 2025 reveal about the Portuguese man o' war and its relatives?
a: There are at least four different Physalia species
All Physalia belong to a single species
12214.e: The study published in 2025 found five genetic lines, which correspond to at least four species. Besides Physalia physalis, these are Physalia utriculus, Physalia megalista and the newly described Physalia minuta.
12214.m: Behind the Portuguese man o' war are several similar species.

12215.q: What is the smaller relative of the Portuguese man o' war, common in Australia, called?
12215.e: The “bluebottle” has a smaller float, usually only about half as long as in the Portuguese man o' war. It is widespread in the Indo-Pacific and very common on Australian beaches.
12215.m: The bluebottle is the little sister of the Portuguese man o' war.

12216.q: Which other blue drifting animal with a sail is often mistaken for the Portuguese man o' war?
12216.e: The by-the-wind sailor also drifts at the surface with a sail. But it is much smaller and has only short tentacles, which are usually harmless to humans.
12216.m: The by-the-wind sailor is smaller and more harmless than the Portuguese man o' war.

12217.q: What colour is the float of the Portuguese man o' war usually?
a: Translucent blue to violet with a pink crest
12217.e: The bubble shimmers bluish to violet, and the crest is often pink. The blue tones match the colour of the sea well.
12217.m: The Portuguese man o' war shimmers blue and violet.

12218.q: How long do the red, whip-like welts usually stay visible after a sting from a Portuguese man o' war?
12218.e: After a sting, red welts that look like whip marks form on the skin. They usually stay visible for two to three days, even when the pain has long since faded.
12218.m: You can usually see the welts of a Portuguese man o' war sting for two to three days.

12219.q: How many Portuguese men o' war can come together in a drifting group?
12219.e: Wind and currents often drive the colonies together. In this way, gatherings of up to about 1000 animals arise.
12219.m: Portuguese men o' war often drift in large groups.

12220.q: Which phylum of animals does coral belong to?
12220.e: Corals are cnidarians and are therefore related to jellyfish and sea anemones. Stinging cells are typical of the phylum.
12220.m: Coral is a cnidarian like the jellyfish.

12221.q: Which class within the cnidarians do stony corals belong to?
12221.e: Stony corals belong to the Anthozoa, which have no free-swimming jellyfish stage. After a short larval stage, they live as polyps, mostly sitting fixed to the ground.
12221.m: Corals are anthozoans with no jellyfish stage.

12222.q: Why are stony corals called that?
a: Because they form a hard limy skeleton
Because they can live only on stones
Because they turn to stone at low tide
12222.e: Stony corals secrete a hard skeleton of lime. Their scientific name Scleractinia also refers to this (Greek skleros, hard).
12222.m: Stony corals build a hard limy skeleton.

12223.q: Which mineral does the skeleton of today's stony corals consist of?
12223.e: Stony corals secrete calcium carbonate in the form of aragonite. Over a long time, whole reefs arise from it.
12223.m: The coral skeleton consists of aragonite, a form of lime.

12224.q: Stony corals belong to the Hexacorallia, soft corals to the Octocorallia. What do these names refer to?
a: The number of tentacles, in sixes or eights
The number of colours in the skeleton
The age of the colony in years
12224.e: Hexa means six, octo eight. In stony corals, tentacles and partitions are laid out in multiples of six, while soft corals have eight tentacles.
12224.m: Stony corals count in sixes, soft corals in eights.

12225.q: How many body openings does a coral polyp have for taking in food and excreting?
12225.e: The polyp has only one mouth opening, which also serves as the anus. Undigested remains are expelled by the same route.
12225.m: In the coral polyp, the mouth is also the exit.

12226.q: What does a coral polyp use to catch small prey from the plankton?
a: Sticky threads of mucus on the foot
12226.e: The tentacles carry stinging cells (nematocysts), which shoot out a poison thread on contact. In this way, zooplankton is paralysed and guided to the mouth.
12226.m: The coral paralyses its prey with stinging cells.

12227.q: What are the zooxanthellae that live in the tissue of many corals?
a: Single-celled algae that carry out photosynthesis
Bacteria that break down the limy skeleton
Fungi that make the coral ill
12227.e: Zooxanthellae are single-celled algae from the group of dinoflagellates. They live in the tissue of the polyps and supply them with sugar from photosynthesis.
12227.m: Zooxanthellae are algae that supply the coral with energy.

12228.q: What share of their energy needs can reef-building corals cover from the photosynthesis of their zooxanthellae?
12228.e: The zooxanthellae pass on a large part of their photosynthesis products, such as sugar, to the coral. In many species, this covers up to about 90 per cent of energy needs.
12228.m: The zooxanthellae supply the coral with most of its energy.

12229.q: What do the zooxanthellae receive from the coral in return?
a: Light from their own light organs
12229.e: The coral offers the algae a sheltered place in the light and supplies carbon dioxide as well as nitrogen and phosphorus compounds from its metabolism. Both partners benefit.
12229.m: The coral gives the algae a home and nutrients.

12230.q: Why do reef-building corals need clear, shallow water?
a: They breathe only at the surface
12230.e: The zooxanthellae carry out photosynthesis and therefore depend on enough light. Murky or deep water greatly slows the growth of reef-building corals.
12230.m: Reef corals need light for their algae partners.

a: The coral forms white protective scales
12231.e: Under stress, mainly from water that is too warm, the coral loses its coloured zooxanthellae. The white limy skeleton then shows through the transparent tissue.
12231.m: In bleaching, the coral loses its coloured algae.

12232.q: Is a bleached coral dead at once?
a: No, it can recover if the water cools quickly
Yes, it dies within a few hours
Yes, because the skeleton falls apart at once
No, it does not need the algae at all
12232.e: A bleached coral is still alive, but starving. If temperatures return to normal in time, it can take in new zooxanthellae; otherwise it dies.
12232.m: A bleached coral is starving, but not yet dead.

12233.q: What main trigger leads to mass coral bleaching worldwide?
a: Sea temperatures that are too high for weeks
Too much plankton in the reef water
Strong winter thunderstorms over the reef
Too many fish in the reef
12233.e: Mass bleaching is triggered mainly by marine heatwaves. Even about 1 °C above the usual summer maximum can cause bleaching over several weeks.
12233.m: Persistently warm water bleaches the corals.

12234.q: How do researchers worldwide monitor whether coral reefs are threatened by bleaching?
a: With satellite measurements of sea temperature
By counting the sharks in the reef
By measuring the salt content in rain
12234.e: Programmes such as NOAA's Coral Reef Watch measure the water temperature by satellite. If it stays above the usual summer maximum for weeks, bleaching threatens.
12234.m: Satellites warn when the sea gets too warm for corals.

12235.q: According to NOAA, what share of the world's reef area was exposed to bleaching-level heat stress in the fourth global bleaching event (2023 to 2025)?
12235.e: The fourth global bleaching event affected about 84 per cent of reef areas in more than 80 countries and territories. It was therefore the largest bleaching event ever observed.
12235.m: The bleaching of 2023 to 2025 hit over four fifths of all reefs.

12236.q: In which year did the first documented global coral bleaching take place?
12236.e: The first global mass bleaching took place in 1998 during a strong El Niño event. Others followed in 2010 and 2014 to 2017.
12236.m: The first worldwide coral bleaching happened in 1998.

12237.q: According to the IUCN assessment of 2024, what share of reef-building warm-water corals is regarded as threatened with extinction?
12237.e: The IUCN reassessed 892 species and classed 44 per cent as threatened. In the earlier assessment in 2008, it was still about a third.
12237.m: Almost half of reef coral species are threatened with extinction.

12238.q: What does the IUCN name as the greatest threat to reef-building corals?
12238.e: According to the IUCN, climate change is the main threat, above all through heatwaves and bleaching. In addition come pollution, agricultural run-off, diseases and overfishing.
12238.m: Climate change is the greatest danger to corals.

12239.q: How does ocean acidification harm stony corals?
a: It makes building the limy skeleton harder
It poisons the stinging cells directly
It makes the tentacles stick together
12239.e: The sea takes up carbon dioxide, which lowers the pH value and leaves fewer carbonate ions available. The coral then needs more energy to deposit lime.
12239.m: Acidic seawater makes building lime harder for corals.

12240.q: How long is the Great Barrier Reef off the coast of Australia?
12240.e: The Great Barrier Reef stretches over more than 2300 kilometres along the coast of Queensland. It is the largest coral reef system on Earth.
12240.m: The Great Barrier Reef is longer than 2300 kilometres.

12241.q: Roughly how big is the area of the Great Barrier Reef?
12241.e: The area covers about 344,400 square kilometres. That is more than eight times the area of Switzerland.
12241.m: The Great Barrier Reef is over eight times as big as Switzerland.

12242.q: Roughly how many individual reefs does the Great Barrier Reef consist of?
12242.e: The Great Barrier Reef is not a single reef, but a system of over 2900 reefs and about 900 islands. Together they form the largest structure created by living things.
12242.m: The Great Barrier Reef consists of thousands of individual reefs.

12243.q: In which year was the Great Barrier Reef declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
12243.e: The Great Barrier Reef was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1981. The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park had already been founded in 1975.
12243.m: The Great Barrier Reef has been a World Heritage Site since 1981.

12244.q: Which animal is known as a coral eater for causing great damage to the Great Barrier Reef?
12244.e: The crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster) eats coral polyps by turning its stomach inside out over them. In outbreaks, it can eat whole stretches of reef bare.
12244.m: In outbreaks, the crown-of-thorns starfish eats corals bare.

12245.q: Which large sea snail is regarded as a natural enemy of the crown-of-thorns starfish, a coral eater?
12245.e: The giant triton (Charonia tritonis) eats crown-of-thorns starfish. Because it was heavily collected for its beautiful shell, it has become rare on many reefs.
12245.m: The giant triton helps the coral because it eats crown-of-thorns starfish.

12246.q: What role do parrotfish play for coral reefs?
a: They scrape off algae and lime and produce sand
They build new reef structures with mucus
They bring zooxanthellae to the corals
12246.e: With their beak-like teeth, parrotfish graze algae off corals and dead limestone. They excrete the ground-up lime as fine sand.
12246.m: Parrotfish keep reefs free of algae and make sand.

12247.q: When does the famous mass spawning of corals on the Great Barrier Reef usually take place?
a: A few nights after a full moon between October and December
At new moon in June or July
At midday at low tide in March
Every day at sunrise in midsummer
12247.e: On the Great Barrier Reef, many coral species release eggs and sperm at the same time about one to six nights after a full moon in the southern spring, that is, between October and December. Water temperature, moon phase and day length control the timing.
12247.m: On the Great Barrier Reef, corals spawn shortly after a full moon in the southern hemisphere's spring.

12248.q: In what form do many hermaphrodite stony corals release their sex cells in mass spawning?
a: As bundles of eggs and sperm
As long strings of spawn on the bottom
12248.e: Many stony corals are hermaphrodites and release eggs and sperm together in small bundles. These float to the surface, where they break up and fertilisation takes place.
12248.m: Many corals spawn bundles of eggs and sperm.

12249.q: How do corals settle new reefs even though the polyps are fixed in place?
a: Their larvae drift with the current and settle
The polyps crawl across the seabed at night
Fish carry whole colonies along in their mouths
Birds spread pieces of coral on their feet
12249.e: Fertilised eggs develop into ciliated larvae, the planulae. They drift in the water for some time and then settle on hard ground to form a new polyp.
12249.m: Coral larvae drift through the water to new places.

12250.q: How does a coral colony grow from a single polyp?
a: By the fusing of many larvae
By moulting of the original polyp
12250.e: The first polyp divides or forms buds, so that genetically identical daughter polyps arise. In this way, colonies with thousands of polyps grow up.
12250.m: A coral colony arises by budding from one polyp.

12251.q: How can broken-off pieces of coral contribute to reproduction?
a: They attach and grow into new colonies
They drift around the world as plankton
12251.e: If a storm, for example, breaks off branches, the fragments can attach and form new colonies. Projects to restore reefs with coral gardens also use this fragmentation.
12251.m: Broken-off coral branches can become new colonies.

12252.q: In which temperature range do reef-building corals thrive best?
12252.e: Reef-building corals prefer warm water of about 23 to 29 °C. Many already live close to their upper temperature limit, which is why heatwaves are so dangerous.
12252.m: Reef corals like warm water, but not too hot.

12253.q: Between which latitudes do most tropical coral reefs lie?
12253.e: Warm-water reefs are largely restricted to the tropics and subtropics. Outside about 30 degrees of latitude, the water is mostly too cool for reef formation.
12253.m: Tropical coral reefs lie around the equator.

12254.q: Which type of reef grows as a ring around a lagoon with no central island?
12254.e: An atoll is a ring-shaped reef that encloses a lagoon. It often forms where a volcanic island has sunk.
12254.m: An atoll is a ring of coral around a lagoon.

12255.q: Which type of reef grows directly at the coast and is separated from the land only by shallow water?
12255.e: Fringing reefs grow directly along the coast and are the commonest type of reef. Barrier reefs, by contrast, lie further out and are separated by a deeper lagoon.
12255.m: The fringing reef borders the coast directly.

12256.q: Which naturalist explained the formation of atolls from coral reefs around sinking volcanic islands?
12256.e: In 1842, in a book on coral reefs, Charles Darwin described how fringing reefs turn into barrier reefs and then atolls when an island slowly sinks. Drilling in the 20th century confirmed his theory.
12256.m: Darwin explained how corals form atolls.

12257.q: What share of marine species do coral reefs shelter, although they cover less than one per cent of the seabed?
12257.e: Coral reefs are among the most species-rich habitats on Earth. Estimates assume that about 25 per cent of all marine species depend on them.
12257.m: In a tiny area, very many marine species live in coral reefs.

12258.q: Where is the Coral Triangle, the region with the greatest coral diversity in the world?
a: Between Indonesia, the Philippines and Papua New Guinea
In the Red Sea off Egypt
In the Indian Ocean off the Maldives
12258.e: The Coral Triangle in the western Pacific covers waters of Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste and the Solomon Islands. About three quarters of all known coral species occur there.
12258.m: Most coral species live in the Coral Triangle of South-East Asia.

12259.q: How do cold-water corals such as Desmophyllum pertusum (formerly Lophelia pertusa) differ from tropical reef corals?
a: They live without zooxanthellae in dark, cold water
They live only in the freshwater of lakes
12259.e: Cold-water corals live at depths without light and feed exclusively on plankton and suspended matter. Off Norway, they form extensive deep-water reefs.
12259.m: Cold-water corals live without algae in the dark depths.

12260.q: Since when have stony corals existed, according to fossil finds?
a: Since the Middle Triassic about 240 million years ago
Since the Cretaceous about 80 million years ago
Since the Cambrian about 520 million years ago
Since the Quaternary about 2 million years ago
12260.e: The oldest stony corals date from the Middle Triassic about 240 million years ago. Older coral groups such as the rugose corals had died out at the end of the Permian.
12260.m: Stony corals have existed for about 240 million years.

12261.q: Roughly how fast do branching stony corals such as staghorn corals grow compared with massive species?
a: Up to about 10 cm a year, massive ones only about 0.3 to 2 cm
About 1 mm a year, massive ones about 1 cm
About 1 m a year, massive ones about 50 cm
Equally fast, about 5 cm a year
12261.e: According to NOAA, branching forms can add up to about 10 cm a year, while dome-shaped colonies manage only 0.3 to 2 cm. Massive corals are often sturdier and very old.
12261.m: Branching corals grow faster than massive ones.

12262.q: Where does the brain coral get its name?
a: From the winding grooves on its surface
From its especially large nervous system
From its position at the head of the reef
12262.e: In brain corals, the polyps are arranged in long, winding valleys. The rounded colony therefore resembles the folds of a brain.
12262.m: The brain coral looks like a brain because of its folds.

12263.q: Which fast-growing corals with antler-like branches shape many reefs but are particularly prone to bleaching?
12263.e: Staghorn corals of the genus Acropora form branching and table-shaped colonies. They grow quickly, but react sensitively to heat stress.
12263.m: Staghorn corals grow fast, but bleach easily.

12264.q: Which group does the red precious coral from the Mediterranean, used for jewellery, belong to?
12264.e: The red precious coral (Corallium rubrum) is an octocoral with eight tentacles per polyp. Its red limy skeleton has been made into jewellery since antiquity.
12264.m: The red precious coral is an octocoral from the Mediterranean.

12265.q: Where does the German word “Koralle” (coral) come from?
12265.e: The word reached German via Latin corallium from the Greek korallion. It originally meant the red precious coral.
12265.m: The word coral comes from Greek.

12266.q: Why are fire corals not true corals in the sense of the anthozoans?
a: They belong to the red algae
12266.e: Fire corals of the genus Millepora do form a limy skeleton, but they are hydrozoans. Their strong stinging cells cause burning pain on contact.
12266.m: Fire corals are hydrozoans and not true corals.

12267.q: Which organisms additionally cement the coral reef together with limy crusts?
12267.e: Limy crustose coralline algae coat coral rubble and bind it into a solid reef body. Their surfaces also help coral larvae to settle.
12267.m: Crustose coralline algae cement the coral reef together.

12268.q: Where has a disease been spreading since 2014 that makes the tissue of many stony coral species die off rapidly?
a: Off Florida and in the Caribbean
12268.e: Stony coral tissue loss disease was discovered off Florida in 2014 and spread through the Caribbean. It attacks many species of stony coral.
12268.m: Since 2014, a tissue disease has been destroying many corals in the Caribbean.

12269.q: What was observed for the first time on the Great Barrier Reef in 2016 and 2017?
a: Mass bleaching in two consecutive years
An ice cover over the reef
The complete death of the whole reef
12269.e: In 2016 and 2017, mass bleaching occurred on the Great Barrier Reef for the first time in two years in a row. The corals therefore had hardly any time to recover.
12269.m: In 2016 and 2017, the Great Barrier Reef bleached two years in a row.

12270.q: Which animal phylum do sponges belong to?
12270.e: Sponges form their own phylum, Porifera. Cnidarians (Cnidaria), bryozoans (Bryozoa) and placozoans (Placozoa) are separate phyla.
12270.m: Sponges form the animal phylum Porifera.

12271.q: What does the scientific name “Porifera” of the sponges mean literally?
12271.e: “Porifera” is made up of Latin “porus” (pore) and “ferre” (to carry). The name describes the many pores through which water flows into the sponge.
12271.m: Porifera means pore bearers, because sponges are full of pores.

12272.q: What did the zoologist Robert Grant observe in sponges that led to the name “Porifera”?
a: Water flows into the sponge through many pores
Sponges wear hard shells like crabs
Sponges glow at night in the water
12272.e: Grant observed the flow of water through sponges. The name Porifera means pore bearers.
12272.m: Porifera means pore bearers, because water flows through pores.

12273.q: Roughly how many sponge species are scientifically described today?
12273.e: Around 9000 sponge species are described in the scientific literature. There are probably many undiscovered species, especially in the deep sea.

12274.q: What does the skeleton of most sponge species, the demosponges, consist of?
a: Silica needles and elastic protein fibres
12274.e: Over 80 per cent of all sponge species are demosponges. Their skeleton consists of needles of silica and fibres of the protein spongin.
12274.m: Most sponges are demosponges with silica needles and spongin fibres.

12275.q: What material do the skeletal needles of the calcareous sponges (Calcarea) consist of?
12275.e: Calcareous sponges form their needles (spicules) from calcium carbonate, that is, lime. Glass sponges and demosponges, by contrast, use silica.
12275.m: Calcareous sponges build their needles from lime.

12276.q: How can you recognise the skeletal needles of glass sponges (Hexactinellida)?
a: They have six rays and are made of silica
They have four rays and are made of lime
They are hook-shaped and made of chitin
12276.e: The name Hexactinellida means roughly “six-rayed”. Their needles consist of silicon dioxide and have three axes with six rays.
12276.m: Glass sponges have six-rayed needles of glass.

12277.q: Which protein forms the elastic fibre framework of many demosponges, such as the bath sponge?
12277.e: Spongin is a collagen-like protein. In the bath sponge, only this soft fibre framework remains once the cells have been removed.
12277.m: The soft framework of the bath sponge consists of spongin.

12278.q: Which cells in a sponge create the water current and catch food particles?
12278.e: Choanocytes beat their flagellum and so drive water through the sponge. Their collar of fine projections holds back bacteria and particles.
12278.m: Collar cells pump the water and catch the food.

12279.q: Which single-celled organisms do the collar cells of sponges resemble so closely that this matters for the evolution of animals?
12279.e: Choanoflagellates also have a flagellum with a collar. They are regarded as the closest single-celled relatives of animals, which makes sponges a key to the origin of multicellular animals.
12279.m: Choanoflagellates are the closest single-celled relatives of animals.

12280.q: By what route does water flow through a sponge?
a: In through many small pores, out through large openings
In through large openings, out through small pores
In through a mouth and out through a gut
Not at all, sponges do not draw in water
12280.e: Water enters through many small pores and leaves the sponge through one or more large exit openings, the oscula. In this way, used water is thrown far away.
12280.m: Water flows into the sponge through pores and out through large openings.

12281.q: Why can sponges regenerate so well?
a: They have cells that can turn into almost all other cell types
They have a brain that plans new body parts
They swap body parts with other sponges
They have an especially strong blood vessel system
12281.e: Amoeba-like cells in the middle layer, the archaeocytes, can become other cell types. This explains the strong regeneration of sponges.
12281.m: Versatile cells make sponges masters of regeneration.

12282.q: What lies in the jelly-like middle layer inside the body of a sponge?
12282.e: The middle layer is called the mesohyl. Cells wander through it, and skeletal needles and spongin are formed there.
12282.m: In the middle layer of the sponge, cells wander and needles form.

12283.q: Which organ systems are missing completely in sponges?
12283.e: Sponges have no nerves, no true muscles and no digestive tract. Food is taken in and digested by individual cells.
12283.m: Sponges live entirely without nerves, muscles and gut.

12284.q: How is food digested in sponges?
12284.e: Sponges digest intracellularly: choanocytes and archaeocytes take in particles and digest them in food vacuoles.
12284.m: Sponges digest their food inside single cells.

12285.q: Why can sponges with many small chambers and canals grow especially large?
a: The chambers have room for many more pumping cells, which filter more water
The canals are lined with muscles
Air is stored in the chambers
The chambers serve as a stomach
12285.e: In the commonest body plan, the leucon type, the collar cells lie in many small chambers. In this way, even a large body can filter enough water.
12285.m: Many small chambers allow sponges to have large bodies.

12286.q: How is the simplest body plan of a sponge built?
a: Like a tube with a single cavity
Like a ball with a gut and a mouth
Like a tree with roots and leaves
Like a star with five arms
12286.e: In the simplest body plan, the ascon type, the sponge is a tube whose cavity is lined directly with collar cells. It occurs only in small calcareous sponges.
12286.m: The simplest sponge is a tube with one cavity.

12287.q: What famous experiment did Henry Van Peters Wilson carry out with sponges in 1907?
a: He pressed them through a cloth, and the cells found each other again
He let them freeze for a year
He dyed their needles with gold
He crossed two species with each other
12287.e: Wilson pressed sponges through fine silk gauze and so broke them into single cells. These found each other again and formed new, working sponges.
12287.m: Sponge cells that have been broken apart can come together again as a sponge.

12288.q: How do freshwater sponges in Switzerland survive the winter?
a: As small resting capsules with dormant cells
They overwinter as whole active sponges under the ice
12288.e: In autumn, freshwater sponges form gemmules, small capsules with dormant stem cells in a protective shell. In spring, these cells build up a new sponge.
12288.m: Freshwater sponges overwinter as resting capsules.

12289.q: In which season do freshwater sponges in Central Europe typically form their gemmules?
12289.e: The gemmules form in autumn, before the sponge dies back. They rest over the winter and germinate in spring.
12289.m: In autumn, freshwater sponges form their gemmules.

12290.q: What are the skeletal needles of a sponge for?
a: They support the body and deter predators
They serve as poison spines for hunting
They are used for walking on the seabed
12290.e: The needles are formed by special cells, the sclerocytes, from lime or silica. They give the soft body support and make it unpalatable to many animals.
12290.m: Skeletal needles support and protect the sponge.

12291.q: Why are freshwater sponges such as Spongilla lacustris sometimes bright green?
12291.e: Green specimens contain single-celled green algae in their cells. In the shade, the same sponges are often whitish to brownish.
12291.m: Green freshwater sponges contain algae in their cells.

12292.q: Where in Central Europe can you find freshwater sponges such as Spongilla lacustris?
a: In lakes and slow waters, on stones and wood
Only in mountain streams above 2000 m
Only in groundwater deep in the soil
12292.e: Freshwater sponges such as Spongilla lacustris and Ephydatia fluviatilis grow as crusts or cushions on stones, wood and plants in lakes and calm flowing waters.
12292.m: Sponges also live in Swiss lakes.

12293.q: Which sponge class do freshwater sponges (Spongillida) belong to?
12293.e: All freshwater sponges belong to the order Spongillida within the Demospongiae. Calcareous and glass sponges live only in the sea.

12294.q: Which insect larvae feed as specialists on freshwater sponges?
12294.e: The larvae of spongillaflies, a family of lacewings, live in the water and suck on freshwater sponges with their mouthparts.
12294.m: Spongillafly larvae live on freshwater sponges.

12295.q: How do most sponges reproduce sexually?
a: They are mostly hermaphrodites and release sperm into the water
They mate with direct body contact
They lay eggs in cocoons on land
They multiply only by spores like fungi
12295.e: Many sponges form both egg cells and sperm. The sperm are expelled with the water current and drawn in by other sponges.
12295.m: Most sponges are hermaphrodites and fertilise through the water.

12296.q: How do sponges that sit fixed in place reach new locations?
a: Through seeds blown by the wind
By detaching from the bottom and swimming over long distances
12296.e: Many sponges form ciliated swimming larvae, such as the parenchymula. The larva swims for a while and then settles in a new place.

a: Yes, some crawl a few millimetres a day
No, they are completely immobile for life
Yes, they swim by jet propulsion like jellyfish
Yes, they roll over long distances with the current
12297.e: For a long time, sponges were thought to be completely fixed in place. Observations show, however, that some marine and freshwater sponges crawl slowly over the ground at about 1 to 4 mm a day.
12297.m: Some sponges crawl very slowly over the ground.

12298.q: How do carnivorous sponges catch their prey?
a: With hook-shaped needles on which small crustaceans get caught
With tentacles full of stinging cells
12298.e: Carnivorous sponges, almost all from the family Cladorhizidae, no longer have a water current. Small crustaceans get tangled on their hooked needles and are enveloped and digested by cells.
12298.m: Carnivorous sponges catch crustaceans with hooked needles.

12299.q: Where was the carnivorous sponge Lycopodina hypogea discovered at a fairly shallow depth?
a: In underwater caves of the Mediterranean
In a mountain lake in the Alps
In the polar ice of the Arctic
In a hot spring in Iceland
12299.e: Lycopodina hypogea lives in Mediterranean caves at a depth of about 17 to 23 m. Most carnivorous sponges, by contrast, live in the deep sea.
12299.m: A carnivorous sponge lives in caves of the Mediterranean.

12300.q: Why is a carnivorous deep-sea sponge off California called the “harp sponge”?
a: Its upright branches resemble a harp
It produces notes like a harp
It stretches long threads between rocks
12300.e: The harp sponge Chondrocladia lyra has upright branches that resemble a harp or lyre. With them, it catches small crustaceans.
12300.m: The harp sponge looks like a harp.

12301.q: Which animals often live as a pair for life in the glass lattice of the Venus' flower basket (Euplectella aspergillum)?
12301.e: Young shrimps slip in through the lattice and grow too big to get out again. They eat the particles drawn in and keep the sponge clean.
12301.m: A pair of shrimps often lives in the lattice of the glass sponge.

12302.q: What are skeletons of the glass sponge Euplectella aspergillum traditionally given as in Japan?
a: As a wedding gift and symbol of eternal love
As a lucky charm for fishermen
As a gift for a birth
12302.e: Because a pair of shrimps often lives inside until death, the skeleton is regarded as a symbol of eternal love and is given as a wedding gift.
12302.m: In Japan, the glass sponge stands for eternal love.

12303.q: Why are optical-fibre researchers interested in the anchor spicules of glass sponges such as Euplectella?
a: They conduct light and are also very resistant to breaking
They conduct electric current better than copper
12303.e: The hair-thin silica needles conduct light much like optical fibres, but because of their layered structure they are far less brittle than technical glass.
12303.m: Glass sponge needles are natural, break-resistant light guides.

12304.q: How old was a specimen of the deep-sea glass sponge Monorhaphis chuni according to researchers' estimates?
12304.e: From the growth layers of its giant needle, a Monorhaphis chuni was estimated to be about 11,000 years old. Sponges are thus among the longest-lived animals.
12304.m: Some glass sponges live to be over 10,000 years old.

12305.q: How long can the giant basal spicule of the glass sponge Monorhaphis chuni grow?
12305.e: The anchor spicule of Monorhaphis chuni reaches up to about 3 m in length. It is regarded as the largest biologically formed silica structure on Earth.
12305.m: Monorhaphis has a glass needle up to three metres long.

12306.q: Where was the largest sponge known at the time discovered in 2015?
a: In the deep sea near Hawaii
12306.e: Researchers found it in the Papahānaumokuākea marine protected area north-west of Hawaii at a depth of over 2000 m. It was about as big as a minibus.
12306.m: The largest known sponge lives in the deep sea near Hawaii.

12307.q: Which sponge group was recognised in 2012 as a fourth class alongside demosponges, calcareous sponges and glass sponges?
12307.e: Genetic and anatomical studies showed in 2012 that the Homoscleromorpha do not belong to the demosponges. Since then they have counted as a separate, fourth class of sponges.
12307.m: Since 2012, the Homoscleromorpha have been the fourth sponge class.

12308.q: Roughly how old are the glass sponge reefs off the coast of British Columbia in Canada?
12308.e: The glass sponge reefs discovered in 1987 in Hecate Strait and Queen Charlotte Sound are about 9000 years old. Such reefs had previously been thought long extinct.
12308.m: The glass sponge reefs of Canada are about 9000 years old.

12309.q: What can glass sponges do thanks to their tissue of fused cells?
a: Stop their pumping instantly when disturbed
12309.e: In glass sponges, many cells are fused into one large syncytium. Electrical signals spread through it, so the sponge can suddenly stop its pumping.
12309.m: Glass sponges can switch off their pumping in a flash.

12310.q: From which geological period do well-preserved sponge fossils of the Doushantuo Formation in China date?
12310.e: The Doushantuo Formation shows sponge fossils from the Ediacaran about 580 million years ago. Sponges are thus among the oldest known animal groups.
12310.m: Sponges have existed for over 500 million years.

12311.q: Which animal group challenges sponges for the position of earliest branch on the animal family tree?
12311.e: For a long time sponges were clearly regarded as the sister group of all other animals. Some genetic studies suggest that comb jellies branched off even earlier, which is disputed among researchers.
12311.m: Whether sponges or comb jellies branched off first is still being researched.

12312.q: Which extinct group of Cambrian reef builders is often counted among the sponges?
12312.e: In the early Cambrian, the archaeocyaths built the first reefs made by animals. Their structure resembles that of sponges, which is why they are usually placed with the Porifera.
12312.m: The archaeocyaths were Cambrian reef sponges.

12313.q: What do boring sponges of the genus Cliona do to shells and corals?
a: They dissolve limestone and bore tunnels into it
They glue them together into reefs
12313.e: Boring sponges use special cells to etch out tiny chips of limestone and live in the tunnels. In this way they contribute strongly to the bioerosion of reefs.
12313.m: Boring sponges dig into limestone and shells.

12314.q: Which sea turtle feeds mainly on sponges?
12314.e: In coral reefs the hawksbill turtle eats mainly sponges, and it tolerates their needles and toxins.
12314.m: The hawksbill turtle lives mainly on sponges.

12315.q: What do some bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay in Australia use sea sponges for?
a: To protect their snouts when foraging on the seabed
12315.e: The dolphins pull a sponge over their snout and use it to poke about on the rough seabed for fish. This tool use is passed on mainly from mothers to daughters.
12315.m: Some dolphins protect their snouts with a sponge.

12316.q: Which cancer drug was developed from a substance found in the sea sponge Halichondria okadai?
12316.e: Eribulin is a synthetic variant of halichondrin B, which was first isolated from Halichondria okadai. It is used against breast cancer.
12316.m: The cancer drug eribulin goes back to a sponge substance.

12317.q: Which Caribbean sponge yielded nucleosides that led to the leukaemia drug cytarabine?
12317.e: Unusual nucleosides were discovered in Tethya crypta (now Tectitethya crypta) in the 1950s. They served as the model for cytarabine, which is used against leukaemia.
12317.m: Cytarabine against leukaemia was modelled on a sponge.

12318.q: What is the Greek island of Kalymnos famous for?
12318.e: On Kalymnos, men have dived for bath sponges of the genus Spongia for centuries. The island is regarded as the traditional centre of sponge diving.
12318.m: Kalymnos is the island of the sponge divers.

12319.q: What does the “sponge loop” in coral reefs describe?
a: Sponges take up dissolved organic matter and pass it on to other animals as particles
Sponges travel in circles around coral colonies
Sponges pump water in a closed circuit
Sponges grow in rings around seagrass
12319.e: Sponges filter dissolved organic matter and constantly shed old cells. Other reef dwellers eat these particles, so nutrients are retained in the nutrient-poor reef.
12319.m: Through the sponge loop, sponges make dissolved food available to reef dwellers.

12320.q: Which animal phylum do tapeworms belong to?
12320.e: Tapeworms form the class Cestoda within the flatworms (Platyhelminthes). They are not closely related to annelids such as the earthworm.

12321.q: How does the body structure of tapeworms differ from that of roundworms?
a: Tapeworms are flat and segmented, roundworms are round
Tapeworms are round, roundworms are flat
Both are built in exactly the same way
Tapeworms have a hard outer skeleton
12321.e: Tapeworms are flatworms and have a flat, usually segmented body. Roundworms (ascarids) are nematodes with a round, unsegmented body.
12321.m: Tapeworms are flat, roundworms are round.

12322.q: Where does the German name “Bandwurm” (ribbon worm) of the tapeworm come from?
a: From its way of moving in groups
From its discoverer, who was called Band
From the ligaments in the joints that it infects
12322.e: Tapeworms are often several metres long but only a few millimetres wide and flat. They look like a ribbon. The scientific name Cestoda also comes from the Greek word for belt.
12322.m: The tapeworm is long and flat like a ribbon.

12323.q: Roughly how many species of tapeworm are known?
12323.e: Depending on the source, about 3,500 to 6,000 tapeworm species have been described. Almost all groups of vertebrates can be infected by tapeworms.
12323.m: There are several thousand known species of tapeworm.

12324.q: How does a tapeworm take in food even though it has no gut?
a: through a mouth on its head
through pores at its tail end
12324.e: Tapeworms have neither a mouth nor a gut. They absorb dissolved nutrients from the host’s gut contents directly through their skin.
12324.m: The tapeworm feeds through its whole skin.

12325.q: Why is a tapeworm not digested itself in its host’s gut?
a: Its skin protects it from the digestive juices
It sits inside a hard limestone shell
It leaves the gut every night
There are no digestive juices in the gut
12325.e: The tapeworm’s special skin is protected against the host’s digestive juices. It also absorbs dissolved nutrients through this same skin.
12325.m: The special skin protects the tapeworm from digestion.

12326.q: What are the tiny projections that densely cover a tapeworm’s skin for?
a: They increase the surface area for absorbing food
12326.e: The fine projections, called microtriches, greatly increase the surface area of the tapeworm’s skin. This lets it absorb more nutrients from the gut.
12326.m: Tiny projections increase the tapeworm’s surface area.

12327.q: What is the head of a tapeworm, which it uses to hold on in the gut, called?
12327.e: Depending on the species, the scolex has suckers, sucking grooves or hooks. With it the tapeworm anchors itself in the gut wall.
12327.m: The tapeworm holds on with its scolex.

12328.q: What are the individual segments of a tapeworm called?
12328.e: The body of true tapeworms consists of segments called proglottids. Each segment usually contains its own set of reproductive organs.
12328.m: The segments of a tapeworm are called proglottids.

12329.q: How many segments can a large beef tapeworm consist of?
12329.e: The chain of segments of a beef tapeworm can include over a thousand, sometimes up to around two thousand segments. New ones are constantly growing behind the head.
12329.m: A beef tapeworm consists of over a thousand segments.
