12330.q: Where do new segments constantly form in a tapeworm?
a: in the neck zone directly behind the head
at the rear end of the body
in the middle of the chain of segments
in every segment at the same time
12330.e: New segments form in the growth zone behind the scolex. The oldest and most mature segments are therefore at the very back.
12330.m: In a tapeworm, the rearmost segments are the oldest.

12331.q: What kind of sexual system do almost all tapeworms have?
12331.e: Almost all tapeworms have both male and female reproductive organs. In true tapeworms, each segment usually has a complete set.
12331.m: A tapeworm is male and female at the same time.

12332.q: Why can a single tapeworm in the gut still produce fertilised eggs?
a: It is fertilised by the host
12332.e: Usually tapeworms fertilise each other, but self-fertilisation is possible, even between segments of the same worm. This allows a single tapeworm to reproduce.
12332.m: A tapeworm does not need a partner to reproduce.

12333.q: What happens to the mature, egg-filled segments of a Taenia tapeworm such as the beef tapeworm?
a: They break off and leave the body with the faeces
They are digested by the worm itself
They stay on the worm for life
They migrate into the host’s blood
12333.e: Mature end segments break off and are excreted in the faeces. This is how the eggs reach the environment and the next host.
12333.m: Mature tapeworm segments leave the host with the faeces.

12334.q: What happens when an intermediate host such as a cow eats tapeworm eggs?
a: Larvae hatch, bore through the gut wall and settle in the tissue
The eggs are excreted again unchanged
An adult tapeworm grows in the gut immediately
The eggs dissolve completely in the stomach
12334.e: A hooked larva with six little hooks hatches from the egg. It penetrates the gut wall, travels with the blood to the muscles and develops there into a bladder worm.
12334.m: In the intermediate host, the larvae travel from the gut into the tissue.

12335.q: What is the bladder-shaped larva that sits in the muscle meat of the beef and pork tapeworm called?
12335.e: The bladder worm is a fluid-filled bladder with an inverted head. If a person eats raw meat containing bladder worms, a tapeworm develops from it.
12335.m: The tapeworm larva sits in the meat as a bladder worm.

12336.q: Who is the only natural definitive host of the beef tapeworm (Taenia saginata)?
12336.e: The adult beef tapeworm lives only in the human gut. Cattle are the intermediate host, in whose muscles the bladder worms sit.
12336.m: The beef tapeworm becomes an adult only in humans.

12337.q: How long does an adult beef tapeworm usually grow?
12337.e: The beef tapeworm is usually about 4 to 10 metres long and only a few millimetres wide. In exceptional cases, even more than 20 metres have been measured.
12337.m: The beef tapeworm usually grows several metres long.

12338.q: How does the head of the beef tapeworm differ from that of the pork tapeworm?
a: It has no ring of hooks
It has two rings of hooks
12338.e: The beef tapeworm holds on only with four suckers and has no ring of hooks. The pork tapeworm also has a ring of hooks.
12338.m: The beef tapeworm’s head is unarmed.

12339.q: What is striking about the detached segments of the beef tapeworm?
a: They are as hard as limestone
They swim away in the water
12339.e: The shed segments of the beef tapeworm are mobile and crawl. This spreads the eggs over a larger area.
12339.m: The segments of the beef tapeworm can crawl.

12340.q: How does a person normally become infected with the pork tapeworm in the gut?
a: Through raw or undercooked pork containing bladder worms
12340.e: The bladder worms of the pork tapeworm sit in the muscle meat of the pig. If a person eats such meat raw or insufficiently cooked, a tapeworm grows in their gut.
12340.m: Well-cooked pork protects against the pork tapeworm.

12341.q: How long does the pork tapeworm grow, roughly?
12341.e: The pork tapeworm usually reaches about 2 to 7 metres. That makes it clearly shorter than the beef tapeworm.
12341.m: The pork tapeworm grows several metres long.

12342.q: Why is the pork tapeworm particularly dangerous for humans?
a: Humans can also become an intermediate host and develop bladder worms
It sucks large amounts of blood
It produces a powerful nerve poison
It regularly bores through the gut wall
12342.e: If a person swallows eggs of the pork tapeworm, bladder worms can form in the body, for example in the muscles or in the brain. This disease is called cysticercosis.
12342.m: Pork tapeworm eggs can form bladder worms in humans.

12343.q: Which illness is a common, preventable consequence when bladder worms of the pork tapeworm reach the brain?
12343.e: According to the WHO, neurocysticercosis is the most common preventable cause of epilepsy worldwide. In affected areas, around a third of all epilepsy cases are due to it.
12343.m: Bladder worms in the brain can trigger epileptic seizures.

12344.q: Why has the pork tapeworm largely disappeared from Europe today?
a: thanks to meat inspection and hygiene
because pigs are vaccinated against it
because the climate is too cold
12344.e: Official meat inspection and better hygiene have largely pushed back the pork tapeworm in Europe. In some countries of Latin America, Africa and Asia it is still widespread.
12344.m: Meat inspection has pushed back the pork tapeworm in Europe.

12345.q: How can you find out whether a person has a tapeworm in the gut?
a: The faeces are examined for segments or eggs
12345.e: Tapeworm segments or eggs passed in the faeces show an infection. In the laboratory, the segments can even reveal which species of tapeworm it is.
12345.m: Tapeworm segments or eggs in the faeces reveal an infection.

12346.q: Which human tapeworm can grow up to about 20 metres long?
12346.e: The fish tapeworm is one of the longest tapeworms of humans. It can grow up to about 20 metres long and form thousands of segments.
12346.m: The fish tapeworm is one of the longest tapeworms of humans.

12347.q: How does the fish tapeworm hold on in the gut?
a: with a ring of hooks alone
12347.e: The head of the fish tapeworm has no hooks but two elongated sucking grooves. They are called bothria.
12347.m: The fish tapeworm clings on with two sucking grooves.

12348.q: Which animals are the first intermediate host of the fish tapeworm?
12348.e: The ciliated larva of the fish tapeworm is eaten in the water by small copepods such as Cyclops. Only after that does it get into fish.
12348.m: Tiny crustaceans are the first host of the fish tapeworm.

12349.q: Why does water play an important role in the life cycle of the fish tapeworm?
a: A swimming larva hatches from its eggs in the water
The adult worm lives freely in the lake
Its eggs need sea water to mature
The worm breathes only under water
12349.e: When fish tapeworm eggs get into water, a ciliated larva hatches. It has to be eaten by a tiny crustacean for the cycle to continue.
12349.m: The fish tapeworm’s larva starts its life in water.

12350.q: How does the fish tapeworm get into humans?
a: Through raw or insufficiently cooked fish containing larvae
12350.e: Larvae of the fish tapeworm sit in the flesh of freshwater fish such as perch or pike. If a person eats the fish raw, a tapeworm grows from them in the gut.
12350.m: Raw fish can contain larvae of the fish tapeworm.

12351.q: Which vitamin deficiency can rarely be caused by the fish tapeworm?
12351.e: The fish tapeworm takes up a lot of vitamin B12. In a small proportion of those infected, this leads to a form of anaemia.
12351.m: The fish tapeworm can snatch away vitamin B12.

12352.q: At which Swiss lake did several wedding guests catch the fish tapeworm in 2006 after eating marinated raw perch from this lake?
12352.e: In the Lake Geneva region, more cases of fish tapeworm have been reported since about 2001. In 2006, guests at a wedding fell ill after eating raw, marinated perch fillets from Lake Geneva.
12352.m: Raw fish from Lake Geneva can transmit the fish tapeworm.

12353.q: What is the safest way to protect yourself from the fish tapeworm?
a: Cook fish thoroughly or deep-freeze it beforehand
Only rinse fish in cold water
12353.e: Cooking thoroughly or sufficiently deep-freezing kills the larvae in the fish. Marinating with acid or salt is not a reliable way of doing this.
12353.m: Well-cooked fish is free of living tapeworm larvae.

12354.q: How big is the adult fox tapeworm (Echinococcus multilocularis)?
12354.e: The fox tapeworm is usually only about 1.5 to 3.5 millimetres long. Even so, it is one of the most dangerous tapeworms for humans.
12354.m: The fox tapeworm is tiny but dangerous.

12355.q: How many segments does the fox tapeworm usually have?
12355.e: The fox tapeworm usually has only four or five segments. The last segment is greatly enlarged and makes up almost half of the body length.
12355.m: The fox tapeworm has only a handful of segments.

12356.q: Which animals are the most important intermediate hosts of the fox tapeworm?
12356.e: Voles eat the eggs with their food, and the larvae grow in their liver. When a fox eats the mouse, the cycle is complete.
12356.m: The mouse is the link in the life of the fox tapeworm.

12357.q: Which organ does the larva of the fox tapeworm most often infect in humans?
12357.e: In humans, the larva of the fox tapeworm usually grows in the liver and invades the tissue like a tumour. The disease is called alveolar echinococcosis.
12357.m: In humans, the fox tapeworm mostly infects the liver.

12358.q: How long can it take for a fox tapeworm infection to cause symptoms in humans?
12358.e: The larva grows very slowly, so symptoms often appear only after 5 to 15 years. Early warning signs are usually absent.
12358.m: A fox tapeworm infection often goes unnoticed for years.

12359.q: Roughly how many people in Switzerland newly fall ill each year with the disease caused by the fox tapeworm?
12359.e: In the 1990s there were only about 10 to 15 cases a year. Since then the number has risen markedly, and a review study from 2025 gives an average of around 70 cases a year.
12359.m: The fox tapeworm disease is rare in Switzerland, but more common than it used to be.

12360.q: What is considered the main reason for the rise in fox tapeworm cases in Switzerland since the 1980s?
a: the sharp rise in fox numbers
12360.e: Fox numbers have increased sharply since the 1980s, including in towns and cities. With a delay of about 10 to 15 years, cases of the disease in humans rose.
12360.m: More foxes mean more fox tapeworm eggs in the environment.

12361.q: How many foxes in the urban area of Zurich were infected with the fox tapeworm in one study?
12361.e: In a Zurich study, around 47 per cent of foxes in the urban area were infected, and as many as around 67 per cent in the neighbouring recreation area. So town foxes often carry the parasite too.
12361.m: Town foxes in Zurich also often carry the fox tapeworm.

12362.q: What do fox tapeworm eggs survive surprisingly well?
a: Cold and frost in a household freezer
Cooking right through in an oven
12362.e: The eggs are very resistant to cold and stay infectious for months. They do not die in a normal freezer compartment, but heating kills them.
12362.m: Frost hardly harms fox tapeworm eggs, but heat does.

12363.q: Which tapeworm forms large, fluid-filled bladders in the intermediate host, for example in the liver or lungs?
12363.e: The larva of the dog tapeworm forms fluid-filled bladders called hydatids. Thousands of tapeworm heads develop inside them.
12363.m: The dog tapeworm forms large bladders in the intermediate host.

12364.q: Which farm animals are the main intermediate hosts of the dog tapeworm (Echinococcus granulosus) in Europe?
12364.e: In Europe, the so-called sheep strain of the dog tapeworm predominates. Dogs become infected when they eat infected organs from sheep.
12364.m: Sheep and dogs share the life cycle of the dog tapeworm.

12365.q: Why should you wash or heat low-growing wild berries and windfall fruit well before eating them in Switzerland?
a: Because fox tapeworm eggs can stick to them
Because the fox tapeworm grows inside the fruit
12365.e: Foxes leave droppings containing tapeworm eggs, which can stick to berries, mushrooms or vegetables. Thorough washing reduces the risk, and heating reliably kills the eggs.
12365.m: Washing and heating protect against fox tapeworm eggs.

12366.q: How do dogs and cats usually become infected with the cucumber seed tapeworm (Dipylidium caninum)?
12366.e: The larvae of the cucumber seed tapeworm develop in fleas. When grooming their fur, dogs and cats swallow the fleas.
12366.m: Fleas transmit the cucumber seed tapeworm.

12367.q: What is special about the dwarf tapeworm (Hymenolepis nana) compared with most tapeworms?
a: It can develop without an intermediate host
It grows to over 20 metres long
12367.e: The dwarf tapeworm can complete its entire life cycle in a single host. This is why it can keep reproducing directly in humans.
12367.m: The dwarf tapeworm does not necessarily need an intermediate host.

12368.q: Which active substance is often used against tapeworms in the gut of humans and pets?
12368.e: Praziquantel is a tried and tested remedy against tapeworms in the gut. Antibiotics such as penicillin, by contrast, do not help against worms.
12368.m: Praziquantel is an important remedy against tapeworms.

12369.q: How was it proved in the 19th century that the bladder worms in pork and tapeworms belong together?
a: Through feeding experiments with infected meat
12369.e: In the 1850s, the physician Friedrich Küchenmeister showed through feeding experiments that bladder worms become tapeworms. This led to an understanding of the tapeworms’ change of host.
12369.m: Feeding experiments showed that bladder worms become tapeworms.

12370.q: Which animal class does the tick belong to?
12370.e: Ticks are arachnids (Arachnida) and, within this class, count as mites. Adult ticks therefore have eight legs and not six like insects.
12370.m: The tick is an arachnid and not an insect.

12371.q: Which larger group of arachnids are ticks assigned to?
12371.e: Ticks form the order Ixodida within the mites (Acari). They are therefore closely related to house dust mites and spider mites.

12372.q: What is the most common tick species in Switzerland called?
12372.e: The sheep tick (Ixodes ricinus) is by far the most common tick in Switzerland. It transmits Lyme disease and TBE.
12372.m: The most common tick in Switzerland is the sheep tick.

12373.q: Which tick family does the sheep tick belong to?
12373.e: The sheep tick belongs to the hard ticks (Ixodidae), which have a hard shield on the back. Soft ticks such as the pigeon tick have no such shield.
12373.m: The sheep tick is a hard tick with a hard shield on its back.

12374.q: The sheep tick is called Ixodes ricinus in scientific terms, like the castor oil plant Ricinus. Why does this name fit?
a: An engorged tick looks like a castor bean
Ticks live only on the castor oil plant
Ticks suck the sap of the castor oil plant
The castor oil plant drives away ticks
12374.e: The seeds of the castor oil plant Ricinus communis are oval, shiny and speckled, similar to an engorged tick. Which was named after the other first is disputed.
12374.m: An engorged tick looks like a castor bean.

12375.q: How many legs does a tick larva of the sheep tick have?
12375.e: The larva of the sheep tick has only six legs. The fourth pair of legs appears only after moulting into a nymph.
12375.m: The tick larva walks on six legs, nymphs and adults on eight.

12376.q: Which stages of development does the sheep tick go through after the egg?
12376.e: A larva hatches from the egg, moults into a nymph and then into an adult. There is no pupal stage as in butterflies.
12376.m: The tick develops from egg to larva and nymph to adult.

12377.q: How many blood meals does a sheep tick normally need over its whole life?
12377.e: The larva, the nymph and the adult female each suck blood once, usually from three different hosts. This is why it is called a three-host tick.
12377.m: The sheep tick sucks blood only three times in its life, once per stage.

12378.q: How long does the development of the sheep tick from egg to adult usually take?
12378.e: Normally the sheep tick needs around three years, or two under good conditions. Under unfavourable conditions it can take up to six years.
12378.m: A tick usually needs around three years to become an adult.

12379.q: Roughly how many eggs does a female sheep tick lay?
12379.e: After her last blood meal, the female lays on average around 2,000, at most about 3,000 eggs on the ground. Then she dies.
12379.m: A female sheep tick lays thousands of eggs once and then dies.

12380.q: How many vertebrate species have been shown to be hosts of the sheep tick?
12380.e: The sheep tick is no specialist: over 300 vertebrate species such as mammals, birds and lizards serve it as hosts. This variety makes it an important carrier of disease.
12380.m: The sheep tick sucks blood from a great many different vertebrates.

12381.q: On which hosts do sheep tick larvae mainly feed?
12381.e: The tiny larvae stay close to the ground and infect mainly mice, voles and songbirds. Adult ticks prefer larger hosts.
12381.m: Tick larvae mostly get their blood from mice.

12382.q: Which wild animals are particularly important hosts for adult sheep ticks in large parts of northern and western Europe?
12382.e: Adult sheep ticks prefer large hosts. In northern and western Europe, roe deer, red deer and fallow deer are the most important.
12382.m: Roe deer and deer feed many adult ticks.

12383.q: Where is the main sense organ with which a tick smells its hosts?
a: On the shield on its back
12383.e: Haller’s organ sits on the foremost pair of legs. This is why a lurking tick stretches its front legs into the air to detect carbon dioxide, body odour and warmth.
12383.m: Ticks smell their hosts with their front legs.

12384.q: Which gas from a host’s breath does the tick detect especially well?
12384.e: Exhaled carbon dioxide tells the tick that a host is near. It detects it with Haller’s organ on its front legs.
12384.m: The tick recognises its prey by the exhaled carbon dioxide.

12385.q: How does a sheep tick normally get onto a person?
a: It is brushed off grass or bushes
It flies at the person deliberately
12385.e: The tick lurks on grass and low plants with its front legs outstretched and is brushed off as someone passes. It can neither jump nor fly, and it does not fall from trees.
12385.m: Ticks lurk in the grass and are brushed off as you walk past.

12386.q: How far does a sheep tick usually move away from its resting place?
12386.e: The sheep tick stays very much in one place and usually moves only 20 to 40 cm, at most about 30 metres. It covers long distances only on a host.
12386.m: Ticks hardly move and travel almost only on their hosts.

12387.q: From roughly what temperature do nymphs and adult sheep ticks become active?
12387.e: Nymphs and adults start looking for a host at around 7 °C. This is why you can be bitten even on mild winter days.
12387.m: Ticks become active at around seven degrees.

12388.q: What humidity does the sheep tick need so that it does not dry out?
a: About 40 to 50 per cent is enough
12388.e: The sheep tick needs a relative humidity of over about 70 to 80 per cent. This is why it lives in damp leaf litter, undergrowth and tall grass.
12388.m: Ticks need damp air, otherwise they dry out.

12389.q: How does the sheep tick take in water?
a: It absorbs water vapour from damp air
It drinks morning dew from leaves
12389.e: The sheep tick cannot drink liquid water and even avoids it. But when the humidity is very high, it can absorb water vapour from the air.
12389.m: The tick tops up on water from damp air instead of drinking.

12390.q: Up to roughly what altitude do ticks occur in Switzerland, according to the authorities?
a: Up to about 1,500 to 2,000 metres above sea level
Only up to about 300 metres above sea level
Up to about 4,500 metres above sea level
Only up to about 800 metres above sea level
12390.e: The federal portal ch.ch gives tick occurrence up to about 1,500 m, and cantonal leaflets such as the one from Zurich up to about 2,000 m above sea level. So care is needed when hiking in the mountains too.
12390.m: In Switzerland there are ticks up to around 1,500 to 2,000 metres.

12391.q: In which months are ticks mainly active in Switzerland?
12391.e: In Switzerland, ticks are mainly active from about March to November. There are peaks in spring and early autumn.
12391.m: In Switzerland, tick season runs from spring to late autumn.

12392.q: Why is a tick so hard to pull out of the skin?
a: It has screwed itself in with its legs
It has suckers on its back
It grows together with the skin
12392.e: The tick cuts the skin open and pushes in a piercing apparatus with barbs, the hypostome. It also often cements it in place with a sticky secretion.
12392.m: Barbs on the piercing apparatus anchor the tick in the skin.

12393.q: Why do you often not notice a tick bite?
a: The tick bites only during sleep
The bite happens only through clothes
12393.e: Tick saliva contains hundreds of proteins, including numbing, anticoagulant and anti-inflammatory substances. This is why the bite usually stays painless and unnoticed.
12393.m: Tick saliva numbs the skin, so you hardly feel the bite.

12394.q: Roughly how long does a female sheep tick suck during one blood meal?
12394.e: A female sheep tick stays on the host for several days, around 80 hours in dogs and cats. Then she drops off, engorged.
12394.m: A tick does not suck blood briefly but for days.

12395.q: How does the shield on the back differ between the male and the female sheep tick?
a: In the male it covers almost the whole back
Only the female has a shield on her back
In the female it covers almost the whole back
Neither has a shield on its back at all
12395.e: In the male the shield covers almost the whole back, in the female only about the front half. This lets the female’s abdomen expand greatly while she sucks.
12395.m: The female tick has a small shield so she can grow while sucking.

12396.q: How does the male sheep tick behave when it comes to sucking blood?
a: It sucks little or no blood
It sucks more blood than the female
It sucks only the blood of birds
It sucks only the blood of fish
12396.e: The male takes in little or no blood. On the host he mainly looks for a feeding female to mate with.
12396.m: In the sheep tick, it is mainly the female that sucks blood.

12397.q: How big is an unfed female sheep tick?
12397.e: Unfed females measure around 3 to 4 mm, males a little less. When engorged, however, females become many times larger and turn grey.
12397.m: A hungry female tick is only a few millimetres small.

12398.q: What does the tick do with the blood it has taken in, so that it can absorb more nutrients?
a: It gives off water and salts again
It spits out the red blood cells
It dilutes it with plant sap
It stores it in a crop on the ground
12398.e: The tick excretes surplus water and salts again. In this way it can concentrate blood components up to about twenty times.
12398.m: The tick thickens the blood by giving off water.

12399.q: Which disease do ticks transmit most often in Switzerland?
12399.e: Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne disease in Switzerland. The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) estimates around 10,000 cases a year.
12399.m: Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne disease in Switzerland.

12400.q: What kind of pathogen causes Lyme disease, which ticks transmit?
12400.e: Lyme disease is caused by bacteria of the group Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato. This is why it can be treated with antibiotics.
12400.m: Lyme disease is caused by bacteria and treated with antibiotics.

12401.q: What kind of pathogen causes tick-borne encephalitis (TBE), which ticks transmit?
12401.e: TBE is caused by a virus. Antibiotics do not work against it, but a vaccination protects you.
12401.m: TBE is a viral disease that you can be vaccinated against.

12402.q: Which researcher, born in Basel, discovered the pathogen of Lyme disease, which ticks transmit?
12402.e: The Swiss scientist Willy Burgdorfer discovered the bacteria in ticks in the USA in 1981. In 1983 the pathogen was named Borrelia burgdorferi in his honour.
12402.m: Willy Burgdorfer of Basel gave the Lyme disease pathogen its name.

12403.q: After which place is Lyme disease, which ticks transmit, named?
a: After a village in the canton of Bern
12403.e: The disease is named after the town of Lyme in the US state of Connecticut. There, a cluster of joint inflammations in children was noticed in the 1970s.
12403.m: Lyme disease bears the name of a town in Connecticut.

12404.q: Which typical skin sign after a tick bite can point to Lyme disease?
a: An itchy blistering rash all over the body
A black scab with a crater
12404.e: The migrating redness (erythema migrans) is a slowly spreading, often ring-shaped redness around the bite site. If you see it, you should go to the doctor.
12404.m: A growing red ring after a tick bite is called erythema migrans.

12405.q: What proportion of ticks in Switzerland carry Borrelia bacteria, according to cantonal leaflets?
a: About 5 to 30 per cent, locally up to 50 per cent
12405.e: Depending on the region, about 5 to 30 per cent, locally up to 50 per cent, of ticks carry Borrelia. By contrast, only around 1 per cent carry TBE viruses.
12405.m: Borrelia bacteria are much more common in ticks than TBE viruses.

12406.q: Roughly how many ticks in Switzerland carry the TBE virus, according to cantonal leaflets?
12406.e: Only around 1 per cent of ticks carry the TBE virus. But because the disease can be severe, vaccination is recommended.
12406.m: Only about one tick in a hundred carries the TBE virus.

12407.q: Which areas of Switzerland count as TBE risk areas, according to the FOPH?
a: Only the cantons of Zurich and Thurgau
Only areas below 500 metres above sea level
12407.e: According to the FOPH, all cantons except Ticino count as TBE risk areas. Anyone who lives or stays there is recommended to be vaccinated.
12407.m: Almost all of Switzerland except Ticino is a TBE risk area.

12408.q: From what age does the FOPH generally recommend the TBE vaccination against viruses transmitted by ticks?
12408.e: The FOPH recommends the vaccination for adults and for children from three years of age in risk areas. For one- and two-year-olds, it is decided case by case.
12408.m: The tick vaccination against TBE is recommended from three years of age.

12409.q: How many doses make up the basic immunisation against TBE, which ticks transmit?
12409.e: Full protection needs three vaccine doses. The first two are about a month apart, and the third follows a few months later.
12409.m: For full TBE protection you need three vaccinations.

12410.q: At what interval is the TBE booster vaccination against tick viruses recommended in Switzerland?
12410.e: If the risk continues, a booster vaccination is recommended every ten years. This is set out in the Swiss vaccination schedule.
12410.m: The TBE vaccination is boosted every ten years.

12411.q: Which disease is transmitted by ticks in Switzerland?
12411.e: Besides Lyme disease and TBE, tularaemia can also be transmitted by ticks. It is caused by a bacterium, and cases of it have increased in Switzerland.
12411.m: Ticks transmit not only Lyme disease and TBE but also rabbit fever.

12412.q: How many TBE cases after tick bites have been reported per year in Switzerland in recent years?
12412.e: Over the last ten years, the reported TBE cases fluctuated between 112 and 434 a year, according to the canton of Zurich. TBE is a notifiable disease in Switzerland.
12412.m: In Switzerland, a few hundred people fall ill with TBE every year.

12413.q: Why is the exact number of Lyme disease cases in Switzerland only an estimate?
a: There is no Lyme disease in Switzerland
12413.e: Unlike TBE, Lyme disease is not notifiable in Switzerland. Its frequency is extrapolated from a voluntary reporting network of GP practices, the Sentinella system.
12413.m: Lyme disease is not notifiable, so the case numbers are estimates.

12414.q: Why should a tick be removed as quickly as possible?
a: The risk of Borrelia transmission rises the longer it sucks
Because otherwise the tick lays eggs in the skin
Because otherwise the tick crawls right into the skin
Because otherwise the tick becomes poisonous
12414.e: Borrelia are usually transmitted only after several hours of sucking, and the risk grows with the duration. TBE viruses, by contrast, can pass over shortly after the bite.
12414.m: The faster the tick is gone, the smaller the risk of Lyme disease.

12415.q: How does one correctly remove a tick, according to the Swiss health authorities?
a: Grip it close to the skin with tweezers and pull it out slowly
Suffocate it with oil or glue and wait
Burn it off with a lighter
Squeeze the body firmly and tear it off
12415.e: You grip the tick as close to the skin as possible with tweezers or a tick remover and pull it out steadily and straight, without squeezing it. Oil, glue or other substances should not be used beforehand.
12415.m: You pull a tick out slowly with tweezers, close to the skin.

12416.q: What should you do with the bite site after removing a tick?
a: Disinfect it and watch it over the following weeks
Cover it immediately with a plaster for a month
Pay no further attention to it
12416.e: The bite site is disinfected and then observed. If redness or fever appears, you should see a doctor.
12416.m: After removal, you disinfect the bite site and keep an eye on it.

12417.q: Which protective measure against ticks does the FOPH recommend when spending time in the forest?
a: Stay on wide paths and avoid undergrowth
Do not check yourself after a visit to the forest
12417.e: The FOPH advises staying on wide paths, avoiding grass and bushes, and wearing well-covering clothing and tick repellent. Afterwards, you should check your body and clothes.
12417.m: If you stay on wide paths, you brush off fewer ticks.

12418.q: What proportion of people who become infected with the TBE virus through a tick bite have no symptoms, according to the canton of Zurich?
12418.e: Around 70 per cent of those infected notice nothing. In some of those who fall ill, inflammation of the meninges or the brain follows after a flu-like phase.
12418.m: Most TBE infections pass without symptoms.

12419.q: What is the free tick prevention app called that was developed at the ZHAW with the support of the FOPH?
12419.e: The ZHAW’s app “Zecke” shows a risk map, explains how to remove ticks and, with a tick diary, reminds you of possible symptoms. It was presented in 2015.
12419.m: The Swiss app “Zecke” helps with protection against tick bites.

12420.q: Which animal class do scorpions (order Scorpiones) belong to?
12420.e: Like spiders, harvestmen and mites, scorpions are arachnids. Like these, they have four pairs of walking legs and chelicerae.
12420.m: The scorpion is an arachnid and not an insect.

12421.q: How many walking legs does a scorpion have?
12421.e: Scorpions have four pairs of walking legs. The big pincers are not legs but modified mouthparts, the pedipalps.
12421.m: Like a spider, a scorpion walks on eight legs.

12422.q: Which body appendages form the big pincers in the scorpion?
a: The first pair of walking legs
12422.e: The scorpion’s pincers are the greatly enlarged pedipalps, the second pair of limbs. It uses them to seize and hold its prey.
12422.m: The scorpion’s pincers are modified pedipalps.

12423.q: What are the small pincer-shaped mouthparts called that a scorpion uses to tear up its prey?
12423.e: The chelicerae are small jaw claws in front of the mouth. In the scorpion they are pincer-shaped and tear the prey into small pieces.
12423.m: The scorpion tears up its food with its small chelicerae.

a: The narrow rear part of the abdomen
12424.e: The “tail” is the narrow rear section of the abdomen, the metasoma. Scorpions are invertebrates and have no spine.
12424.m: The scorpion’s tail is part of its abdomen.

12425.e: The scorpion’s tail consists of five armoured segments that are joined by joints. This is why the scorpion can bend it and use the sting accurately.
12425.m: The scorpion’s tail has five segments and the venomous sting behind them.

12426.q: Where does a scorpion produce its venom?
a: In venom glands in the last segment of the tail
In glands on the head beside the eyes
In the stomach from digested prey
12426.e: The last segment behind the tail, the telson, contains a pair of venom glands. It ends in the pointed sting.
12426.m: The scorpion’s venom sits in the last segment of the tail.

a: With four pairs of book lungs
12427.e: Scorpions have four pairs of book lungs on the underside of the abdomen. These consist of many thin plates and evolved from the gills of their ancestors.
12427.m: The scorpion breathes with eight book lungs on its belly.

12428.q: What does a scorpion use the comb-like organs (pectines) on its underside for?
12428.e: The pectines sit on the second segment of the abdomen and are full of sensory cells. With them the scorpion tests the ground, for example to find a place to deposit the spermatophore.
12428.m: With its pectines, the scorpion feels the ground beneath it.

12429.q: What is the maximum number of eyes a scorpion can have?
12429.e: Scorpions have a middle pair of eyes on the back and, at the sides, up to five pairs of small simple eyes. Even so, they see poorly, because the eyes serve mainly to tell light from dark.
12429.m: A scorpion has many eyes but sees only roughly with them.

12430.q: With which sense do many scorpions mainly track down their prey?
12430.e: Scorpions pick up ground vibrations and air movements through slit sense organs on the legs and sensory hairs. This lets them locate a burrowing prey animal from a distance of about 50 cm.
12430.m: The scorpion feels its prey rather than seeing it.

12431.q: What happens when you shine UV light on a scorpion at night?
12431.e: The outer body covering (cuticle) of scorpions fluoresces blue-green under UV light. Researchers use this to find the nocturnal animals in the field.
12431.m: Under UV light, a scorpion glows blue-green.

12432.q: Where are the substances that make a scorpion glow under UV light?
a: In the venom of the venom gland
12432.e: The glowing substances are in the cuticle, the hard body covering. This is why even a dead scorpion or a shed skin still glows under UV light.
12432.m: The scorpion’s body covering glows in UV light.

12433.q: Roughly how many scorpion species have been described worldwide?
12433.e: Depending on how they are counted, about 2,000 to over 2,500 scorpion species have been described. New ones are constantly being added, mainly from the tropics and deserts.
12433.m: There are around 2,500 different scorpion species worldwide.

12434.q: What is true of the scorpions that are dangerous to humans?
a: Almost all belong to a single scorpion family
They are spread evenly across all families
They are always the biggest species
12434.e: Almost all scorpions with a strong venom belong to the species-rich family Buthidae, such as Leiurus, Androctonus, Tityus and Centruroides.
12434.m: The most dangerous scorpions mostly belong to the family Buthidae.

12435.q: Roughly how many scorpion species are considered potentially deadly to humans?
12435.e: Only about 25 scorpion species have a venom that can kill a person. The great majority cause at most a painful sting similar to a wasp sting.
12435.m: Only a few scorpion species are truly life-threatening to humans.

12436.q: Which scorpion is regarded as one of the most dangerous in the world?
12436.e: Leiurus quinquestriatus from North Africa and the Middle East, also called the “deathstalker” or yellow scorpion, has a very strong nerve poison. It is often named as the most dangerous scorpion.
12436.m: The deathstalker Leiurus is one of the most venomous scorpions.

12437.q: What does the genus name of the dangerous scorpion Androctonus mean?
12437.e: Androctonus is made up of the Greek words for “man” and “to kill”. The fat-tailed scorpions of this genus really do have a very strong venom.

12438.q: Which rule of thumb often applies to how dangerous a scorpion is?
a: A thick tail and thin pincers suggest a strong venom
Big pincers suggest a strong venom
A dark colour suggests a strong venom
Big animals always have a strong venom
12438.e: Species with strong pincers often overpower prey by force and have a rather weak venom. Species with slender pincers and a thick tail rely more on their venom, but the rule has exceptions.
12438.m: Thin pincers and a thick tail are a warning sign in a scorpion.

12439.q: Roughly how many scorpion stings are estimated worldwide each year?
12439.e: Estimates put the figure at over a million scorpion stings a year, often around 1.2 to 1.5 million. Most are harmless, but a few thousand people die each year.
12439.m: Every year, over a million people worldwide are stung by scorpions.

12440.q: In which country are particularly many scorpion stings registered, with around 200,000 cases a year?
12440.e: In Mexico, around 200,000 scorpion stings are reported each year. Species of the genus Centruroides are mainly responsible.
12440.m: Mexico is one of the countries with the most scorpion stings.

12441.q: Which organ system does the venom of dangerous scorpions mainly affect?
12441.e: The venoms of the Buthidae contain neurotoxins that affect ion channels of nerve cells. This can lead to cramps, breathing difficulties and cardiovascular problems.
12441.m: Dangerous scorpion venom attacks the nerves.

12442.q: What is a substance from the venom of a scorpion being researched for in medicine?
a: To make brain tumours visible during operations
12442.e: Chlorotoxin from the venom of Leiurus binds preferentially to cells of certain brain tumours. Coupled with a fluorescent dye, it is meant to help identify tumour tissue during operations (“tumour paint”).
12442.m: A substance from scorpion venom can make brain tumours visible.

12443.q: What is the “prevenom” of some scorpions?
a: A scent mark in the territory
A digestive juice in the stomach
12443.e: Some scorpions first release a clear, salt-rich pre-venom that quickly causes pain. Only afterwards does the milky, protein-rich main venom follow, which costs more energy.
12443.m: With the prevenom, the scorpion saves its valuable main venom.

12444.q: How far can some scorpions (for example of the genus Parabuthus) spray their venom?
12444.e: Some species can spray their venom up to about a metre in defence. If it gets into the eyes, it can cause severe pain.
12444.m: Some scorpions spray their venom up to a metre.

12445.q: How does a scorpion take in its food?
a: It digests it outside the body and sucks it up
It filters it from the water
12445.e: Scorpions release digestive juices onto the torn-up prey. They then suck up the resulting liquid mush, because they cannot swallow solid pieces.
12445.m: The scorpion digests its prey before it even reaches its mouth.

12446.q: What do most scorpions mainly feed on?
12446.e: Scorpions hunt mainly crickets, grasshoppers, beetles, termites and spiders. Large species occasionally also catch small lizards or mice.
12446.m: The scorpion is a hunter of insects and other arthropods.

12447.q: How long can many scorpions survive without food?
12447.e: Thanks to their very low metabolism, many scorpions can go without food for up to twelve months. This is an important adaptation to barren habitats.
12447.m: A scorpion can go hungry for up to a year.

12448.q: What is the mating dance of scorpions called, in which the male leads the female by the pincers?
12448.e: In the “promenade à deux”, the male holds the female by the pincers and leads her back and forth, sometimes for hours. In this way he draws the female over a sperm packet he has deposited beforehand.
12448.m: Before mating, scorpions dance the promenade à deux.

12449.q: How do the sperm get to the female in the scorpion?
a: Via a sperm packet deposited on the ground
Via direct mating with a penis
12449.e: The male deposits a spermatophore on the ground. During the dance he draws the female over it, so that she takes up the sperm packet with her genital opening.
12449.m: The scorpion hands over its sperm in a packet on the ground.

a: They hatch from eggs in the sand
They develop as larvae in the water
12450.e: Scorpions give birth to live young: the young develop inside the mother’s body. Among arachnids, this is unusual.
12450.m: Scorpions give birth to live young.

12451.q: How long can the gestation period last in some scorpion species?
12451.e: Depending on the species, gestation lasts from a few months to over a year. For an invertebrate, this is exceptionally long.
12451.m: A scorpion mother can be pregnant for over a year.

12452.q: Where do young scorpions stay straight after birth?
a: In an earth nest without the mother
12452.e: The young climb onto the mother’s back at once. There they stay protected until their first moult.
12452.m: Young scorpions travel on their mother’s back.

12453.q: How many young can a female scorpion have per litter, depending on the species?
12453.e: Litter size depends greatly on the species and lies between a few and over 100 young. Small species usually have fewer young.
12453.m: The number of baby scorpions varies greatly from species to species.

12454.q: Roughly how many times does a scorpion moult before it is an adult?
12454.e: After the first moult on the mother’s back, usually five to eight more follow. The moults stop when the scorpion reaches sexual maturity.
12454.m: A scorpion grows up through several moults.

12455.q: How old can some scorpions get?
12455.e: For invertebrates, scorpions live surprisingly long. Many species live several years, a few up to about 25 years.
12455.m: Some scorpions can reach around a quarter of a century.

12456.q: What does parthenogenesis, which occurs in some scorpions such as Tityus serrulatus, mean?
a: Females have offspring entirely without males
Males carry the young to term
Young arise by the mother dividing
The young hatch from eggs in the sand
12456.e: In parthenogenesis, offspring develop without fertilisation. Females of the Brazilian Tityus serrulatus do not need a male, which is why this dangerous species can spread quickly in cities.
12456.m: Some Tityus females do not need a male to have offspring.

12457.q: Which West African scorpion, at around 20 cm long, is among the largest scorpions in the world?
12457.e: The emperor scorpion (Pandinus imperator) grows to around 20 cm long and weighs about 30 g. Despite its size, its sting is usually not dangerous for healthy people.
12457.m: The emperor scorpion is a harmless giant among scorpions.

12458.q: Why is the emperor scorpion listed in the Washington Convention on endangered species (CITES Appendix II)?
a: Because of heavy collection for the pet trade
Because it is dangerous to humans
Because it has already died out
Because it lives only in zoos
12458.e: The emperor scorpion is a popular terrarium animal and was caught in large numbers. The listing in Appendix II is meant to control trade and prevent overexploitation.
12458.m: CITES protects the emperor scorpion from being sold off by the pet trade.

12459.q: How small is one of the smallest known scorpion species (Typhlochactas mitchelli)?
12459.e: Typhlochactas mitchelli from Mexico grows only about 9 mm long and is regarded as one of the smallest scorpions. It has no eyes and lives in the leaf litter.
12459.m: Some scorpions are shorter than a centimetre.

12460.q: In which geological period do the oldest known scorpion fossils appear?
12460.e: The oldest scorpion fossils, such as Dolichophonus loudonensis from Scotland, date from the Silurian, around 430 million years ago. Scorpions are therefore among the oldest groups of land animals.
12460.m: Scorpions have existed for over 400 million years.

12461.q: How big could some prehistoric scorpions grow in the Carboniferous?
12461.e: Fossils from the Carboniferous, around 330 million years ago, show scorpions well over half a metre long. Today’s species grow at most to a good 20 cm.
12461.m: Prehistoric scorpions were much bigger than today’s.

a: Only in the rain by day
12462.e: Most scorpions hide by day under stones, bark or in burrows. At night they come out to catch prey as ambush hunters.
12462.m: The scorpion is a night hunter.

12463.q: Which mammal is almost immune to the venom of some scorpions?
12463.e: The North American grasshopper mouse hunts bark scorpions. Its nervous system is altered in such a way that the venom hardly causes any pain.
12463.m: The grasshopper mouse eats scorpions without being stopped by the venom.

12464.q: How can some scorpions defend themselves acoustically when in danger?
a: By chirping with parts of their body
By loud whistling with the mouth
12464.e: Some species rub bristles, pincers or the sting against each other and thus produce sounds (stridulation). They use this to warn predators.
12464.m: Some scorpions chirp to warn enemies.

12465.q: What can scorpions of the genus Ananteris shed when in danger?
12465.e: Ananteris scorpions can shed parts of the metasoma to escape an attacker. The tail does not grow back, and the anus is lost with it, but the animals live on for months and can reproduce during this time.
12465.m: In an emergency, Ananteris sacrifices part of its tail.

12466.q: Which is the largest of the scorpions native to Switzerland?
12466.e: The Italian scorpion (today usually Polytrichobothrius italicus, formerly Euscorpius italicus) grows up to about 5 cm long and lives mainly in Ticino and in the Misox. Its sting is about as harmless as a wasp sting.
12466.m: The Italian scorpion is the largest scorpion in Switzerland.

12467.q: In which part of Switzerland do native scorpions mainly live?
a: On the south side of the Alps, for example in Ticino
In the Central Plateau around Zurich
In the high mountains above 3,000 m
12467.e: Scorpions like it warm and dry. In Switzerland they live mainly on the south side of the Alps, for example in Ticino, in the Misox and in southern Grisons valleys.
12467.m: Swiss scorpions live mainly in the warm south of the country.

12468.q: Which word does the name “scorpion” come from?
12468.e: The name comes via the Latin “scorpio” from the Greek “skorpios”. The Greek word is probably a loanword from a non-Indo-European language.
12468.m: The name scorpion comes from Greek.

12469.q: Which bright red star forms the “heart” in the constellation Scorpius?
12469.e: Antares is a red supergiant and the brightest star in the constellation Scorpius. In Greek myth, a scorpion kills the hunter Orion.
12469.m: Antares shines red in the heart of the constellation Scorpius.

12470.q: What distinguishes tarantulas from most spiders in Swiss gardens?
a: They belong to a more primitive group of spiders
They have six legs instead of eight
They are insects and not spiders
They are the only spiders with venom
12470.e: Tarantulas belong to the Mygalomorphae, a primitive group of spiders. Most native spiders such as the garden spider belong to the more modern Araneomorphae.
12470.m: Tarantulas are among the primitive spiders.

12471.q: How do tarantulas strike their fangs into their prey?
a: From top to bottom, parallel to each other
Sideways against each other like pincers
Not at all, they kill only with their legs
12471.e: A tarantula’s fangs point parallel to the body axis and strike from above. Most other spiders, by contrast, have fangs that work against each other like pincers.
12471.m: Tarantulas strike their fangs downwards into the prey.

12472.q: What does a tarantula breathe with?
a: With book lungs in the abdomen
With lungs in the chest like mammals
12472.e: Tarantulas have two pairs of book lungs. These are pockets with many thin plates, arranged like the pages of a book.
12472.m: A tarantula breathes with book lungs.

12473.q: What do tarantulas mainly use their silk for, since they do not build catching webs?
a: To line their burrow and for the egg sac
To fly on a thread across the sea
Not at all, they cannot make silk
12473.e: Tarantulas hunt as ambush hunters without a catching web. With their usually four spinnerets they line the burrow and spin cocoons.
12473.m: Tarantulas spin silk for their home and egg sac rather than for webs.

12474.q: How many eyes does a tarantula have?
12474.e: Tarantulas have eight small eyes, usually arranged in two rows on a little mound. They see poorly and rely mainly on touch and vibrations.
12474.m: Despite eight eyes, a tarantula sees poorly.

12475.q: Which artist and naturalist is the German name “Vogelspinne” (bird spider) probably traced back to?
12475.e: In 1705, Maria Sibylla Merian published her work “Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium”. It shows a large spider eating a bird.
12475.m: Maria Sibylla Merian indirectly gave the tarantula its German name.

12476.q: Which bird is the tarantula eating in Maria Sibylla Merian’s famous copper engraving of 1705?
12476.e: Merian’s picture from Suriname shows a spider overpowering a hummingbird. This gave rise to the German name Vogelspinne (bird spider), although birds are only rarely prey.
12476.m: A hummingbird in a copper engraving made the tarantula famous.

12477.q: What does the Latin species name “avicularia” mean in the tarantula Avicularia avicularia?
12477.e: Linnaeus described the species in 1758 as Aranea avicularia. The name derives from the Latin “avis”, meaning bird.

12478.q: Roughly how many species does the tarantula family comprise according to the World Spider Catalog?
12478.e: The World Spider Catalog today lists around 1,100 to 1,200 tarantula species in over 150 genera. New species are described every year.
12478.m: There are well over a thousand species of tarantula.

12479.q: Which tarantula is regarded as the heaviest spider in the world?
12479.e: The Goliath birdeater Theraphosa blondi is the heaviest known spider by mass. Its name refers to the biblical giant Goliath.
12479.m: The Goliath birdeater is the heaviest spider in the world.

12480.q: What is the most a Goliath birdeater can weigh?
12480.e: Weights of up to about 170 to 175 g are given for the Goliath birdeater. That corresponds roughly to the weight of an apple.
12480.m: A large Goliath birdeater weighs about as much as an apple.

12481.q: What leg span can a Goliath birdeater reach?
12481.e: The Goliath birdeater reaches a leg span of up to about 28 to 30 cm. That is enough to cover a dinner plate.
12481.m: A Goliath birdeater can grow as big as a dinner plate.

12482.q: How long can the fangs of a Goliath birdeater grow?
12482.e: The fangs of the Goliath birdeater reach 2 to 4 cm in length. They can pierce human skin without difficulty.
12482.m: The Goliath birdeater has fangs several centimetres long.

12483.q: Where does the Goliath birdeater live in the wild?
a: In the rainforest in the north of South America
In the savannahs of East Africa
In the mountain forests of South East Asia
12483.e: Theraphosa blondi occurs in Suriname, Guyana, French Guiana, northern Brazil, eastern Colombia and southern Venezuela. There it lives in burrows in the damp rainforest.
12483.m: The Goliath birdeater lives in the rainforest of northern South America.

12484.q: What does the name of the Goliath birdeater refer to?
a: Its discoverer, who was called Goliath
12484.e: The name alludes to the giant Goliath from the Bible, because it is the heaviest spider in the world. It was scientifically described in 1804 by Pierre André Latreille.
12484.m: The Goliath birdeater is named after a biblical giant.

12485.q: What does the Goliath birdeater mainly eat in the wild?
12485.e: Despite its name, the Goliath birdeater mostly eats large arthropods, earthworms and frogs. It only rarely catches birds.
12485.m: The Goliath birdeater eats worms far more often than birds.

12486.q: How does a threatened Goliath birdeater warn its enemies, among other things?
a: It makes sounds by rubbing bristles (stridulation)
It lights up brightly in the dark
It gives off a foul-smelling mist
It changes colour in a flash
12486.e: The Goliath birdeater rubs bristles on its palps and legs against each other and so produces a hissing sound. This stridulation is meant to scare off attackers.
12486.m: A Goliath birdeater can hiss by rubbing bristles together.

12487.q: How many eggs does a female tarantula lay in an egg sac, depending on the species?
12487.e: Depending on the species, an egg sac contains around 50 to 2,000 eggs. In the Goliath birdeater it is about 100 to 200.
12487.m: A tarantula egg sac can contain up to two thousand eggs.

12488.q: How long does a female tarantula typically guard her egg sac?
a: Not at all, she leaves it at once
12488.e: The female usually guards the egg sac for six to eight weeks and turns it regularly. After that the spiderlings hatch.
12488.m: A tarantula mother guards her egg sac for weeks.

12489.q: Which tarantulas have urticating hairs for defence?
a: Almost only species from the Americas (New World)
12489.e: Urticating hairs occur in around 90 per cent of American tarantula species. Species from Africa, Asia and Australia have none.
12489.m: Urticating hairs are a weapon of the American tarantulas.

12490.q: How do the urticating hairs of American tarantulas work?
a: They have barbs and irritate skin and mucous membranes
They contain a deadly nerve poison
They dissolve in water to form acid
They glow and dazzle the enemy
12490.e: Urticating hairs are tiny and covered with barbs. Research distinguishes seven types, which are shaped differently depending on the species.
12490.m: Urticating hairs irritate with tiny barbs.

12491.q: How do typical ground-dwelling tarantulas from the Americas use their urticating hairs?
a: They brush them off the abdomen with their hind legs
They spit them out of the mouth
They shoot them from the spinnerets
They throw them with their fangs
12491.e: Bombardier spiders turn to face the attacker and rub their hind legs over the abdomen. In doing so, clouds of fine barbed hairs are whirled up.
12491.m: Bombardier spiders flick their urticating hairs away with their hind legs.

12492.q: How do tree-dwelling tarantulas of the genus Avicularia usually release their urticating hairs?
a: By direct contact, pressing the abdomen against the attacker
By flicking them off forcefully with the hind legs
By shedding the hairs when jumping
By weaving them into a catching web
12492.e: Avicularia species have type II urticating hairs, which are mostly transferred by touch. They thrust their abdomen at the enemy instead of brushing off hairs.
12492.m: Avicularia tarantulas use their urticating hairs by touch.

12493.q: Why should you protect your eyes when handling tarantulas that have urticating hairs?
a: The hairs can lodge in the cornea and cause inflammation
The spiders aim venom directly at the eyes
The hairs contain a solvent that damages glasses
12493.e: If urticating hairs get into the eye, they can hook into the cornea. This ophthalmia nodosa can cause problems for a long time.
12493.m: Tarantula urticating hairs must never get into the eye.

12494.q: How can you often recognise a tarantula that has recently brushed off urticating hairs?
a: By a bald patch on the abdomen
By red spots on the front part of the body
12494.e: After brushing them off, a bald patch remains on the abdomen. New urticating hairs grow back only with the next moult.
12494.m: A tarantula’s bald patch disappears only after the next moult.

12495.q: What do some tarantulas such as the Goliath birdeater use urticating hairs for, besides defence?
a: They weave them into the egg sac to protect it
They eat them as a source of protein
They keep warm with them on cold nights
12495.e: Urticating hairs are worked into cocoons and webbing. Presumably this keeps fly larvae and other parasites away from the eggs.
12495.m: In tarantulas, urticating hairs also protect the young in the egg sac.

12496.q: Where do most American tarantulas carry their urticating hairs?
a: Under the soles of the feet
12496.e: In most species the urticating hairs sit on the abdomen. An exception is the genus Ephebopus, which carries them on the palps.
12496.m: Most tarantulas carry their urticating hairs on the abdomen.

12497.q: How does a tarantula extend its legs?
a: By raising the pressure of its body fluid (haemolymph)
By powerful extensor muscles in every joint
By elastic springs made of chitin alone
By breathing air into the legs
12497.e: Muscles bend the leg joints, and they are extended hydraulically by haemolymph pressure. This is why dying or dried-out spiders draw their legs in.
12497.m: Tarantulas extend their legs with fluid pressure, like a hydraulic system.

12498.q: Which substance carries oxygen in the haemolymph of tarantulas?
12498.e: The haemolymph of the tarantula contains the copper-containing haemocyanin. Loaded with oxygen, it turns the blood bluish.
12498.m: Tarantulas have bluish blood with copper instead of iron.

12499.q: How old can females of some tarantula species get?
12499.e: Female tarantulas are among the longest-lived spiders and, depending on the species, can reach 30 years and more. They go on moulting even as adults.
12499.m: Female tarantulas can live for several decades.

12500.q: What is typical of male tarantulas after the final moult?
a: They no longer moult and usually live only another year or two
They keep growing and outlive the females
They turn back into young animals
They lose all their legs and stay in the burrow
12500.e: After the final moult, males do not moult any more. They search for females and usually die within about a year and a half.
12500.m: Male tarantulas live only a short time after maturity.

12501.q: What are the tibial hooks on the first pair of legs of many adult male tarantulas used for?
a: They hold the female’s fangs in place during mating
They are used for digging the burrow
They anchor the catching web to the ground
12501.e: With the tibial apophyses, the male clamps the female’s chelicerae. This allows him to mate without being bitten.
12501.m: Tibial hooks protect the male tarantula during mating.

12502.q: How does a male tarantula transfer his sperm to the female?
a: With the bulbs at the ends of the palps, which he fills beforehand on a sperm web
Directly via the spinnerets on the abdomen
Via the fangs during a bite
By depositing a sperm packet on the ground
12502.e: The male spins a sperm web, puts a drop of sperm on it and sucks it up with the bulbs of the palps. During mating, he inserts the bulbs into the female’s genital opening.
12502.m: Male tarantulas load their sperm into the palps via a sperm web.

12503.q: What does a tarantula renew when it moults?
a: The outer skin and also the lining of internal cavities
Only the hairs on its back
12503.e: In moulting, not only the outer skin is shed but also the lining of the book lungs, foregut and sperm storage pouches. This is why a female also loses stored sperm in the process.
12503.m: When moulting, a tarantula also renews the lining of its internal cavities.

12504.q: How does a male tarantula announce himself to the female?
a: With drumming signals using the palps and legs
With light signals on the abdomen
By presenting her with a nest he has built
12504.e: The male drums with his palps and legs on the ground or the webbing. A female ready to mate also replies by drumming.
12504.m: Tarantulas communicate with drumming signals before mating.

12505.q: Roughly how often do fully grown female tarantulas moult?
a: About once a year or less often
12505.e: Young animals moult several times a year, at first every four to eight weeks. Adult females usually moult only about once a year, and old animals even less often.
12505.m: Adult female tarantulas moult about once a year.

12506.q: What happens to a lost leg of a young tarantula?
a: It grows back over the following moults
It is replaced by an extra palp
The spider dies of it at once
12506.e: Tarantulas can regenerate lost legs. The new leg appears after a moult and reaches full size again after further moults.
12506.m: A tarantula can regrow lost legs over several moults.

12507.q: Which insects are particularly feared enemies of tarantulas?
a: Spider wasps such as tarantula hawks (Pepsis)
12507.e: Spider wasps of the genus Pepsis paralyse a tarantula with their sting and lay an egg on it. The larva then eats the living spider from the inside.
12507.m: Tarantula hawks paralyse tarantulas as food for their larvae.

12508.q: What is the IUCN status of the blue-shimmering tarantula Poecilotheria metallica?
12508.e: Poecilotheria metallica is regarded as critically endangered. Its habitat in India is being destroyed by logging, and animals are also being collected for the pet trade.
12508.m: The Gooty sapphire ornamental tarantula is critically endangered.

12509.q: In which country does the tarantula Poecilotheria metallica live?
12509.e: The species lives in forests in Andhra Pradesh in southern India. More recent finds also come from Tamil Nadu.
12509.m: The Gooty sapphire ornamental tarantula comes from southern India.

12510.q: What produces the blue colour of the tarantula Poecilotheria metallica?
12510.e: The blue is a structural colour, produced by the bending of light at nanostructures in the hairs. No blue pigment is involved.
12510.m: The blue of the Gooty sapphire ornamental tarantula is a structural colour.

12511.q: Roughly how small is the known range of the tarantula Poecilotheria metallica?
12511.e: For a long time the species was found only in a disturbed reserve forest of under 100 km². The tiny area makes it especially vulnerable.
12511.m: The Gooty sapphire ornamental tarantula lives in a very small area.

12512.q: In which tarantulas can a bite exceptionally cause muscle cramps in humans?
a: In Old World species such as Poecilotheria from Asia
In the Chilean rose from South America
In pinktoe tarantulas from the Americas
12512.e: Bites from Old World species such as Poecilotheria or Pterinochilus murinus can rarely cause cramps and dizziness. These species have no urticating hairs and defend themselves more with bites.
12512.m: Old World tarantulas usually have the stronger venom.

12513.q: Besides pain, what is a relatively common result of a tarantula bite in humans?
a: A wound infection from bacteria on the fangs
A breakdown of the red blood cells
12513.e: The venom of most tarantulas is harmless to humans, and the bite mainly hurts. But because bacteria cling to the fangs, a wound infection is common.
12513.m: After a tarantula bite, an infection is more likely than poisoning.

12514.q: Which international agreement has regulated trade in the Mexican red-knee tarantula since 1985?
12514.e: Brachypelma smithi was put in Appendix II of CITES in 1985, and all other Brachypelma species followed in 1994. Since then, trade has needed permits.
12514.m: Red-knee tarantulas are protected by the CITES agreement.

12515.q: In which habitat does the red-knee tarantula Brachypelma smithi live in Mexico?
a: In hilly dry forests on the Pacific coast
In swamps on the Gulf of Mexico
In mangroves on the Caribbean coast
In the high mountains above 4,000 m
12515.e: Brachypelma smithi lives in dry forests in the state of Guerrero on the Pacific coast. There it digs burrows with one entrance.
12515.m: The red-knee tarantula comes from the Pacific coast of Mexico.

12516.q: How long can it take for a Mexican red-knee tarantula to reach sexual maturity?
12516.e: Brachypelma smithi grows very slowly and matures only after about seven to ten years. Other species such as Psalmopoeus cambridgei manage it in around a year.
12516.m: Red-knee tarantulas need many years to reach sexual maturity.

12517.q: Are there wild tarantulas living in Europe?
a: Yes, a small species in Spain and Sicily
No, only in zoos and terrariums
Yes, they are common in Switzerland
12517.e: The small tarantula Ischnocolus valentinus lives in Spain, Sicily and North Africa under flat stones.
12517.m: A small wild tarantula lives in Spain too.

12518.q: With which animal does the tarantula Xenesthis immanis in South America often live peacefully in the same burrow?
12518.e: The tiny frog Chiasmocleis ventrimaculata lives with the tarantula and presumably eats ants that could threaten its eggs. The spider spares it and offers it protection.
12518.m: Some tarantulas share their burrow with a small frog.

12519.q: Where does the word “tarantula”, the English name for large hairy spiders such as the tarantulas (Vogelspinnen), come from?
a: From the southern Italian town of Taranto
From the Spanish word for spider
From the Latin word for hair
12519.e: Originally, a wolf spider from the area around Taranto was called a “tarantula”. Later the name, especially in English, was transferred to the large tarantulas.
12519.m: The name tarantula comes from the town of Taranto in Italy.

12520.q: Which subphylum of arthropods do horseshoe crabs belong to, despite their name?
12520.e: Horseshoe crabs have chelicerae instead of jaws and antennae. This puts them closer to arachnids and scorpions than to true crabs.
12520.m: The horseshoe crab is not a crab but a chelicerate.

12521.q: Why are horseshoe crabs often called living fossils?
a: Their body structure has hardly changed for hundreds of millions of years
They live only in places with many fossils
Their shell is made of petrified limestone
They live for several hundred years
12521.e: Fossils show that horseshoe crabs looked much as they do today over 400 million years ago. Scientifically, they form the order Xiphosura, which means roughly “sword tail”.
12521.m: Horseshoe crabs look almost like their ancestors of hundreds of millions of years ago.

12522.q: How many species of horseshoe crab are still alive today?
12522.e: There are only four living species: Limulus polyphemus in America and Tachypleus tridentatus, Tachypleus gigas and Carcinoscorpius rotundicauda in Asia.
12522.m: Today only four species of horseshoe crab are left.

12523.q: Which horseshoe crab species lives on the Atlantic coast of North America?
12523.e: Limulus polyphemus is the only American species. The other three species occur in South, South East and East Asia.
12523.m: The American horseshoe crab is called Limulus polyphemus.

12524.q: Why is the blood of the horseshoe crab blue?
a: It contains blue pigments from algae
12524.e: In the horseshoe crab, oxygen is carried by haemocyanin, which contains copper. Loaded with oxygen, it turns the blood blue.
12524.m: Copper in the haemocyanin makes the horseshoe crab’s blood blue.

12525.q: What is an extract from the blood of the horseshoe crab used for in medicine?
a: For testing vaccines and syringes for bacterial toxins
As a substitute for human blood donations
As a blue dye for tablets
12525.e: Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL) is obtained from the blood cells (amoebocytes) of the horseshoe crab Limulus. It reliably shows contamination by bacterial toxins.
12525.m: The horseshoe crab’s blood helps to make medicines safe.

12526.q: What does the LAL test from horseshoe crab blood detect?
a: The genetic material of flu viruses
12526.e: The lysate clots as soon as it comes into contact with endotoxins (lipopolysaccharides) from the cell wall of Gram-negative bacteria. This is how vaccines, syringes and implants are tested.
12526.m: The LAL test from the horseshoe crab detects bacterial endotoxins.

12527.q: Which animal test did the LAL test with horseshoe crab blood largely replace?
a: The irritation test on hens’ eggs
The allergy test on guinea pigs
12527.e: In the past, fever-causing contamination was tested by injecting the sample into rabbits. The LAL test is quicker and cheaper.
12527.m: The horseshoe crab test replaced the slow rabbit test.

12528.q: Since when has the test with horseshoe crab blood been officially used for medicines in the USA?
12528.e: The FDA approved the LAL test in 1977 for testing medicines and devices that come into contact with blood.
12528.m: The LAL test has been approved in the USA since 1977.

12529.q: Which researcher discovered in the 1950s in Woods Hole that horseshoe crab blood clots when bacteria are present?
12529.e: The physician Frederik Bang observed at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole that bacteria make the blood clump. Later he developed the test from this with Jack Levin.
12529.m: Frederik Bang laid the foundation for the test with horseshoe crab blood.

12530.q: Which genetically engineered alternative can replace the test with horseshoe crab blood?
12530.e: Factor C is the protein that starts clotting in the blood in response to endotoxins. Produced by genetic engineering (rFC), it does the same job without animal blood.
12530.m: Recombinant factor C spares the horseshoe crab.

12531.q: What is the great advantage of genetically engineered factor C over the test with horseshoe crab blood?
a: No horseshoe crabs have to be caught for it
It works entirely without a laboratory
12531.e: The biologist Jeak Ling Ding of the National University of Singapore developed a method to produce factor C by genetic engineering. It has been on the market since 2003, and it needs no animal blood.
12531.m: The replacement test for horseshoe crab blood needs no animals.

12532.q: What has made it easier for pharmaceutical companies in Europe to give up horseshoe crab blood since 2020?
a: A separate chapter on the factor C test in the European Pharmacopoeia
A worldwide ban on catching horseshoe crabs
A duty to use rabbits again
A ban on all tests for bacteria
12532.e: On 1 July 2020, the chapter on recombinant factor C became available in the European Pharmacopoeia. This makes it easier for companies to use the animal-free test.
12532.m: Europe has recognised the animal-free replacement test since 2020.

12533.q: How much of their blood is taken from horseshoe crabs during blood collection at most, according to the pharmaceutical industry?
12533.e: According to the pharmaceutical industry, up to around a third of the blood is taken from the animals, after which they are returned to the sea. Critical reports sometimes speak of even more.
12533.m: A horseshoe crab loses up to a third of its blood when it is bled.

12534.q: How high is the death rate of horseshoe crabs after blood collection estimated to be?
a: Around 3 to 30 per cent, depending on the study
12534.e: Estimates vary, depending on the study, between about 3 to 15 and 10 to 30 per cent of the animals dying after being bled. So most survive, but by no means all.
12534.m: Many horseshoe crabs survive being bled, but by no means all.

12535.q: What is the job of the amoebocytes in the blood of the horseshoe crab?
12535.e: On contact with bacterial toxins, the amoebocytes clump together and so seal wounds. They work in a similar way to white blood cells.
12535.m: Amoebocytes protect the horseshoe crab against bacteria.

12536.q: From which genus of horseshoe crabs is the lysate TAL obtained in Asia?
12536.e: TAL stands for Tachypleus amoebocyte lysate. It comes from Tachypleus gigas or Tachypleus tridentatus and is sometimes used in Asia instead of LAL.
12536.m: Asian horseshoe crabs supply the TAL.

12537.q: Roughly how old is the oldest known fossil horseshoe crab, Lunataspis aurora?
12537.e: Lunataspis aurora dates from the Ordovician and is around 445 million years old. Horseshoe crabs are therefore regarded as living fossils.
12537.m: Horseshoe crabs existed long before the dinosaurs.

12538.q: Which extinct animal group is regarded as a close relative of the horseshoe crabs?
12538.e: The sea scorpions were also chelicerates and are closely related to the horseshoe crabs. Trilobites, by contrast, are a group of arthropods in their own right.
12538.m: The sea scorpions were relatives of the horseshoe crab.

12539.q: What is the long tail spine (telson) of the horseshoe crab used for?
a: For steering and for turning over
12539.e: The horseshoe crab is not venomous. With the movable telson it steers when swimming and pushes itself back onto its underside when it is lying on its back.
12539.m: The horseshoe crab’s tail is a lever, not a venomous sting.

12540.q: How is the body of the horseshoe crab divided?
a: Horseshoe-shaped front body, abdomen and tail spine
Head, thorax and abdomen as in insects
Head, trunk and two tail spines
12540.e: At the front is the horseshoe-shaped front body (prosoma), behind it the abdomen (opisthosoma) with the gills, and at the end the tail spine (telson).
12540.m: The horseshoe crab has a front body, abdomen and tail spine.

12541.q: Which organs does the horseshoe crab breathe with?
12541.e: The gills consist of many thin plates lying on top of one another like the pages of a book. Hence the name book gills.
12541.m: The horseshoe crab breathes with gills that look like books.

12542.q: How many pairs of book gills does an adult horseshoe crab have?
12542.e: On the abdomen there are five pairs of book gills, so ten gills. Newly hatched larvae still lack three of these pairs.
12542.m: Five pairs of gills supply the horseshoe crab with oxygen.

12543.q: What does the horseshoe crab use to crush its food?
a: Chewing plates at the bases of its legs
12543.e: The horseshoe crab has no jaws. Spiny chewing plates (gnathobases) at the bases of the legs grind up the food as it walks and push it to the mouth.
12543.m: The horseshoe crab chews with its legs.

12544.q: What does the American horseshoe crab mainly feed on?
12544.e: It ploughs through the seabed for small bivalves, bristle worms and other invertebrates.
12544.m: The horseshoe crab looks for its prey in the sand of the seabed.

12545.q: Roughly how many single eyes (ommatidia) does a compound eye of the horseshoe crab have?
12545.e: Each of the two compound eyes at the sides consists of about 1,000 ommatidia. These are unusually large and therefore easy to study.
12545.m: A compound eye of the horseshoe crab has about a thousand single eyes.

12546.q: Why were the eyes of the horseshoe crab so valuable for research into vision?
a: Their large visual cells are easy to study
They work entirely without nerve cells
They are the largest eyes in the animal kingdom
12546.e: Haldan Keffer Hartline used the large visual cells of Limulus to study how nerve cells process light signals. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1967.
12546.m: The horseshoe crab’s eyes helped us understand vision.

12547.q: Besides visible light, which radiation can the median eyes of the horseshoe crab detect?
12547.e: Besides the compound eyes, the horseshoe crab has two median eyes at the front of the shell. They have a second visual pigment with a peak at about 360 nanometres and so see UV light.
12547.m: The horseshoe crab can see ultraviolet light.

12548.q: Where does the horseshoe crab have light-sensing cells besides its eyes?
a: In the tips of its legs
12548.e: In the horseshoe crab, photoreceptors are also found on the abdomen and on the telson. So it can tell light from dark even with its tail.
12548.m: Even the horseshoe crab’s tail senses light.

12549.q: How many pairs of limbs does the front body of the horseshoe crab have?
12549.e: On the prosoma there is one pair of chelicerae and five pairs of walking legs. That makes six pairs of limbs.
12549.m: The horseshoe crab has chelicerae and five pairs of legs.

12550.q: In which position does the horseshoe crab usually swim?
12550.e: When swimming, the horseshoe crab turns over and rows with its gill plates, underside up. It steers with the telson.
12550.m: The horseshoe crab swims upside down.

12551.q: What is the larval stage of the horseshoe crab called?
12551.e: The larvae, about 1 cm in size, resemble the extinct trilobites. Hence their name. Nauplius, zoea and megalopa are larvae of true crustaceans.
12551.m: Young horseshoe crabs look like little trilobites.

12552.q: Roughly how many times does an American horseshoe crab moult before it is an adult?
12552.e: The rigid shell does not grow with the animal. Up to sexual maturity, the horseshoe crab sheds it about 17 times.
12552.m: The horseshoe crab grows only through many moults.

12553.q: At roughly what age does the American horseshoe crab reach sexual maturity?
12553.e: The American horseshoe crab grows slowly and reproduces only at about nine to twelve years, females usually a little later than males. This makes populations vulnerable to overexploitation.
12553.m: A horseshoe crab needs almost a decade before it can reproduce.

12554.q: How old can an American horseshoe crab get, according to estimates?
12554.e: The lifespan is estimated at around 20 to 40 years. It is hard to measure exactly, because adult animals no longer moult.
12554.m: A horseshoe crab can live for decades.

12555.q: How long do female American horseshoe crabs grow at most, including the tail?
12555.e: Large females reach about 60 cm in length, including the tail spine, and a weight of nearly 5 kg.
12555.m: A large female horseshoe crab is as long as an arm.

12556.q: How do the sexes of the American horseshoe crab differ in size?
a: Females are 25 to 30 per cent bigger
Both are exactly the same size
Males are 25 to 30 per cent bigger
12556.e: The females are clearly larger than the males and can become more than twice as heavy.
12556.m: In the horseshoe crab, the female is the larger animal.

12557.q: What does the male horseshoe crab use to cling to the female during mating?
a: His first pair of legs, modified into hooks
12557.e: In sexually mature male American horseshoe crabs, the first pair of legs is modified into strong clasping hooks. With them they hold on to the female’s abdomen.
12557.m: The male horseshoe crab has clasping hooks on his front legs.

12558.q: What are horseshoe crab males called that settle beside a pair without clasping on and also fertilise eggs?
12558.e: Besides the male that is clasped on, other males often crowd round the female. Because fertilisation takes place outside the body, they can also father offspring.
12558.m: Satellite males sneak in when horseshoe crabs mate.

12559.q: How does the fertilisation of the eggs take place in the horseshoe crab?
a: Outside the body in the nest
12559.e: The female lays the eggs in a pit in the sand, and the males release their sperm over them. This is external fertilisation.
12559.m: In the horseshoe crab, the eggs are fertilised only in the sand.

12560.q: When do American horseshoe crabs come to the beaches to spawn in particularly large numbers?
a: In spring at spring tides around full and new moon
In high summer at low tide at midday
In autumn in storms and rain
In winter with ice on the water
12560.e: In Delaware Bay, the peak of the spawning season is in May and June. At the especially high spring tides around full and new moon, the females lay their eggs high up on the beach.
12560.m: The moon decides when horseshoe crabs come ashore.

12561.q: Where does the female American horseshoe crab lay her eggs?
a: In pits 15 to 20 cm deep in the sandy beach
On seagrass blades in deep water
In empty shells on the seabed
12561.e: The female digs nests on the beach near the high-water line and buries the greenish eggs there. Sun and sand keep them warm.
12561.m: Horseshoe crabs bury their eggs in the beach sand.

12562.q: In which bay in the USA does the largest population of the American horseshoe crab spawn?
