12562.e: On the beaches of Delaware Bay between New Jersey and Delaware, most horseshoe crabs gather to spawn every spring. The other bays are on the Pacific.
12562.m: Delaware Bay is the biggest spawning ground of the horseshoe crabs.

12563.q: How far does the range of the American horseshoe crab extend?
a: From Maine to the Yucatán Peninsula
12563.e: Limulus polyphemus lives on the Atlantic coast of North America from Maine southwards into the Gulf of Mexico and to the Yucatán Peninsula.
12563.m: The American horseshoe crab lives on the east coast of North America.

12564.q: Which migratory bird depends on horseshoe crab eggs in Delaware Bay as a source of energy?
12564.e: On its long journey to the Arctic, the red knot (Calidris canutus rufa) eats horseshoe crab eggs in huge numbers. Fewer eggs mean fewer red knots.
12564.m: Without horseshoe crab eggs, the red knot lacks fuel.

12565.q: For which catch are horseshoe crabs used as bait on the US east coast?
12565.e: Horseshoe crabs are cut up and put in traps for eels and whelks. Besides blood collection, this fishery is a main threat.
12565.m: Many horseshoe crabs end up as bait in traps.

12566.q: How has the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classified the American horseshoe crab since 2016?
12566.e: Since the 2016 assessment, the IUCN has listed Limulus polyphemus as vulnerable, mainly because of overexploitation and loss of habitat.
12566.m: The American horseshoe crab is regarded as vulnerable.

12567.q: What has seriously endangered the tri-spine horseshoe crab in East Asia?
12567.e: The tri-spine horseshoe crab is losing its spawning beaches to land reclamation and coastal building, and is also being caught. The IUCN classifies it as endangered.
12567.m: The tri-spine horseshoe crab is especially threatened.

12568.q: Which poison can occur in the flesh and eggs of the mangrove horseshoe crab?
12568.e: Tetrodotoxin has been found in the mangrove horseshoe crab Carcinoscorpius rotundicauda. In South East Asia, poisonings have already occurred after eating it.
12568.m: Anyone who eats mangrove horseshoe crabs risks poisoning.

12569.q: Which figure from Greek myth does the species name of the horseshoe crab Limulus polyphemus go back to?
12569.e: Polyphemus is the one-eyed Cyclops from Homer’s Odyssey. The name is based on the earlier mistaken belief that the animal had only a single eye.
12569.m: The horseshoe crab bears the name of a Cyclops.

12570.q: What do leafcutter ants mainly do with the leaves they cut?
a: They grow a fungus on them as food
They feed the leaves to aphids
They store the leaves as a winter supply
12570.e: The pieces of leaf are chewed and serve as a growing medium for a fungus. The ants feed themselves and their larvae on the fungus, not on the leaves themselves.
12570.m: Leafcutter ants are fungus farmers, not leaf eaters.

12571.q: How do leafcutter ants and the fungus they cultivate depend on each other?
a: Neither can hardly survive without the other
The fungus only harms the ants
The ants eat the fungus only in an emergency
The fungus also grows wild everywhere in the forest
12571.e: The ants feed on the fungus, and the fungus is fed and cared for by the ants. The main fungus, Leucoagaricus gongylophorus, hardly occurs in nature without the ants.
12571.m: Ant and fungus depend on each other.

12572.q: Which part of the fungus serves as the main food for the larvae of leafcutter ants?
a: Swollen, nutrient-rich tips of the fungal threads
Pieces of wood the fungus has broken down
12572.e: The fungus forms swollen thread ends full of sugars, fats and proteins, the gongylidia. They are the main food of the larvae.
12572.m: Swollen fungal threads are the larvae’s food.

12573.q: Which insects are ants such as the leafcutter ants most closely related to?
12573.e: Like wasps and bees, ants belong to the Hymenoptera. Termites also live in colonies, but they are more closely related to cockroaches.
12573.m: Like bees and wasps, ants belong to the Hymenoptera.

12574.q: What do all ants of the tribe Attini, to which the leafcutter ants belong, have in common?
a: They keep aphids as milk cows
12574.e: All fungus-growing ants of the Americas are grouped in the tribe Attini. The leafcutter ants are the most advanced group among them.
12574.m: All Attini ants are fungus growers.

12575.q: What significance do leafcutter ants have for agriculture in Central and South America?
a: They are regarded as major pests in plantations
They have no influence at all
They are deliberately sold as fertiliser
12575.e: A large colony can strip whole trees and fields of leaves in a short time. This is why leafcutter ants are regarded as major pests in plantations.
12575.m: In plantations, leafcutter ants are regarded as major pests.

12576.q: How many workers can a queen of the leafcutter ant genus Atta produce in total over her life?
12576.e: An Atta queen lays eggs continuously over many years. In total, up to around 150 million workers can arise in this way, even though they never all live at the same time.
12576.m: An Atta queen can produce over a hundred million daughters in her life.

12577.q: How much soil can a large colony of leafcutter ants excavate when building its nest?
12577.e: The underground nests of large Atta colonies have hundreds of chambers. In one nest that was studied, around 40 tonnes of soil were excavated.
12577.m: For a large nest, leafcutter ants move tonnes of soil.

12578.q: How far does the range of the leafcutter ants extend?
a: From the south of the USA to Argentina
From Canada to Tierra del Fuego
From South East Asia to Australia
12578.e: Leafcutter ants live only in the Americas. Their range extends from Texas and Louisiana to Patagonia in Argentina.
12578.m: Leafcutter ants occur only in the Americas, from Texas to Patagonia.

12579.q: Why does the leafcutter ant Atta texana worry foresters in Texas?
a: It strips young pines of their needles
It eats the wood of houses
12579.e: Atta texana lives in the south of the USA, mainly in Texas and Louisiana. Especially in winter, when little other greenery is available, it strips young pines in plantings.
12579.m: In Texas, leafcutter ants harm young pines.

12580.q: Up to how many workers can a large Atta colony of leafcutter ants contain at one time?
12580.e: Mature Atta colonies have several million workers. This makes them among the largest insect societies of all.
12580.m: An Atta colony can have millions of workers.

12581.q: How many queens does a typical colony of the leafcutter ant genus Atta have?
12581.e: Atta colonies are usually founded and led by a single queen. She lays all the eggs for the whole colony.
12581.m: An Atta colony usually has only one queen.

12582.q: How old can a queen of the leafcutter ant genus Atta get?
12582.e: Atta queens are among the longest-lived insects and can reach 10 to 20 years of age. When she dies, the colony dies, because she is not replaced.
12582.m: An Atta queen can live for over a decade.

12583.q: Roughly how many sperm does a leafcutter ant queen store after the nuptial flights?
12583.e: The queen mates with several males and stores around 300 million sperm. She lives off these for her whole life.
12583.m: A leafcutter queen collects hundreds of millions of sperm when she mates.

12584.q: How can a leafcutter ant queen still lay fertilised eggs many years after mating?
a: She stores the sperm in a sperm pouch
12584.e: The sperm pouch, called the spermatheca, is a storage organ in the abdomen. There the sperm stay viable for years.
12584.m: The queen stores sperm for years in a sperm pouch.

12585.q: What does a young leafcutter ant queen take with her on her nuptial flight?
a: A piece of fungus in a pouch in her mouth
A piece of leaf between her legs
An egg of the mother queen
12585.e: In the infrabuccal pocket in her mouth, the young queen carries a piece of fungus from the mother nest. With it she starts the first fungus garden in the new nest.
12585.m: The young queen takes her fungus along in her mouth as starting capital.

12586.q: What does a queen of the leafcutter ant genus Atta use to fertilise her first fungus garden when founding the nest?
12586.e: When founding a nest, the Atta queen stays shut in the nest and cuts no leaves. She feeds the small fungus garden with drops of her faeces.
12586.m: The founding queen fertilises her fungus with her own droppings.

12587.q: What does a leafcutter ant queen do shortly after mating, before she digs her nest?
a: She seeks out a foreign nest
12587.e: After mating, the queen no longer needs wings and sheds them. Her flight muscles later serve her as an energy reserve.
12587.m: After the nuptial flight, the queen sheds her wings.

12588.q: What percentage of young leafcutter ant queens successfully found a long-lived colony?
12588.e: The vast majority of young queens are eaten or fail when founding. Only around 2.5 per cent build a lasting colony.
12588.m: Very few young queens found a successful colony.

12589.q: What happens to the male leafcutter ants after the nuptial flight?
a: They return to the mother nest
They help to dig the nest
12589.e: The males’ only job is to mate. They die shortly after the nuptial flight.
12589.m: Male leafcutter ants live only to mate.

12590.q: At what time do the nuptial flights of leafcutter ants usually take place?
a: At the start of the rainy season
In the middle of the dry season
Only at full moon in winter
12590.e: After the first rains, the ground is soft and damp. The young queens can then dig a nest more easily.
12590.m: Leafcutter ants usually swarm at the start of the rainy season.

12591.q: How many worker castes are usually distinguished in mature colonies of the leafcutter ant genus Atta?
12591.e: A distinction is made between minimae, minores, mediae and majores. They differ greatly in size and task.
12591.m: Atta colonies have four size classes of workers.

12592.q: What is the main job of the tiniest workers (minimae) of the leafcutter ants?
a: Caring for the fungus garden and the brood
12592.e: The smallest workers have a head width of under 1 mm. They tend the fungus and the larvae in the narrow passages of the garden.
12592.m: The smallest are the gardeners in the fungus garden.

12593.q: What is the main job of the largest workers (majores) of the leafcutter ants?
a: Defending the nest and clearing roads
12593.e: The majores, or soldiers, have huge heads with strong chewing muscles. They defend the colony and clear large obstacles from the paths.
12593.m: The big soldiers defend the leafcutter ants’ nest.

12594.q: How big can the soldiers of the leafcutter ant Atta laevigata grow?
12594.e: The largest soldiers of Atta laevigata reach about 16 mm in body length and 7 mm in head width. With their jaws they can even cut through leather.
12594.m: Atta soldiers grow up to about 16 mm long.

12595.q: What is the job of the small leafcutter ant workers that ride along on the pieces of leaf being carried?
a: They fend off parasitic phorid flies
They steer the carrier to the nest
They eat the leaf on the way
12595.e: Phorid flies try to lay eggs on carrying workers. The small hitchhikers chase them away, since the carrier itself does not have its jaws free.
12595.m: Small hitchhikers protect the leaf carriers from flies.

12596.q: How do leafcutter ants react when a plant they have brought in proves harmful to their fungus?
a: They avoid this plant for a long time afterwards
They bring in the plant all the more eagerly afterwards
They eat the plant themselves afterwards
They leave the whole nest at once
12596.e: If a plant material harms the fungus, the workers stop collecting it after about a day. This delayed rejection can last for weeks, so the colony learns from the fungus’s reaction.
12596.m: Leafcutter ants learn to avoid plants that harm their fungus.

12597.q: What especially threatens the fungus gardens of the leafcutter ants?
a: A specialised parasitic fungus that attacks the cultivated fungus
Too much sunlight in the nest
Fish that get into the passages
12597.e: The sac fungus Escovopsis attacks the cultivated fungus. A heavy infestation can destroy the whole garden.
12597.m: A parasitic fungus is the greatest enemy of the fungus gardens.

12598.q: Which helpers do leafcutter ants of the genus Acromyrmex carry on their armour to protect the fungus garden from pests?
12598.e: Pseudonocardia bacteria grow on the body of Acromyrmex. They produce substances that inhibit the parasitic fungus Escovopsis.
12598.m: Acromyrmex uses bacteria on its armour as a living pharmacy.

12599.q: How do leafcutter ants deal with the waste from their fungus garden?
a: They take it to separate waste chambers or dumps
They leave it lying in the fungus garden
They bury it in the brood chamber
12599.e: Used plant material and dead ants go into special waste chambers or onto dumps outside. Mostly older workers work there, and they no longer enter the nest.
12599.m: Leafcutter ants keep their waste strictly away from the fungus garden.

12600.q: What do older leafcutter ant foragers do when their jaws have become blunt?
a: They only carry leaves instead of cutting
They leave the colony for ever
12600.e: Over time the cutting edges of the jaws wear down, and cutting costs more time and energy. The workers then switch to carrying the pieces of leaf.
12600.m: With blunt jaws, leafcutter ants switch from cutting to carrying.

12601.q: Which metal is concentrated in the cutting edges of the leafcutter ants’ jaws, making them harder?
12601.e: Zinc is stored in the cutting edges of the mandibles. It makes them harder and more resistant to wear.
12601.m: Zinc hardens the jaws of leafcutter ants.

12602.q: How do leafcutter ants help themselves when cutting a leaf, so that the cut is cleaner?
a: They produce vibrations with a sound-making organ
They spit acid on the edge of the leaf
They bite into cold leaves only at night
They rub the leaf on the ground
12602.e: By stridulating with the abdomen, they make the jaw vibrate. This makes the leaf stiffer and easier to cut.
12602.m: Leafcutter ants cut with vibrating jaws.

12603.q: Up to roughly what multiple of their body weight were workers of the leafcutter ant Atta cephalotes able to lift in measurements?
12603.e: In laboratory tests, Atta cephalotes workers lifted at most around 9 times their body weight, big and small alike. The often-quoted figure of 50 times is exaggerated.
12603.m: Leafcutter ants can carry a multiple of their own weight.

12604.q: How do leafcutter ants find the way between the nest and the food plant?
a: By scent trails from the venom gland
Only with the help of the stars
12604.e: Workers mark their routes with trail pheromones from the venom gland. Even the tiniest amounts of these substances are enough to recognise the trail.
12604.m: Leafcutter ants follow scent trails to their food plants.

12605.q: How deep into the ground can a nest of the leafcutter ant genus Atta reach?
12605.e: Large Atta nests reach several metres deep. A nest dug up in Brazil extended over around 50 square metres and reached about 8 metres deep.
12605.m: Atta nests reach several metres into the ground.

12606.q: Roughly how many tonnes of soil were excavated from a single large nest of the leafcutter ant Atta sexdens in Brazil?
12606.e: In the classic excavation of an Atta sexdens nest in Brazil, the loose soil that was dug out weighed around 40,000 kilograms. The nest had over 1,000 chambers, 390 of them with fungus gardens.
12606.m: A large Atta nest contains tonnes of excavated soil.

12607.q: What are the many openings and channels in the mound of an Atta leafcutter ant nest for?
a: As an exit for males only
12607.e: The fungus and the ants use a lot of oxygen and produce carbon dioxide. The wind drives air through the openings, so that the nest is ventilated.
12607.m: Atta nests are built with a ventilation system.

12608.q: Roughly how much vegetation can a large colony of leafcutter ants cut per day?
a: As much as a fully grown cow eats
As much as a single leaf
As much as a mouse eats
As much as a whole forest
12608.e: A large Atta colony brings in huge amounts of plant material every day. The amount is compared with the daily needs of a cow.
12608.m: An Atta colony harvests as much each day as a cow eats.

12609.q: Why are leafcutter ants in Brazil and other countries of South America often regarded as pests?
a: They strip crops and plantations of leaves
12609.e: Large colonies cut huge amounts of leaves every day, including in plantations, gardens and on pastures. This is why they are regarded as major pests in agriculture.
12609.m: Leafcutter ants can strip whole plantations of their leaves.

12610.q: In which country are roasted young leafcutter ant queens, called “hormigas culonas”, regarded as a delicacy, especially in the department of Santander?
12610.e: In Santander, the winged young queens of Atta laevigata are collected as they swarm and roasted. The “hormigas culonas” (“big-bottomed ants”) are an expensive speciality there.
12610.m: In Colombia, people eat roasted leafcutter queens as “hormigas culonas”.

12611.q: How do leafcutter ants defend their nest against attackers such as predatory ants?
a: With especially large soldiers with powerful jaws
With a poisonous sting like bees
By leaving the nest at once
12611.e: Leafcutter ants have different castes. The large soldiers defend the nest with their strong jaws, for example against army ants.
12611.m: Large soldiers with strong jaws defend the ants’ nest.

12612.q: Roughly how many million years ago did ants in the Americas begin fungus farming, from which the leafcutter ants later emerged?
12612.e: Family tree analyses show that the fungus farming of the Attini arose around 55 to 65 million years ago. The leafcutter ants are a much younger branch of it.
12612.m: Ants have been farming for many millions of years.

12613.q: What do leafcutter ants use the cut pieces of leaf for?
a: As a growing medium for a fungus that they eat
As direct food for the workers
As building material for the nest walls
As a roof against the rain
12613.e: The ants do not eat the leaves themselves. They chew them and grow a fungus on them, on which mainly the larvae feed.
12613.m: Leafcutter ants are fungus growers, not leaf eaters.

12614.q: What are the chambers in the leafcutter ants’ nest in which they grow their fungus called?
12614.e: The ants lay out fungus gardens in underground chambers. Large nests have hundreds of such chambers.
12614.m: Leafcutter ants lay out underground fungus gardens.

12615.q: How do the digestive enzymes of the leafcutter ants’ fungus get back into the fungus garden?
a: Through the wind in the nest
12615.e: The ants eat fungal enzymes along with the fungus, and these pass through their gut undigested. With their droppings, they apply them to fresh leaf material and so speed up its breakdown.
12615.m: The ants’ droppings bring the fungal enzymes back into the garden.

12616.q: What do adult leafcutter ant workers feed on in addition to the fungus?
a: The plant sap of the cut leaves
12616.e: When cutting, the workers lick up the plant sap that comes out. It gives them a lot of energy, while the larvae live mainly on the fungus.
12616.m: Adult leafcutter ants drink plant sap while cutting.

12617.q: Why are grass-cutting ants such as Atta vollenweideri in South America feared by cattle farmers?
a: They cut a lot of grass and so damage pastures
They bite cows and transmit diseases
They eat the concentrate feed in the barn
12617.e: Some Atta species cut mainly grass instead of leaves. Large colonies can therefore badly damage pastures.
12617.m: Grass-cutting ants compete with cattle for the grass.

12618.q: Which special sense of orientation could be shown in the leafcutter ant Atta colombica in experiments?
12618.e: Field experiments gave signs that Atta colombica can sense the Earth’s magnetic field. This presumably helps it to find its way to the nest.
12618.m: Atta colombica can probably orient itself by the Earth’s magnetic field.

12619.q: How does a leafcutter ant nest affect the soil in the tropical forest?
a: The soil becomes markedly more fertile
12619.e: Through the waste and the digging, many nutrients reach the soil. Jungle soil can become many times more fertile as a result.
12619.m: Leafcutter ants improve the soil through waste and digging.

12620.q: Which insect order are termites counted in today?
12620.e: Comparisons of genetic material have shown that termites arose from cockroaches. The former order of their own, Isoptera, is now regarded only as a subgroup of the Blattodea.
12620.m: Termites are cockroaches that form colonies.

12621.q: What do the wood roaches of the genus Cryptocercus have in common with termites that shows their close relationship?
a: They eat wood with the help of similar single-celled organisms in the gut
They build earth mounds metres high
They have soldiers with poison sprayers
They form colonies with millions of animals
12621.e: The wood roaches of the genus Cryptocercus eat wood, live in family groups and carry similar gut flagellates to lower termites. They are the sister group of the termites.
12621.m: The wood roach Cryptocercus is the closest relative of the termites.

12622.q: What does the former scientific order name of the termites, Isoptera, mean?
12622.e: Isoptera comes from Greek: “isos” means equal and “pteron” means wing. In the reproductive termites, both pairs of wings are almost the same size and shape.
12622.m: Termites have two almost equal pairs of wings.

12623.q: Where does the word “termite” come from?
a: From the Arabic “tarmit” for earth mound
From the French “terminer” for to end
12623.e: The Latin word “termes” (genitive “termitis”) referred to a wood-eating worm. The name of the termites arose from it.
12623.m: The name termite goes back to the Latin word for woodworm.

12624.q: Roughly how many termite species have been described worldwide?
12624.e: Around 2013, just under 2,930 termite species were known, and today it is a little more. Most of them live in the tropics.

12625.q: Which termite family is by far the richest in species?
12625.e: The Termitidae comprise around 2,000 species and so a good two thirds of all termites. They include the fungus-growing and the humus-eating species.
12625.m: Most termite species belong to the higher termites.

12626.q: Why is the Australian termite Mastotermes darwiniensis called a “living fossil”?
a: It is the last living species of a formerly large group
It was found alive in a piece of amber
It has lived in the same nest for a thousand years
It was bred anew after it died out
12626.e: Mastotermes darwiniensis is the last living representative of the family Mastotermitidae, which was much richer in species as fossils. It is regarded as especially primitive.
12626.m: Mastotermes darwiniensis is a living fossil among termites.

12627.q: Which observation about the primitive termite Mastotermes darwiniensis supports the relationship between termites and cockroaches?
a: It lays its eggs in packets like a cockroach
It lives alone instead of in a colony
It eats only carrion like many cockroaches
It has a venomous sting like some cockroaches
12627.e: Like cockroaches, Mastotermes lays its eggs in connected packets. In cockroaches, such an egg packet is called an ootheca.
12627.m: Mastotermes lays egg packets like a cockroach.

12628.q: From which geological period do the oldest reliably known termite fossils come?
12628.e: The oldest termite fossils are around 130 million years old and come from the Early Cretaceous. Their origin is presumed to be even earlier, in the Jurassic.
12628.m: There were termites in the time of the dinosaurs.

12629.q: What kind of development do termites go through, unlike ants?
a: Direct development in the egg without moulting
Alternation of generations with larval polyps
12629.e: Termites are hemimetabolous: larvae hatch from the egg and develop through several moults into the finished animal, without a pupal stage. Ants, by contrast, have a larva and a pupa.
12629.m: Termites become adults without a pupal stage.

12630.q: How do worker termites differ genetically from worker ants?
a: In termites there are male and female workers
In termites all workers are male
In termites all workers are cloned
In termites the workers are haploid
12630.e: Termites are diploid in both sexes, and workers and soldiers can be male or female. In ants, all workers are females, and the males are haploid.
12630.m: Termite workers can be male or female.

12631.q: Which three main castes are typically found in a termite colony?
12631.e: A termite colony usually consists of reproductives that can breed, wingless workers and soldiers. Workers and soldiers do not normally reproduce.
12631.m: A termite colony has reproductives, workers and soldiers.

12632.q: What distinguishes the royal pair of termites from that of ants?
a: The king lives permanently with the queen
The king dies straight after mating
The king leaves the nest after founding
The king eats the queen’s first eggs
12632.e: In termites, the king stays with the queen for life in the royal chamber and mates with her again and again. Male ants, by contrast, die shortly after the nuptial flight.
12632.m: In termites, a royal pair rules.

12633.q: Up to how many eggs per day can a queen of the higher termites lay?
12633.e: The queens of large species such as Macrotermes lay up to around 30,000 eggs a day. Over her life, it can be millions.
12633.m: A termite queen is a real egg factory.

12634.q: Why can the queen of large termite species hardly move any more?
a: Her abdomen has swollen hugely because of the ovaries
She has had no legs from birth
She is stuck fast in the royal chamber
She lies in a permanent cold sleep
12634.e: The queen’s abdomen expands so much because of the huge ovaries that she can hardly move any more. Experts call this physogastry. Workers look after and clean her.
12634.m: Because of her fat abdomen, the queen is almost immobile.

12635.q: How long can the queen of the African termite Macrotermes natalensis grow?
12635.e: With her swollen abdomen, the queen of Macrotermes natalensis reaches up to about 14 cm in length. The workers, by contrast, are only a few millimetres in size.
12635.m: A termite queen can grow as long as a finger.

12636.q: Why do termites pass food and gut fluid to each other mouth to mouth or via the anus?
a: To distribute nutrients, messenger substances and gut microbes
To save water for building the mound
To scare off enemies with the smell
12636.e: This exchange of food is called trophallaxis. In this way nutrients, messenger substances and gut symbionts are distributed throughout the whole colony.
12636.m: Termites share their food and their gut microbes.

12637.q: Why do young and freshly moulted termites depend on the droppings of nestmates?
a: This gives them the gut microbes for digesting wood
This gives them limestone for their shell
This gives them water for breathing
This gives them pigments for camouflage
12637.e: At every moult, the lining of the hindgut with its symbionts is also shed. Through anal fluid from nestmates, the animals take the microbes up again.
12637.m: Without the gut microbes of nestmates, a termite cannot make use of wood.

12638.q: Which microorganisms in the hindgut especially help lower termites to break down cellulose?
12638.e: Lower termites harbour single-celled flagellates as well as bacteria and archaea in the hindgut. These break down the cellulose of the wood.
12638.m: Flagellates in the gut digest the wood for the termite.

12639.q: Termites cannot digest wood on their own. Where does the energy they get from the wood come from in the end?
a: From breakdown products that gut microbes make from cellulose
From sunlight that they store in their shell
From minerals in the soil of their nest
From resin that they suck from the bark
12639.e: Gut microbes break the cellulose down into acetic acid, carbon dioxide and hydrogen. The termite takes up the acetic acid through the gut wall and gets energy from it.
12639.m: Termites live mainly on acetic acid from the wood.

12640.q: Which greenhouse gas do termites give off when digesting plant material?
12640.e: Archaea in the termite gut produce methane. Because of the huge number of termites in the tropics, this contributes measurably to worldwide methane emissions.
12640.m: Termites give off methane when they digest.

12641.q: How do higher termites digest plant material even though they lack flagellates in the gut?
a: With bacteria, their own enzymes and in some cases fungus gardens
With small stones in the stomach like a hen
Not at all, they eat only other insects
With the help of ants that digest for them
12641.e: The higher termites have lost the flagellates. They digest with bacteria, their own enzymes and in some cases with the help of fungus gardens.

12642.q: What is special about the single-celled organism Mixotricha paradoxa from the gut of an Australian termite?
a: It is moved along by thousands of bacteria sitting on it
It eats the termite from the inside
It also lives freely in the sea
12642.e: The single-celled organism Mixotricha paradoxa moves mainly with the help of thousands of spirochaetes sitting on it, not with its few flagella of its own. It is a textbook example of symbiosis.
12642.m: Mixotricha is moved by bacteria as if by oars.

12643.q: On which continents do fungus-growing termites live?
12643.e: The fungus-growing termites (Macrotermitinae) lay out fungus gardens in their nests. This farming arose in Africa, and today such termites live in Africa and Asia.
12643.m: Fungus-growing termites live in Africa and Asia.

12644.q: What do fungus-growing termites build the combs on which their fungus grows from?
a: From droppings containing roughly pre-digested plant material
12644.e: The workers eat plant parts, excrete them barely digested and form fungus combs from them. The fungus breaks the material down and is then eaten itself.
12644.m: The termites’ fungus garden grows on their own droppings.

12645.q: What is the termite fungus Termitomyces titanicus known for?
a: It is regarded as the largest edible mushroom in the world
It is regarded as the most poisonous mushroom in Africa
It is regarded as the oldest fungus on Earth
It is regarded as the only glowing fungus
12645.e: The cap of Termitomyces titanicus can grow around a metre across. The mushroom grows out of termite mounds in West Africa and is eaten.
12645.m: The world’s largest edible mushroom grows on termite mounds.

12646.q: What does a comparison of the family trees of fungus-growing termites and their Termitomyces fungi show?
a: The two developed together over a long time
The fungi are older than all insects
The fungi descend from ant gardens
The fungi change species every year
12646.e: The family trees of termites and fungi largely match. This points to coevolution, that is, the partners developing together.
12646.m: Termites and their fungi arose together.

12647.q: How tall can the largest termite mounds in Africa get?
12647.e: Large termite mounds of species such as Macrotermes reach over 8 metres in height. In proportion to the animals’ body size, these are enormous structures.
12647.m: Termites build towers taller than a house.

12648.q: What are the walls of a typical termite mound mainly made of?
a: Soil, glued with saliva and droppings
12648.e: Termites mix soil particles with saliva and droppings. When dry, this material becomes almost as hard as concrete.
12648.m: Termite mounds are built of soil and saliva.

12649.q: At roughly what temperature do fungus-growing termites keep the inside of their nest as constant as possible?
12649.e: Ventilation shafts in the nest carry heat away and bring fresh air in. In this way the temperature stays close to 30 °C, which also benefits the fungus garden.
12649.m: A termite nest is a natural air-conditioning system.

12650.q: Which building in Zimbabwe uses ventilation modelled on termite mounds?
12650.e: The architect Mick Pearce designed the Eastgate Centre with natural ventilation inspired by termite mounds. The building manages without conventional air conditioning.
12650.m: Termites are models for energy-saving architecture.

12651.q: Why does the Australian “compass termite” Amitermes meridionalis align its flat mounds north and south?
a: So that the nest does not overheat at midday
So that the queen can see the stars
So that the rain runs off faster
So that enemies cannot find the entrance
12651.e: The narrow sides point to the midday sun, and the broad faces to the east and west. In this way the nest warms up in the morning and evening and stays cooler at midday.
12651.m: Compass termites build like a sundial.

12652.q: How old, in some cases, are the roughly 200 million termite mounds described in north-eastern Brazil in 2018?
12652.e: The earth mounds of the species Syntermes dirus cover an area about the size of Great Britain. Dating gave an age of up to around 4,000 years.
12652.m: Brazilian termites have been building a huge field of mounds for thousands of years.

12653.q: What is the mating flight called in which winged termites swarm out of the nest in large numbers?
12653.e: Usually after rain, thousands of reproductives fly out at the same time. Afterwards, females and males form pairs and found new colonies.
12653.m: New termite colonies begin with the nuptial flight.

12654.q: What do termite reproductives do shortly after landing from the nuptial flight?
a: They shed their wings at breaking seams
They lay eggs in the air at once
12654.e: The wings break off at pre-formed seams. Afterwards, the partners walk one behind the other in tandem and look for a place to found the colony.
12654.m: After the nuptial flight, termites no longer need wings.

12655.q: What are termites called that can replace a dead queen or king in the nest?
12655.e: Replacement reproductives develop from larvae or workers and become able to breed without growing wings. In this way a colony can survive the loss of the royal pair.
12655.m: Termite colonies keep replacement kings in reserve.

12656.q: How does the Japanese termite Reticulitermes speratus produce its replacement queens?
12656.e: The queen lays unfertilised eggs, from which successors with her own genes hatch. Workers and soldiers, by contrast, arise from fertilised eggs.
12656.m: Some termite queens produce their successors without males.

12657.q: What weapon do the soldiers of nasute termites (Nasutitermitinae) have?
a: A frontal gland with a sticky spray secretion
A venomous sting on the abdomen
A covering of urticating hairs on the back
12657.e: Their jaws are stunted, but they have a beak-like projection on the head. From this they spray a sticky, poisonous secretion at attackers.
12657.m: Nasute termites defend themselves with a glue sprayer on the head.

12658.q: What do the soldiers of the termite Globitermes sulphureus do in an attack?
a: They burst open and glue up the enemy
They play dead and give off a stench
They fly away and warn other colonies
They dig into the sand in a flash
12658.e: The soldiers tear their body wall open, and a yellow, sticky liquid comes out. This suicide to protect the colony is called autothysis.
12658.m: Some termite soldiers sacrifice themselves by bursting.

12659.q: What do old workers of the termite Neocapritermes taracua from French Guiana carry on their backs?
a: Blue crystals that produce a poison when they burst
Eggs of the queen for the move
12659.e: Older workers accumulate blue crystals in pouches. If they burst in a fight, these react with gland secretion to form a poisonous liquid.
12659.m: Old termite workers carry an explosive backpack.

12660.q: How do some termite soldiers defend the passage with their flattened, hard heads?
a: They plug the passage with them like a cork
They dig new escape passages with them
They knock enemies off the ceiling with them
They produce light in the dark with them
12660.e: In dry-wood termites such as Cryptotermes, the head is flat and thick at the front. The soldiers use it to block openings, a behaviour called phragmosis.
12660.m: Some termite soldiers are living door plugs.

12661.q: How do termites warn each other of danger in the dark nest?
a: By head banging, which produces vibrations
By whistling sounds with the wings
By changing the colour of the body
12661.e: Soldiers and workers bang their heads rhythmically against the ground. The vibrations are sensed by nestmates through their legs.
12661.m: Termites drum an alarm with their heads.

12662.q: Why do termites sometimes follow lines drawn with certain ballpoint pens?
a: A substance in the ink resembles their trail pheromone
The line shines like a thread of water
The ink contains cellulose as food
12662.e: Some inks contain 2-phenoxyethanol, which acts in a similar way to a trail pheromone. The mostly blind workers orient themselves strongly by such scent trails.
12662.m: Termites follow scent trails, not pictures.

12663.q: Which African predator related to the hyenas feeds almost only on termites?
12663.e: At night, the aardwolf licks up large numbers of termites of the genus Trinervitermes from the ground. It tolerates the defensive substances of their soldiers, which other animals avoid.
12663.m: The aardwolf is a hyena that licks up termites.

12664.q: Which tool-using behaviour in chimpanzees did Jane Goodall first observe in connection with termites?
a: Fishing for termites with stalks and twigs
12664.e: In 1960, Jane Goodall saw in Gombe how chimpanzees pushed blades of grass into termite nests and pulled out the termites that had bitten on. This changed the view of tool use in animals.
12664.m: Chimpanzees fish for termites with little sticks.

12665.q: Which termite from East Asia has spread as a feared pest in the south of the USA and in Hawaii?
12665.e: The Formosan termite was carried around the world with timber and shiploads. Its large underground colonies cause considerable damage to buildings in New Orleans, for example.
12665.m: The Formosan termite is a wood pest that has been spread worldwide.

12666.q: Where does the yellow-necked drywood termite, native to the Mediterranean region, mostly nest?
a: In dead wood of old trees, sometimes in roof beams
12666.e: The yellow-necked drywood termite is one of the drywood termites and lives in small colonies of usually around 1,000 to 2,000 animals. It nests mainly in old trees and sometimes in roof beams.
12666.m: The yellow-necked drywood termite lives in the wood that it eats.

12667.q: Where in Germany was a well-known infestation with introduced termites discovered in the 1930s?
12667.e: In the Hamburg harbour area and in Altona, introduced termites of the genus Reticulitermes had settled. Warm district heating pipes helped them survive the winters.
12667.m: Termites survived in Hamburg thanks to warm heating pipes.

12668.q: What do the African harvester termites of the family Hodotermitidae mainly feed on?
12668.e: Harvester termites such as Hodotermes mossambicus cut off blades of grass and carry them into their underground nest. Unlike most species, their workers have functioning eyes.
12668.m: Harvester termites mow grass for their store.

12669.q: What is typical of the way of life of drywood termites such as Cryptotermes brevis?
a: They live entirely in the wood that they eat, without contact with the ground
They build tall earth mounds in the savannah
They grow fungi in underground gardens
They mow grass and store it in the nest
12669.e: Drywood termites form small colonies and live entirely in the wood that they eat. Species such as Cryptotermes brevis also infest furniture and roof frames.
12669.m: Drywood termites live inside their own food.

12670.q: Which insect order do stick insects belong to?
12670.e: Stick insects, together with the leaf insects, form the order Phasmatodea of their own, the phasmids. Despite the German name Stabheuschrecke (“stick grasshopper”), they are not closely related to the jumping grasshoppers.
12670.m: Stick insects are phasmids and not true grasshoppers.

12671.q: What does the Greek word “phasma”, from which the order name of the stick insects is derived, mean?
12671.e: “Phasma” means ghost or apparition in ancient Greek. The name alludes to the fact that the animals become practically invisible in their surroundings.
12671.m: The stick insect is a ghost because you can hardly see it.

12672.q: Why is the German name “Heuschrecke” (grasshopper) for stick insects actually inaccurate?
12672.e: True grasshoppers have powerful jumping legs. Stick insects, by contrast, move by walking slowly and do not jump.
12672.m: A stick insect walks instead of jumping.

12673.q: Roughly how many valid species of phasmids (stick insects and relatives) have been described?
12673.e: Today over 3,500 valid species have been described, and new ones are added every year. Many species in tropical forests are probably still undiscovered.
12673.m: There are around 3,500 known species of phasmids.

12674.q: How long, with its legs outstretched, was the stick insect from China that was presented in 2016 as the longest insect in the world?
12674.e: In 2014, the researcher Zhao Li found a stick insect in the Chinese region of Guangxi that was 62.4 cm long with its legs outstretched. In 2016 it was presented as the longest insect in the world.
12674.m: The longest insect in the world is a stick insect from China.

12675.q: Which insect group do the longest insects in the world belong to?
12675.e: The record holders are stick insects. Phobaeticus chani from Borneo measures 56.7 cm with its front legs outstretched, and a species from China even over 62 cm.
12675.m: Phobaeticus chani from Borneo held the length record for a long time.

12676.q: What does the name part “chani” mean in the giant stick insect Phobaeticus chani?
a: It honours a person called Chan
It names the place it was found in China
12676.e: The species was named in 2008 after the Malaysian naturalist Datuk Chan Chew Lun, who had handed the specimen to the researcher. Many species are named after people.
12676.m: Phobaeticus chani honours a Malaysian nature lover called Chan.

12677.q: Why is the total length of record-breaking stick insects much greater than the body length?
a: Because the outstretched legs are included in the measurement
Because the antennae are several metres long
Because the body shrinks after death
Because the wings stick out far beyond the body
12677.e: In Phobaeticus chani, the body alone measures about 36 cm. Only with the front legs outstretched does the animal reach around 57 cm.
12677.m: Even the body of Phobaeticus chani is longer than a ruler.

12678.q: How heavy can the females of the Malaysian jungle nymph get?
12678.e: The females of the Malaysian jungle nymph (Heteropteryx dilatata) weigh about 30 to 65 g. This makes them among the heaviest living insects.
12678.m: The heaviest stick insect is a green giant from Malaysia.

12679.q: What colour are the females of the giant stick insect Heteropteryx dilatata usually?
12679.e: The females are usually lime green, more rarely yellow or reddish brown. The males, by contrast, are smaller, slimmer and brownish.
12679.m: Heteropteryx females usually wear a light green dress.

12680.q: How does the spiny stick insect Heteropteryx dilatata defend itself when touched?
a: It snaps its spiny hind legs together
It rolls up into a ball
12680.e: When threatened, it hisses with its wings, raises its abdomen and spreads its hind legs. If touched, it snaps the spiny lower legs against the thighs and so painfully pinches the attacker.
12680.m: Heteropteryx defends itself with spiny hind legs like a pair of pincers.

12681.q: How does the stick insect Heteropteryx dilatata lay its eggs?
a: It pushes them into the ground one by one with its ovipositor
It sticks them to branches in foam nests
It carries them in a brood pouch on its belly
It lays them in the water of tree holes
12681.e: The females bore each egg singly into the soil with an ovipositor. The nymphs hatch only after about 7 to 14 months.
12681.m: Heteropteryx buries its eggs singly in the ground.

12682.q: Roughly how long do the females of the smallest known phasmids grow?
12682.e: The females of Miniphasma prima from Sri Lanka grow only around 17.5 mm long. The largest species, by contrast, measure over 60 cm.
12682.m: Some stick insects are shorter than two centimetres.

12683.q: Between which countries does Lord Howe Island, home of the Lord Howe stick insect, lie?
12683.e: The small Lord Howe Island lies in the Pacific between Australia and New Zealand. Politically it belongs to the Australian state of New South Wales.
12683.m: The Lord Howe stick insect comes from a tiny Pacific island.

12684.q: Which nickname is used for the large, dark Lord Howe stick insect?
12684.e: Because of its massive, glossy black body, it is called a “tree lobster”. It grows up to about 20 cm long.
12684.m: The Lord Howe stick insect is called the tree lobster because of its looks.

12685.q: What triggered the disappearance of the Lord Howe stick insect from its home island?
a: Black rats from a stranded supply ship
A volcanic eruption on the island
12685.e: In 1918, the supply ship Makambo ran aground off the island, and black rats came ashore. The rats ate the stick insects, which were no longer found after about 1920.
12685.m: Introduced rats wiped out the Lord Howe stick insect on its island.

12686.q: Why do several zoos around the world keep Lord Howe stick insects?
a: As a reserve stock in case the wild population disappears
Because they serve as food animals for reptiles
Because they are dangerous to visitors and therefore exciting
Because they can lay eggs only in a zoo
12686.e: The wild population is tiny. Zoos such as Melbourne, Budapest, Bristol, San Diego and Toronto therefore keep reserve populations so that the species does not die out.
12686.m: Lord Howe stick insects are also bred as a reserve in Europe.

12687.q: Where was the Lord Howe stick insect, thought to be extinct, rediscovered in 2001?
a: On the rock Ball’s Pyramid in the Pacific
In a botanical garden in Sydney
On the North Island of New Zealand
12687.e: In 2001, researchers found a tiny remnant population on the barren rock spire of Ball’s Pyramid, about 23 km from Lord Howe Island. It lived under a single bush.
12687.m: On a lonely sea rock, the Lord Howe stick insect survived unnoticed.

12688.q: How many Lord Howe stick insects did the researchers find when it was rediscovered in 2001?
12688.e: Nicholas Carlile and the ranger Dean Hiscox discovered 24 animals at night under a bush on Ball’s Pyramid. This tiny group was the last known wild population.
12688.m: Just two dozen animals saved the Lord Howe stick insect from oblivion.

12689.q: Where exactly were the last wild Lord Howe stick insects found on Ball’s Pyramid?
a: Under a single bush on the barren rock
In a dense forest on the summit
In a cave below sea level
In birds’ nests on the steep coast
12689.e: The small remnant population lived on a single bush of the species Melaleuca howeana, a member of the myrtle family. The bare rock offered hardly any more habitat.
12689.m: A single bush on a rock was the home of the last Lord Howe stick insects.

12690.q: In which zoo did the breeding of the Lord Howe stick insect begin in 2003, using animals from Ball’s Pyramid?
12690.e: In 2003, a pair from Ball’s Pyramid was brought to Melbourne Zoo, where, after initial difficulties, breeding succeeded. By 2016, around 13,000 eggs had hatched there.
12690.m: Melbourne Zoo has saved the Lord Howe stick insect from extinction.

12691.q: What conservation status does the Lord Howe stick insect have on the IUCN Red List?
12691.e: The species is classified as “Critically Endangered”. The wild population is tiny and restricted to a single rock.
12691.m: The Lord Howe stick insect is one of the rarest insects in the world.

12692.q: What is very unusual for an insect in the social behaviour of the Lord Howe stick insect?
a: Males and females sometimes form lasting pairs
They live in colonies with a queen
The males guard nests with young
12692.e: In some animals, males and females form a bond and rest close together. In insects, something like this occurs only very rarely.
12692.m: Lord Howe stick insects often stay together as a pair.

12693.q: How do Lord Howe stick insects change as they grow up?
a: They change from green and active by day to black and active at night
They change from black to bright red
They lose their legs and crawl
They grow big wings and fly
12693.e: Young Lord Howe stick insects are green and active by day. The adults are glossy black and come out mainly at night.
12693.m: Young Lord Howe stick insects are green, adults are black.

12694.q: Which precondition for a return of the Lord Howe stick insect to its home island was created in 2019?
a: The island was cleared of rats and mice
A new rock was piled up
The island was fenced in completely
All the birds on the island were relocated
12694.e: After a large eradication programme, Lord Howe Island was declared free of rats and mice at the end of 2019. This made reintroducing the stick insect possible in the first place.
12694.m: Without rats, the Lord Howe stick insect can go home again.

12695.q: What does parthenogenesis mean in many stick insects?
a: Females lay eggs capable of developing without fertilisation
Young arise by the mother dividing
Eggs are fertilised by two males
12695.e: In parthenogenesis, unfertilised eggs develop into offspring. Many stick insects can in this way reproduce entirely without males.
12695.m: A stick insect often does not need a male to have offspring.

12696.q: What sex are the offspring that usually hatch from unfertilised eggs in stick insects?
12696.e: In stick insects, unfertilised eggs as a rule produce females. They are mostly genetic copies of the mother.
12696.m: Daughters hatch from unfertilised stick insect eggs.

12697.q: How rare are males in the Indian stick insect (Carausius morosus)?
a: About one male to 500 to 1,000 females
About one male to two females
About one male to ten females
Males are more common than females
12697.e: Males of the Indian stick insect are extreme exceptions. The species reproduces almost only by parthenogenesis.
12697.m: Indian stick insects consist almost entirely of females.

12698.q: Which country does the popular terrarium stick insect Carausius morosus originally come from?
12698.e: The Indian stick insect originally comes from southern India. Today it is one of the most common insects in schools and terrariums around the world.
12698.m: The Indian stick insect carries its homeland in its name.

12699.q: How long do the females of the Indian stick insect grow?
12699.e: The females reach around 8 to 9 cm, the rare males only 5 to 6 cm. This makes the species fairly medium-sized.
12699.m: An Indian stick insect is about as long as a finger.

12700.q: Which food plant is often used in Europe for keeping Indian stick insects?
12700.e: Bramble stays green in winter too and is eaten with relish by many stick insects. Raspberry, hazel or ivy, for example, are also offered.
12700.m: Bramble leaves are the favourite food of many stick insects in the terrarium.

12701.q: Roughly how many eggs can a female Indian stick insect lay over her lifetime?
12701.e: A female lays up to three eggs a day and so comes to about 1,200 eggs in her life. For stick insects overall, the number is around 100 to 1,200, depending on the species.
12701.m: A female Indian stick insect lays over a thousand eggs.

12702.q: What ability for camouflage does the Indian stick insect have?
a: It can change its colouring between green and brown
It can double its body length
It can spin foliage out of silk
It can glow like a glow-worm
12702.e: The females adapt their colour depending on light, temperature and humidity and become lighter or darker. In this way they remain hard to spot on leaves or twigs.
12702.m: The Indian stick insect changes colour like a little chameleon.

12703.q: What can young stick insects do after losing a leg?
a: Regrow it almost completely over the next moults
Stick it back on with saliva
Walk with an antenna as a replacement leg
Take over a leg from a partner
12703.e: Stick insects can shed a leg at a breaking point when an enemy grabs them. Nymphs largely regrow the leg over the following moults.
12703.m: A young stick insect lets go of a leg and lets it grow back.

12704.q: What do many stick insects do to look like a twig in the wind?
a: They sway slowly back and forth
They roll up into a spiral
They hop jerkily up and down
12704.e: Many species rock gently back and forth as if a twig were swaying in the wind. This movement makes their camouflage even more convincing.
12704.m: The stick insect dances with the wind to look like a branch.

12705.q: What is the catalepsy that stick insects show when in danger?
a: A rigid state in which they stay motionless
12705.e: In the startle rigidity, stick insects stay motionless for minutes, often with their legs held close. This makes them look just like a dead twig.
12705.m: When in danger, the stick insect freezes into a little stick.

12706.q: What does the North American stick insect Anisomorpha buprestoides use to defend itself against attackers?
a: An irritating secretion from glands on the front of the body
A poisonous sting on the abdomen
A bite from its strong jaws
12706.e: The species from the south-east of the USA has defensive glands in the thorax region and can spray a stinging secretion accurately. It can cause severe pain in the eyes of humans and animals.
12706.m: Some stick insects defend themselves with chemical weapons.

12707.q: What do the eggs of many stick insects most resemble?
12707.e: The hard eggs with a lid often look like seeds. In this way they are overlooked by predators and even spread like seeds.
12707.m: Stick insect eggs are disguised as seeds.

12708.q: What is the job of the fatty appendage (capitulum) on some stick insect eggs?
a: It attracts ants, which carry the eggs into their nest
It serves the embryo as a breathing tube
It sticks the egg to leaves
It scares off birds with poison
12708.e: Ants drag the eggs into their nest because of the nutritious capitulum and eat only the appendage. The egg then lies well protected in the ants’ nest.
12708.m: Ants become babysitters for stick insect eggs.

12709.q: What did a Japanese study from 2018 show about stick insect eggs and birds?
a: Some of the eggs survive digestion in the bird’s gut
Birds avoid stick insects because of poison
Birds use the eggs as nesting material
12709.e: Researchers fed brown-eared bulbuls with females full of eggs. About 5 to 20 per cent of the eggs were excreted undamaged, and in one tested species nymphs hatched from them.
12709.m: A bird can unwittingly carry stick insect eggs to new areas.

12710.q: How do freshly hatched nymphs of the Australian stick insect Extatosoma tiaratum resemble their surroundings?
a: They look and move like ants
12710.e: The tiny, dark nymphs with a red head scurry about nimbly and resemble ants of the genus Leptomyrmex. In this way they escape many predators that avoid well-defended ants.
12710.m: Young Extatosoma stick insects disguise themselves as ants.

12711.q: What do stick insects feed on?
a: On the blood of larger animals
12711.e: All phasmids are plant eaters and mostly eat leaves of trees and bushes. Some species can strip large areas of forest bare when their numbers explode.
12711.m: Stick insects are pure leaf eaters.

12712.q: What was discovered in 2016 about the digestive enzymes of stick insects?
a: Their genes for pectin-degrading enzymes originally come from bacteria
They have no gut at all
They digest leaves only with stomach acid
They live only on sugar from plant sap
12712.e: Stick insects make pectinases themselves, whose genes were once taken over from bacteria by horizontal gene transfer. This lets them break open the cell walls of leaves.
12712.m: Stick insects borrowed digestive genes from bacteria.

12713.q: What kind of development do stick insects go through?
a: Incomplete metamorphosis without a pupal stage
Direct birth as a finished animal without moulting
12713.e: A nymph hatches from the egg, already resembling the adult animal. It grows up through several moults without ever forming a pupa.
12713.m: A stick insect grows up moult by moult without a pupa.

12714.q: What do freshly moulted stick insect nymphs often eat first?
12714.e: After moulting, many nymphs eat their old skin. In this way they recover valuable nutrients and leave no telltale traces.
12714.m: A stick insect eats up its old skin after moulting.

12715.q: How long can mating last in the Indian stick insect Necroscia sparaxes?
12715.e: In this species, pairs stayed joined together for up to 79 days. This is regarded as a record among insects.
12715.m: Some stick insects stay paired for weeks.

12716.q: Where do the stick insects of the primitive genus Timema live?
a: In the west of North America, mainly in California
In the rainforests of the Congo Basin
12716.e: Timema species live in the west of North America, mainly in California. The roughly 20 species alone form the primitive suborder Timematodea.
12716.m: The primitive Timema stick insects are at home in California.

12717.q: For how long have some Timema stick insects been reproducing without sex?
12717.e: Genetic studies showed that several asexual Timema lines have been reproducing without males for over a million years. For animals, that is an exceptionally long period.
12717.m: Some Timema stick insects have done without males for millions of years.

12718.q: What is true of the wings of many stick insects?
a: They are often missing or greatly shortened, especially in females
They always have four wings of equal size
Their wings are covered with scales like those of butterflies
They have only a single pair of wings on the head
12718.e: Many species are wingless or have only stub wings. Often the males have wings, while the heavier females cannot fly.
12718.m: Many female stick insects cannot fly.

12719.q: Roughly how many species of stick insects and relatives live in Europe?
12719.e: About 17 species are known in Europe, mainly in the Mediterranean region. They include the Mediterranean stick insect Bacillus rossius and Clonopsis gallica.
12719.m: Southern Europe has its own stick insects too.

12720.q: Which insect order do leaf insects belong to?
12720.e: Leaf insects are phasmids and so close relatives of the stick insects. They are not closely related to the mantises, which live as predators.
12720.m: Leaf insects are leaf-shaped relatives of the stick insects.

12721.q: What did the order name Phasmatodea, to which the leaf insect belongs, originally mean?
a: It goes back to the Greek word for ghost or apparition
It goes back to the Greek word for leaf green
It goes back to the Latin word for twig
It goes back to the Latin word for herbivore
12721.e: “Phasma” means ghost or apparition in Greek. The name alludes to the ghostly invisibility of these masters of camouflage.
12721.m: Phasmids are called that because, like ghosts, they are hardly to be seen.

12722.q: Where does the genus name Phyllium of the leaf insect come from?
12722.e: “Phyllon” means leaf in Greek, as also in the word chlorophyll. The name describes the leaf-like shape of the animals.
12722.m: Phyllium contains the Greek word for leaf.

12723.q: How do leaf insects strengthen their camouflage when they move?
a: They sway back and forth like a leaf in the wind
They change colour like a chameleon
They roll up into a ball
They move only in heavy rain
12723.e: When walking, leaf insects rock their body back and forth. In this way they look like a leaf moving in the wind.
12723.m: Leaf insects sway like a leaf in the wind.

12724.q: How do males and females differ in many leaf insects?
a: Males are slimmer and fly, females are broader and cannot fly
Females are slim and fly, males do not
Only the males are coloured green
12724.e: Females have a broad, leaf-like body but cannot fly. The slimmer males have long hind wings and fly.
12724.m: In leaf insects, usually only the males fly.

12725.q: Roughly how many valid species of leaf insect have been described?
12725.e: About 120 species are known today. Around half of them have been scientifically described only since 2016.
12725.m: There are around 120 species of leaf insects, and new ones are constantly being added.

12726.q: What has been especially striking in research on leaf insects in recent years?
a: About half of the species have been described only since 2016
Since 2016 almost all species are regarded as extinct
Since 2016 all species are counted as mantises
Since 2016 no new species have been discovered
12726.e: New field research and genetic methods have brought to light many previously overlooked species. Several new genera have also been established since 2017.
12726.m: The diversity of leaf insects has been properly recognised only for a few years.

12727.q: Which fossil site in Germany yielded a leaf insect around 47 million years old?
12727.e: The Messel Pit is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and famous for fossils from the Eocene. There, in 2005, the fossil Eophyllium messelensis was found.
12727.m: An ancient leaf insect was found in the Messel Pit.

12728.q: Roughly how old is the fossil Eophyllium messelensis, an ancestor of the leaf insects?
12728.e: The fossil comes from the Eocene and is around 47 million years old. It already looks very much like today’s males.
12728.m: Leaf-like phasmids already existed around 47 million years ago.

12729.q: What does the find of Eophyllium in Germany show about the history of leaf insects?
a: Their range used to be much larger than today
They originally come from the Arctic
They used to live exclusively in water
They used to be unable to eat leaves
12729.e: Today leaf insects live only in the tropics of Asia and Oceania. The fossil from Europe proves that the group used to be much more widespread.
12729.m: The fossil from Messel proves that leaf insects once lived in Europe too.

12730.q: Which insect researcher, born in Bern, established the family of leaf insects (Phylliidae) in 1893?
12730.e: The Bernese entomologist Carl Brunner von Wattenwyl established the family Phylliidae in 1893. He was an important researcher of grasshoppers and phasmids.
12730.m: The family of leaf insects was established by a Swiss researcher.

12731.q: What does the fossil Eophyllium suggest about the behaviour of leaf insects?
a: Leaf camouflage and swaying behaviour probably already existed millions of years ago
They lived back then as predators of other insects
They built nests out of leaves back then
They lived back then in large colonies like ants
12731.e: The fossil already shows the leaf-like body shape. Researchers conclude from this that mimicry and swaying are very old.
12731.m: The leaf camouflage of leaf insects is an ancient invention.

12732.q: Where is the natural range of leaf insects today?
a: From South Asia through South East Asia to Melanesia and northern Australia
In the rainforests of Central and South America
In tropical West and Central Africa
In the Mediterranean region and North Africa
12732.e: Leaf insects live from South Asia through South East Asia to New Guinea, Melanesia and northern Queensland. They do not occur naturally in the Americas.
12732.m: Leaf insects are tropical dwellers of Asia and Oceania.

12733.q: Which island group in the Indian Ocean marks the western limit of the range of leaf insects?
12733.e: The genus Pulchriphyllium has the westernmost range and reaches the Seychelles. Further west there are no leaf insects.
12733.m: The Seychelles are the westernmost outpost of the leaf insects.

12734.q: In which region of the world do leaf insects live in the wild?
a: In South and South East Asia as far as Melanesia
In the Sahara and on the Arabian Peninsula
12734.e: Leaf insects live in tropical forests from India and South East Asia through New Guinea to Pacific islands such as Fiji. They do not occur wild in Europe.
12734.m: Leaf insects are tropical dwellers of Asia and the western Pacific.

12735.q: Why are many species of leaf insect found on only a single island or island group?
a: They are poor at spreading and developed separately on islands
They are deliberately released there by humans
They migrate from island to island every year
They can tolerate only sea water as drinking water
12735.e: The females usually cannot fly, and the animals hardly migrate. On isolated islands such as New Caledonia, genera of their own with small ranges have arisen in this way.
12735.m: Isolation on islands promotes the emergence of species of their own.

12736.q: Leaf insects also live on New Guinea, east of Wallace’s Line. What does this line separate?
a: The northern from the southern hemisphere
Two time zones in the Pacific
12736.e: Wallace’s Line runs between Borneo and Sulawesi and between Bali and Lombok. West of it the wildlife is Asian, and east of it it is increasingly Australian in character.
12736.m: Wallace’s Line separates the wildlife of Asia and Australia.

12737.q: Which animal group is most closely related to leaf insects?
12737.e: Leaf insects belong to the order of the phasmids, which also includes the stick insects. Both disguise themselves as plant parts: one as a leaf, the other as a twig.
12737.m: Leaf insects and stick insects are phasmids.

12738.q: Which sex is the larger one in leaf insects, growing, for example in the largest species, up to about 12 cm long?
a: Both are always the same size
12738.e: The largest leaf insects are females, for example of Pulchriphyllium giganteum with up to around 12 cm. The males are smaller and slimmer.
12738.m: The giants among the leaf insects are females.

12739.q: How long can the females of the largest leaf insects grow?
12739.e: The largest females, for example of Pulchriphyllium giganteum, reach around 10.5 to 12 cm. That makes them clearly shorter than the longest stick insects.
12739.m: Large leaf insects are about as long as the palm of a hand.

12740.q: How big are the smallest known leaf insects, roughly?
12740.e: Males of Microphyllium spinithorax from the Philippines measure only about 24 mm. The largest females of other species grow about five times as long.
12740.m: The smallest leaf insects are only about as long as a finger joint.

12741.q: What clear difference in body structure exists between the sexes in most leaf insects?
a: Females are bigger and broader, males smaller and slimmer
Males are bigger and broader, females smaller and slimmer
Both sexes are the same size and shape
Only the males have a leaf-like body
12741.e: The females are large, broad and very leaf-like. The males are smaller, slimmer and therefore less perfectly camouflaged.
12741.m: In leaf insects, the females are the big, broad leaves.

12742.q: What is the flying ability of the females like in most leaf insects?
a: They largely lack hind wings and cannot fly
They are better fliers than the males
They fly long distances only at night
They fly only briefly after the last moult
12742.e: The females’ hind wings are mostly missing or only rudimentary. Their front wings serve as leaf-like wing covers and not for flying.
12742.m: Female leaf insects look like leaves but cannot fly.

12743.q: What are the males’ hind wings like in the leaf insect?
a: They are fully developed and allow short flights
They are stunted and only stumps
They serve exclusively as swimming fins
They are fused with the front wings into a shell
12743.e: Males have fully developed, mostly transparent hind wings. With them they can fly short distances, for example when searching for females.
12743.m: Male leaf insects can fly, the females mostly cannot.

12744.q: What are the front wings of the females used for in most leaf insects?
a: As leaf-like wing covers for camouflage
For fast flying over long distances
12744.e: The females’ front wings are modified into leathery wing covers that look like a leaf with veins. The females usually cannot fly, because the hind wings are missing or stunted.
12744.m: The females’ wings are mainly camouflage, not flying equipment.

12745.q: What does the pattern on the front wings of a female leaf insect imitate?
a: The eyes of a bird of prey
The bark of a tree trunk
12745.e: The females’ front wings are modified into leathery wing covers, the tegmina. They often cover the whole abdomen and carry a pattern like a midrib and leaf veins.
12745.m: The females’ wing covers look like a leaf with veins.

12746.q: How can you easily tell male and female leaf insects apart?
a: Males have much longer antennae than females
Females have much longer antennae than males
Males have eight legs, females six
12746.e: The females’ antennae are short, about as long as the head. The males have long, bristly antennae with clearly more segments.
12746.m: Long antennae give away a male leaf insect.

12747.q: How do the males’ antennae in the leaf insect differ from those of the females?
a: They are longer, bristly and have 20 to 26 segments
They are shorter and have only 3 segments
They are completely absent in males
They are the same length but coloured bright red
12747.e: Male antennae are much longer than the female ones and covered with bristles. They consist of 20 to 26 segments.
12747.m: You recognise male leaf insects by their long, bristly antennae.

12748.q: Which additional sense organs do male leaf insects usually have on the head?
12748.e: Males usually have three ocelli, simple light-sensing organs. They presumably help with flying, which only the males can do.
12748.m: The males, which can fly, usually have three simple eyes.

12749.q: With which behaviour does a leaf insect strengthen its camouflage in addition to its body shape?
a: It sways back and forth like a leaf in the wind
It rolls up into a ball
It glows green in the dark
It quickly digs into the ground
12749.e: When walking and when disturbed, many species sway back and forth. In this way they look like a leaf moving in the wind.
12749.m: Leaf insects sway as they walk, like a leaf in the wind.

12750.q: Which detail on the body edge makes the camouflage of some leaf insects especially realistic?
a: Edges that look like feeding damage on a leaf
Spines that look like rose thorns
Spots that look like bird droppings
12750.e: In some species the body edges look as if someone had already eaten at the leaf. This makes the animal look like a perfectly ordinary, nibbled leaf.
12750.m: Some leaf insects even have fake feeding damage.

12751.q: Which body parts of the leaf insect, besides the abdomen, are also broadened like a leaf?
12751.e: The legs also have flat, lobed widenings. In this way the whole animal looks like a leaf with small side leaflets.
12751.m: Even the legs of leaf insects look like little leaves.

12752.q: What does the colouring of many leaf insects depend on?
a: On humidity, temperature, food and light
On the age of the mother alone
On the phase of the moon alone
On the sex of the siblings alone
12752.e: Leaf insects can be green, yellow, brown or reddish. In many species, environmental conditions such as humidity, temperature, food and light determine the colour.
12752.m: The colour of a leaf insect depends greatly on its surroundings.

12753.q: What do freshly hatched leaf insect nymphs usually look like?
a: Red to blackish brown, often with white spots
Already exactly the same green as the adults
12753.e: The young hatch coloured red, reddish brown or blackish brown. Only over the course of a few days do they gradually turn green.
12753.m: Young leaf insects are dark at first and later turn green.

12754.q: What do leaf insects feed on?
a: Small insects that they catch with their front legs
Fungi that they grow in the ground
12754.e: Leaf insects are pure plant eaters. In the wild they eat, for example, leaves of guava, cacao, mango and tea.
12754.m: Leaf insects eat just what they imitate, namely leaves.

12755.q: Which food plants are often offered to leaf insects in terrariums in Europe?
12755.e: Since tropical plants are hard to get here, keepers often use bramble, raspberry, oak or rose. Roses from shops can, however, be contaminated with insecticides.
12755.m: In the terrarium, leaf insects often eat bramble leaves.

12756.q: At what time of day are leaf insects mainly active?
12756.e: Leaf insects are nocturnal. By day they stay motionless and rely entirely on their camouflage.
12756.m: By day, leaf insects pretend to be just a leaf.

12757.q: How can some leaf insects (for example species of the genera Phyllium and Cryptophyllium) defend themselves chemically?
a: They spray a milky, caustic secretion
They sting with a venomous sting
They spit sticky threads from the mouth
They release a numbing gas from the abdomen
12757.e: From openings on the front thoracic shield, they can spray a milky, sharp-smelling secretion. The smell differs from species to species.
12757.m: Some leaf insects defend themselves with a caustic spray secretion.

12758.q: What is the ability of male leaf insects and nymphs to shed a leg when in danger called?
12758.e: In autotomy, a leg is shed at a breaking point. The predator is distracted while the animal flees.
12758.m: Through autotomy, a leaf insect sacrifices a leg in order to survive.

12759.q: How do female leaf insects make sounds when disturbed?
a: By knocking on wood with the abdomen
By rapid whirring of the wings
12759.e: The females rub parts of their antennae against each other and so produce chirping sounds, called stridulation. This presumably serves to deter predators.
12759.m: Female leaf insects chirp with their antennae when in danger.

12760.q: Which special way of reproducing is possible in leaf insects?
a: Live birth of fully developed young
Reproduction by budding as in corals
12760.e: Females can also lay eggs capable of developing without males. In parthenogenesis, females usually hatch from them again.
12760.m: Leaf insects can also reproduce without males.

12761.q: How do male leaf insects find the females?
a: They follow a light signal on the abdomen
They hear a loud mating song over kilometres
They follow a slime trail on the ground
12761.e: The males sense the vibrations that the females produce. Their long, bristly antennae help them in the search.
12761.m: Males track down the females through fine vibrations.

12762.q: How do male leaf insects transfer their sperm to the female?
a: With a spermatophore, a sperm packet
Via an egg that the male lays
By releasing it into the water
By a bite into the abdomen
12762.e: The male pushes a sperm packet, the spermatophore, under the female’s subgenital plate. There it empties by itself.
12762.m: The male hands over his sperm in a small sperm packet.

12763.q: Roughly how many eggs does a female leaf insect lay over her lifetime?
12763.e: From three to four weeks after her last moult, a female lays one to three eggs a week. In total, depending on the species, 100 to 300 eggs add up.
12763.m: A female gradually lays a few hundred eggs.

12764.q: How do female leaf insects lay their eggs?
a: They drop them or flick them away
They glue them to leaves in packets
They bury them deep in the ground
They carry them on their body until they hatch
12764.e: The eggs are simply dropped to the ground or flicked away. They often resemble plant seeds and so do not stand out there.
12764.m: Leaf insects simply drop their seed-like eggs.

12765.q: Why are the eggs so important for identifying leaf insects?
a: They are shaped specifically for each species and are often the most important identifying feature
They are exactly the same colour in all species
They contain a visible species number
They are known in only a single species
12765.e: The shape, surface and lid of the eggs differ from species to species. Some resemble the seeds of rhubarb or four o’clock flowers.
12765.m: In leaf insects, the egg often reveals which species it is.

12766.q: Roughly how long does it take for a nymph to hatch from the egg of a leaf insect?
12766.e: Egg development is long and takes four to eight months, depending on the species and conditions. After that, the nymph needs several more months to become an adult.
12766.m: Leaf insect eggs need several months to hatch.

12767.q: Why do leaf insects often eat their old skin after moulting?
a: It contains valuable nutrients and trace elements
It protects them from catching cold
They need it to lay eggs
12767.e: Leaf insects grow through several moults, females moulting six times and males four. The shed skin is usually eaten so that the substances it contains are not lost.
12767.m: Leaf insects recycle their old skin as food.

12768.q: On which famous voyage of discovery were leaf insects probably first reported in Europe?
a: On the first circumnavigation of the world under Magellan
On James Cook’s South Seas voyage
On Vasco da Gama’s voyage to India
12768.e: Antonio Pigafetta accompanied Magellan’s circumnavigation (1519 to 1522) as chronicler. He reported on trees whose leaves walk about.
12768.m: Even Magellan’s circumnavigators marvelled at walking leaves.

12769.q: What is especially important when keeping leaf insects in a terrarium?
a: A large pool of water to swim in
Dry air as in the desert
12769.e: Leaf insects are plant eaters from damp tropical forests. In the terrarium they are given bramble leaves, for example, and the air must be damp enough for moulting to succeed.
12769.m: Leaf insects need fresh foliage and damp air.

12770.q: What is the scientific name of the European rhinoceros beetle?
12770.e: The European rhinoceros beetle is called Oryctes nasicornis in scientific terms. Lucanus cervus is the stag beetle, and Melolontha melolontha the cockchafer.
12770.m: The European rhinoceros beetle bears the name Oryctes nasicornis.

12771.q: Which beetle group do the rhinoceros beetle and tropical species such as the Hercules beetle belong to together?
12771.e: The European rhinoceros beetle belongs to the Dynastinae, the rhinoceros beetles. This group also includes the tropical Hercules and Atlas beetles.
12771.m: The rhinoceros beetle is a member of the Dynastinae.

12772.q: Which beetle family does the rhinoceros beetle belong to?
12772.e: The rhinoceros beetle belongs to the large family of scarab beetles (Scarabaeidae). This also includes cockchafers, flower chafers and dung beetles.
12772.m: The rhinoceros beetle is a scarab beetle like the cockchafer.

12773.q: How are the antennae of the rhinoceros beetle built at the end?
a: With a three-segmented club of plates
With a feathery tuft of hair
12773.e: Like all scarab beetles, the rhinoceros beetle has a club of movable plates at the end of the antenna. In the rhinoceros beetle it consists of three segments.
12773.m: The rhinoceros beetle’s antennae end in a club of plates.

12774.q: Roughly how long does an adult European rhinoceros beetle grow?
12774.e: Adult rhinoceros beetles usually measure around 2 to 4 cm. This makes them among the largest beetles in Europe.
12774.m: A rhinoceros beetle usually measures between two and four centimetres.

12775.q: How can you most easily recognise the male of the European rhinoceros beetle?
a: By the long, curved horn on the head
12775.e: The male has a long horn on its head, curved backwards. Antler-like jaws, by contrast, belong to the stag beetle.
12775.m: The male rhinoceros beetle has a long horn on its head.

12776.q: What does the female of the European rhinoceros beetle have instead of a long horn?
