12776.e: Females have at most a short bump or a little stump of a horn on the head. Their pronotum also has no bumps.
12776.m: The female rhinoceros beetle has only a small bump.

12777.q: What is on the pronotum of the male rhinoceros beetle?
a: A pair of white tufts of hair
12777.e: In the male, the pronotum forms a transverse ridge that is bent up into three bumps in the middle. In the female, these bumps are absent.
12777.m: The male rhinoceros beetle’s pronotum carries three bumps.

12778.q: What colour is the hair on the underside of the rhinoceros beetle?
12778.e: The shiny upper side is bare, while the underside is conspicuously covered in fox-red hair. This is a good identifying feature.
12778.m: The rhinoceros beetle has a fox-red hairy underside.

12779.q: How are the legs of the rhinoceros beetle built?
a: As digging legs with toothed shins
As swimming legs with fringes of hair
As jumping legs with thick thighs
12779.e: The shins of all three pairs of legs are modified into digging legs and are coarsely toothed on the outside. This lets the beetle dig itself well into mould and soil.
12779.m: The rhinoceros beetle digs in with toothed digging legs.

12780.q: At what time of day is the European rhinoceros beetle mainly active?
12780.e: Rhinoceros beetles are mostly active at dusk and at night. By day they usually stay hidden.
12780.m: The rhinoceros beetle flies mainly at dusk and at night.

12781.q: In which months do adult rhinoceros beetles mainly fly in central Europe?
12781.e: Depending on the weather, the beetles fly from about the end of May to August, most commonly in June and July. Before and after that, hardly any beetles are about.
12781.m: You see the rhinoceros beetle mainly on warm summer nights.

12782.q: Which human-made danger affects flying rhinoceros beetles especially?
a: They are attracted by artificial light
They get caught in plastic spiders’ webs
They are paralysed by mobile phone radiation
They drown in garden ponds because of noise
12782.e: At night, rhinoceros beetles fly towards artificial light sources. In doing so they can become exhausted, have accidents or become easy prey.
12782.m: Artificial light lures the rhinoceros beetle into dangerous traps.

12783.q: How do adult European rhinoceros beetles feed?
a: Hardly at all, they live mainly on reserves from their larval period
12783.e: Adult rhinoceros beetles probably take in little or no food and live off the reserves that the larva built up. This is not entirely clear, and they probably occasionally lick tree sap.
12783.m: The adult rhinoceros beetle lives off the stores from its larval period.

12784.q: Roughly how long does an adult European rhinoceros beetle live?
a: Only a few weeks to a few months
12784.e: Life as a beetle is short and, depending on the source, lasts only weeks to a few months in summer. The rhinoceros beetle spends the greatest part of its life as a larva.
12784.m: As a finished beetle, the rhinoceros beetle lives only a short time.

12785.q: How long does the larval development of the European rhinoceros beetle usually take?
12785.e: Depending on temperature and food, the larva usually needs two to four years until pupation. The action plan of the canton of Bern generally assumes three years.
12785.m: The rhinoceros beetle larva grows for several years.

12786.q: How long can a fully grown larva of the European rhinoceros beetle get?
12786.e: The grubs of the rhinoceros beetle usually grow 6 to 10 cm long, sometimes even a little longer. This makes them clearly bigger than the finished beetle.
12786.m: The rhinoceros beetle larva is bigger than the beetle itself.

12787.q: What typical body shape does the rhinoceros beetle larva have?
a: A flat, black caterpillar with bristles
12787.e: The larva is a typical grub: whitish, cylindrical and curved in a C shape towards the belly. It has a brown head capsule and three pairs of legs.
12787.m: The rhinoceros beetle larva is a fat, curved grub.

12788.q: How many larval stages does the rhinoceros beetle go through?
12788.e: The larva moults twice and so goes through three larval stages. Only in the third stage does it reach its full size.
12788.m: The rhinoceros beetle grows up in three larval stages.

12789.q: What do the larvae of the rhinoceros beetle feed on?
12789.e: The larvae eat rotten wood mould and other crumbling plant fibres. In central Europe they do not harm living plants.
12789.m: The rhinoceros beetle larva eats rotten wood.

12790.q: How can the rhinoceros beetle larva make use of the hard-to-digest cellulose?
a: With the help of bacteria in a fermentation chamber of the hindgut
With its own digestive enzymes in the saliva
By pre-digestion in the crop with stomach acid
By taking in small stones in the gizzard
12790.e: In the enlarged hindgut, symbiotic bacteria break down the cellulose without air. The larva itself has no cellulose-splitting enzymes.
12790.m: Bacteria in the gut help the rhinoceros beetle larva to digest wood.

12791.q: Which gas is produced when cellulose is broken down in the gut of the rhinoceros beetle larva?
12791.e: Methane is produced during fermentation by the gut bacteria. The microorganisms also serve the larva as an important source of protein.
12791.m: Methane is produced in the gut of the rhinoceros beetle larva.

12792.q: Where does the rhinoceros beetle larva pupate?
a: In a cocoon the size of a hen’s egg made of soil and mould
In a silk web on a branch
In the water of a pond
12792.e: The larva builds a pupal cell the size of a hen’s egg from clay, soil and wood mould. Inside, it transforms into the beetle.
12792.m: The rhinoceros beetle pupates in an egg-sized pupal cell.

12793.q: What was the original, natural habitat of rhinoceros beetle larvae?
a: Wood mould in old, dead broadleaf trees
Damp sand dunes by the sea
Bare rock crevices in the high mountains
Mud at the bottom of lakes
12793.e: Originally, the larvae developed in the decomposed mould of dead trunks and thick branches of old broadleaf trees. In near-natural forests, this habitat is rare today.
12793.m: The rhinoceros beetle originally lived in the mould of old broadleaf trees.

12794.q: Where are rhinoceros beetle larvae often found near settlements today?
a: In compost heaps and sawdust heaps
In flower pots on the balcony
12794.e: The rhinoceros beetle has moved to human-made substitute habitats. These include compost heaps, and heaps of sawdust and bark mulch.
12794.m: The rhinoceros beetle uses compost heaps as a nursery.

12795.q: Which former substitute habitat of the rhinoceros beetle came from the tanner’s trade?
12795.e: Tanneries used crushed oak bark, called tanbark. The old tanbark heaps were ideal breeding places but disappeared with the tanneries.
12795.m: In the past, the rhinoceros beetle often grew up in heaps of tanbark.

12796.q: Which mistake in the garden often destroys the development of rhinoceros beetle larvae?
a: Spreading the compost before the larvae are finished
Watering the compost well regularly in summer
Putting a lot of fresh lawn clippings on the compost
Setting up the compost in a sunny place
12796.e: If the compost is spread in the garden while larvae are still living in it, they cannot complete their development, which lasts several years. In addition, the larvae are often mistaken for harmful grubs and killed.
12796.m: A compost heap with rhinoceros beetle larvae should be left to rest for a long time.

12797.q: How do scoliid wasps harm the larvae of the rhinoceros beetle?
a: Their larva eats the grub from the outside
They carry the larvae into their nest
They steal the wood from the larva
12797.e: Scoliid wasps such as the yellow-headed scoliid wasp lay their egg on the rhinoceros beetle larva. The wasp larva then eats the grub from the outside.
12797.m: Scoliid wasps are dangerous enemies of rhinoceros beetle larvae.

12798.q: How is the rhinoceros beetle legally protected in Switzerland?
a: It is protected in the Nature and Cultural Heritage Ordinance
It may be collected only in winter
It counts as a huntable animal
It is not protected at all in Switzerland
12798.e: The rhinoceros beetle is listed in Annex 3 of the Ordinance on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage (NHV). This makes it one of the protected animal species of Switzerland.
12798.m: In Switzerland, the rhinoceros beetle is protected by law.

12799.q: Up to roughly what altitude does the rhinoceros beetle occur in Switzerland?
a: Up to about 600 m above sea level
Up to about 2,500 m above sea level
Up to about 1,800 m above sea level
Only above 1,500 m above sea level
12799.e: The warmth-loving rhinoceros beetle inhabits only the lowlands in Switzerland, up to about 600 m above sea level at most. At higher altitudes it is too cool for it.
12799.m: In Switzerland, the rhinoceros beetle lives mainly in the warm lowlands.

12800.q: Which canton has drawn up its own action plan to promote the rhinoceros beetle?
12800.e: The canton of Bern published an action plan for the rhinoceros beetle in 2024. The measures begin in the city of Biel and along the southern foot of the Jura.
12800.m: The canton of Bern promotes the rhinoceros beetle with an action plan.

12801.q: With which measure can new breeding sites be created for the rhinoceros beetle?
a: With heaps of dead wood and wood chips
With nest boxes high in conifers
With small ponds full of water plants
12801.e: In the Bernese action plan, so-called “wood beetle heaps” are built from dead wood and wood chips, in some cases inoculated with fungal mycelium. The larvae can develop in them for years.
12801.m: Wood beetle heaps offer the rhinoceros beetle new nurseries.

12802.q: In which European country is the European rhinoceros beetle absent?
12802.e: The rhinoceros beetle is distributed from North Africa through Europe to Central Asia. In Great Britain, however, it does not occur to this day.
12802.m: There is no rhinoceros beetle in Great Britain.

12803.q: What is special about the occurrence of the rhinoceros beetle in northern Europe?
a: It is the only representative of the Dynastinae there
It lives only in caves there
It is active only by day there
12803.e: In northern Europe, the rhinoceros beetle is the only species of the subfamily Dynastinae. It arrived there only in historical times.
12803.m: In the north of Europe, the rhinoceros beetle is the only Dynastinae beetle.

12804.q: What do male rhinoceros beetles mainly use their horn for?
a: For fights with rivals over females
12804.e: The males fight each other with the horn and try to heave the rival out of the way. The winner has better chances with the females.
12804.m: The male rhinoceros beetle fights with his horn over a female.

12805.q: What mainly determines how big a rhinoceros beetle and its horn become?
a: The amount and quality of the larval food
The number of moults of the beetle
The phase of the moon at hatching
The age of the beetle after hatching
12805.e: Beetles do not grow after hatching. Their final size and horn length depend on how well the larva was able to feed.
12805.m: A well-fed larva becomes a big rhinoceros beetle.

12806.q: What is special about small, hornless males of the rhinoceros beetle?
a: They look very much like the females
12806.e: Small males without a horn closely resemble the females. They can be told apart by the bare tip of the abdomen, which is hairy in females.
12806.m: Hornless male rhinoceros beetles look almost like females.

12807.q: On the Canary Islands lives a rhinoceros beetle subspecies that exists only there. What are such forms called?
12807.e: Endemics occur only in a narrowly limited area, for example on an island group. The subspecies Oryctes nasicornis prolixus lives only on the Canary Islands.
12807.m: Endemics exist only in a particular area.

12808.q: Who scientifically described the European rhinoceros beetle in 1758?
12808.e: Carl Linnaeus described the rhinoceros beetle in 1758 in his work “Systema Naturae”. This is why the name is often followed by “L.” or “Linnaeus”.
12808.m: Carl Linnaeus gave the rhinoceros beetle its scientific name.

12809.q: What does the species name “nasicornis” mean in the rhinoceros beetle?
12809.e: “Nasicornis” is made up of the Latin words “nasus” for nose and “cornu” for horn. The name alludes to the male’s horn on its head.
12809.m: The name nasicornis means nose horn.

12810.q: Roughly how many species does the subfamily of rhinoceros beetles (Dynastinae), to which the rhinoceros beetle belongs, comprise?
12810.e: The Dynastinae comprise over 1,500 species worldwide in around 225 genera. Most live in the tropics.
12810.m: The rhinoceros beetle has over a thousand related species of Dynastinae worldwide.

12811.q: How long can a male Hercules beetle, a tropical relative of the rhinoceros beetle, grow, including the horn?
12811.e: Male Hercules beetles reach up to about 17 cm with the horn. This makes them among the longest beetles in the world.
12811.m: With its horn, the Hercules beetle is one of the longest beetles in the world.

12812.q: Where does the Hercules beetle, a relative of the rhinoceros beetle, live?
12812.e: The Hercules beetle lives in rainforests from Mexico to Bolivia and has also been observed in the Lesser Antilles. It is named after the Greek hero Heracles.
12812.m: The Hercules beetle lives in the rainforests of the Americas.

12813.q: What happens to the wing cases of the Hercules beetle, a relative of the rhinoceros beetle, in high humidity?
12813.e: In dry air, the wing cases are olive green to yellowish. When the humidity rises, they turn dark to black.
12813.m: The Hercules beetle turns dark in damp air.

12814.q: How heavy can the larva of the Hercules beetle, a relative of the rhinoceros beetle, get?
12814.e: The larvae of the Hercules beetle grow up to about 11 cm long and weigh around 100 grams or even a little more. They are among the heaviest insect larvae.
12814.m: The Hercules beetle larva weighs about as much as a bar of chocolate.

12815.q: Where is the larger of the two horns on the male Hercules beetle, a relative of the rhinoceros beetle?
12815.e: The male has one horn on the head and a clearly longer horn on the pronotum. Together they work like a pair of pincers with which he grips rivals.
12815.m: The long horn of the Hercules beetle grows on the pronotum.

12816.q: What do adult Hercules beetles, tropical relatives of the rhinoceros beetle, feed on?
12816.e: Adult Hercules beetles eat fresh and rotting fruit as well as tree sap. In captivity they ate bananas, apples, grapes and mangoes, for example.
12816.m: The Hercules beetle likes to eat ripe fruit.

12817.q: Which plants does the coconut rhinoceros beetle (Oryctes rhinoceros), a close relative of the European rhinoceros beetle, damage?
12817.e: The beetles bore into the heart of coconut and oil palms and eat the young leaves that have not yet unfolded there. The European rhinoceros beetle, by contrast, is not a pest.
12817.m: The coconut rhinoceros beetle harms palms in the tropics.

12818.q: What is used for the biological control of the coconut rhinoceros beetle, a relative of the European rhinoceros beetle?
12818.e: The Oryctes nudivirus was discovered in Malaysia in 1963. It infects larvae and beetles and is used deliberately for control.
12818.m: A special virus helps against the coconut rhinoceros beetle.

12819.q: Where does the Atlas beetle, a tropical relative of the rhinoceros beetle from the genus Chalcosoma, live?
12819.e: The Atlas beetle (Chalcosoma atlas) lives in South East Asia. Its males have three conspicuous horns.
12819.m: The Atlas beetle is a rhinoceros beetle from South East Asia.

12820.q: Which moth family does the death’s-head hawkmoth belong to?
12820.e: The death’s-head hawkmoth is a moth of the hawkmoth family, Sphingidae in Latin. Typical of hawkmoths are powerful bodies and narrow, fast wings.
12820.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth belongs to the hawkmoth family.

12821.q: What is the scientific name of the death’s-head hawkmoth?
12821.e: The death’s-head hawkmoth is called Acherontia atropos in scientific terms. The other names belong to the privet hawkmoth, the elephant hawkmoth and the hummingbird hawkmoth.
12821.m: Acherontia atropos is the scientific name of the death’s-head hawkmoth.

12822.q: What does the genus name Acherontia of the death’s-head hawkmoth go back to?
a: Acheron, a river of the Greek underworld
Acheron, a Roman god of war
A town called Acheron in Egypt
12822.e: Acherontia derives from Acheron, a river that leads to the underworld in Greek myth. The name suits the moth’s gloomy image.
12822.m: The genus name of the death’s-head hawkmoth recalls the underworld river Acheron.

12823.q: Who was Atropos, after whom the species name of the death’s-head hawkmoth is named?
a: One of the three Fates, who cuts the thread of life
The Greek goddess of hunting and the moon
A nymph who was turned into a moth
The ferrywoman who takes the dead across the river
12823.e: Atropos is one of the three Greek goddesses of fate, the Moirai. She cuts off the thread of life and so stands for death.
12823.m: In myth, Atropos cuts the thread of life, which is why the death’s-head hawkmoth bears her name.

12824.q: Who first scientifically described the death’s-head hawkmoth in 1758?
12824.e: Carl Linnaeus described the species in 1758 in the 10th edition of his work “Systema Naturae”, then still as Sphinx atropos.
12824.m: Linnaeus described the death’s-head hawkmoth in 1758.

12825.q: Linnaeus first placed the death’s-head hawkmoth in the genus Sphinx. Why are hawkmoths also called sphinx moths to this day?
a: Their caterpillars raise the front of the body at rest like a sphinx
The moths originally come from Egypt
The moths have a face like a human
The moths were first discovered at the pyramids
12825.e: Hawkmoth caterpillars often sit at rest with the front of the body raised, like the Egyptian sphinx. This is why Linnaeus called the death’s-head hawkmoth Sphinx atropos; the genus Acherontia followed only in 1809.
12825.m: To Linnaeus, the death’s-head hawkmoth was still Sphinx atropos.

12826.q: Which feature gave the death’s-head hawkmoth its name?
a: A skull-like yellow marking on the thorax
Black eyespots on the hind wings
A bone-white pattern on the abdomen
A grey head shape resembling a skull
12826.e: On the thorax, the moth has a yellowish marking that recalls a skull. It varies in how clear it is and can even be missing.
12826.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth has a yellow skull on the back of its thorax.

12827.q: What wingspan does a female death’s-head hawkmoth reach?
a: Around 10 to 12 cm, rarely up to 13 cm
12827.e: Females reach about 100 to 122 mm, exceptionally up to 130 mm wingspan. Males are a little smaller, at about 90 to 115 mm.
12827.m: A female death’s-head hawkmoth spreads her wings to a good ten centimetres.

12828.q: What record does the death’s-head hawkmoth hold among hawkmoths?
a: It is the largest hawkmoth in Europe
It is the fastest moth in the world
It is the lightest hawkmoth in Africa
It is the oldest known hawkmoth
12828.e: With a body length of up to about 6 cm and a wingspan of over 12 cm, the death’s-head hawkmoth is the largest hawkmoth in Europe.
12828.m: No hawkmoth in Europe is bigger than the death’s-head hawkmoth.

12829.q: Roughly how heavy does a female death’s-head hawkmoth become as a moth?
12829.e: Females weigh about 3 to 8 g, males about 2 to 6 g. For a moth, that is very heavy.
12829.m: A death’s-head hawkmoth weighs as much as a few paper clips together.

12830.q: What colour are the hind wings of the death’s-head hawkmoth?
a: Ochre yellow with two dark bands
12830.e: The hind wings are ochre yellow and have two dark crossbands. The front wings, by contrast, are marbled dark brown to grey.
12830.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth hides yellow hind wings beneath its dark front wings.

12832.q: Which plants does the caterpillar of the death’s-head hawkmoth especially like to eat in Europe?
12832.e: The caterpillar eats mainly leaves of nightshades such as potato, tomato or thorn apple. This is why it is often found in potato fields.
12832.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar often lives on potato plants.

12833.q: What is special about the proboscis of the death’s-head hawkmoth?
a: It is short, strong and ribbon-like instead of tubular
It is longer than the whole body
It is split into two separate tubes
The adult moth lacks it entirely
12833.e: The proboscis is only about 12 to 18 mm long, broad and ribbon-like. The moth can hardly suck flower nectar with it, but it can pierce wax cells well.
12833.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth has a short, strong proboscis for piercing honeycombs.

12834.q: What is the main food of the adult death’s-head hawkmoth?
12834.e: The moth enters honeybee nests and sucks honey from the combs. Because of its short proboscis, it hardly visits flowers.
12834.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth is a honey thief in beehives.

12835.q: How does the death’s-head hawkmoth disguise itself chemically in the beehive?
a: Its body scent matches the honeybees’ mixture of fatty acids
It secretes a poison that stuns the bees
It covers itself with pollen from the hive
It smells of the queen and so lures bees away
12835.e: Its surface carries four fatty acids, including palmitic and oleic acid, in almost the same proportion as honeybees. In this way the bees do not recognise it as an intruder.
12835.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth smells like a bee and is therefore tolerated in the hive.

12836.q: Which sound, unusual for butterflies and moths, can the death’s-head hawkmoth make?
a: A whistle, by forcing air through the proboscis
A chirp, by rubbing its hind legs
A drumming, with the abdomen on wood
12836.e: When disturbed, the moth forces air through the short proboscis and produces a high whistle. This is very unusual among butterflies and moths.

12837.q: What protects the death’s-head hawkmoth when it enters a beehive and is stung?
a: It tolerates a lot of bee venom and has a thick, hairy body
It secretes an antidote with its proboscis
It wears a hard shell like a beetle
It enters only in winter, when the bees are asleep
12837.e: In experiments, the moths survived a dose of venom equal to about four bee stings. Their thick, hairy body also protects them.
12837.m: A death’s-head hawkmoth survives even several bee stings.

12838.q: What does the death’s-head hawkmoth get when it enters a beehive?
a: Bee larvae as a source of protein
12838.e: The moth pierces comb cells with its short, strong proboscis and sucks out the honey. In a quarter of an hour it empties about five cells.
12838.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth is a honey thief in the beehive.

12839.q: How does the adult death’s-head hawkmoth produce its whistle?
a: It sucks air in through the proboscis, and a flap in the pharynx vibrates
It rubs its wings on its hind legs
It beats its abdomen on the ground
12839.e: Muscles raise the roof of the pharynx and draw air in through the proboscis. The epipharynx vibrates in the process and produces a squeaking tone, rather like a siren.
12839.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth whistles with air that it draws in through its proboscis.

12840.q: How does a person perceive the sound that the death’s-head hawkmoth makes when drawing in air?
a: As a high, clearly audible squeak
Not at all, the sound is in the ultrasound range
As a deep hum like a bumblebee
Only as a vibration that you feel
12840.e: The sound is at a few thousand hertz, so high but clearly audible. If you pick up a moth, you can clearly hear a squeak.
12840.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth’s whistle is high but clearly audible to humans.

12841.q: Which sexes of the death’s-head hawkmoth can whistle?
a: Only the caterpillars, not the moths
12841.e: Both sexes produce the whistling sounds. Males in particular can also be heard near a female.
12841.m: In the death’s-head hawkmoth, males and females whistle.

12842.q: What hypothesis is there about the whistling of the death’s-head hawkmoth in the beehive?
a: It could imitate the “piping” of the queen bee
It attracts wasps, which distract the bees
It serves the moth for echolocation of combs
It calls other moths to a joint attack
12842.e: One suspicion is that the sound resembles the piping of a queen, at which workers keep still. This is not proven, and another interpretation is defence against enemies.
12842.m: Whether the death’s-head hawkmoth imitates the queen is still uncertain.

12843.q: How does the caterpillar of the death’s-head hawkmoth defend itself when disturbed?
a: It clicks loudly with its mandibles and can bite
It sprays formic acid from a gland
It rolls up and plays dead
It stabs with its tail horn
12843.e: The caterpillar makes clicking sounds with its mandibles and bites if need be. For humans the bite is practically harmless.
12843.m: Even the death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar makes noises.

12844.q: Which plant is the most important food plant of the death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar in central Europe?
12844.e: The main food plant is the potato. The caterpillars also eat other nightshades such as tomato or thorn apple, but also plants such as lilac or oleander.
12844.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar likes potato leaves best.

12845.q: As far as which northern country does the death’s-head hawkmoth, migrating in from Africa, occasionally travel?
12845.e: On its migratory flights, the death’s-head hawkmoth occasionally reaches northern Europe and even Iceland. It does not migrate to America or East Asia.
12845.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth sometimes flies from Africa all the way to Iceland.

12846.q: Which widespread mistaken belief about the origin of the death’s-head hawkmoth in Europe has been disproved?
a: That it came to Europe only with the potato
That it was introduced from South America
That it was deliberately bred by beekeepers
That it arose from a cross between two species
12846.e: The potato came to Europe only around 1565, but the moth had lived here before that and fed on other nightshades such as thorn apple.
12846.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth was in Europe before the potato.

12847.q: How long does a fully grown caterpillar of the death’s-head hawkmoth get?
12847.e: In the last stage, the caterpillar measures about 120 to 130 mm, stretched out up to 150 mm. It then weighs around 18 to 22 g.
12847.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar grows as long as a hand is wide.

12848.q: In which colour forms does the fully grown caterpillar of the death’s-head hawkmoth occur?
12848.e: The caterpillar is usually coloured green-yellow, brown or yellow-orange. In addition there are slanting, bluish-violet stripes in a V shape.
12848.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar comes in several colour forms.

12849.q: Which feature does the caterpillar of the death’s-head hawkmoth have at the rear end, like many hawkmoth caterpillars?
12849.e: Hawkmoth caterpillars have a horn at the rear end, the anal horn. In the death’s-head hawkmoth it is yellow, granular and curved in an S shape. It is harmless.
12849.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar has a yellow, curved horn.

12850.q: How does the caterpillar of the death’s-head hawkmoth grow from a few millimetres to over 12 cm?
a: It moults several times because its skin does not grow with it
It grows without moulting like an earthworm
It only takes in water and swells up
12850.e: The caterpillar moults four times and so goes through five stages. At each moult it sheds the skin that has become too tight.
12850.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar grows up in five stages.

12851.q: Where does the caterpillar of the death’s-head hawkmoth pupate?
a: In an earth chamber, usually 15 to 40 cm deep in the ground
In a silk cocoon high up in a tree
Hanging free on a leaf stalk
12851.e: The caterpillar digs itself in and builds an egg-shaped earth chamber of about 8 by 6 cm. It usually lies 15 to 40 cm deep.
12851.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth pupates deep in the earth.

12852.q: What colour is the pupa of the death’s-head hawkmoth a few hours after pupation?
12852.e: Fresh pupae are yellow to cream-coloured and, after about 12 hours, turn a shiny mahogany brown.
12852.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth pupa soon turns reddish brown.

12853.q: What can the pupa of the death’s-head hawkmoth do shortly before hatching?
a: It can give out squeaking sounds
It can glow in the dark
It can bore to the surface and fly
It can change its colour to green
12853.e: The pupa can move and, shortly before hatching, produce short, simple squeaks.
12853.m: In the death’s-head hawkmoth, even the pupa can squeak.

12854.q: How many eggs does a female death’s-head hawkmoth lay on average?
12854.e: A female lays on average about 150, at most around 200 eggs, up to about 75 in a single day.
12854.m: A female death’s-head hawkmoth lays around 150 eggs.

12855.q: Where does the female death’s-head hawkmoth lay her eggs?
a: Mostly singly on the underside of older leaves
In large packets in the ground
12855.e: The eggs are glued mostly singly to the underside of older leaves of the food plant. In this way they are well hidden.
12855.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth lays its eggs singly under leaves.

12856.q: What do freshly hatched caterpillars of the death’s-head hawkmoth eat first?
12856.e: Like many butterfly and moth caterpillars, they eat the eggshell first after hatching. Then they nibble small holes in the leaves.
12856.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar’s first meal is its eggshell.

12857.q: Where is the main range of the death’s-head hawkmoth?
a: In Africa south of the Sahara and in the Mediterranean region
12857.e: The species comes from Africa and also lives in North Africa, the Mediterranean area and the Middle East. From there it migrates north every year.
12857.m: The home of the death’s-head hawkmoth is mainly Africa.

12858.q: Why is the death’s-head hawkmoth regarded as a migratory moth in central Europe?
a: It migrates in from the south every year and hardly survives the winter here
It migrates to Scandinavia every autumn
It switches daily between forest and lake
It moves into caves in the Alps in winter
12858.e: The moths fly in from the south from May and again in August and September. Their offspring only rarely survive the central European winter.
12858.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth comes to us as a visitor from the south.

12859.q: At what altitude have migrating death’s-head hawkmoths already been recorded in the canton of the Grisons?
a: At around 3,000 m above sea level
At 400 m above sea level at most
At exactly 800 m above sea level
At over 6,000 m above sea level
12859.e: Migrating moths have been found in the Grisons at around 3,000 m on glaciers. Caterpillars, by contrast, are found in southern Germany, for example, only up to around 700 m.
12859.m: On its migration, the death’s-head hawkmoth even flies over the Alps.

12860.q: In which stage does the death’s-head hawkmoth try to overwinter in Europe?
a: As a pupa in the ground
As an egg on the bark
12860.e: Overwintering takes place as a pupa. In central Europe, however, it only rarely survives the cold.
12860.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth overwinters as a pupa, but mostly without success.

12861.q: Why do caterpillars of the death’s-head hawkmoth that grow up in the central European summer often not produce fertile moths?
a: The long summer days disturb their development
The potatoes here are not nutritious enough
There are too few beehives here
The caterpillars eat too much here
12861.e: The critical day length is about 14 hours of light. If caterpillars grow up with 15 or more hours of light, as in the central European summer, fertile moths rarely result.
12861.m: Long summer days often make the death’s-head hawkmoth infertile.

12862.q: How does a disturbed death’s-head hawkmoth typically behave?
a: It spreads its wings, hops about and whistles
It flies steeply upwards at once
It digs into the ground in a flash
12862.e: Instead of flying away, it spreads its wings, hops about restlessly and whistles. Afterwards it crawls under plant parts or into crevices.
12862.m: A disturbed death’s-head hawkmoth relies on threats rather than flight.

12863.q: What else do male death’s-head hawkmoths use to defend themselves when strongly threatened?
a: An unpleasant scent from glands on the abdomen
A sticky liquid from the mouth
12863.e: Males have scent glands with brush-like tufts of hair on the abdomen. When strongly disturbed, they give off a smell reminiscent of mouldering fungi.
12863.m: A threatened male death’s-head hawkmoth smells of musty fungi.

12864.q: Which parasites infest the caterpillars of the death’s-head hawkmoth?
a: Lice and mites from birds’ nests
12864.e: Ichneumon wasps (Ichneumonidae) and tachinid flies (Tachinidae) lay their eggs in the caterpillars. The larvae then eat the host from the inside.
12864.m: Ichneumon wasps and tachinid flies are enemies of the death’s-head hawkmoth caterpillar.

12865.q: What causes many caterpillars and pupae of the death’s-head hawkmoth to be lost in central Europe?
a: Forest fires in the high mountains
12865.e: Since the caterpillars often live in potato fields, many pupae are destroyed at harvest or killed by sprays.
12865.m: The potato harvest is dangerous for the death’s-head hawkmoth.

12866.q: How is the conservation status of the death’s-head hawkmoth classified in central Europe?
a: Not threatened, since it constantly migrates in from the south
12866.e: The species is missing from most Red Lists of central Europe. Local losses hardly matter, because populations are topped up every year by immigration from the south.
12866.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth is regarded as not threatened here.

12867.q: What do the three species of the genus Acherontia, to which the death’s-head hawkmoth belongs, have in common?
a: A skull-like marking on the back
They all live only in Africa
They are all active by day and colourful
12867.e: Besides Acherontia atropos, there are Acherontia lachesis and Acherontia styx in Asia. All three have a marking that recalls a skull.
12867.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth has two close relatives in Asia.

12868.q: In which thriller of 1991 do pupae of the death’s-head hawkmoth or its close relatives play an important role?
12868.e: In the film, the murderer puts moth pupae in his victims’ mouths. The script speaks of Acherontia styx, but death’s-head hawkmoths were filmed, and they can also be seen on the famous poster.
12868.m: The death’s-head hawkmoth became world-famous through “The Silence of the Lambs”.

12869.q: In which novel by Bram Stoker from 1897 does the death’s-head hawkmoth appear?
12869.e: In “Dracula”, the asylum inmate Renfield tells how the Count sent him large moths with a death’s head on their backs at night. Van Helsing calls them Acherontia atropos.
12869.m: Count Dracula, too, had dealings with the death’s-head hawkmoth.

12870.q: What did the Earth form from?
12870.e: Dust and lumps of rock were circling in space. They crashed into each other and stuck together into bigger and bigger lumps until the Earth was formed.
12870.m: The Earth formed from dust and rock circling in space.

12871.e: The Sun formed first. Then the planets, including the Earth, formed from what was left around the Sun.
12871.m: The Sun is older than the Earth.

12872.q: What was the Earth like at the very beginning?
12872.e: The young Earth was so hot that its rock glowed and was liquid. Only slowly did it cool down.
12872.m: The young Earth was glowing hot.

12873.e: Lava is rock that is so hot it becomes liquid. It comes out of the Earth at volcanoes.
12873.m: Lava is liquid, glowing hot rock.

12874.q: According to scientists today, how was the Moon formed?
12874.e: Scientists think that a large body in space crashed into the young Earth. The Moon formed from the debris.
12874.m: The Moon probably formed after a big collision with the Earth.

12875.q: Where did the first life on Earth appear?
12875.e: Scientists think that the first living things appeared in water. The water probably protected them from the Sun’s dangerous rays.
12875.m: The first life probably appeared in water.

12876.q: How big were the first living things?
12876.e: The first living things were so small that you can only see them with a microscope. They were single-celled organisms like bacteria.
12876.m: The first living things were tiny single-celled organisms.

12877.q: Which planet is the Earth, counting from the Sun?
12877.e: From the Sun, first come Mercury and Venus, then the Earth. That is why the Earth is the third planet.
12877.m: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun.

12878.e: The Earth is almost as round as a ball. You can see this clearly on photos taken from space.
12878.m: The Earth is almost the shape of a ball.

12879.q: What was there a lot of on the young Earth?
12879.e: On the young Earth volcanoes erupted everywhere. There were no plants or animals yet.
12879.m: There were very many volcanoes on the young Earth.

12880.q: What formed when the Earth slowly cooled down and it rained for a long time?
12880.e: When the Earth cooled down, water vapour turned into rain. The water collected in the low places and formed the seas.
12880.m: When the Earth cooled down, the seas formed.

12881.q: What is it like deep inside the Earth?
12881.e: Inside the Earth it is still very hot today. The deeper you go, the hotter it gets.
12881.m: Inside the Earth it is very hot.

12882.q: What is the centre of the Earth called?
12882.e: Right in the middle of the Earth is the core. It is made mainly of iron.
12882.m: The centre of the Earth is called the core.

12883.q: What is the outermost, solid layer of the Earth that we live on called?
12883.e: The Earth’s crust is the outer, solid layer of the Earth. Compared with the whole Earth it is as thin as the skin of an apple.
12883.m: We live on the Earth’s crust.

12884.q: Who lived on Earth first: fish or dinosaurs?
12884.e: Fish existed long before the dinosaurs. The dinosaurs came much later.
12884.m: Fish existed long before the dinosaurs.

12885.q: Do the continents always stay in the same place?
a: Yes, they are tied to the seabed.
12885.e: The continents move only a few centimetres each year. But over millions of years they travel a long way.
12885.m: The continents move very slowly across the Earth.

12886.q: What was the name of the huge continent at the time of the first dinosaurs, in which almost all land was joined together?
12886.e: More than 200 million years ago, when the first dinosaurs lived, almost all the land on Earth was joined together. This giant continent is called Pangaea.
12886.m: The giant continent Pangaea later broke up into today’s continents.

12887.e: Africa slowly pushed against Europe. The rock was squeezed together and folded upwards, and that is how the Alps were formed.
12887.m: The Alps were formed because rock was pushed together.

12888.q: What do people sometimes find high up in the Swiss Alps?
12888.e: The rock of the Alps used to lie on the seabed. That is why fossilised shells and snails are found up there.
12888.m: Fossilised sea creatures are found in the Alps.

12889.e: The word comes from Greek. “Deinos” means terrible and “sauros” means lizard.

a: They were born alive like calves.
They grew in their mother’s pouch.
12890.e: Dinosaurs laid eggs, just as birds and crocodiles do today. Scientists have found many fossilised dinosaur eggs.

12891.e: Tyrannosaurus rex was a big meat-eater. It had a huge mouth with sharp teeth.

12892.q: What was strikingly small on Tyrannosaurus rex?
12892.e: Tyrannosaurus rex had a huge head and strong legs. But its arms were very short.
12892.m: Tyrannosaurus rex had very short arms.

12893.q: On how many legs did Tyrannosaurus rex walk?
12893.e: Tyrannosaurus rex walked on its two powerful back legs. It kept its balance with its long tail.
12893.m: Tyrannosaurus rex walked on two legs.

12894.q: How many horns did Triceratops have on its face?
12894.e: “Triceratops” means three-horned face. It had two long horns above its eyes and a short one on its nose.
12894.m: Triceratops had three horns on its face.

12895.e: Triceratops was a plant-eater. It used its beak to pluck plants.

12896.q: What was especially long on Brachiosaurus?
12896.e: Brachiosaurus had a very long neck. This let it eat leaves high up in the trees.
12896.m: Brachiosaurus had a very long neck.

12897.q: What did Stegosaurus have on its back?
12897.e: Stegosaurus had a row of large bony plates on its back. On its tail it had sharp spikes.
12897.m: Stegosaurus had large plates on its back.

12898.q: What did Ankylosaurus have at the end of its tail?
12898.e: Ankylosaurus had armour made of bony plates. At the end of its tail it had a heavy club of bone that it could use to defend itself.
12898.m: Ankylosaurus had a bony club on its tail.

12899.q: What did some dinosaurs, for example Velociraptor, have?
12899.e: Scientists have found out that many smaller dinosaurs had feathers. Velociraptor was one of them.

12900.q: Which animals today are descended from dinosaurs?
12900.e: Birds developed from small, feathered dinosaurs. You could say that birds are today’s dinosaurs.

12901.q: What do we call scientists who study dinosaur fossils?
12901.e: Palaeontologists study living things from prehistoric times. They dig up fossils and examine them.

12902.q: How do we know what dinosaurs looked like?
12902.e: Nobody has ever seen a dinosaur. Scientists put fossilised bones together and so find out how the animals were built.
12902.m: Fossilised bones show us what dinosaurs looked like.

12903.q: Did humans and dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus rex live at the same time?
12903.e: Many millions of years lie between the big dinosaurs and the first humans. Films in which people fight dinosaurs are made up.
12903.m: Humans and big dinosaurs never lived at the same time.

12904.q: Which period of Earth’s history is named after the Jura mountains?
12904.e: The Jurassic is a period when many dinosaurs lived. It is named after the Jura mountains, where rock from this time was studied.
12904.m: The Jurassic period is named after the Jura mountains.

12905.q: Which dinosaur has often been found in Frick in the canton of Aargau?
12905.e: Many Plateosaurus skeletons were found in a clay pit in Frick. You can see them in the dinosaur museum in Frick.
12905.m: Many Plateosaurus were found in Frick in Aargau.

12906.q: What can you see near Lommiswil in the canton of Solothurn?
12906.e: In an old quarry near Lommiswil you can see many dinosaur footprints on a large slab of rock. They are about 145 million years old.
12906.m: There are dinosaur footprints near Lommiswil.

a: No, some were as small as a chicken.
Yes, all were bigger than a house.
Yes, all were bigger than an elephant.
No, all were as tiny as ants.
12907.e: There were huge dinosaurs, but small ones too. Some were only as big as a chicken.

12908.q: Roughly how many years ago did the dinosaurs die out?
12908.e: That is so long ago that it is hard to imagine. At that time the age of the big dinosaurs came to an end.
12908.m: The dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.

12909.q: What hit the Earth shortly before the dinosaurs died out?
12909.e: A huge asteroid crashed into the Earth. That was the main reason the dinosaurs died out.
12909.m: A huge asteroid hit the Earth.

a: A lump of rock in space
A small moon of the Earth
12910.e: Asteroids are lumps of rock or metal that circle the Sun. Some are small, others are many kilometres across.
12910.m: An asteroid is a lump of rock in space.

12911.q: Roughly how big was the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs?
a: About as big as a car
About as big as a football
12911.e: The asteroid was about 10 to 15 kilometres across. That is more than the height of the highest mountain on Earth.
12911.m: The asteroid was many kilometres across.

12912.q: In which present-day country is the asteroid’s crater?
12912.e: The crater is on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. It is called the Chicxulub crater and is covered over today.
12912.m: The asteroid’s crater is in Mexico.

12913.q: What happened to the sky after the impact?
a: There were never any clouds again.
12913.e: The impact threw huge amounts of dust and soot into the air. They darkened the sky for a long time.
12913.m: After the impact, dust darkened the sky.

12914.q: Why did it become cold on Earth after the impact?
a: Sunlight could no longer get through.
12914.e: The dust in the air blocked the sunlight. That is why it became dark and cold all over the Earth for a long time.
12914.m: Without sunlight it became cold on Earth.

12915.q: Roughly how many kinds of animals and plants died out at that time?
a: About three out of four kinds
About one out of a hundred kinds
12915.e: Scientists estimate that about three quarters of all kinds of animals and plants died out at that time. It was one of the biggest mass extinctions in Earth’s history.
12915.m: About three out of four kinds died out at that time.

12916.q: Why did the big plant-eaters also have problems afterwards?
12916.e: Because many plants died, the big plant-eaters could no longer find enough to eat. After that the meat-eaters had no prey either.
12916.m: Without plants the plant-eaters had no food.

12917.q: Apart from the asteroid, what probably also had an effect?
a: Huge forest fires started by people
12917.e: At about the same time huge volcanoes erupted in India. They also changed the climate on Earth.
12917.m: Huge volcanic eruptions also made life hard for the animals.

12918.q: Which animals survived when the dinosaurs died out?
12918.e: Small mammals needed little food and could hide. So many of them survived.
12918.m: Small mammals survived the extinction of the dinosaurs.

12919.q: Which group of animals survived the extinction and still lives today?
12919.e: Crocodiles already existed at the time of the dinosaurs. Some smaller crocodiles survived the great extinction.
12919.m: Crocodiles survived the extinction of the dinosaurs.

12920.q: Which plants were the first to spread again in many places after the impact?
12920.e: Ferns were able to spread again quickly after the disaster. In some places scientists find especially many fern spores in rock layers from this time.
12920.m: After the impact, ferns were the first to spread.

12921.q: With which period of Earth’s history did the age of the big dinosaurs end?
12921.e: The last big dinosaurs lived in the Cretaceous period. At the end of the Cretaceous they died out, long before there were humans.
12921.m: The age of the big dinosaurs ended with the Cretaceous.

12922.q: Which sea creatures with coiled shells died out together with the dinosaurs?
12922.e: Ammonites were sea creatures with a coiled shell, related to squid. They died out in the same great extinction as the dinosaurs.
12922.m: Ammonites died out together with the dinosaurs.

12923.q: Did the dinosaurs die out in a single day?
12923.e: Many animals died right at the impact. Others only died later, because the cold and hunger lasted a long time.
12923.m: The dinosaurs took longer than one day to die out.

12924.q: What formed when the asteroid struck a sea?
12924.e: The asteroid crashed into a shallow sea. This created huge flood waves that rushed far over the coasts.
12924.m: The impact set off huge flood waves.

12925.q: Which big meat-eater was one of the last dinosaurs?
12925.e: Tyrannosaurus rex lived at the very end of the age of the dinosaurs. It died out in the great extinction.
12925.m: Tyrannosaurus rex was one of the last dinosaurs.

12926.q: How do scientists know that an asteroid struck at that time?
a: From stories told by early humans
12926.e: Scientists have found a thin layer of rock from that time all over the world. It contains substances that come from space.
12926.m: Traces in the rock reveal the asteroid impact.

12927.q: Kinds of animals are dying out today too. Who is often to blame for this today?
12927.e: Today kinds of animals often die out because people destroy their habitats or hunt them too much. That is why protecting nature is important.
12927.m: Today kinds of animals often die out because of people.

12928.q: On which continent did the first humans live?
12928.e: The first humans lived in Africa. From there they later spread all over the world.
12928.m: The first humans lived in Africa.

12929.q: What could early humans do better than apes?
12929.e: Early humans walked upright on two legs. This left their hands free for tools.
12929.m: Early humans walked upright on two legs.

12930.q: What is the name of the famous skeleton of an early human female from Ethiopia?
12930.e: Lucy was found in Ethiopia in Africa. She lived more than 3 million years ago and already walked upright.
12930.m: Lucy is a famous skeleton from Africa.

12931.q: What did the first humans make their tools from?
12931.e: The first humans shaped stones so that they had sharp edges. They did not yet know about metal and glass.
12931.m: The first tools were made of stone.

12932.q: Why is the Stone Age called that?
a: Because tools were made of stone
Because all houses were made of stone
12932.e: In the Stone Age people made many tools and weapons from stone. They did not yet know about metal.
12932.m: The Stone Age is called that because the tools were made of stone.

12933.q: What is the name of a large stone tool that was held in one hand?
12933.e: The hand axe was a stone that was chipped sharp on both sides. It fitted well in the hand.
12933.m: The hand axe was an important Stone Age tool.

12934.q: Which stone was especially popular for sharp tools in the Stone Age?
12934.e: Flint is easy to split and gets very sharp edges. It is also called silex.
12934.m: Flint was especially popular for sharp tools.

12935.q: What gave early humans warmth and light at night?
12935.e: Early humans learned to use fire. It gave warmth and light, kept wild animals away and made food softer.
12935.m: Fire gave early humans warmth and light.

12936.q: How did the first humans get their food?
12936.e: The first humans were hunter-gatherers. They hunted animals and gathered berries, nuts, roots and mushrooms. Fields and farm animals only came much later.

12937.q: Where did early humans often live?
12937.e: Many early humans lived in caves or under rock overhangs. They also built tents from wood and animal skins.
12937.m: Early humans often lived in caves and tents.

12938.q: Why did early humans often move on?
a: They followed the animals and the food.
12938.e: Hunter-gatherers followed the herds of animals and looked for new plants. That is why they rarely stayed in the same place for long.

12939.q: What did Stone Age people make their clothes from?
12939.e: Stone Age people sewed their clothes from furs and leather. This kept them warm in winter.
12939.m: In the Stone Age people wore clothes made of fur.

12940.q: What did Stone Age people sew with?
12940.e: Stone Age people carved fine needles from bone. They did not yet know about metal.
12940.m: Stone Age people sewed with bone needles.

12941.q: What did Stone Age people paint on cave walls?
12941.e: Many cave paintings show animals such as horses, bison and deer. The pictures are many thousands of years old.
12941.m: Stone Age people painted animals on cave walls.

12942.q: In which country is the famous painted cave of Lascaux?
12942.e: The cave of Lascaux is in France. Its animal pictures are many thousands of years old.
12942.m: The painted cave of Lascaux is in France.

12943.q: Which animal was probably the first pet of humans?
12943.e: The dog is descended from the wolf. According to what we know today, it was the first animal to live together with people. One of the oldest dog finds comes from the Kesslerloch cave near Thayngen.
12943.m: The dog was probably the first pet of humans.

12944.q: What are the early humans called who lived in Europe before us?
12944.e: The Neanderthals lived in Europe for a long time, including during the Ice Age. They are named after the Neander Valley in Germany.
12944.m: The Neanderthals lived in Europe before us.

12945.q: What is the name of the human species that all people today belong to?
12945.e: All people today belong to the species Homo sapiens. This is Latin and means “wise human”.
12945.m: All people today belong to Homo sapiens.

12946.q: Which musical instrument did Stone Age people already make?
12946.e: Scientists have found flutes made of bird bones and mammoth ivory. The oldest are more than 40,000 years old.
12946.m: There were bone flutes even in the Stone Age.

12947.q: What did Stone Age people often hunt with?
12947.e: Stone Age hunters used spears with tips made of stone or bone. They often hunted together.
12947.m: Stone Age hunters hunted with spears.

12948.q: What was it like in the Ice Age?
12948.e: In the Ice Age it was much colder than today. Large parts of the Earth were covered with ice.
12948.m: In the Ice Age it was much colder than today.

12949.q: What covered large parts of Switzerland in the Ice Age?
12949.e: In the Ice Age the glaciers from the Alps grew far out into the Swiss Plateau. At the coldest times most of Switzerland lay under ice.
12949.m: In the Ice Age a large part of Switzerland lay under glaciers.

12950.q: Which animal with long fur and tusks lived in the Ice Age?
12950.e: The mammoth had long, curved tusks. Thick, long fur protected it from the cold.
12950.m: The mammoth had thick fur against the cold.

12951.q: Which animal today is the mammoth related to?
12951.e: The mammoth belongs to the elephant family. Like elephants, it had a trunk and tusks.
12951.m: The mammoth is related to the elephant.

12952.q: In which village in the canton of Zurich were many mammoth bones found?
12952.e: Bones of several mammoths were found in Niederweningen in the canton of Zurich. You can see the finds in the Mammoth Museum.
12952.m: Many mammoth bones were found in Niederweningen.

12953.q: Which rhinoceros lived in Europe in the Ice Age?
12953.e: The woolly rhinoceros had thick, shaggy fur. This let it live in the cold of the Ice Age.
12953.m: The woolly rhinoceros lived in Europe in the Ice Age.

12954.q: Which big bear from the Ice Age is extinct today?
12954.e: The cave bear was bigger than today’s brown bear and spent the winter resting in caves. Its bones have also been found in Swiss caves such as the Wildkirchli in the Alpstein.
12954.m: The cave bear lived in the Ice Age and is extinct today.

12955.q: Which cat with very long canine teeth lived in the Ice Age?
12955.e: The sabre-toothed cat had two very long upper canine teeth. It is extinct today.
12955.m: The sabre-toothed cat had very long canine teeth.

12956.q: Which animals that live in the far north today also lived in Switzerland in the Ice Age?
12956.e: In the cold Ice Age reindeer also lived in Switzerland. Today they live only in the far north.
12956.m: There were reindeer in Switzerland in the Ice Age.

a: A big stone carried along by a glacier
An animal frozen in the ice
A bird from the Ice Age
12957.e: Glaciers carried huge stones far away from their mountains. When the ice melted, they were left behind. They are called erratic boulders.
12957.m: An erratic boulder is a stone brought by a glacier.

12958.q: What helped to shape many Swiss lakes, for example Lake Zurich?
12958.e: The Ice Age glaciers carved out deep valleys. When the ice melted, they filled with water and became lakes.
12958.m: Many Swiss lakes were shaped by glaciers.

12960.q: Roughly how many years ago did the last ice age end?
12960.e: The last ice age came to an end about 12,000 years ago. After that it became warmer and the glaciers melted.
12960.m: The last ice age ended about 12,000 years ago.

12961.q: What happened when the Ice Age came to an end?
12961.e: At the end of the Ice Age it became warmer. The glaciers melted and retreated into the Alps.
12961.m: At the end of the Ice Age the glaciers melted.

12962.q: What was the sea level like in the Ice Age?
12962.e: In the Ice Age a lot of water was frozen in glaciers. That is why the sea level was lower than today.
12962.m: In the Ice Age the sea level was lower than today.

12963.q: Were there already people in the Ice Age?
a: Yes, they hunted wild horses, for example.
12963.e: People lived long before the end of the Ice Age. They hunted wild horses and bison, for example.
12963.m: There were already people in the Ice Age.

12964.q: What is the name of the largest glacier in the Alps?
12964.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais is the largest and longest glacier in the Alps. But in the Ice Age the glaciers were much bigger still.
12964.m: The Great Aletsch Glacier is the largest glacier in the Alps.

12965.q: Which large animal did people in the Ice Age sometimes hunt together?
12965.e: A mammoth was too big for a single hunter. That is why people sometimes hunted it in groups.
12965.m: In the Ice Age, people sometimes hunted mammoths.

12966.q: What did Ice Age people use from a mammoth?
12966.e: People used almost everything from a mammoth: meat for eating, fur for clothes and bones for tools.
12966.m: People used the meat, fur and bones of the mammoth.

12967.q: Which tool did not exist yet in the Stone Age?
12967.e: People in the Stone Age did not yet know about iron. Tools were made of stone, wood and bone.
12967.m: There were no iron tools in the Stone Age.

12968.q: Which age followed the Stone Age in Europe?
12968.e: After the Stone Age, people learned how to make bronze. That is why the next great age is called the Bronze Age.
12968.m: The Bronze Age followed the Stone Age.

12969.q: What is the oldest part of the Stone Age called?
12969.e: The Old Stone Age is the oldest and longest part of the Stone Age. It lasted much longer than all the later parts put together.
12969.m: The Old Stone Age is the oldest part of the Stone Age.

12970.q: What is the last part of the Stone Age called?
12970.e: The New Stone Age is the most recent part of the Stone Age. After it came the age of metals.
12970.m: The New Stone Age is the last part of the Stone Age.

12971.q: Roughly how long did the Stone Age last?
12971.e: The oldest stone tools are more than two million years old. This makes the Stone Age the longest period in human history.
12971.m: The Stone Age is the longest period in human history.

12972.q: What did NOT exist yet in the Stone Age?
12972.e: Stone Age people in Europe could not write yet. That is why much of what we know about them comes only from finds in the ground.
12972.m: Stone Age people could not write yet.

12973.q: Who searches the ground for traces from the Stone Age?
12973.e: Archaeologists dig carefully in the ground. They find tools, bones and the remains of houses.
12973.m: Archaeologists find traces of the Stone Age in the ground.

12974.q: What is the name of the famous glacier mummy found in the Alps?
12974.e: Ötzi was found in 1991 in the ice of the Ötztal Alps. He lived around 5300 years ago, at the end of the Stone Age.
12974.m: Ötzi is a man from the Stone Age who was found in the ice.

12975.q: What was it like in the Ice Age, when many Stone Age people lived?
12975.e: In the Ice Age it was much colder than today. Huge glaciers also covered large parts of Switzerland.
12975.m: In the Ice Age, most of Switzerland was covered in ice.

12976.q: What did people gather in the Stone Age?
12976.e: People gathered berries, nuts, mushrooms, roots and herbs. This was an important part of their food.
12976.m: Hunter-gatherers also ate berries, nuts and mushrooms.

12978.q: What do we call people who do not live in one fixed place?
12978.e: Nomads move from place to place. Hunter-gatherers lived like this.
12978.m: Nomads do not always live in the same place.

12980.q: What did hunters use from an animal they had killed?
12980.e: They ate the meat and made clothes from the fur. They made tools from bones and antlers.
12980.m: Hunters used almost everything from an animal.

12981.q: Which animal did people often hunt in the Ice Age?
12981.e: In the Ice Age, large herds of reindeer lived in our region. They were very important for hunters.
12981.m: In the Ice Age, people often hunted reindeer.
